Limits of size, tolerances, clearance or interference and fit type from the hole and shaft deviations. Enter the deviations from the ISO 286 tables.

ISO 286-1
Dmax = D + ES Dmin = D + EI dmax = D + es dmin = D + ei max clearance = Dmax − dmin min clearance = Dmin − dmax min clearance ≥ 0 → clearance fit max clearance ≤ 0 → interference fit otherwise → transition fit

  1. ISO 286-1:2010, Geometrical product specifications (GPS) — ISO code system for tolerances on linear sizes. Deviations must be read from the standard tables.

Torsion & angle of twist

Torque from power and speed, then shear stress and angle of twist for a solid or hollow circular shaft.

τ = Tρ / J
T = 9550·P / n (N·m, P in kW, n in rpm) J = π(d⁴ − dᵢ⁴) / 32 τ = T·ρ / J τmax = T·c / J φ = T·L / (J·G)
References
  1. F. P. Beer, E. R. Johnston & J. T. DeWolf, Mechanics of Materials, 3rd ed., ch. 3 (torsion): τ = Tρ/J, φ = TL/JG.
  2. Power–torque relation T = 9550·P/n as used in the course notes: Forces, stress & strain, section G.

δ = PL / EA

Line conventions

[S1] Drawing book Part 1, §3.2

  • Thick continuous: visible outlines ≈ 0.7 mm; border 1.0–2.0 mm.
  • Thin continuous 0.25–0.35 mm: dimension, extension and hatching lines.
  • Hidden (short dashes): dashes 4–6 mm, gaps 2–3 mm. Start and end with a dash that touches the outline.
  • Centre line (thin long chain): long dash 8–30 mm, short dash 1.5 mm, gaps ≈ 3 mm.
  • Cutting plane: thin chain, thick at the ends, arrows show the viewing direction, labelled A–A [S2 §4.1].
  • Short thin chain: adjacent parts, alternative positions. Break lines: thick wavy for short breaks, thin for long breaks.

Sheets, scales and pencils

[S1] §2.3–2.4, §2.2-7

Dimensions on a drawing are always the real size, whatever the scale.

Enlarged 2:1, 2.5:1, 5:1, 10:1, 20:1 … 1000:1 · Full 1:1 · Reduced 1:2, 1:2.5, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20 … 1:1000.

Pencils: 7H–9H extremely hard → H medium hard → HB medium soft → B soft → 5B–7B extremely soft. Hard leads for thin lines, soft leads for thick continuous lines.

Dimensioning

[S1] §3.4

  • Series: one dimension after another. Errors add up.
  • Parallel: all from one reference surface. Errors much smaller.
  • Progressive: from one origin, one arrowhead per dimension. Combined mixes series and parallel.
  • Figures above and parallel to the dimension line, near its middle; stagger close ones.
  • Each dimension once. No over-dimensioning. Don't cross extension and dimension lines.
  • Never use outlines, centre lines or extension lines as dimension lines.
  • Circles get the diameter ⌀ (what the lathe or drill needs); arcs get R. Equal holes: dimension one and give the count.
  • Narrow spaces: dots instead of arrowheads; oblique but parallel extension lines are allowed.

First- and third-angle projection

[S1] ch.5 §5.3

Three planes: V gives the front view (elevation), H the plan, W the side view. Use at least two views, three for complex parts. The front view is the face that shows the most.

Plan widths come from the front view; side-view heights come from the front view.

  • First angle (European / ISO, used in the course examples): plan below the front view; the view from the left goes on the right.
  • Third angle (American): plan above; the view from the right goes on the right.

The views are identical in both systems; only their positions change.

Isometric and oblique views

[S2] Part 2, ch.1

  • Isometric: verticals stay vertical; horizontal edges at 30° each side. Measure only along isometric lines; other lines (e.g. a cube's diagonals) are distorted.
  • Complex shapes: enclose them in a box ("crating") and measure along its edges. Hidden lines are normally left out.
  • Isometric circle, four-arc method: draw the isometric square (side = D). The two corners on the short diagonal are two centres; lines from them to the midpoints of the opposite sides cross at the other two.
  • Oblique: front face true shape and size; receding edges at 30° or 45° (45° most common). Depth may be drawn at half size so it looks natural. Put circular features on the front face so they stay true circles.

Sections and sectional views

[S2] ch.4

  • Hatching: thin parallel lines at 45°, evenly spaced, not closer than ≈ 2 mm. Break it around dimensions and notes. Very large areas: hatch the edges only.
  • Assemblies: adjacent parts hatched in opposite directions; if they must go the same way, change the spacing.
  • Types: full, half (symmetrical parts; halves split by a centre line), offset/staggered, aligned, local part section (thin irregular boundary), revolved (thin outline), removed (thick outline, may be enlarged).
  • Ribs and webs cut lengthwise are not hatched; cut across, they are.
  • Not sectioned when cut lengthwise in assemblies: shafts, bolts, nuts, screws, studs, keys, pins, cotters, dowels, rivets, rods, washers, balls, rollers, gear teeth.

Fits and tolerances

[S5] fits summary · checked against ISO 286-2

Capital letter = hole, small letter = shaft: ⌀25 H8/f6. Table values are in µm; divide by 1000 for mm.

Hole-basis system: hole H, lower deviation 0. Shaft-basis: shaft h, upper deviation 0.

Fit type from the shaft letter (hole-basis) [S5]: a…h clearance · j, k, m, n transition · p, r, s, t, u, z interference.

Clearance max = Dmax − dmin min = Dmin − dmax Interference max = dmax − Dmin min = dmin − Dmax Transition max clearance = Dmax − dmin max interference = dmax − Dmin

Worked example from [S5], ⌀25 H8/f6: hole 25.000–25.033, shaft 24.967–24.980 → max clearance 0.066, min clearance 0.020 mm.

Check this in the summary. [S5] says to "keep Lh fixed for a shaft" when a grade is missing from the table. In ISO 286 that holds for shafts a–h only (upper deviation is the fundamental one); for j–zc the lower deviation ei is fixed instead.

Surface texture

[S10] notebook ch.7 §7-4 · [S6] Fig 7.14

  • Roughness: fine, closely spaced irregularities left by the tool or abrasive grains.
  • Waviness: wider-spaced irregularities; lay: direction of the dominant pattern; flaws: isolated defects.
  • Roughness width: distance between successive peaks. Roughness-width cut-off: greatest spacing included when measuring Ra, in mm.
Ra = (1/n) · Σ |hᵢ| arithmetic mean deviation from the mean line, in µm

The symbol [S10 pp.138–143]: a check mark with legs at 60° whose point touches the surface, an extension line or a leader; the long leg is on the right as the drawing is read.

  • Bar on the short leg: machining required. Circle inside the V: material removal prohibited (as cast, forged, die-cast, extruded). Number left of the V: stock to remove.
  • Ra (max, µm) above the V; two values = allowed range. Waviness height and spacing above the horizontal line; sampling length (cut-off) below it; lay symbol to the right of the long leg. No cut-off given → 0.8 mm applies.
  • General finish as a note: "Unless otherwise specified, all surfaces 3.2". Rough work: V with R or G, symbol f, or "FAO" (finish all over).

Machining marks on drawings carry the value, e.g. reaming 2.5/0.32, grinding 2.5/0.160, drilling Rz80 [S6].

Expected Ra for each process: see Roughness by process.

Welding symbols

[S7] welding summary · [S10] §7-3-4

  • Bolts and nuts are temporary joints; welds are permanent. Basic joints: lap and butt.
  • Weld symbols: fillet (triangle, size = leg length), bevel, V, J, U; single (one side) or double (both sides). Groove data: size s, root opening, groove angle.
  • Arrow at about 60°. Symbol below the reference line means the weld is on the arrow side; above means the other side.
  • Flag at the elbow: field (site) weld. Circle at the elbow: weld all round.
  • Never put a weld symbol on a hidden line, and use orthographic views, not isometric ones. Don't repeat the same weld in several views.
  • Spot and projection welds: circle symbol with number of welds, pitch and strength (N) or nugget diameter, placed on the joint centre line.
  • A welding working drawing states the process/electrode, location, shape and size [S10].
  • The arrow points to the member that gets the groove; one size is enough when both sides are equal [S10 §8.6].
  • Fillet: size left of the triangle's perpendicular leg (always drawn on the left), length right of it, then the pitch for intermittent welds. Chain intermittent = opposite triangles; staggered = staggered triangles. Faces at 45° unless two leg sizes are given. Throat t = 0.707 h.
  • Grooves: V and bevel get size, root opening and included angle; U and J get size. Plug and slot welds use a rectangle; below the line = hole in the arrow-side member.
  • Finish/contour symbols (flush, convex) go on the weld symbol; the tail carries the process or specification and is left off when not needed.

Keys, splines, cotters and pins

[S3] keys handout · [S10] notebook §5.1–5.11, §4.6

  • Sunk keys: half in the shaft, half in the hub; taper 1:100 on the top face only.
  • Rectangular sunk key w = d/4, t = 2w/3 = d/6; square w = t = d/4; gib-head same, with a head to drive it out.
  • Parallel/feather keys: no taper, sliding fit, let the hub slide along the shaft (peg, single- or double-headed).
  • Woodruff: disc segment, self-aligning, for tapered shaft ends; weakens the shaft. Pick width ≈ d/4 and radius ≈ shaft radius [S10].
  • Saddle keys (flat, hollow) hold by friction → light duty. Tangent keys: a pair at 90° for heavy shafts. Round keys: taper 1:50, ⌀ ≈ 0.25D.
  • Splines: 4, 6, 10 or 16; carry more load, centre the hub better. Profiles: parallel-side, involute, serrations. Designation D 6 × 28 × 34 × S2X = centred on D, 6 splines, minor ⌀28, major ⌀34.
  • Cotters: wedge, taper usually 1:30, for rods in tension or compression, not rotation. Knuckle joint: eye + fork + pin in clearance fit.

Gears: terms, formulas and drawing

[S10] notebook ch.9 (pp.165–197)

  • Spur: parallel shafts; speed ratio inversely proportional to the teeth. Helical: teeth on a helix, smoother and quieter, more power; double helical (herringbone) cancels the axial thrust. Bevel: intersecting shafts, usually 90°. Worm: shafts at 90°, not intersecting, ratios up to about 300:1. Also rack & pinion, internal and epicyclic gears.
  • Pinion = the smaller gear of the pair.
m = D / z module (standard value, mm) P = z / D = 1/m diametral pitch (teeth/in) pc = π m = S + w circular pitch a = m dedendum = 1.25 m h = 2.25 m De = D + 2m outside (addendum) circle Dd = D − 2.5m root (dedendum) circle C = (D1 + D2) / 2 centre distance T = Ft·D/2 Fr = Ft tan φ n2 = n1·(R1/R2)
  • Involute construction: pressure angle 20°, base circle tangent to the line of action; root fillet r = 0.4m (spur, helical), 0.2m (bevel).
  • Drawing conventions: tip circles thick continuous; pitch circle thin chain; root circles broken (or thin), usually left off the side view; tooth profile only in a local or removed view marked "Working profile".
  • Working drawing must give the outside diameter and the tooth thickness. Don't dimension on the circular view; put the gear data table in the top-right corner.
  • From a real gear: measure De and count z, then m = De/(z+2), rounded up to the standard value. Bevel: m = De/(z + 2cos δ), tan δ = z1/z2.
  • Helical: mn = m cos ψ; bevel pitch angle tan γ = Np/NG; worm lead L = px·Nw, tan λ = L/(π dw).
Typo in the notebook. Eq. 9.20 prints the helical axial force as F cos φn cos ψ. The axial component is Fa = F cos φn sin ψ; the printed form repeats the tangential force Ft.

Studs, cap screws and machine screws

[S10] notebook §5-5, 5-6 · [S8] fasteners sheet

  • Stud: threaded both ends; used where a bolt won't fit or the part comes off often (cylinder heads, pumps). Screw it permanently into the tapped part; the nut goes on the free end. Dimension the thread length at both ends and the overall length.
  • Spec: DOUBLE-END STUD M10 × 1.5 × 100, STEEL, CADMIUM PLATED.
  • Blind hole for a stud: drill with a 120° cone; drilled depth l₂ = l₁ + 0.5d; tap; screw the stud home.
  • Cap screw: through a clearance hole, into a tapped hole. Hex heads have a 0.4 mm washer face, diameter = width across flats; ≤ 25 mm long → threaded almost to the head. Spec M6 × 1 × 40 HEX CAP SCREW.
  • Blind hole with no depth limit: drill one diameter past the screw end, tap to half a diameter past it.
  • Machine screw spec order: size × pitch × length, head type, material: M10 × 1.5 × 40 SLOTTED FLAT HEAD MACHINE SCREW.
  • Nut locking: lock (jam) nut, castle nut + split pin, spring washers, locking plates.

Riveted joints

[S4] riveted joints handout

  • Permanent joints for boilers, tanks, bridges and trusses. Hot riveting gives the tighter joint because the shank shrinks as it cools.
  • Air-tight joints: caulking (blunt chisel on the bevelled edge) or fullering (tool as wide as the bevel). Lap-joint edges are bevelled at about 80°.
  • Pitch p ≈ 3d · margin m ≈ 1.5d · row pitch 0.8p (chain) or 0.6p (zig-zag).
  • Butt joints with cover straps: single strap t₁ = 1.125 t; double straps t₂ = 0.75 t each. Stronger than lap joints.
  • Lap joints for circumferential seams; butt joints for longitudinal seams (except small tanks under 100 lb/in²) [S10 §8.10].
  • Failure: tearing of the plate at the edge (prevented by margin m = 1.5d, d = hole diameter) and tearing across a row of rivets (net section p − d) [S10 §8.10].
Likely typo in the handout. It prints rivet diameter "d = 6 t mm". Machine-drawing texts use Unwin's formula d = 6√t (t in mm). Confirm against the notebook before using it.

Assembly and working drawings

[S10] notebook ch.6–7

Assembly drawing: shows how parts fit in their working positions. Types: general, detailed, working, sub-assembly, installation, outline, diagram, exploded.

  • General assembly: one or two views (principal + section; half section if symmetrical), only principal dimensions, hidden lines usually left out.
  • Parts identified by leaders ending in balloons; leaders not horizontal or vertical; balloons in rows. Numbering by size, by assembly order, or bought-in parts first.
  • Part list: number, name, quantity, material. Title: machine name + "ASSEMBLY".

Working drawing: everything needed to make the part: shape, sizes, notes (material, finish, geometric tolerances, heat treatment) and title block.

  • Steps: choose views → choose scale (small parts at 2:1 or more) → centre lines → draw from the characteristic view → lines, lettering, dimensions → size tolerances on key dimensions → geometric tolerances on functional surfaces → notes → check and fill the title block.
  • Checking is done by someone who did not draw it: clearances with neighbouring parts, all views and scales, missing or repeated dimensions, fits that add no needless cost, finishes, materials, stock sizes for standard parts.

Forces, stress and strain

Index
  1. Forces, moments and equilibrium
  2. The four internal loads
  3. Stress
  4. Strain and Hooke's law

  6. Torsion of circular shafts

Forces, moments and equilibrium

[M7] Hibbeler Statics · [M1] Stress Analysis §1.2

  • A force tends to translate a body; a moment tends to rotate it: M = F·d (d ⟂ distance), vector form M = r × F.
  • A distributed load is replaced by its resultant = area under the load curve, acting at its centroid. Triangle w over L → ½wL at L/3 from the large end.
  • Method of sections: if the whole body is in equilibrium, so is every piece cut from it.
  • Compound beams with hinges: split at the hinges (a hinge carries force, not moment) when unknowns exceed three.
3D ΣFx = ΣFy = ΣFz = 0 ΣMx = ΣMy = ΣMz = 0 2D ΣFx = 0 ΣFy = 0 ΣMo = 0

Other statics topics in the course: 3D force systems, moment about a line, equivalent systems, friction, centroids and Pappus, moments of inertia, trusses (joints, sections, space), frames and machines, virtual work, potential energy.

The four internal loads

[M1] §1.3–1.4 · [M8] structure lectures

  • Normal force N ⟂ to the section: tension (elongation) or compression (shortening).
  • Shear force V in the plane of the section: layers slide, a rectangle becomes a parallelogram.
  • Bending moment M about an axis in the section: the member bends.
  • Torque T about the axis ⟂ to the section: the member twists (angle of twist).

N, V and M diagrams come from writing N(x), V(x), M(x) for each loading segment [M1 Ex. 1.3].

Stress

[M1] §1.6–1.7 · [M6]

Stress is internal force per unit area at a point, always on a named plane. Unit: Pa = N/m² (1 MPa = 1 N/mm²). A stress needs a magnitude, a direction and the plane it acts on.

σ = N / A normal (tension +) τ = V / A shear σb = P / A_contact bearing σ_allow = σ_fail / FoS (or σy / FoS)
  • Single shear: one sheared section. Double shear: two sections, each carries P/2.
  • Course example: σ_fail = 510 MPa, FoS = 1.75 → σ_allow = 291.4 MPa [M1 Ex. 1.6].
  • A part has failed when it can no longer do its job: σ_eq > σ_all, δ_max > δ_cr, or ω_max > ω_cr.

Strain and Hooke's law

[M1] ch.2 · [M2] · [M4] · [M6]

ε = ΔL / L0 normal strain (µm/m or %) γ = π/2 − θ′ shear strain (rad) σ = E ε τ = G γ Hooke's law ν = −ε_lateral / ε_axial 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5 true ε = ln(L/L0) true σ = P / A_i
  • Normal strains change volume; shear strains change shape.
  • Small-strain analysis: sin θ ≈ θ, cos θ ≈ 1, tan θ ≈ θ.
  • True strains add up over successive steps; engineering strains don't (stretch to 2L0 and back gives e = +1 then −½) [M4].
  • For isotropic materials G = E / [2(1 + ν)] (standard relation).

Axially loaded members

[M2] axial loading lecture (2P, Flexibility & plasticity)

δ = ∫ P(x) dx / (E A(x)) general δ = P L / (E A) constant P, A, E δ = Σ Nᵢ Lᵢ / (Eᵢ Aᵢ) stepped bar (superposition) δ_th = α ΔT L thermal
  • Superposition is valid only for linear-elastic material.
  • Statically indeterminate bar: equilibrium and compatibility (e.g. fixed at both ends → total δ = 0).
  • Free bar heated: ε = αΔT, σ = 0. Fully restrained: ε = 0, σ = E α ΔT (compressive when heated).
  • With a gap: if δ_th ≤ δ_gap nothing happens; otherwise α ΔT L = δ_gap + R L / (E A).

Torsion of circular shafts

[M3] Beer & Johnston ch.3

  • Cross-sections of circular shafts stay plane and undistorted. Shear strain grows linearly with radius: γ = ρφ / L.
  • Hollow and solid circular shafts behave the same way because they are axisymmetric.
τ = T ρ / J τ_max = T c / J J = π c⁴ / 2 (solid) J = π (c₂⁴ − c₁⁴) / 2 (hollow) φ = T L / (J G) φ = Σ Tᵢ Lᵢ / (Jᵢ Gᵢ)
  • Elastoplastic shaft: first yield at T_Y = (π/2) c³ τ_Y. With an elastic core of radius ρ_Y: T = (4/3) T_Y [1 − ¼ (ρ_Y/c)³]. Fully plastic T_P = (4/3) T_Y.
  • Unloading is elastic, so residual stresses come from superposing the load and an equal opposite elastic torque.

Pure bending

[M3] Beer & Johnston ch.4

  • A symmetric beam in pure bending bends into a circular arc; plane sections stay plane.
  • The neutral surface keeps its length and passes through the centroid of the section.
  • Top shortens (compression), bottom lengthens (tension) for a sagging moment.
ε_x = − y / ρ σ_x = − M y / I σ_max = M c / I = M / S S = I / c
  • Elastoplastic rectangular beam: M_Y = σ_Y I / c; with elastic core half-thickness y_Y: M = (3/2) M_Y [1 − ⅓ (y_Y/c)²]; plastic moment M_P = (3/2) M_Y.

Yield criteria

[M5] Mendelson, Plasticity, ch.6 · course: 2P Flexibility & plasticity

Principal stresses σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ σ₃; σ_Y = yield stress in simple tension.

  • Max principal stress (Rankine): σ₁ = σ_Y.
  • Max principal strain (Saint-Venant): σ₁ − ν(σ₂ + σ₃) = σ_Y.
  • Max shear (Tresca): σ₁ − σ₃ = σ_Y; shear yield k = σ_Y / 2. A hexagon in the σ₁–σ₂ plane.
  • Total strain energy (Beltrami): σ₁² + σ₂² + σ₃² − 2ν(σ₁σ₂ + σ₂σ₃ + σ₃σ₁) = σ_Y².
  • Distortion energy (von Mises): (σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)² = 2σ_Y²; plane stress σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂² = σ_Y², an ellipse; k = σ_Y/√3.

For ductile metals Tresca and von Mises agree best with tests; Tresca is always the more conservative of the two.

Plastic deformation in metals

[M4] plasticity chapter (Dr. M. Agwa)

  • Plastic deformation = permanent deformation that stays after the loads are removed.
  • Mechanisms: slip (dislocation motion, the main one), twinning, phase transformation, and creep mechanisms (grain-boundary sliding, vacancy diffusion, dislocation climb).
  • Volume does not change during slip or twinning. Pure hydrostatic stress cannot cause plastic flow; it takes shear.
  • Slip starts when the resolved shear stress on a slip plane reaches the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS); in a tension test the inclined planes carry that shear.
  • Most metals are BCC, FCC or HCP.
  • Models: linear elastic → non-linear elastic → elastic–perfectly plastic → linear hardening → non-linear hardening.
  • Aluminium is easier to bend than steel; steel is easier to deform hot than cold [M4].

The tension test

[M4] plasticity chapter · [M6] tension laws · [M9] testing lectures

  • Specimens: short L0 = 5 d0 (round) or 5.65 √A0; long L0 = 10 d0 or 11.3 √A0. L0 is the gauge length, not the specimen length.
  • O–Y elastic · Y yield · Y–N uniform plastic flow with strain hardening · N necking starts (max load, UTS) · N–F localised necking, triaxial stress · F fracture (cup-and-cone in ductile metals).
  • Engineering stress falls after N only because A0 is used; true stress keeps rising.
  • Unloading from the plastic range follows a line parallel to the elastic line.
  • No clear yield point → 0.2 % proof stress: offset strain 0.002, line parallel to the elastic part.
% elongation = ΔL_max / L0 × 100 % reduction of area = ΔA / A0 × 100 modulus of resilience = ½ σ_pl ε_pl flow curve σ = K εⁿ
Check the ductility bands. [M6] lists brittle / semi-ductile / ductile by % elongation, but the labels are hard to read. The usual convention is brittle below 5 % elongation.

Compression test

[M15] compression notes · 1st-year Mechanical, Material

  • Used mainly for brittle materials that carry compression in service: concrete, stone, cast iron.
  • Ductile metals flatten into a barrel and do not fracture. Brittle ones shear on a plane at θ = 45° + φ/2 ≈ 55–60° (φ = angle of internal friction), with no yield point.
  • Specimen: circular section, parallel ends, 2 ≤ L/D ≤ 10. Below 2 the end friction dominates; above 10 the specimen buckles. A spherical seating block corrects ends that are not parallel.
  • The barrel comes from friction at the ends. Reduce it by lubricating the ends, testing a three-part specimen and studying the middle part, or using grooved heads.
  • Measured strength drops as L/D or specimen size increases, and rises with loading rate.
engineering σ = P / A0 ε = ΔL / L0 true σt = P / Ai εt = ln(A0/Ai) = 2 ln(D0/Di) % contraction = (L0 − Lf) / L0 × 100 % increase of section = (Af − A0) / A0 × 100

Bending test

[M14] bending test notes · 1st-year Mechanical, Material

  • Assumptions: pure bending, the same E in tension and compression, plane sections stay plane, a homogeneous beam symmetric about the loading plane.
  • 4-point loading is preferred: the middle third carries zero shear, so it is in pure bending.
  • Flexural strength σ_PL = M_PL y / I; modulus of rupture σ_max = M_max y / I. Take P and δ for E from the elastic range only.
  • Brittle beams break suddenly on a plane ⟂ to the neutral axis (tension side). Ductile beams do not break; they form a plastic hinge.
  • Cold bend test (ductility check): mandrel radius R = D if D ≤ 25 mm, R = 1.5 D if D > 25 mm. Inspect for cracks on the outer fibres (tension), inner fibres (compression), 45° shear cracks, and random cracks from defects. Other variants: hot bend, nick-bend, quench-bend.
σ = M y / I 3-point (P at mid-span) M = P L / 4 E = P L³ / (48 δ I) 4-point (P at each third) M = P L / 3 cantilever (P at the tip) M = P L E = P L³ / (3 δ I) resilience R = ½ P_PL δ_PL toughness ≈ ⅔ P_max δ_max section y = D/2, I = πD⁴/64 · y = h/2, I = bh³/12

Shear and torsion tests

[M13] shear & torsion notes + ZigZag "Shear _ Torsion tests" summary

Direct shear (force parallel to the section):

riveted joint τ = P / (n · x · A) n = rivets, x = shear planes = plates − 1 punching τ = P / (π D t) (square column: Q / 4bh) beam τ = Q S / (I b)

Torsion test: record T against the angle of twist θ, then:

τ = T r / J J = πD⁴/32 · J = π(Do⁴ − Di⁴)/32 γ = r θ / L0 G = T L / (J θ) θ in rad = θ° · π/180 elastic shear strength τ_el = 16 T_el / (π d³) ultimate, ductile solid τ_u = 12 T_max / (π d³) ultimate, brittle solid τ_u = 14 T_max / (π d³) ultimate, hollow τ_u = 4 T_max / (π d² t) d = (do + di)/2, t = (do − di)/2
Check the 14 and the 4. Both course sources write them. The elastic formula gives 16 for a brittle solid (it stays linear to fracture), and thin-wall theory (Beer [M3], τ = T / 2tA with A = πd²/4) gives 2T/(πd²t). Ask the lecturer which to use.
  • Resilience R = ½ T_PL θ_PL; toughness ≈ ⅔ T_max θ_max; moduli = value ÷ (A0 L0).
  • Ductility: Lf = √(L0² + (r θ_max)²), % elongation = (Lf − L0)/L0 × 100.
  • E ≈ 2.5 G (from G = E / 2(1 + ν)). Design stress τ = τ_PL / FoS, FoS 1.5–3.

Hardness tests

[M10] hardness notes · 1st-year Mechanical, Material · [M17] Callister

  • Hardness: resistance of the surface to permanent deformation (scratching, abrasion, cutting, indentation). Kinds: indentation, rebound, scratch, wear, machinability.
  • Indentation tests are static and practically non-destructive: Brinell, Vickers, Rockwell. Rockwell reads the number straight off the dial.

Brinell: hardened-steel ball D = 1, 2, 5 or 10 mm, load P (kg) held 15–20 s, measure the impression diameter d.

BHN = P / (π D h) = 2P / (π D [D − √(D² − d²)]) kg/mm² choose P from K = P / D² valid if d/D = 0.25 – 0.5 σ_ult ≈ 0.36 × BHN kg/mm²
MaterialK = P/D²P with D = 10 mm
Steel (hard metals)303000 kg
Copper and Al alloys (intermediate)151500 kg
Aluminium (soft)5500 kg
  • 0.36 BHN agrees with Callister's TS(MPa) ≈ 3.45 HB for steels (= 0.352 HB in kg/mm²).
  • Specimen: thickness ≥ 10 × impression depth; impression centre ≥ 2.5 d from the edge; ≥ 4 d between impressions.
  • Unsuitable for very hard materials (the ball deforms), thin sheet, and surface-hardened parts (the ball passes through the case).
Worked example in [M10] (D = 10 mm, P = 3000 kg, d = 4.5 mm) gives BHN = 196. The formula gives ≈ 179 for d = 4.5 (σ_ult ≈ 64 kg/mm²); 196 matches d = 4.3 mm.

Vickers: diamond square-based pyramid, 136° between opposite faces, loads 10–120 kg. The number does not change with load for the same material, which makes it suitable for very hard materials and thin sheet.

VHN = 2P sin(136°/2) / d² = 1.854 P / d² d = (d1 + d2) / 2 depth h = d / (2√2 · tan 68°) ≈ d / 7
Depth in [M10]. The example uses h = (d/2)/tan 68°. The 68° is measured across the faces, where the half-width is d/(2√2), so h ≈ d/7 (0.107 mm for d = 0.75 mm, not 0.15 mm).
RockwellIndenterMajor loadUsed for
Adiamond cone (Brale)60 kghardened steel, very hard metals, small impressions
Bsteel ball 1/16 in (1.588 mm)100 kgmild and medium-carbon steel sheet
Cdiamond cone (Brale)150 kgalloy steel, anything harder than B100

Impact loading and tests

[M11] impact test notes · 1st-year Mechanical, Material

A load applied suddenly causes more stress than the same load applied slowly. Weight P dropped from height h onto a bar of length L and area A:

σ_st = P / A δ_st = P L / (E A) impact factor I = 1 + √(1 + 2h / δ_st) σ_d = σ_st · I δ_d = δ_st · I ε_d = δ_d / L0 suddenly applied (h = 0): σ_d = 2 σ_st, δ_d = 2 δ_st strain energy U = σ_d² A L / (2E) modulus of resilience u = σ_d² / (2E)

Weight dropped at mid-span of a simply supported beam:

δ_st = P L³ / (48 E I) δ_d = δ_st · I σ_d = 12 E y δ_d / L² y = D/2 or h/2 U = σ_d² V / (18E) rectangle · σ_d² V / (24E) circle
  • Charpy: 10 × 10 × 55 mm, 45° V-notch 2 mm deep, simply supported on a 40 mm span, struck behind the notch.
  • Izod: 10 × 10 × 75 mm cantilever, struck in front of the notch, 22 mm above it.
  • Energy absorbed U = W H − W H′ (pendulum weight × drop in height). The notch makes sure the specimen breaks: without it a ductile bar only bends. Both strikes put the notch on the tension side.
  • Stress concentration: Kt = σ_notch / σ_applied = 1 + 2√(D/ρ), D = notch depth, ρ = notch radius. Semicircular notch (D = ρ) → Kt = 3.

Fatigue

[M12] fatigue theory notes + problems · 1st-year Mechanical, Material

  • Sudden failure under repeated or fluctuating loads, at stresses below the static strength and often with no warning.
  • Stages: crack initiation (usually at the surface or a stress concentration) → crack growth (beach marks) → final fracture of the remaining section (rough zone).
  • S–N curve: stress amplitude against cycles to failure. The endurance (fatigue) limit Se is the amplitude below which a fully reversed cycle never breaks the part.
Sm = (Smax + Smin)/2 Sa = (Smax − Smin)/2 Smax = Sm + Sa Smin = Sm − Sa fully reversed Sm = 0, Sa = Smax pulsating Smin = 0 → Sm = Sa = Smax/2
RuleFailure lineNote
GoodmanSa/Se + Sm/Sut = 1straight line Se → Sut
SoderbergSa/Se + Sm/Sy = 1most conservative, ends at yield
GerberSa/Se + (Sm/Sut)² = 1parabola, least conservative
Modified GoodmanGoodman ∩ Sa + Sm = SyGoodman line cut by the yield line
  • Procedure [M12]: divide Sy and Sut by the static factor of safety and Se by the fatigue factor, draw the line, plot (Sm, Sa). Inside → safe.
  • Example [M12]: σmax = +12, σmin = −8 kg/mm² → Sm = 2, Sa = 10. With Se = 20 and fatigue FoS 3, the allowed amplitude is at most 6.67 → not safe.

Rectilinear motion and motion graphs

[D3-a] "Straight line motion (2): graphical solutions" · [D1-1] pp.2–3

constant a v = v0 + a t v² = v0² + 2a (s − s0) s − s0 = v0 t + ½ a t² a = f(t) v − v0 = ∫ a dt s − s0 = ∫ v dt a = f(s) ∫ a ds = ∫ v dv (a = v dv/ds)
  • Differentiating lowers the degree of the curve by one: slope of s–t = v, slope of v–t = a.
  • Integrating raises it by one: area under a–t = Δv, area under v–t = Δs.
  • A rising a-line integrates to a concave curve, a falling one to a convex curve. The notes' area rule for a curve of degree n inside its enclosing rectangle: concave = rectangle/(n+1), convex = n·rectangle/(n+1).
  • The number of intervals on the graph equals the number of different accelerations. Total distance = sum of |Δs| between turning points (v = 0). Average speed = Δs/Δt.
Area rule. It is exact only for a pure power curve whose vertex sits at a corner of the rectangle. [D3-a p.24] applies it to v = 8t − 25t³ and gets 0.21 m, but ∫v dt = 0.15 m. Also in [D3-a]: p.3 the slope on 2–4 s is 4, not 2; p.6 S(60) = 10 293.3, not 10 373.3.

Projectile motion

[D3-b] "Curvilinear motion: projectile" · Prep, 2nd term

Gravity is the only force: ax = 0, ay = −g (−9.81 m/s², −32.2 ft/s²) with y upward.

x Vx = V0 cos θ (constant) x − x0 = V0 cos θ · t y Vy = V0 sin θ − g t y − y0 = V0 sin θ · t − ½ g t² Vy² = (V0 sin θ)² − 2g (y − y0) top of the path Vy = 0, V = Vx, y = h speed V = √(Vx² + Vy²)
  • Steps: x horizontal, y vertical; coordinates of the launch point (x0, y0) and end point (x, y); resolve V0; apply the laws. The x-equation gives the range R = x − x0, the y-displacement equation the flight time, the Vy² equation the maximum height h.
  • Two possible launch angles: eliminate t and use sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ, which leaves a quadratic in tan θ.
  • Smallest launch speed: write V0² as a function of the angle and set its derivative to zero.
Two checks in [D3-b]. p.3 writes ay = 9.81 without a sign; every example uses −9.81 with y up. p.7 assumes the water jet is at its peak when it reaches the wall; the true maximum height on the wall is 32.5 ft at θ = 67.3°, not 11.1 ft.

Curvilinear motion: x–y, n–t and polar

[D3-c] "Polar coordinates" and its summary table, p.6

AxesVelocityAcceleration
Cartesian x, yVx = ẋ, Vy = ẏax = ẍ, ay = ÿ
Normal–tangentialVt = V, Vn = 0at, an = V²/ρ
Polar r, θVr = ṙ, Vθ = r θ̇ar = r̈ − r θ̇²
aθ = r θ̈ + 2 ṙ θ̇
ρ = [1 + (dy/dx)²]^(3/2) / (d²y/dx²) r = r(θ) ṙ = (dr/dθ) θ̇ r̈ = (d²r/dθ²) θ̇² + (dr/dθ) θ̈ polar → x–y Vx = Vr cos θ − Vθ sin θ Vy = Vr sin θ + Vθ cos θ ax = ar cos θ − aθ sin θ ay = ar sin θ + aθ cos θ magnitudes V = √(Vr² + Vθ²) a = √(ar² + aθ²)
  • Polar coordinates give V and a only, not the displacement. Two problem types: r and θ as functions of time (differentiate), or r(θ) with θ, θ̇, θ̈ given (use the ṙ and r̈ rules above).
  • From x–y to n–t: t lies along v. With β = angle between a and v, at = a cos β, an = a sin β.
Follower rods. [D3-c p.4] reports only Vr and ar for a rod driven by a cam, while p.9–10 reports the full polar V and a for the same kind of question. A rod sliding along a fixed line through O has v = ṙ and a = r̈; check which the lecturer expects.

Impulse, momentum and impact

[D4-4] ZigZag summary, ch.4 (Prep, 2nd term)

impulse ∫ ΣFx dt = m v2x − m v1x (same in y) momentum m1 v1 + m2 v2 = m1 v1′ + m2 v2′ restitution e = (v1′ − v2′) / (v2 − v1)
  • Steps: free-body diagram, ΣF, then find t0, the instant motion starts (when the applied force first exceeds the resistance), and integrate from t0. The integral is the area under the F–t curve.
  • Elastic e = 1, no energy lost (an idealisation). Semi-elastic 0 < e < 1, energy lost. Plastic e = 0, the bodies stick and move with one velocity.
  • Combined problems chain work–energy (ΣU = T2 − T1, weight work −mg(h2 − h1), friction work −μk N d), then the impact, then the impulse.
Check [D4-4]. A margin note calls impulse a "difference of energies"; it is the change in momentum. p.2: V2 = 110.25 m/s, not 111. p.4: V_A = √19.6 m/s with g = 9.8 (√20 needs g = 10).

Rigid-body motion and fixed-axis rotation

[D1-1] "Planar kinematics of a rigid body" · [D4-5] · [D2-d]

  • Translation (rectilinear or curvilinear): every point has the same s, v and a, so the body acts as a point. Rotation about a fixed axis: every point moves on a circle. General plane motion (GPM): translation + rotation.
  • ω and α act along k̂: positive counter-clockwise, negative clockwise. î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ; reversing the order changes the sign.
constant α ω = ω0 + α t ω² = ω0² + 2α Δθ Δθ = ω0 t + ½ α t² α = f(t) ω − ω0 = ∫ α dt α = f(θ) ∫ α dθ = ∫ ω dω point P v = ω × r a_t = α × r a_n = −ω² r magnitudes v = ω r a_t = α r a_n = ω² r a = √(a_t² + a_n²) units ω = 2π N / 60 (N in rpm) rev = θ / 2π
ConnectionRelation
Cord on a drum, rack on a pinions = θ r · v = ω r · a = α r
Belt, or two meshing gearsω1/ω2 = α1/α2 = θ1/θ2 = r2/r1
Two wheels on one shaftsame θ, ω, α

Meshing gears turn in opposite senses [D1-1 p.12].

Check [D1-1] p.13. ω = 13/0.12 = 108.33 rad/s should be 13/1.2 = 10.83 rad/s (the radius is 1.2 m). [D4-5] p.4: θ_A at t = 2 s is 2 rad, not −0.25.

Absolute (position) analysis

[D1-2] "Absolute analysis of general plane motion"

  • Relate the displacement S of a point to the body angle θ, then differentiate with respect to time: θ̇ = ω, θ̈ = α.
  • Measure S from a fixed point (a pin, or where the fixed paths of the moving points cross) to the moving part.
  • Example: S = 5 sin θ → v = 5ω cos θ → a = 5(α cos θ − ω² sin θ).
  • Slider–crank: the cosine rule gives S(θ); take the positive root. That single equation cannot give ω of the connecting rod. For it, write a second equation linking the two angles, e.g. AB sin θ_AB = BC sin θ_BC → ω_BC = AB ω_AB cos θ_AB / (BC cos θ_BC).
  • A negative v means motion opposite to the assumed displacement; a negative ω means the angle is decreasing.
  • Signs differ from the vector method: the same ladder problem gives α = +11/3 rad/s² here and −11/3 rad/s² with the counter-clockwise-positive k̂ convention [D1-3 p.4].

Relative velocity and acceleration

[D1-3] "Relative motion analysis of general plane motion" · [D2-a] · [D2-b]

v_B = v_A + ω_AB × r_B/A a_B = a_A + α_AB × r_B/A − ω_AB² r_B/A
  • v_B/A is perpendicular to r_B/A. The tangential acceleration term follows the relative velocity; the normal term points from B toward A.
  • Steps: name the motion of each body (rotation or GPM). For a rotating link use v = ω × r; for a GPM link use the relative equation. Write every term in î and ĵ and equate components: two equations, two unknowns.
  • Solve all velocities first, because the normal terms need every ω; then the accelerations.
  • Assume unknown ω and α positive (counter-clockwise); a negative answer means clockwise. A slider moves only along its guide; on an inclined guide use the slope ratios (e.g. 4/5, 3/5).
  • Chains of links: find B from the driving link, then C from B; or write v_C from both links and equate.
Check [D1-3]. p.7: ω_CD = −4 rad/s (clockwise), not +4; then α_BC = −6.16 and α_CD = −21.86 rad/s² (printed −6.03 and −21.56). p.3: k̂ × (−0.2 ĵ) = +0.2 î; the final α = −95 rad/s² is still right.

Instantaneous centre of zero velocity

[D1-4] "Instantaneous center of rotation" · [D2-c] summary

  • At a given instant a body in GPM rotates about a point of zero velocity, the IC: v_P = ω · r_P/IC, perpendicular to r_P/IC in the sense of ω.
  • It gives velocities only. For accelerations use the relative-acceleration equation.

Finding the IC [D1-4 pp.2–3]:

  • ω and one velocity v_P known: on the perpendicular to v_P, at distance v_P/ω.
  • Two velocity directions known, not parallel: where the perpendiculars cross.
  • Parallel velocities on a common perpendicular: join the tips. Same sense → IC outside the two points; opposite senses → between them. Equal parallel velocities → no IC, ω = 0.
  • Rolling without slipping: the contact point, so v_centre = ω R.
  • Rod end on a slider → perpendicular to the slider's path; on a rotating link → the line through that link's pin; on a GPM body → the line to that body's IC [D2-c].
  • A slipping wheel's contact point is not the IC: use r_O/IC = v_O/ω. The IC triangle is usually solved with the sine rule.

Kinetics: translation

[D1-5] "Kinetics of translation motion"

Every problem is drawn as F.B.D = K.D: external forces on one side, m a_G (and I_G α when the body rotates) on the other.

rectilinear ΣFx = m aG ΣFy = 0 ΣMG = 0 curvilinear ΣFt = m α R ΣFn = m ω² R ΣMG = 0 (α, ω of the links that carry the body) moments about any other point P include the moment of m aG friction at rest F_f = F ≤ μs N sliding F_f = μk N
  • Incline: x along the slope (positive with the motion), y normal to it: w sin θ − F_f = m aG, N = w cos θ.
  • Vehicles: friction on the driven wheels pushes the car forward (rear-wheel drive → rear wheels only, front-wheel → front only, 4×4 → both). Each axle carries 2N.
  • No slipping: F_f ≤ μs N. No tipping: the normal reaction must stay under the body, 0 ≤ x ≤ l/2 from the weight line; at the tipping limit the whole reaction is at one edge.
  • When a supporting wire is cut, the body starts from rest, so the normal term m ω² R is zero at that instant.
Check [D1-5]. p.1–2 writes F_f = μs N for a body at rest; that is only the limit at impending slip, in general F_f = F ≤ μs N. p.9 states the range "0 ≤ h ≤ 0.8" and then finds h_max = 1.414 m, so the stated range contradicts its own answer.

Kinetics: rotation about a fixed axis

[D1-6] "Kinetics of rotation motion" · [D4-6] ZigZag summary, ch.6

ΣFt = m aGt = m α R ΣFn = m aGn = m ω² R ΣMG = IG α or about the pin ΣMO = IO α, IO = IG + m R² I = m k² (k = radius of gyration)
  • Axes: n toward the pin O, t in the sense of rotation. Draw the F.B.D and the K.D (m aGt, m aGn, IG α); a moment is positive when it acts with the rotation.
  • IG from the tables: rod ml²/12 (about an end ml²/3), disc ½mR², sphere ⅖mR², plate m(b² + h²)/12. For a composite body find G first, then IO = Σ(Ii + mi di²).
  • Released from rest (cord cut, support removed): ω = 0, so aGn = 0; α cannot be zero.
  • Cord on a disc without slipping: a_block = α R. Spring on a cylinder: F = k R θ.
Check. [D4-6 p.4]: α = −2.625/2.5 = −1.05 rad/s², so the wheel stops after 19.0 s (printed −26 and 0.76 s). [D1-6 p.15]: B_x and B_y are swapped; they are 88.29 N and 179.03 N. [D1-6 p.18]: 8.97 is ω², so ω ≈ 3.0 rad/s.

Kinetics: general plane motion and rolling

[D1-7] "Kinetics of GPM"

ΣFx = m aGx ΣFy = m aGy ΣMG = IG α rolling, no slip aG = α R F_f unknown, then check F_f ≤ μs N rolling, slipping aG ≠ α R F_f = μk N
  • Procedure: assume no slipping and solve. If F_f ≤ μs N the assumption holds; if not, re-solve with F_f = μk N and aG ≠ αR. Do not put μs N into the no-slip equations. The least μs for rolling is F_f/N from the no-slip solution.
  • Friction direction: if the applied load turns the cylinder (a couple, a cord wound on it), friction opposes the rotation. If the load does not turn it (w sin θ, a force through G), friction supplies the rotation. A negative F_f just means the other direction; the results stand.
  • When aG is hard to see, use relative acceleration from a point of known acceleration: aG = aA + α × r_G/A − ω² r_G/A.

Work and energy

[D1-8] "Planar kinetics of rigid body: work and energy"

T1 + ΣU1→2 = T2
Work ofUNote
Weight−W Δypositive when G moves down
Spring−½ k (s2² − s1²)s = deformation from the free length
CoupleM (θ2 − θ1)∫ M dθ if M varies with θ
Friction−μk N sonly when slipping; zero for rolling without slip
ForceF cos θ · s∫ F·ds if F varies; a force kept ⟂ to a bar: P θR
MotionKinetic energy T
Translation½ m vG²
Rotation about O½ IO ω²
General plane motion½ m vG² + ½ IG ω² = ½ I_IC ω²
  • No work is done by pin reactions, the normal reaction, the weight in horizontal motion, or friction in rolling without slipping. Internal forces cancel.
  • For a system add the T of every member according to its own motion (links rotating, a bar in curvilinear translation, a disc in GPM). At an extreme position a rolling disc stops and its centre becomes the IC of the rod attached to it.
Check [D1-8]. p.3 says spring work is always negative; that holds only while the deformation grows. p.8: the spring already holds the disc in equilibrium, so s1 = 0.4905 m and the answer is S = 1.5 m, not 2.481 m. p.6: s2 = 2.25 m (the −75 J is right).

Potential energy, conservation and stability

[D1-9] "Conservation of energy" · [D1-11] "Potential energy"

Vg = ± W yG + above the datum, − below Ve = ½ k s² always positive T1 + V1 = T2 + V2 (conservative forces only) equilibrium dV/dθ = 0 stable d²V/dθ² > 0 · neutral = 0 · unstable < 0
  • Weight and spring forces are conservative (their work depends only on the end positions). Friction is not: its work depends on the path and turns into heat.
  • Procedure: draw both positions; put the datum through a fixed point (a pin, or where fixed paths cross); find each ΔyG and spring deformation from the geometry; add T of each member; substitute.
  • Stability: write V = Ve + Vg as a function of θ, solve dV/dθ = 0, then test the sign of d²V/dθ² at each root. A disc pinned above G is stable, pinned at G neutral, pinned below G unstable.
Check [D1-11]. p.13–14 reports only θ = 62.65° (stable); dV/dθ = 0 also has θ = 27.81°, which is unstable. p.8 prints the numeric d²V/dθ² line with three signs reversed; the values given are right.

1.1 Course data

  • Lecture #1 is titled "Mechanical Systems Design (DPE 301): Course Description and Introduction to Mechanical Systems Design", by Professor Dr. Mohamed Agwa [MD-1 p.1].
  • Design (1) syllabus: code DPE202, "Machine elements Design", prerequisites DPE102 & DPE103 [MD-1 p.2].
    • Contact hours: Cr 3, Lec 2, Tutorial 3, Lab –, Total 5. Marks: CW 50 (50%), O/P –, FE 50 (50%), total 100 [MD-1 p.2].
    • Category: Compulsory (MR) [MD-1 p.2].
    • Objective: knowledge about different machine elements, their application and methods of design under different static and fatigue loads [MD-1 p.2].
    • Topics: fundamentals of machine design; fits and tolerance, geometrical tolerances and machine marks; design considerations (design criteria, selection of materials, dimensions and shapes, production, assembly and maintenance, etc.); design for static loads; design for dynamic loads and fatigue strength; design of riveted joints; design of power screws and threaded joints; design of welded joints; design of helical and leaf springs; design of shrink-fitted joints; design of axles and shafts for strength, rigidity and critical speed [MD-1 p.2].
    • Textbook for Design (1): Chapters 1–9 of Richard Budynas and Keith Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, McGraw-Hill Education (2019) [MD-1 p.2].
  • Design (2) syllabus (this course): code DPE 301, "Mechanical Systems Design", prerequisite DPE202 [MD-1 p.3].
    • Contact hours: Cr 3, Lec 2, Tutorial 2, Lab –, Total 4. Marks: CW 50 (50%), O/P –, FE 50 (50%), total 100 [MD-1 p.3].
    • Category: Compulsory (MR) [MD-1 p.3].
    • Objective: knowledge about different mechanical systems, its components, application and methods of design under different static and fatigue loads [MD-1 p.3].
    • Topics: fundamentals of power transmission elements design; design of rolling bearing; design of sliding bearing; design of rigid and flexible couplings; design of brakes and clutches; design of flat and V belts; design of sprockets and chains; design of spur, helical, bevel and worm gears (printed "warm gears") [MD-1 p.3].
  • Shigley chapters shown as the course material (Shigley lecture-slide covers) [MD-1 p.4–10]:
    • Chapter 11 Rolling-Contact Bearings (10th ed.) [p.4]; Chapter 12 Lubrication and Journal Bearings (9th ed.) [p.5];
    • Chapter 13 Gears – General [p.6]; Chapter 14 Spur and Helical Gears [p.7]; Chapter 15 Bevel and Worm Gears [p.8] (10th ed. in SI units);
    • Chapter 16 Clutches, Brakes, Couplings, and Flywheels (9th ed.) [p.9]; Chapter 17 Flexible Mechanical Elements (10th ed. in SI units) [p.10].

1.4 Student advice note "ملف مهم جدا جدا" (Machine Design, تصميم الماكينات) [MD-IMP]

A handwritten Arabic note (6 pp) by a former student, signed but unnamed, titled "تصميم الماكينات" (Machine Design). It contains advice and course organisation only, no technical content. The year it describes is not stated. The points, translated:

  • The design course this year is easier than the second-year one [MD-IMP p.1].
  • The course is out of 150 marks: 50 coursework (أعمال سنة), split among the midterm, the project, and attendance at lectures and sections; 100 for the final (⚠ F21: [MD-1 p.3] gives CW 50 + FE 50 = 100) [MD-IMP p.1].
  • "Of course no need to say that the midterm and the final are رش" (student slang; the note does not explain it), followed by a sad face [MD-IMP p.1].
  • The course is taught by Dr. Mohamed Agwa (د. محمد عجوة) and Eng. Mohamed Ashry (م. محمد عشري) [MD-IMP p.2]. (The section handouts used in these notes are by Eng. Ehsan Khaled.)
  • The writer's opinion: Dr. Agwa is, without exaggeration, the best in the faculty for marking, explanation and the way he treats students. Eng. Ashry explains well, but the writer advises relying on the doctor first and last [MD-IMP p.2].
  • Lecture rules the writer reports: nobody enters the lecture late, nobody brings food or drink, and nobody uses a mobile phone during the lecture [MD-IMP p.2].
  • Midterm and final: the doctor offers two options [MD-IMP p.3]:
    1. Enter the exam with whatever you want (including the problems you solved), but the exam will contain problems you have never seen.
    2. The students collect money and photocopy the lectures, without the problems in them; the exam problems then come from the lectures or from the reference (those he asked the students to solve), 3 to 5 problems per chapter.
    • The writer strongly recommends the second option.
  • The doctor asks for any papers or tables students want added to be sent to him to collect. Files named "ورق الميدترم" (midterm papers) and "ورق الفاينال" (final papers) hold all the additions; students should go through them well and talk to the doctor if they want to add something [MD-IMP p.4].
  • For the teaching assistant (المعيد): the syllabus may not be finished in the sections; this is no problem because the doctor's explanation is sufficient [MD-IMP p.4].
  • While studying, print the doctor's lectures, because these are the papers taken into the exam. Studying from a laptop leaves you confused in the exam; printing is better so you are used to the paper [MD-IMP p.4–5].
  • A file named "محاضرات صوتية" (audio lectures) holds recordings of the doctor's lectures; listen to them when something is unclear, with the lecture paper in front of you [MD-IMP p.5].
  • Most important: beware of studying from any material of the Power department (قسم باور). Its requirements and problem data are completely different, as is the order of explanation; the syllabus is the same, but each doctor has his own requirements in the problems [MD-IMP p.5].
  • The note closes with good wishes and a signature, and a joke picture captioned "لما تصمم Brake وتطلع Non safe" (when you design a brake and it comes out non-safe): a sofa built from car seats and wheels [MD-IMP p.6].

2.1 Types and arrangements

  • Belt types (Table 17-1): flat, round, V and timing [MD-2 p.4].
  • Flat belt: joint yes; size t = 0.03–0.20 in (0.75–5 mm); no upper limit on center distance [MD-2 p.4].
  • Round belt: joint yes; d = 1/8 to 3/4 in; no upper limit on center distance [MD-2 p.4].
  • V belt: no joint; b = 0.31–0.91 in (8–19 mm); center distance limited [MD-2 p.4].
  • Timing belt: no joint; p = 2 mm and up; center distance limited [MD-2 p.4].
  • Fig 17-2 shows (a) a nonreversing open belt, (b) a reversing crossed belt and (c) a reversing open-belt drive. Crossed belts must be separated to prevent rubbing if high-friction materials are used [MD-2 p.5].
  • Open belt compared with crossed belt [MD-2 p.6]:
    • open: shafts in the same plane; crossed: two planes.
    • open: pulleys turn in the same direction; crossed: opposite directions.
    • open: wrap angle < 180°; crossed: > 180°.
    • open: lower power capacity; crossed: higher.
    • open: shorter belt; crossed: longer.
    • open: no rubbing, so longer life; crossed: rubs, so shorter life.
    • open: vibrates (whips) at larger center distance; crossed: free from such vibration.
  • Quarter-twist drive (Fig 17-3): an idler guide pulley must be used if motion is to be in both directions [MD-2 p.7].
  • Loose-pulley drive (Fig 17-4): it removes the need for a clutch; a fork shifts the belt. Fig 17-5 shows variable-speed belt drives [MD-2 p.8].

2.2 Geometry

Figure: md-belt-open-geometry.jpg (Fig 17-1a) [MD-2 p.9].

  • Open belt: θd = π − 2 sin⁻¹[(D − d)/(2C)]; θD = π + 2 sin⁻¹[(D − d)/(2C)] (17-1). D = large pulley diameter, d = small pulley diameter, C = center distance, θ = angle of contact [MD-2 p.9].
  • Open belt length: L = [4C² − (D − d)²]^½ + ½(D θD + d θd) (17-2) [MD-2 p.10].
  • Crossed belt: θ = π + 2 sin⁻¹[(D + d)/(2C)] (17-3); L = [4C² − (D + d)²]^½ + ½(D + d)θ (17-4) [MD-2 p.11].

2.3 Tensions (belting equation)

  • Belt element (Fig 17-6): F = (F2 − m r² ω²) exp(fθ) + m r² ω² (17-5). F1 = tight-side tension, F2 = loose-side tension, b = width, t = thickness, m = mass per unit length, ω = angular velocity. θd = φ [MD-2 p.12].
  • F1 = (F2 − m r² ω²) exp(fφ) + m r² ω² (17-6) [MD-2 p.13].
  • (F1 − Fc)/(F2 − Fc) = exp(fφ) (17-7), where Fc = m r² ω² [MD-2 p.13].
  • F1 − F2 = (F1 − Fc)[exp(fφ) − 1]/exp(fφ) (17-8) [MD-2 p.13].
  • Centrifugal (hoop) tension: Fc = m r² ω², with ω = V/r [MD-2 p.14].
  • US form: V = π d n/12 ft/min; w = 12 γ b t lbf/ft (γ in lbf/in³; b, t in in); Fc = (w/g)(V/60)² = (w/32.17)(V/60)² [MD-2 p.14].
  • SI form: w = γ b t; Fc = (w/g)V² [MD-2 p.14].
  • Torque: ΔF = F1 − F2 = 2T/d [MD-2 p.15].
  • F1 = Fi + Fc + ΔF/2 = Fi + Fc + T/d (f); F2 = Fi + Fc − ΔF/2 = Fi + Fc − T/d (g) [MD-2 p.16].
    • Fi = initial tension, Fc = hoop tension, ΔF/2 = tension due to torque T.
  • F1 − F2 = 2T/d (h); F1 + F2 = 2Fi + 2Fc [MD-2 p.16].
  • Fi = (F1 + F2)/2 − Fc (i) [MD-2 p.17].
  • Fi = (T/d)[exp(fφ) + 1]/[exp(fφ) − 1] (17-9) [MD-2 p.17].
  • F1 = Fc + Fi · 2exp(fφ)/[exp(fφ) + 1] (17-10) [MD-2 p.17].
  • F2 = Fc + Fi · 2/[exp(fφ) + 1] (17-11) [MD-2 p.18].
  • Power: H = (F1 − F2)V/33 000 (j), in hp with lbf and ft/min [MD-2 p.18].

2.4 Allowable tension and correction factors (flat belts)

  • Manufacturers give an allowable tension Fa (or σall) per unit width. Belt life is several years [MD-2 p.19].
  • The severity of flexing gives the pulley correction factor Cp. Speeds above 600 ft/min need the velocity correction factor Cv [MD-2 p.19].
  • Cv = 1 for polyamide and urethane belts. For leather, read Cv from Fig 17-9 [MD-2 p.19–20].
  • Ks is the service factor for excursions of load; nd is the design factor for exigencies [MD-2 p.19].
  • Design power: Hd = Hnom Ks nd. The highlighted box on the slide prints "Ha = Hnom Ks nd" (⚠ F1) [MD-2 p.19].
  • Allowable largest tension: (F1)a = b Fa Cp Cv (17-12) [MD-2 p.20].
    • (F1)a in lbf; b = belt width, in; Fa = manufacturer's allowed tension, lbf/in; Cp from Table 17-4; Cv from Fig 17-9 (leather) or 1 (polyamide, urethane).
  • Fig 17-9 (Cv for leather belts): Cv against V (0–30 m/s) for 4.5 mm, 5 mm, 7 & 8 mm and 9 mm thicknesses. Cv falls from 1.0 to about 0.7 at 30 m/s. Data: Machinery's Handbook, 20th ed., 1976, p. 1047 [MD-2 p.21].
  • The same chart in ft/min (0–6000) is on p.22, for thicknesses 11/64, 13/64, 18/64 & 20/64 and 25/64 in [MD-2 p.22].

2.5 Flat-belt analysis steps [MD-2 p.24]

  1. Find exp(fφ) from the belt-drive geometry and friction.
  2. Find Fc from the geometry and speed.
  3. Find the torque: T = 63 025 Hnom Ks nd/n (US). The box on the slide gives T = Hnom Ks nd/(2πn).
  4. Find (F1)a − F2 = 2T/d.
  5. Find (F1)a from Tables 17-2 and 17-4 and Eq (17-12).
  6. F2 = (F1)a − [(F1)a − F2].
  7. Find Fi from Eq (i).
  8. Check the friction development: f′ < f, where f′ = (1/φ) ln{[(F1)a − Fc]/(F2 − Fc)}.
  9. Factor of safety: nfs = Ha/(Hnom Ks).

2.6 Worked example 17-1 (flat belt) [MD-2 p.28–31]

  • Data [p.28]:
    • Polyamide A-3 belt, 150 mm wide (belt 150 × 3.3 mm, γ = 11 kN/m³), 11 kW.
    • Light shock, Ks = 1.25; nfs ≥ 1.1.
    • Horizontal drive, shafts 2.4 m apart, loose side on top.
    • Driving pulley 150 mm at 1750 rpm; driven pulley 450 mm.
  • Solution chain [p.29–31]:
    • φ = 3.0165 rad; exp(0.8 × 3.0165) = 11.17.
    • V = 13.7 m/s.
    • w = 11 000(0.15)(0.0033) = 5.4 N/m; Fc = (5.4/9.81)(13.7)² = 103.3 N.
    • T = 1.25(1.1)(11 000)/(2π·1750/60) = 82.5 N·m.
    • (F1)a − F2 = 2(82)/0.15 = 1093.3 N (⚠ F2).
    • Fa = 18 kN/m, Cv = 1, Cp = 0.70 → (F1)a = 0.15(18 000)(0.70)(1) = 1890 N.
    • F2 = 796.7 N; Fi = 1240.4 N.
    • Design power = 11(1.25)(1.1) = 15.125 kW.
    • f′ = 0.314 < 0.8, so no slip.
    • nfs = 15.125/(11 × 1.25) = 1.1.
  • Sheet problems: Shigley 17-2 and 17-4 [MD-2 p.31]. Both are solved in [MD-S1] (2.7 below).

  • Formula sheet (US units) [MD-S1 p.2–3]:
    • Allowable largest tension: F1a = b Fa Cp Cv; Cp from Table 17-4; Cv = 1 for polyamide and urethane, Fig 17-9 for leather [p.2].
    • Linear speed of belt: v (ft/min) = π d(in) n(rpm)/12 [p.3].
    • Centrifugal force: Fc = m r² ω² = (w/g)(V/60)² = (w/32.17)(V/60)², with w = 12γbt lbf/ft [p.3].
    • Transmitted torque: H = Hnom Ks nd; T (lbf·in) = 63 025H/n [p.3].
    • Transmitted horsepower: H = (F1 − F2)V/33 000 [p.3].
    • Loose-side tension: F1a − F2 = 2T/d [p.3].
    • Initial tension: Fi = (F1a + F2)/2 − Fc [p.3].
    • Coefficient of friction: φ = φd = π − 2 sin⁻¹[(D − d)/2C]; f′ = (1/φ) ln[(F1a − Fc)/(F2 − Fc)] [p.3].
    • Factor of safety: nfs = Ha/(Hnom Ks) [p.3].
  • Dip: when flat belts were used for long center distances, the weight of the belt itself can provide the initial tension. The static belt deflects to a curve (a word is missing in the handout: "deflects to an curve"), and the dip from a straight belt can be measured against a stretched music wire [MD-S1 p.4]:
    • dip = C² w/(96 Fi); dip in in, C = center-to-center distance in in, w = weight per foot of the belt in lbf/ft, Fi = initial tension in lbf. Sketch: two pulleys at distance C, tension Fi at each end, dip at mid-span.
  • Sheet problem P17-2 [MD-S1 p.5–8]:
    • Statement: a 6 in wide polyamide F-1 flat belt connects a 2 in diameter pulley with an angular velocity ratio of 0.5; center distance 9 ft; the smaller pulley turns at 1750 rpm delivering 2 hp; Ks = 1.25. (a) Find Fc, Fi, (F1)a and F2 at the maximum tension limit. (b) Find Ha, nfs and the belt length. (c) Find the dip [p.5].
    • Given: b = 6 in; d = 2 in; d/D = 1/2 → D = 4 in; C = 9 ft; n = 1750 rpm; Hnom = 2 hp; Ks = 1.25. Table 17-2: t = 0.05 in, γ = 0.035 lbf/in³ [p.5].
    • w = 12(0.035)(6)(0.05) = 0.126 lbf/ft; V = π(2)(1750)/12 = 916.3 ft/min; Fc = (0.126/32.17)(916.3/60)² = 0.9134 lbf [p.6].
    • Fa = 35 lbf/in (Table 17-2); Cp = 0.7 (Table 17-4); Cv = 1 → (F1)a = 6(35)(0.7)(1) = 147 lbf [p.6].
    • H = Hnom Ks nd = 2(1.25)(1) = 2.5 hp; T = 63 025(2.5)/1750 = 90 lbf·in; 147 − F2 = 2(90)/2 → F2 = 147 − 90 = 57 lbf [p.6].
    • Fi = (147 + 57)/2 − 0.9134 = 101.08 lbf [p.7].
    • Ha = (147 − 57)(916.3)/33 000 = 2.5 hp; nfs = 2.5/(2 × 1.25) = 1 ("as expected") [p.7].
    • Arabic note: the friction coefficient is checked to make sure the friction the design relies on is below the material's friction coefficient; if not, the belt slips, F1 and F2 change, and Ha (and so nfs) changes [p.7].
    • θd = π − 2 sin⁻¹[(4 − 2)/(2 × 9 × 12)] = 3.123 rad; f′ = (1/3.123) ln[(147 − 0.9134)/(57 − 0.9134)] = 0.307; Table 17-2 gives f = 0.5, so f′ < f as required [p.7].
    • θD = π + 2 sin⁻¹[(4 − 2)/(2 × 9 × 12)] = 3.16 rad; L = [4(9 × 12)² − (4 − 2)²]^½ + ½(4 × 3.16 + 2 × 3.12) = 225.4 in [p.8].
    • dip = (9 × 12)²(0.126)/(96 × 101.08) = 0.1515 in [p.8].
  • Sheet problem P17-4 [MD-S1 p.9–11]:
    • Statement: a flat-belt drive of two 4 ft diameter cast-iron pulleys spaced 16 ft apart; select a belt type to transmit 60 hp at a pulley speed of 380 rpm; service factor 1.1, design factor 1 [p.9].
    • Function: Hnom = 60 hp, n = 380 rpm, Ks = 1.1, C = 16 ft; nd = 1; belt material polyamide; d = D = 4 × 12 = 48 in; unknowns t and b [p.9].
    • Table 17-2: d = 48 in is available with a wide range of materials; choose one and calculate the other variables. Choosing polyamide A-3: t = 0.13 in, γ = 0.042 lbf/in³, Fa = 100 lbf/in, f = 0.8. Solve for the unknown width b [p.9].
    • Cp = 1 (Table 17-4); Cv = 1 (polyamide) → (F1)a = b(100)(1)(1) = 100b lbf [p.9–10].
    • V = π d n = π(4)(380) = 4775 ft/min (d in ft); w = 12(0.042)b(0.13) = 0.0655b lbf/ft; Fc = (0.0655b/32.17)(4775/60)² = 12.89b lbf [p.10].
    • T = 63 025 Hnom Ks nd/n = 63 025(60)(1.1)(1)/380 = 10 946.44 (unit written "lbf/in") [p.10].
    • 100b − F2 = 2(10 946.44)/48 → F2 = 100b − 456.1 lbf [p.10].
    • φ = φd = π − 2 sin⁻¹(0) = π. Assuming full friction development: 0.8 = (1/π) ln[(100b − 12.89b)/(100b − 456.1 − 12.89b)], written as "π × 0.8 = (1/π) ln(…)"; e^(0.8π) = 87.11b/(87.11b − 456.1); 87.11b = 12.34(87.11b − 456.1) → b = 5.6 in (⚠ F19) [p.11].
    • A belt width greater than 5.6 in will develop friction less than 0.8, so b = 6 in is taken [p.11].

3.2 Power rating

3.3 Tensions, number of belts, factor of safety

  • The Gates Rubber Co. gives an effective friction coefficient of 0.5123 for grooves: (F1 − Fc)/(F2 − Fc) = exp(0.5123 φ) (17-18) [MD-3 p.15].
  • Design power: Hd = Hnom Ks nd (17-19), with Ks from Table 17-15 [MD-3 p.16].
  • Number of belts: Nb ≥ Hd/Ha, Nb = 1, 2, 3, … (17-20) [MD-3 p.16].

Table 17-15. Suggested service factors Ks for V-belt drives [MD-3 p.17]

Driven machinery Normal-torque source High or nonuniform-torque source
Uniform 1.0–1.2 1.1–1.3
Light shock 1.1–1.3 1.2–1.4
Medium shock 1.2–1.4 1.4–1.6
Heavy shock 1.3–1.5 1.5–1.8
  • Centrifugal tension: Fc = Kc(V/2.4)² with V in m/s; Fc = Kc(V/1000)² with V in ft/min (17-21). Kc is from Table 17-16 [MD-3 p.18].
  • Tension difference: ΔF = 63 025(Hd/Nb)/[n(d/2)] (17-22). ΔF in lbf, Hd in hp, n in rpm, d in in [MD-3 p.18].
  • F1 = Fc + ΔF exp(fφ)/[exp(fφ) − 1] (17-23) [MD-3 p.18].
  • F2 = F1 − ΔF (17-24); Fi = (F1 + F2)/2 − Fc (17-25) [MD-3 p.19].
  • Factor of safety: nfs = Ha Nb/(Hnom Ks) (17-26) [MD-3 p.21].

3.4 Belt life (passes)

  • Bending induces flexural stresses in the belt [MD-3 p.22–23].
  • Number of passes: Np = [(K/T1)^−b + (K/T2)^−b]^−1 (17-27) [MD-3 p.22–23].
  • Peak tensions: T1 = F1 + (Fb)1 = F1 + Kb/d; T2 = F1 + (Fb)2 = F1 + Kb/D [MD-3 p.22–23].
  • Life in hours: t = Np Lp/(720 V) (17-28), with Lp in in and V in ft/min [MD-3 p.23].

3.5 V-belt design procedure (the chain used in Example 17-4) [MD-3 p.9, p.15–21, p.25–29]

  1. Find Lp: inside circumference plus the Table 17-11 addition.
  2. Find C from Eq (17-16b).
  3. Find φ = θd from Eq (17-1).
  4. Find Htab from Table 17-12, interpolating in speed.
  5. Find K1 (Table 17-13) and K2 (Table 17-14); Ha = K1 K2 Htab.
  6. Hd = Hnom Ks nd; Nb ≥ Hd/Ha.
  7. Tensions: Fc (Kc), ΔF, F1, F2, Fi.
  8. nfs from Eq (17-26).
  9. Life: T1, T2, Np, t.

3.6 Worked example 17-4 [MD-3 p.25–29]

  • Data [p.25]:
    • 7.46 kW split-phase motor at 1750 rpm driving a rotary pump, 24 h/day.
    • d = 188 mm, D = 280 mm; three B2800 belts.
    • Ks = 1.2, plus 0.1 for continuous duty.
  • Geometry and power rating [p.26–27]:
    • V = 17 m/s; Lp = 2800 + 45 = 2845 mm; C = 1054 mm; φ = 3.054 rad; exp(0.5123 × 3.054) = 4.781.
    • Htab: interpolating 3.35 kW (15 m/s) and 3.74 kW (20 m/s) at 17 m/s gives 3.506 kW per belt (3.5 kW).
    • Wrap angle 175°, so K1 = 0.99; K2 = 1.05; Ha = 3.64 kW.
    • Hd = 7.46(1.2 + 0.1)(1) = 9.7 kW; Nb ≥ 2.67, so 3 belts.
  • Tensions and factor of safety [p.27–28]:
    • Kc = 0.965 → Fc = 0.965(17/2.4)² = 48.4 N.
    • ΔF = (9700/3)/[π(1750/60)(0.188)] = 188 N.
    • F1 = 286 N; F2 = 286 − 188 = 98 N; Fi = (286 + 98)/2 − 48.4 = 144 N.
    • nfs = 3.64(3)/[7.46(1.3)] = 1.13.
  • Life [p.28–29]:
    • Kb = 576 lbf·in ≈ 65 N·m → Fb1 = 65/0.188 = 346 N; Fb2 = 65/0.28 = 232 N.
    • T1 = 286 + 346 = 632 N; T2 = 286 + 232 = 518 N.
    • K = 5309, b = 10.926 → Np = 11(10⁹) passes.
    • This is outside the validity range of Eq (17-27), so life is reported as > 10⁹ passes: t > 10⁹(2.845)/[3600(17)] = 46 487 h.

3.7 Timing belts and roller chain (descriptive only)

  • Timing belts are made of rubberized fabric and steel wire. Their teeth fit into grooves on the sprockets (Fig 17-15) [MD-3 p.30].
  • A timing belt does not stretch or slip, so it transmits power at a constant angular-velocity ratio. It needs no initial tension, so fixed-center drives can be used [MD-3 p.30].
  • Timing belts remove the restriction on speed [MD-3 p.31].
  • Disadvantages: first cost, the need to groove the sprockets, and dynamic fluctuations at the belt-tooth meshing frequency [MD-3 p.31].
  • Roller chain (Fig 17-16: roller diameter, width, pitch p, strand spacing) and chain–sprocket engagement (Fig 17-17) are shown as pictures only [MD-3 p.32–33].
  • Sheet problems: Shigley 17-18, 17-19, 17-20 [MD-3 p.33]. 17-18 and 17-19 are solved in [MD-S2] (3.8 below).

  • Sheet problem P17-18 [MD-S2 p.7–9]:
    • Statement: two B85 V belts drive a 5.4 in driving sheave at 1200 rpm and a 16 in driven sheave. Find the power capacity based on a service factor of 1.25, and the center distance [p.7].
    • Given: Nb = 2, B85, d = 5.4 in, D = 16 in, n = 1200 rpm, Ks = 1.25; required Hnom and C [p.7].
    • Table 17-11: Lp = 85 + 1.8 = 86.8 in. C = 0.25[A + √(A² − B)] with A = Lp − (π/2)(D + d) = 86.8 − (π/2)(16 + 5.4) = 53.185 and B = 2(D − d)² = 2(16 − 5.4)² = 224.72 → C = 26.05 in [p.7].
    • θd = 180° − 2 sin⁻¹[(16 − 5.4)/(2 × 26.05)] = 156.5°; (D − d)/C = 0.407 → K1 = 0.94 (Table 17-13); K2 = 1 (Table 17-14) [p.8].
    • V = π(1200)(5.4)/12 = 1696.46 ft/min; interpolating between 1000 ft/min (1.59) and 2000 ft/min (2.62) in Table 17-12: Htab = 2.31 hp/belt; Ha = 0.94(1)(2.31) = 2.17 hp/belt [p.8].
    • Assuming nfs = 1: 1 = 2.17 × 2/(Hnom × 1.25) → Hnom = 3.49 hp [p.9].
  • Sheet problem P17-19 [MD-S2 p.10–13]:
    • Statement: a 60 hp four-cylinder internal-combustion engine drives a medium-shock brick-making machine on two shifts per day. Two 26 in sheaves about 12 ft apart, sheave speed 400 rpm. Select a Gates Rubber V-belt arrangement, find the factor of safety, and estimate the life in passes and hours [p.10].
    • Given: Hnom = 60 hp, medium shock, D = d = 26 in, C = 12 ft, n = 400 rpm [p.10].
    • C = 144 in: Lp = 2(144) + π(26 + 26)/2 + 0 = 369.68 in. Choosing a D360 belt: Lp,new = 360 + 3.3 = 363.3 in (Table 17-11) [p.10].
    • A = 363.3 − (π/2)(2 × 26) = 281.62 in; B = 2(D − d)² = 0 → C = 0.25[281.62 × 2] = 140.8 in [p.10–11].
    • θd = 180°, (D − d)/C = 0 → K1 = 1; K2 = 1.1 (Table 17-14) [p.11].
    • V = π(400)(26)/12 = 2722.7 ft/min; interpolating D, 17.0 in and up, between 2000 (13.9) and 3000 ft/min (18.1): Htab = 16.94 hp/belt; Ha = 1(1.1)(16.94) = 18.63 hp/belt [p.11].
    • Table 17-15: Ks = 1.4; Hd = 60(1.4)(1) = 84 hp; Nb = 84/18.63 = 4.51 → 5 belts [p.11–12].
    • nfs = 18.63(5)/(60 × 1.4) = 1.109 [p.12].
    • ΔF = 63 025(84/5)/(400 × 13) = 203.62 lbf/belt; Kc = 3.498 → Fc = 3.498(2722.7/1000)² = 25.9 lbf/belt [p.12].
    • exp(0.5123π) = 5; F1 = 25.9 + 203.62(5)/(5 − 1) = 280.425 lbf/belt; F2 = 280.425 − 203.62 = 76.805 lbf/belt; Fi = 152.715 lbf/belt [p.12].
    • T1 = T2 = F1 + Kb/d (as d = D); Kb = 5680 → T1 = T2 = 280.425 + 5680/26 = 498.9 lbf [p.13].
    • K = 4208, b = 11.105 (Table 17-17): Np = [2(4208/498.9)^−11.105]^−1 = 9.6(10⁹) passes [p.13].
    • t = 10⁹(363.3)/(720 × 2722.7) = 185 324.6 h (Np capped at 10⁹) [p.13].
  • Problem 17-20 (listed in [MD-3 p.33]) is not solved in the section handout.

3.9 Sheet 2: V-belt and flat-belt problems (Shigley 17-15 to 17-24) [MD-SH2]

The file is a screenshot of Shigley problems 17-15 to 17-24 (the top line is the end of 17-14, "… stainless steel belt."); statements only [MD-SH2 p.1]. Short statements:

  • 17-15: beryllium-copper metal flat belt, Sf = 56.67 kpsi, transmits 5 hp at 1125 rev/min with a life goal of 10⁶ belt passes; shafts 20 in apart, centerlines horizontal; f = 0.32; Ks = 1.25, design factor 1.1; driven shaft at one-third of the motor-pulley speed. Specify the belt, pulley sizes and initial tension at installation.
  • 17-16: for the conditions of 17-15 use a 1095 plain carbon-steel heat-treated belt; the driving pulley hub requires a pulley outside diameter of 3 in or more. Specify belt, pulley sizes and initial tension.
  • 17-17: a single Gates Rubber V belt delivers engine power to the wheel-drive transmission of a riding tractor; 5 hp single-cylinder engine, at most 60% of this power transmitted to the belt; driving sheave 6.2 in, driven 12.0 in; belt as close to a 92 in pitch length as possible; engine governed to a maximum of 3100 rev/min. Select a belt and assess the factor of safety and the belt life in passes.
  • 17-18: two B85 V belts, 5.4 in driving sheave at 1200 rev/min, 16 in driven sheave; power capacity for Ks = 1.25, and the center distance. Solved in [MD-S2 p.7–9] (2.8): C = 26.05 in, Ha = 2.17 hp/belt, Hnom = 3.49 hp.
  • 17-19: 60 hp four-cylinder IC engine, medium-shock brick-making machine, two shifts per day; two 26 in sheaves about 12 ft apart at 400 rev/min. Select a Gates Rubber V-belt arrangement, find the factor of safety and the life in passes and hours. Solved in [MD-S2 p.10–13] (2.8): five D360 belts, nfs = 1.109, Np = 9.6(10⁹) passes (report 10⁹), t = 185 324.6 h.
  • 17-20: reciprocating air compressor with a 5 ft diameter flywheel 14 in wide at 170 rev/min; eight-pole squirrel-cage induction motor, nameplate 50 bhp at 875 rev/min. (a) Design a Gates Rubber V-belt drive from the motor to the compressor flywheel. (b) Can cutting V-belt grooves in the flywheel be avoided by using a V-flat drive?
  • 17-21: geometry of a V-flat drive: (a) if the earth's equator were an inextensible string snug to a spherical earth and 6 ft of string were spliced in and arranged concentric to the equator, how far off the ground is the string? (b) Using this, formulate the modifications to mG, φd, φD, Lp and C for a V-flat drive. (c) How would you revise part (b) of Problem 17-20?
  • 17-22: 2 hp electric motor at 1720 rev/min drives a blower at 240 rev/min. Select a V-belt drive, specify standard V belts, sheave sizes and the center distance; the motor size limits the center distance to at least 22 in.
  • 17-23: the standard roller-chain number gives pitch, proportions, series and strands, e.g., 100H-2: pitch 10/8 in, standard proportions, heavy series, two strands. In Example 17-5, ascertain the pitch from the selected chain number and confirm from Table 17-19.
  • 17-24: equate Eqs (17-32) and (17-33) to find the rotating speed n1 at which the power equates and marks the division between the premaximum and postmaximum power domains; (a) show that n1 = [0.25(10⁶)Kr N1^0.42/p^(2.2−0.07p)]^(1/2.4) (the rest is cut off).

4.1 Types and nomenclature

  • Types shown: spur, helical, rack and pinion, bevel, miter, worm and worm gear, screw gears, internal gears (Figs 13-1 to 13-4) [MD-4 p.2–4].
  • Fig 13-5 nomenclature: top land, face width, addendum circle, face, flank, circular pitch, tooth thickness, width of space, pitch circle, addendum, dedendum, clearance, fillet radius, dedendum circle, clearance circle, bottom land [MD-4 p.5].
  • Diametral pitch P = N/d (13-1): teeth per inch of pitch diameter [MD-4 p.6].
  • Module m = d/N (13-2), mm [MD-4 p.6].
  • Circular pitch p = πd/N = πm (13-3); pP = π (13-4) [MD-4 p.6].

  • Table 13-2, tooth sizes in general use. Cutters are generally available for these sizes [MD-4 p.8]:
    • Diametral pitch, coarse: 2, 2¼, 2½, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16.
    • Diametral pitch, fine: 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80, 96, 120, 150, 200.
    • Module, preferred: 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 25, 32, 40, 50.
    • Module, next choice: 1.125, 1.375, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75, 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 22, 28, 36, 45.
  • Table 13-4, standard helical-gear dimensions (in, deg) [MD-4 p.9]:
    • addendum 1.00/Pn; dedendum 1.25/Pn;
    • pinion pitch diameter NP/(Pn cos ψ); gear pitch diameter NG/(Pn cos ψ);
    • normal arc tooth thickness π/Pn − Bn/2 (Bn = normal backlash) (⚠ F20);
    • base diameters: pinion d cos φt, gear D cos φt;
    • base helix angle tan⁻¹(tan ψ cos φt);
    • external gears: center distance (D + d)/2; outside diameters D + 2a and d + 2a; root diameters D − 2b and d − 2b;
    • internal gears: center distance (D − d)/2; inside diameter D − 2a; root diameter D + 2b.
  • Table 13-3, 20° straight bevel gears [MD-4 p.10]:
    • working depth hk = 2.0/P; clearance c = (0.188/P) + 0.002 in;
    • gear addendum aG = 0.54/P + 0.460/[P(m90)²]; gear ratio mG = NG/NP;
    • equivalent 90° ratio: m90 = mG when Γ = 90°; m90 = √(mG cos γ/cos Γ) when Γ ≠ 90°;
    • face width F = 0.3A0 or F = 10/P, whichever is smaller (A0 = cone distance);
    • minimum numbers of teeth (pinion/gear): 16/16, 15/17, 14/20, 13/30.
  • Common pressure angles are 20° and 25°; the old standard was 14.5° [MD-4 p.11].
  • Face width: 3p < F < 5p, i.e., 3π/P < F < 5π/P [MD-4 p.11].

4.2 Action, contact ratio, interference

  • Line cd is the pressure line (generating line, line of action). It gives the direction of the resultant force between the gears [MD-4 p.12].
  • Layout: draw the pitch circles in contact, then the pressure line at the desired pressure angle, then the base circles tangent to the pressure line [MD-4 p.13].
  • Base radius: rb = r cos φ (13-6) [MD-4 p.14].
  • First contact (point a) is where the pinion flank touches the gear tip. Last contact (point b) is where the pinion tip touches the gear flank. ab is the line of action; the angle of action is the angle of approach plus the angle of recess [MD-4 p.15].
  • A rack is a spur gear of infinite pitch diameter; its sides are straight lines at the pressure angle to the line of centers. Base pitch pb = pc cos φ (13-7) [MD-4 p.16].
  • Arc of action qt = qa + qr [MD-4 p.20].
  • Contact ratio mc = qt/p (13-8): the average number of pairs of teeth in contact [MD-4 p.20].
  • mc = Lab/(p cos φ) (13-9). It should be at least 1.2 (mounting inaccuracies, impact, noise) [MD-4 p.21].
  • Interference is contact of non-conjugate portions; it occurs when contact falls below the base circle. The generating process removes the interfering portion (undercutting) [MD-4 p.22].
  • Smallest pinion for a one-to-one ratio: NP = [2k/(3 sin²φ)](1 + √(1 + 3 sin²φ)) (13-10). k = 1 for full depth, 0.8 for stub [MD-4 p.23].
  • Smallest pinion for ratio mG = NG/NP = m: NP = {2k/[(1 + 2m) sin²φ]}(m + √(m² + (1 + 2m) sin²φ)) (13-11) [MD-4 p.23].
  • Largest gear with a given pinion: NG = (NP² sin²φ − 4k²)/(4k − 2NP sin²φ) (13-12) [MD-4 p.24].
  • Smallest pinion that runs with a rack: NP = 2k/sin²φ (13-13) [MD-4 p.24].

Interference limits (full depth) [MD-4 p.25–26]

4.3 Bevel and helical geometry

  • Straight bevel gears transmit motion between intersecting shafts (Fig 13-3) [MD-4 p.27].
  • Pitch angles: tan γ = NP/NG, tan Γ = NG/NP (13-14). Fig 13-20 shows the cone distance A0, face F, back cone, back-cone radius rb and pitch diameter DG [MD-4 p.28].
  • Helical teeth are cut at the helix angle to the axis. They add an axial force on the shaft and bearings, and engage gradually, giving a smoother transition [MD-4 p.29].
  • ψ = helix angle; the normal pressure angle φn differs from the transverse pressure angle φt [MD-4 p.30].
  • pt = transverse circular pitch (plane of rotation) [MD-4 p.31].
  • pn = pt cos ψ (13-16); px = pt/tan ψ (13-17); Pn = Pt/cos ψ (13-18); pn Pn = π [MD-4 p.31].
  • cos ψ = tan φn/tan φt (13-19) [MD-4 p.32].
  • Helical, smallest pinion for 1:1: NP = [2k cos ψ/(3 sin²φt)](1 + √(1 + 3 sin²φt)) (13-21) [MD-4 p.36].
  • Helical, ratio m: NP = {2k cos ψ/[(1 + 2m) sin²φt]}[m + √(m² + (1 + 2m) sin²φt)] (13-22) [MD-4 p.36].
  • Helical, largest gear: NG = (NP² sin²φt − 4k² cos²ψ)/(4k cos ψ − 2NP sin²φt) (13-23) [MD-4 p.37].
  • Helical, smallest pinion with a rack: NP = 2k cos ψ/sin²φt (13-24) [MD-4 p.37].

4.4 Gear trains

  • n3 = |N2/N3| n2 = |d2/d3| n2 (13-29), n in rev or rpm [MD-4 p.38].
  • For the train of Fig 13-27: n6 = −(N2 N3 N5)/(N3 N4 N6) n2 [MD-4 p.39].
  • Train value e = (product of driving tooth numbers)/(product of driven tooth numbers) (13-30); nL = e nF (13-31) [MD-4 p.39].
  • Rough guide: one pair gives up to 10:1. Beyond that, compound two gears on the same shaft (Fig 13-28) [MD-4 p.40].

4.5 Worked examples [MD-4]

  • Ex 13-1 [p.18–19]:
    • 16T pinion, 40T gear, P = 2, a = 1/P, b = 1.25/P, φ = 20°.
    • p = π/2 = 1.571 in; dP = 8 in, dG = 20 in; C = 14 in.
    • Base radii: pinion 3.759 in, gear 9.397 in.
    • With C increased by ¼ in: dP′ = 8.143 in, dG′ = 20.357 in; φ′ = cos⁻¹[3.759/(8.143/2)] = 22.59°.
  • Ex 13-2 [p.33]:
    • Stock helical gear: φn = 20°, ψ = 25°, Pt = 6 teeth/in, 18T.
    • d = 3 in; pt = 0.5236 in; pn = 0.4745 in; px = 1.123 in; Pn = 6.620 teeth/in; φt = 21.88°.
  • Helical pinion 17T driving 34T [p.34–35] (⚠ F11 on the example labels):
    • RH, ψ = 30°, φn = 20°, Pn = 5.
    • pn = 0.6283 in; pt = 0.7255 in; px = 1.25 in; pnb = 0.590 in; Pt = 4.33.
    • φt = 22.8°; a = 0.200 in; b = 0.250 in; dP = 3.926 in; dG = 7.852 in.
  • Two-stage 30:1 (±1%) train [p.41–42]:
    • Each stage √30 = 5.4772; minimum pinion 16T by Eq (13-11) at 20°; 16√30 = 87.64 ≈ 88; e = (88/16)² = 30.25, within 1%.
    • Exact 30:1: e = (6)(5); N3 = N5 = 16 → N2 = 96, N4 = 80; e = (96/16)(80/16) = 30.
