About these notes

Every line is taken from the source named in its tag. Page numbers are PDF page numbers (for [MC-MID] the number of the captured image cap/mcmid-NNN.jpg); the slide decks have no printed page numbers. Nothing is added from memory. Where the sources say nothing, the notes say so (see "Not covered by the sources"). Suspected source errors are not corrected in place; they are listed under ⚠ Flags. Several worked examples are copied from textbooks and keep their equation, table and example numbers ("Equation 2.6", "Table 2.1", "Example 2.3/2.7/2.9", "Table 21.2", "Example 9.1"); those numbers refer to the books, not to the lecture slides. Where two sources contain the same fact, the tags are joined in one line; where they differ in numbers or method, both versions are kept and marked.

Layout: 1 fundamentals; 2 chip formation; 3 tool geometry; 4 forces, Merchant, power; 5 operations and machine tools (turning, facing, drilling, milling, other machines); 6 cutting temperature; 7 tool wear and tool life; 8 tool materials, surface finish, economics (coverage note); 9 exam and oral questions. Then Calculator candidates, ⚠ Flags and Worked-example checks.

Fundamentals of machining

In this section (5)
  1. 1.1 Manufacturing and material-removal processes
  2. 1.2 What machining is and why it is used
  3. 1.3 Cutting conditions, roughing and finishing
  4. 1.4 Part geometry and how operations produce it
  5. 1.5 Single-point and multi-point tools

1.1 Manufacturing and material-removal processes

  • Manufacturing, technically: the application of physical, chemical and/or assembly processes to alter the geometry, properties and/or appearance of a starting material to produce the final parts or product. Economically: the transformation of materials into items of greater value by one or more processing operations (figure: starting material → manufacturing process → processed part, with machinery, tooling, power, labor inputs and scrap/waste; value added $ → $$$) [MC-G1 p.1].
  • Contents of the course: (1) theory of metal machining, (2) machining operations and machine tools, (3) cutting tool technology [MC-G1 p.1].
  • Material removal processes: a family of shaping operations whose common feature is removal of material from a starting workpart so that the remaining part has the desired geometry (Fig. 1.1) [MC-G1 p.1]:
    • machining: a sharp cutting tool (turning, milling, drilling, shaping, planing, broaching, sawing);
    • abrasive processes: hard abrasive particles (grinding, honing, lapping, super-finishing);
    • non-traditional processes: other energy forms — mechanical, electrochemical, thermal, chemical. Some mechanical non-traditional processes use abrasive particles and so overlap with abrasive processes.
    • Fig. 1.1 tree: conventional machining (turning and related, drilling and related, milling, other); abrasive (grinding operations, other abrasive); non-traditional (mechanical energy, electrochemical machining, thermal energy, chemical machining).
  • Chapter contents: 21.1 overview; 21.2 chip formation (21.2.1 orthogonal model, 21.2.2 actual chip formation); 21.3 forces and Merchant equation; 21.4 power and energy; 21.5 cutting temperature (21.5.1 analytical methods, 21.5.2 measurement) [MC-G12 p.2].
  • Conventional machining is the most important branch of material removal; the three principal processes are turning, drilling and milling; "other machining operations" are shaping, planing, broaching, sawing; "other abrasive processes" are honing, lapping, superfinishing [MC-G12 pp.3–4].
  • Contents of CH 22: machining and part geometry; turning and related operations (cutting conditions, related operations, engine lathe, other lathes, boring machines); drilling (cutting conditions, related operations, drill presses); milling (types, cutting conditions, machines); machining and turning centers; other operations (shaping and planing, broaching, sawing); special geometries (screw threads, gears, high-speed machining) [MC-G31 p.2].

1.2 What machining is and why it is used

  • Machining: a sharp cutting tool cuts away material to leave the desired shape; the cutting action is shear deformation of the work to form a chip; removing the chip exposes a new surface (Fig. 1.2: (a) positive rake, chip, rake face, flank, shear deformation; (b) negative rake angle, relief angle) [MC-G1 p.2].
  • Advantages [MC-G1 p.2; MC-G12 pp.5–7; MC-Q p.2]: (i) wide variety of work materials — virtually all solid metals, plastics and plastic composites (ceramics are difficult because of hardness and brittleness, but most can be cut by abrasive machining); (ii) any regular geometry (flat planes, round holes, cylinders) and, by varying tool shape and path, irregular ones (screw threads, T-slots); (iii) close tolerances, some processes ± 0.025 mm; (iv) very smooth finishes, roughness below 0.4 µm in conventional machining, better by some abrasive processes.
  • Disadvantages [MC-G1 p.2; MC-G12 p.8; MC-Q p.2]: (i) wasteful of material (chips, recyclable but waste for the unit operation); (ii) takes more time than casting or forging; (iii) high cost of machines, power and labour.
  • Reasons machining is important: variety of work materials, variety of part shapes and geometric features (combining operations in sequence gives shapes of almost unlimited complexity), dimensional accuracy (0.025 mm), good surface finish (< 0.4 µm) [MC-G12 pp.5–7]. Disadvantages: wasteful of material, time consuming (vs casting or forging, حدادة) [MC-G12 p.8].
  • Machining generally follows casting or bulk deformation (forging, bar drawing), which create the general shape; machining gives final geometry, dimensions and finish [MC-G1 p.2].
  • A primary relative motion (cutting speed) and a secondary motion (feed) are required; tool shape and penetration plus these motions produce the surface [MC-G1 p.2].
  • Machine tool: holds the workpart, positions the tool relative to the work, and provides power at the set speed, feed and depth; applies to any power-driven machine performing machining (including grinding), and also to metal-forming and press-working machines. Lathes, drill presses and milling machines perform turning, drilling and milling; conventional machines are tended by an operator; many modern ones use CNC [MC-G1 pp.2–3].
  • Common features of machining: (1) a cutting tool forms a chip removed from the workpart; (2) relative motion — primary motion (cutting speed) and secondary motion (feed) [MC-G12 p.10].
  • By controlling tool, work and cutting conditions, machine tools make parts with great accuracy and repeatability [MC-G12 p.17].

1.3 Cutting conditions, roughing and finishing

  • Cutting conditions: cutting speed v (primary motion), feed f (slower lateral motion), depth of cut d (penetration below the original surface) — "the three dimensions of the machining process" [MC-G1 p.4].
  • Roughing cuts remove large amounts quickly, leaving material for finishing; finishing cuts achieve final dimensions, tolerances and finish. Usually one or more roughing cuts then one or two finishing cuts. Roughing: high feeds and depths; finishing: low feeds and depths; cutting speeds are lower in roughing than in finishing [MC-G1 p.4].
  • A cutting fluid is often applied to cool and lubricate; its choice is usually within the scope of cutting conditions [MC-G1 p.4].
  • Material removal rate R_MR = v·f·d (printed unit "mm/min3", ⚠ F26) [MC-G12 p.15].

1.4 Part geometry and how operations produce it

  • Machining is the most versatile and accurate of all manufacturing processes in producing diverse geometries and features; casting also gives a variety of shapes but lacks precision and accuracy [MC-G31 p.3].
  • Rotational parts (cylindrical or disk-like; e.g. turning, boring; drilling is closely related but makes an internal cylinder with a rotating tool) vs non-rotational (prismatic, block- or plate-like; linear work motions combined with rotating or linear tool motions; milling, shaping, planing, sawing) [MC-G31 p.4].
  • Each operation's geometry comes from (1) the relative motions between tool and work and (2) the tool shape [MC-G31 p.5].
  • Generating: geometry determined by the feed trajectory of the tool — straight, taper and contour turning, peripheral (plain) milling, profile milling (Fig. 22.2) [MC-G31 pp.5–6]. Forming: shape created by the tool geometry, the cutting edge having the reverse of the shape — form turning, drilling, broaching (Fig. 22.3) [MC-G31 p.7]. Combined forming and generating: thread cutting on a lathe, slot milling with a T-slot cutter (Fig. 22.4) [MC-G31 p.8].
  • Copying process: the shape of the work-piece depends on the tool shape. Generation process: the shape depends on the relative motion between tool and work-piece [MC-Q p.1].

1.5 Single-point and multi-point tools

  • Single-point vs multi-point tools [MC-G1 p.4]:
Single point Multi point
one main cutting edge, continuously in contact with the work more than one (up to hundreds) edges; two-edged cutters are usually also counted as multi-point
e.g. turning, shaping, planing, slotting, boring tools e.g. milling cutters, drills, reamers, saws
edge prepared by grinding —
low MRR and productivity high MRR and productivity
simple design and fabrication, comparatively low cost complicated design and fabrication, comparatively high cost

Chip formation and orthogonal cutting

In this section (3)
  1. 2.1 The orthogonal cutting model
  2. 2.2 Actual chip formation and chip types
  3. 2.3 Chip thickness ratio, shear angle and shear strain

2.1 The orthogonal cutting model

  • Orthogonal cutting model: a wedge-shaped tool whose cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting-speed direction; the chip forms by shear along the shear plane at angle φ to the work surface; material fails only at the sharp edge; the bulk of the energy is consumed in the shear plane (Fig. 1.5: 3-D and 2-D side view with t0, tc, w, ls, α, φ) [MC-G1 pp.4–5].
  • The rake angle α determines the chip flow direction; the clearance angle gives clearance between flank and new surface [MC-G1 p.5].
  • Orthogonal model: a simplified model neglecting many geometric complexities; only two dimensions play active roles (Fig. 21.6) [MC-G12 p.19].
  • Orthogonal vs oblique cutting, bullets [MC-G12 p.18] (figure: orthogonal and oblique cutting geometry with chip flow angle η and cutting-edge inclination angle):
    • orthogonal: edge at right angle to the feed direction; oblique: edge inclined to it;
    • orthogonal: only two mutually perpendicular force components (cutting and thrust); oblique: three (thrust, radial, cutting);
    • a tool cutting orthogonally has a shorter life than one cutting obliquely;
    • orthogonal cutting has a high heat concentration at the cutting region; oblique cutting less.
  • Comparison table [MC-G12 p.48]:
Orthogonal metal cutting Oblique metal cutting
Cutting edge perpendicular to the direction of tool travel Edge inclined at an angle less than 90° to the direction of tool travel
Chip flows perpendicular to the cutting edge Chip flows on the tool face making an angle
Chip coils in a tight flat spiral Chip flows sideways in a long curl
For the same feed and depth, the shearing force acts on a smaller area, so tool life is less Cutting force acts on a larger area, so tool life is more
Produces sharp corners Produces a chamfer at the end of the cut
Smaller length of cutting edge in contact with the work For the same depth of cut, greater length of edge in contact
Generally parting-off on the lathe, broaching and slotting Used in almost all machining operations

2.2 Actual chip formation and chip types

  • Chip formation depends on the work material and cutting conditions. Fig. 21.8: a more realistic view shows a primary shear zone (not a plane), an "effective φ", and a secondary shear zone from tool–chip friction [MC-G12 p.21].
  • Four chip types [MC-G12 pp.22–24]:
    • Discontinuous: relatively brittle materials (e.g. cast irons) at low cutting speeds; separate (sometimes loosely attached) segments; irregular texture on the surface; promoted (يعزز) by high tool–chip friction and large feed and depth.
    • Continuous: ductile materials at high speeds and relatively small feeds and depths; good surface finish; encouraged by a sharp edge and low tool–chip friction; long chips (as in turning) cause disposal problems and tangling about the tool, so turning tools often have chip breakers.
    • Continuous with built-up edge (BUE): ductile materials at low-to-medium speeds; friction makes work material adhere to the rake face near the edge; BUE formation is cyclical (forms, grows, becomes unstable, breaks off); detached BUE carried away with the chip sometimes takes portions of the rake face (reduces tool life); BUE not carried off becomes embedded in the new surface, making it rough.
    • Serrated: semi-continuous, saw-tooth appearance from cyclic alternating high and low shear strain; associated with difficult-to-machine metals (titanium alloys, nickel-base superalloys, austenitic stainless steels) at higher speeds, and also with steels at high speeds.
  • The shorter chip-type list of [MC-Q p.1] (three types, with work-material examples and surface notes):
    • continuous chip, from ductile materials (e.g. Al, Cu, mild steel);
    • discontinuous chip, from cast iron and cast brass;
    • continuous chip with built-up edge.
    • The figure notes an irregular surface for discontinuous chips, BUE particles on the new surface, and "good finish typical" for continuous chips.

2.3 Chip thickness ratio, shear angle and shear strain

  • Chip thickness ratio r = t0/tc < 1 [MC-G1 p.5].
  • With shear-plane length ls: t0 = ls sin φ, tc = ls cos(φ − α) ⇒ r = sin φ / cos(φ − α) ⇒ tan φ = r cos α / (1 − r sin α) [MC-G1 p.5].
  • Shear strain γ = tan(φ − α) + cot φ [MC-G1 p.5].
  • Example 1.1: α = 10°, t0 = 0.50 mm, tc = 1.125 mm → r = 0.444, tan φ = 0.4738, φ = 25.4°, γ = tan(15.4°) + cot 25.4° = 2.386 (⚠ F23) [MC-G1 p.5].
  • Example 1 (US units): tool width 0.250 in, α = 5°, t0 = 0.010 in, tc = 0.027 in → r = 0.3701; φ = tan⁻¹(0.3701 cos 5/(1 − 0.3701 sin 5)) = tan⁻¹(0.3813) = 20.9°; γ = cot 20.9 + tan(20.9 − 5) = 2.623 + 0.284 = 2.907 [MC-G12 p.40].
  • Cutting ratio: r_cu = a1/a2 < 1, where a1 is the uncut chip thickness and a2 the chip thickness (a2 > a1) [MC-1 p.16].
    • Lamellar shearing and positive strain make the chip thicker than the uncut chip, especially in conventional macro-scale cutting [MC-1 p.16].
    • r_cu is unitless (a ratio of two lengths) [MC-1 p.18].
  • The exam question on the orthogonal model and the same numbers as Example 1.1 are in §9.3 [MC-GQD pp.1–2].

Single-point cutting tool geometry

In this section (5)
  1. 3.1 Cutting angles
  2. 3.2 The single-point tool: surfaces, edges and angles
  3. 3.3 Recommended angles
  4. 3.4 Lathe set-up: centre height, clearance and relief
  5. 3.5 Side cutting edge (lead) angle: effects and tool life

3.1 Cutting angles

  • Three main cutting angles: clearance, rake, wedge (Fig. 1.4: rough/shiny chip surfaces, tool face, flank, relief/clearance angle, shear plane, shear angle, t0, tc, V) [MC-G1 p.3]. Definitions [MC-G1 p.4]:
    • clearance angle: between the flank face (bottom face) of the tool and the tangent to the work at the cutting edge; protects the surface from abrasion that would degrade the finish;
    • rake angle: between the top face of the tool and the normal to the work at the cutting edge; "improves the cutting process and reduce chip formation" (as printed);
    • wedge angle: between the flank face and the top face.
  • Cutting tool: one or more sharp edges; made of a material harder than the work. The rake face directs chip flow and is oriented at the rake angle, measured from a plane perpendicular to the work surface; it can be positive or negative. The flank gives clearance to the new surface and is oriented at the relief angle [MC-G12 p.14].

3.2 The single-point tool: surfaces, edges and angles

  • Geometry, orientation and material of the tool are the three factors that determine the economy and performance of machining (machinability) [MC-1 p.4].
  • Tool geometry consists of rake angles, clearance angles, auxiliary clearance angles, cutting angles and the nose radius [MC-1 p.4].
  • The three important surfaces of a single-point turning tool (SPTT) [MC-1 p.4]:
    • the rake surface, over which the chip flows;
    • the principal flank, which contacts the machined surface over a small length;
    • the auxiliary flank, which in some operations also contacts the finished surface.
  • The principal cutting edge is the line where the rake surface meets the principal flank [MC-1 p.5].
  • Tool designation systems named: ASA; ORS (the old ISO system); NRS (the new ISO system); and MRS (maximum rake system). The systems use different names for the cutting-edge angles [MC-1 p.5].
  • The principal cutting edge angle (PCEA, Φ) is the angle between the cutting plane π_C and the longitudinal feed direction, measured in the reference plane π_R. ORS and NRS both use it [MC-1 p.6; MC-MID p.1].
  • Usual ranges: 45° ≤ φ ≤ 90°. The auxiliary cutting edge angle φ1 is usually 10° ≤ φ1 ≤ 20° [MC-1 p.6].
  • The PCEA figure labels the unmachined, transient and machined surfaces, the chuck, the feed and N [MC-1 p.6].
  • Labels on the tool figures: face, cutting edge, flank, nose radius, side-rake angle + (SR), back-rake angle + (BR), side-relief angle, end-cutting edge angle (ECEA), side-cutting edge angle (SCEA), and clearance or end-relief angle [MC-1 p.2, p.3].
  • Lead angle, definition 1: the angle between the side cutting edge and a plane perpendicular to the direction of feed travel [MC-1 p.11; MC-MID p.2].
  • Lead angle, definition 2: an angular dimension measured parallel to the cutting edge of the tool and to the face of the part being produced [MC-1 p.11].
  • The figure's labels include "Lead angle equal to side cutting angle", plus back relief angle, side flank angle, true rake angle, cutting edge inclination (−), main cutting edge, end cutting edge angle and corner radius [MC-1 p.11].
  • In milling, the lead angle is the angle between the insert's cutting edge and a line perpendicular to the feed direction (typically parallel to the spindle axis). The cutting edge angle is the angle between the cutting edge and the face of the part being produced [MC-3 p.10].
  • p.1 Principal cutting edge angle (PCEA) φ: the angle between the cutting plane (containing the principal cutting edge) and the longitudinal feed direction. Sketch labels: unmachined/unfinished surface, transient surface, machined/finished surface, work piece, chuck, feed, cutting tool; φ principal (side, main) cutting edge angle; φ1 auxiliary (end) cutting edge angle. The line of intersection between rake surface and principal flank surface is the principal cutting edge. Tool sketch: shank; rake surface = "the face on which the chip flows, used to separate the chip from the work piece"; principal (main, side) cutting edge = intersection line between face and flank; main (side) flank; end (auxiliary) cutting edge; end (aux.) flank; nose = junction of side and auxiliary cutting edges (with radius) [MC-MID p.1].
  • p.2 Lead angle: the angle between the side cutting edge and the plane perpendicular to the direction of feed travel; sketches of lead angle in a single-point tool; "lead angle equal the side cutting angle". Arabic note: anything related to the rake face is related to the chip (أي حاجة ليها علاقة بالـ Rake face يبقى ليها علاقة بالرايش) [MC-MID p.2].

3.3 Recommended angles

Recommended values [MC-1 p.2]:

Parameter Value
Nose radius As large as possible
Front relief (clearance) 4 to 8
Side relief (clearance) 6 to 10
Side rake, hard and/or abrasive work 2 to 10
Side rake, soft and/or gummy work 10 to 22
Back rake, hard/or abrasive work Negative to 0
Back rake, soft and/or gummy work 0 to 10 Positive
Material Top rake Side clearance
Aluminium 15°–20° 10°–15°
Brass 10°–12° 8°–10°
Mild steel 8°–10° 7°–9°
Stainless steel 6°–7° 6°–7°
Cast iron 7°–9° 7°–9°

3.4 Lathe set-up: centre height, clearance and relief

  • Setting up tools for facing: the cutting edge should be about 5° above the centre of the work piece, which equates to about 3/64 in. for each inch of work diameter [MC-GT p.1]. Two advantages of the point above centre: it prevents the tool digging into the material, and if the tool moves in the tool post it moves away from the work piece [MC-GT p.1].
  • Cutting angles for lathe set-up: two basic angles, (i) the front clearance angle and (ii) the tool's relief (side clearance) angle [MC-GT p.2].
    • The tool face is not vertical to the work; because the tool is typically 5° above the centre line, a vertical face would rub before cutting; the compensating angle is called the clearance angle [MC-GT p.2].
    • Metals are compressible: the tool first compresses the material, and once fully compressed further movement removes material. As the work rotates the compression is relieved and the OD grows; without clearance for this, the material rubs the tool face. The additional angle added to the clearance angle for this is called the relief angle [MC-GT pp.2–3].
    • During cutting: (i) the material is compressed, (ii) sheared by the tool, (iii) the compressed material springs back; "the angle required to compensate for this interference is called the front clearance angle" [MC-GT p.3] (⚠ F29).
    • Figures: material compresses / springs back; outside diameter, work surface, true rake angle, lip angle, cutting angle, clearance angle, centreline of work, finished surface [MC-GT pp.2–3]. Tool drawing: side rake angle, side clearance angle (section A-A), sharp point with 30° and 30°, back rake angle 16½°, front clearance angle; top, side and front views [MC-GT p.3].

3.5 Side cutting edge (lead) angle: effects and tool life

Effects of the side cutting edge angle (lead angle) [MC-1 p.12–13]:

  • At the same feed, a larger SCEA increases the chip contact length and decreases the chip thickness. The force is spread over a longer edge, so tool life is longer [MC-1 p.12; MC-MID pp.3–4].
  • A larger SCEA increases the force a′, so thin, long work-pieces can bend. It also decreases chip control, and gives thinner, wider chips that are hard to break [MC-1 p.12; MC-MID pp.3–4].
  • Chart values at the same feed f [MC-1 p.12; MC-MID p.3]:
    • kr = 0°: chip thickness h and width B;
    • kr = 15°: 0.97h and 1.04B;
    • kr = 30°: 0.87h and 1.15B.
  • Decrease the lead angle for: finishing with a small depth of cut; thin, long work-pieces; a machine with poor rigidity [MC-1 p.13; MC-MID p.5].
  • Increase the lead angle for: hard work-pieces that give high cutting temperature; roughing a large-diameter work-piece; a machine with high rigidity [MC-1 p.13; MC-MID p.5].
  • Force figure: with no lead angle the insert receives force A; with a lead angle, A is divided into a and a′ [MC-1 p.13].
  • Tool-life chart (a single chart; the Taylor tool-life treatment is in §7) [MC-1 p.13; MC-MID p.5]:
    • conditions: alloy steel, grade STi120, depth of cut 3 mm, feed 0.2 mm/rev, dry cutting;
    • tool life (min, log scale) against cutting speed (m/min, log scale);
    • the SCEA = 15° line lies above the SCEA = 0° line, i.e. longer life at the same speed.
  • pp.3–4 Effects of SCEA (lead angle): at the same feed, sketches for Kr = 0 (chip width B, thickness h), Kr = 15° (1.04B, 0.97h), Kr = 30° (1.15B, 0.87h). At the same feed rate, increasing SCEA increases chip contact length and decreases chip thickness; increasing SCEA increases the force, so thin long work pieces can suffer from bending; it decreases chip control; it decreases chip thickness and increases chip width, so breaking the chip is difficult (Arabic: a very thin, wide strip is hard to break; same with increased SCEA) [MC-MID pp.3–4].
  • p.5 Side cutting edge and tool life: decrease the lead angle for finishing with small depth of cut, thin long work pieces, machines with poor rigidity; increase it for hard work pieces producing high cutting temperature, roughing large-diameter work, machines with high rigidity. Arabic margin: a small lead angle keeps the cutting force low so thin work does not deflect and a non-rigid ("rigid = متين") machine does not vibrate; with a large depth of cut and hot, hard work the lead angle is raised. Chart: tool life (min) vs cutting speed 100–300 m/min, SCEA 15° line above SCEA 0° [MC-MID p.5].

Cutting forces, Merchant's circle and power

In this section (5)
  1. 4.1 Forces on the chip and the tool (orthogonal model, Merchant's circle)
  2. 4.2 Force components in turning (oblique and orthogonal systems)
  3. 4.3 Measured cutting forces (Kennametal test data)
  4. 4.4 Power, unit power and specific cutting energy
  5. 4.5 Forces on lathe slideways [MC-P]

4.1 Forces on the chip and the tool (orthogonal model, Merchant's circle)

  • Forces on the chip (Fig. 1.6a): from the tool, friction force F (resisting chip flow along the rake face) and normal force N; μ = F/N; resultant R at friction angle β, μ = tan β. From the work: shear force Fs and normal force Fn; resultant R′ equal, opposite and collinear with R [MC-G1 pp.5–6].
  • Shear stress τ = Fs/As, with As = t0·w / sin φ; τ equals the shear strength S of the work under cutting conditions [MC-G1 p.6].
  • F, N, Fs, Fn cannot be measured directly; a dynamometer measures the cutting force Fc (in the direction of v) and thrust force Ft (perpendicular, associated with t0), resultant R″ (Fig. 1.6b) [MC-G1 p.6].
  • p.32 Forces on the chip (sketch: shear plane, shear speed, chip speed, tool face, F, N, R, F_s, F_n, R′): the chip and tool face rub against each other, giving a friction force F opposite to the chip speed; N normal to the friction force; their resultant R. On the shear plane: F_s opposite to the shear motion, F_n normal to shear; resultant R′. R = R′ → F_n² + F_s² = F² + N²; Arabic: this is where the Merchant circle comes from [MC-MID p.32].
  • From the force diagram (Fig. 1.7, Merchant's circle) [MC-G1 p.6]:
    • F = Fc sin α + Ft cos α
    • N = Fc cos α − Ft sin α
    • Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ
    • Fn = Fc sin φ + Ft cos φ
    • Special case α = 0: F = Ft and N = Fc, so they can be measured directly.
  • Example 1.2 (shear stress): Fc = 1559 N, Ft = 1271 N, w = 3.0 mm, data of Ex. 1.1 → Fs = 1559 cos 25.4 − 1271 sin 25.4 = 863 N; As = 0.5 × 3.0 / sin 25.4 = 3.497 mm²; τ = 863/3.497 = 247 MPa [MC-G1 pp.6–7].
  • With Fs = S·As [MC-G1 p.7]:
    • Fc = S t0 w cos(β − α) / [sin φ cos(φ + β − α)] = Fs cos(β − α)/cos(φ + β − α)
    • Ft = S t0 w sin(β − α) / [sin φ cos(φ + β − α)] = Fs sin(β − α)/cos(φ + β − α) (the first form is printed "S_t * w", ⚠ F20)
  • Merchant equation: τ = (Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ)/(t0 w / sin φ). Shear occurs at the angle where the shear stress just equals the shear strength; the angle minimising energy is found by dS/dφ = 0, giving φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2. It assumes a constant shear strength unaffected by strain rate, temperature etc., so it is approximate [MC-G1 p.7].
  • Example 1.3 (friction angle): β = 2(45) + α − 2φ, printed "2 (45) + α − φ = 2 (25) + 10 − 2 (25.4) = 49.2°"; μ = tan 49.2 = 1.16 [MC-G1 p.7] (⚠ F21).
  • To increase φ: increase the rake angle (tool design) and decrease the friction angle (lubricant cutting fluid). A higher φ gives a smaller shear-plane area, so a lower shear force, lower cutting energy, lower power and lower cutting temperature — so φ should be as large as possible (Fig. 1.8) [MC-G1 p.8].
  • Figures: mc2-forces-on-chip.jpg (Fig. 1.6) and mc2-merchant-circle.jpg (Fig. 1.7) [MC-G1 p.6].

4.2 Force components in turning (oblique and orthogonal systems)

  • pp.28–31 Forces in metal cutting: topics (1) acting forces in oblique cutting, (2) acting forces in orthogonal cutting, (3) force relationships, (4) power induced while cutting [MC-MID p.28].
    • Oblique cutting system (القطع المائل) (sketch: turning, F_x, F_y, F_z, feed): F_x thrust (axial) force, opposite to the feed (Arabic: resistance of the work to the tool's movement); F_z cutting force, from the work's resistance to the cutting motion (rotation). Arabic: oblique because the tool angle φ lies between 0 and 90°; the φ angle produces a component along the main cutting edge, F_y [MC-MID p.28].
    • If the main edge is perpendicular (angle 90°) we get the orthogonal cutting system: F_y = 0 and only F_z and F_x remain. F_x axial force due to (feed) motion; F_y radial force due to edge inclination; F_z tangential force due to cutting motion (cutting force); R = √(F_x² + F_y² + F_z²) [MC-MID p.29].
    • Orthogonal (sketch): F_x = F_t axial (thrust) force; F_y = F_r = 0 (no edge inclination; edge at 90°); F_z = F_c tangential (cutting) force; R = √(F_x² + F_z²) = √(F_t² + F_c²). Arabic: this is the case we will work with; orthogonal cutting is a special case of oblique cutting [MC-MID p.30].
    • 2-D sketch (Arabic: if we draw it in 2-D): F_x = F_t (thrust) and F_z = F_c on the tool, and equal and opposite reactions on the work — two external forces between cutting tool and work during cutting; for static equilibrium ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_z = 0 [MC-MID p.31].
  • There are three components: tangential F_Z (the largest), feed F_Y (smaller) and radial F_X (the smallest) [MC-1 p.7].
  • A rule of thumb (a "theoretical assumption", not good practice): F_Y = 0.50 F_Z and F_X = 0.25 F_Z [MC-1 p.7].
  • Figure notation: F_c cutting, F_f feed, F_p passive, F_a active and R resultant force, with F_a = √(F_c² + F_f²) and R = √(F_c² + F_f² + F_p²) [MC-1 p.7].
  • Notation conflict: [MC-P p.6] calls P_z tangential and P_y radial, whereas [MC-1 p.7] makes Y the feed direction.

4.4 Power, unit power and specific cutting energy

  • Power: Pc = Fc·v (W; ft·lb/min in US units); hp_c = Fc·v/33,000. Gross power Pg = Pc/η, η typically about 90 % [MC-G1 p.8].
  • Unit power Pu = Pc/MRR, MRR = v·t0·w (mm³/s); also the specific energy U = Pu = Fc·v/(v t0 w) = Fc/(t0 w); units N·m/mm³ (J/mm³), reducible to N/mm² but better kept as N·m/mm³ [MC-G1 p.8].
  • Example 1.4: v = 100 m/min, t0 = 0.50 mm, w = 3.0 mm, Fc = 1557 N → Pc = 1557 × 100/60 = 2595 W; U = 1557/(0.5 × 3.0) = 1038 N/mm² = 1.038 N·m/mm³ [MC-G1 pp.8–9] (⚠ F22).
  • Table 1.1 assumes a sharp tool and t0 = 0.25 mm. Worn tools: multiply by 1.0–1.25 (sharp 1.0; finishing tool nearly worn out ≈ 1.10; roughing tool nearly worn out 1.25) [MC-G1 p.9].
  • Table 1.1 (unit horsepower and specific energy, sharp tools, t0 = 0.25 mm) [MC-G1 p.9; MC-U22 p.13]:

For t0 ≠ 0.25 mm multiply Table 1.1 values by the correction factor of Fig. 1.9 (factor falls from above 1.6 at very small t0, through about 1 near t0 ≈ 0.25–0.3 mm, to about 0.65 at 1.25 mm; mm axis 0.125–1.25, inch axis 0.005–0.050) [MC-G1 pp.9–10].
  • Rake angle, cutting speed and cutting fluid also matter: increasing rake angle or speed, or adding fluid, reduces U and HPu slightly [MC-G1 p.9].

4.5 Forces on lathe slideways [MC-P]

The file title says "orthogonal cutting", but its content is the slideway analysis (see Sources). Set-up (figure) [MC-P p.1]:

  • The carriage sits on a flat way (reaction C, vertical) and a V-way (reactions A and B, at angles α and β to the vertical). The ways are a distance b apart.
  • The work-piece centre is at height h above the ways. The cutting forces on the tool are P_z (vertical, downward) and P_y (horizontal). The carriage weight is G.
  • Equilibrium [MC-P p.1]:
    • (1) ΣF_y = 0: A sin α − B sin β + P_y = 0.
    • (2) ΣF_z = 0: A cos α + B cos β + C − P_z − G = 0.
    • ΣM_o = 0: A cos α·b/2 + B cos β·b/2 − C·b/2 ∓ P_z·d/2 − P_y·h = 0. The source writes ∓; the derivation continues with the minus sign.
  • Isolate C and divide by b/2 [MC-P p.2]:
    • (3) C = A cos α + B cos β − P_z·d/b − P_y·2h/b.
    • (4), substituting (3) into (2): A cos α + B cos β = P_z(d + b)/(2b) + P_y·h/b + G/2.
  • To express the result in α only, assume α + β = 90°, so sin β = cos α and cos β = sin α (5) [MC-P p.2] (⚠ F17).
  • Back-substitution [MC-P p.3]:
    • (6) A cos α + B sin α = P_z(b + d)/(2b) + P_y·h/b + G/2.
    • (7), from (1): B = (A sin α + P_y)/cos α.
    • (8) A = (B cos α − P_y)/sin α.
  • Results [MC-P pp.4–5], using sin²α + cos²α = 1:
    • A = P_z((b + d)/2b) cos α + P_y(h/b) cos α − P_y sin α + (G/2) cos α
    • B = P_z((b + d)/2b) sin α + P_y(h/b) sin α + P_y cos α + (G/2) sin α
    • C = P_z((b − d)/2b) − P_y(h/b) + G/2
  • Slideway face widths [MC-P p.5]: pressure = force/area = force/(width × length), so width = force/(pressure × length). This is applied to each of A, B and C.
  • Exam problem [MC-P p.6], not solved in the source: flat plus V cast-iron ways; α = β = 45°; b = 40 cm; h = 30 cm; work diameter 100 mm; P_z = 350 kgf; P_y = 100 kgf; carriage 150 kgf, 25 cm long; allowable pressure 2 kgf/cm². Asks (a) derive the normal forces, (b) find their values, (c) estimate the slideway face widths. A computed answer is under Worked-example checks.

Machining operations and machine tools

In this section (11)

  2. 5.2 Turning

  4. 5.3 Facing
  5. Worked example: Example 2.9 (face turning of an aluminium tube flange)
  6. 5.4 Drilling and core drilling [MC-2 pp.14–20]
  7. Worked example: Solved Problem 02 (drilling a magnesium alloy)
  8. 5.5 Milling

5.1 The main operations

  • The metal cutting operations listed are turning, boring, drilling, reaming and milling [MC-1 p.1].
  • Turning: single-edge tool, rotating work, cylindrical shape; speed motion from the rotating work, feed by the tool moving slowly parallel to the work axis. Drilling: rotating tool with typically two edges, fed parallel to its axis. Milling: rotating multi-edge tool fed slowly across the work, feed perpendicular to the tool axis; peripheral and face milling (Fig. 1.3 a–d) [MC-G1 p.3].
  • Other conventional operations: shaping, planing, broaching, sawing; grinding and similar abrasive operations follow conventional machining for superior surface finish [MC-G1 p.3].
  • Drilling vs milling: in drilling the feed direction is parallel to the drill's axis of rotation. In milling the feed direction is normal to the cutter's axis of rotation [MC-Q p.5].
  • The two basic milling operations are peripheral (plain) milling and face milling. The figures also show end milling, with depth of cut d and cutting width b [MC-3 p.1].

5.2 Turning

  • Turning has a rotary motion of the work-piece about its axis, plus a linear motion of the tool. The tool's linear motion is perpendicular to the w.p axis (for a flat w.p) or at an angle to the w.p axis [MC-Q p.4]. See ⚠ F18 for the "cylindrical w.p" item.
  • Turning: single-point tool, rotating work, tool fed parallel to the axis to generate a cylinder; done on a lathe, which powers the rotation and feeds the tool at a specified rate and depth (Fig. 22.5: D0, Df, d, f, v, L) [MC-G31 p.9].
  • Cutting conditions in turning [MC-G31 pp.10–12]:
    • N = v/(π D0) (N rev/min, v m/min, D0 in m);
    • Df = D0 − 2d;
    • fr = N·f (mm/min);
    • Tm = L/fr (L = length of the cylindrical part), or directly Tm = π D0 L/(f v) (v in mm/min);
    • in practice an approach and overtravel distance is added, so the feed motion lasts longer than Tm;
    • R_MR = v f d (mm³/min); f is expressed simply in mm, neglecting the rotational character; units of speed must be consistent with f and d.
  • Turning formulas of the Unit 1 lecture (the same relations appear in the mid-term notes and the section notes):
  • Cutting speed (m/min): V = πN(D1 + D2)/2 = πN·D_avg. For small d, V ≅ πN·D1 [MC-1 p.14; MC-MID p.6; MC-ES p.1].
  • Rearranged for spindle speed: N = 2V/(π(D1 + D2)) [MC-1 p.20; MC-MID p.10].
  • Feed rate: f_r = f·N [MC-1 p.14; MC-MID p.6; MC-ES p.1].
  • Uncut (nominal) chip thickness: a = f cos κ, with κ the lead angle [MC-1 p.14; MC-MID p.6; MC-ES p.1]. A handwritten note derives it: cos κ = a/f, so a = f cos κ [MC-2 p.1; MC-F24 p.1].
  • The same thickness in PCEA form: a1 = s·sin φ, with s the feed in mm/rev (not mm/min) and φ the principal cutting edge angle; for pure orthogonal turning φ = 90° [MC-1 pp.16–17]. (The two forms agree when κ = 90° − φ; this is not stated in the source.)
  • Depth of cut: d = (D1 − D2)/2 [MC-1 p.14; MC-MID p.6; MC-ES p.1]. Hence D2 = D1 − 2d [MC-1 p.20].
  • Material removal rate: Q = V·f·d = [π(D1² − D2²)/4]·f_r [MC-1 p.15; MC-MID p.7; MC-ES p.1].
  • Spindle power: P_s ≅ Q·u_s, where u_s is the power needed to cut a unit volume of work material [MC-1 p.15; MC-MID p.7; MC-ES p.1].
  • Motor power: P_m = P_s/η, where η is the efficiency of the drive system [MC-1 p.15; MC-MID p.7; MC-ES p.1].
  • Spindle torque: P = Tω = T(2πN), so T = P/(2πN), with W = J/s = N·m/s [MC-1 p.20; MC-MID p.10; MC-ES p.2].
  • Cutting-edge engagement (nominal width of cut): L_m = doc/cos κ [MC-2 p.8; MC-MID p.9; MC-F24 p.1]. [MC-1 p.21] prints this as "(doc)s(κ)" (⚠ F1).
  • p.6 Turning parameters (sketch: D0, D1, d, N, f mm/rev, lead angle, feed): d depth of cut (mm); N rev speed (rpm); f feed (mm/rev); f_r feed rate = f·N (mm/min). Chip-section sketch: PCEA φ, lead angle K, L contact (chip contact) length, a uncut chip thickness; cos K = a/f → a = f cos K; d = (D0 − D1)/2; V = πDN with D_avg = (D0 + D1)/2 → V = π(D0 + D1)N/2 [MC-MID p.6].
  • p.7 Power: spindle power (Arabic: the power the spindle takes — the one holding the work) P = Q·U_s, Q material removal rate, U_s specific cutting energy (Arabic: scientists made experiments for each material and got U_s; it is taken from the table). Q ≡ MRR = A_chip·V_c (mm³/min). Also Q = (π/4)(D0² − D1²)·L_m / T_m (L_m machined length, T_m machining time). P_s = Q·U_s (spindle power); P_m = P_s/η (motor power; Arabic: some power is lost between motor and spindle) [MC-MID p.7].
  • p.1 Turning operation (figure: D1, D2, N, V, d, f, feed, lead angle K): V = π((D1 + D2)/2)N (m/min), D1 initial diameter of the work (القطر الابتدائي للشغلة), D2 final diameter (القطر النهائي), N rotational speed (rpm); for small d, V = πD1N; d = (D1 − D2)/2; feed rate F_r = F·N (mm/min), F feed mm/rev; uncut (nominal) chip thickness a = F cos K (K lead angle); metal removal rate Q = VFd = (π/4)(D1² − D2²)F_r (mm³/min); spindle power P_s = Q·U_s (W), U_s power required to cut unit volume; motor power P_m = P_s/η (W); cutting time t_m = L/F_r (min), L = length to cut [MC-ES p.1].
  • Operations related to turning (Fig. 22.6) [MC-G31 pp.13–16]: (a) facing — tool fed radially on one end to make a flat end surface; (b) taper turning — tool fed at an angle to the axis, giving a tapered cylinder or cone; (c) contour turning — tool follows a non-straight contour; (d) form turning (forming) — shaped tool plunged radially; (e) chamfering — cuts an angle on the corner; (f) cutoff (parting) — tool fed radially to cut off the end; (g) threading — pointed tool fed parallel to the axis at a large effective feed rate; (h) boring — single-point tool fed parallel to the axis on the inside diameter of an existing hole; (i) drilling on a lathe (drill fed along the axis of the rotating work; reaming similarly); (j) knurling — not machining but metal forming, producing a regular cross-hatched pattern.
  • Taper turning, done by swivelling the compound rest (figure) [MC-Q p.2]:
    • advantages: any angle, any taper direction;
    • disadvantages: tool travel is limited, and manual feed must be used.
  • Work-holding methods in turning are the three-jaw self-centering chuck, the four-jaw chuck, between centres, and the mandrel (figure: parallel mandrel with locking nut; between centres with a catch plate and driving dog) [MC-Q p.3].
  • Engine lathe components (diagram): headstock, spindle, speed controls, feed controls, tool post, cross slide, carriage, ways, lead screw (threaded), tailstock, bed [MC-G31 p.17].
  • Work-holding on a lathe: between centres, chuck, collet, face plate [MC-G31 p.18]:
    • between centres with a "dog" (lathe carrier: clamps around the work and transmits spindle rotation; dog plate driven by the spindle; centre at each end) [MC-G31 p.19];
    • three-jaw chuck (jaws adjustable to clamp the work) [MC-G31 p.20];
    • collet (three slits; a sleeve advances to squeeze it on the work bar) [MC-G31 p.21];
    • face plate with clamps, for non-cylindrical workparts [MC-G31 p.22].
  • Turret lathe: tailstock replaced by a turret holding up to six tools, rapidly indexed; tool post replaced by a four-sided turret; for high-production work needing a sequence of cuts [MC-G31 p.23].
  • Boring: like turning (single-point tool, rotating work) but on the inside diameter of an existing hole — internal turning; done on boring machines (boring mills) or lathes; horizontal or vertical (orientation of the spindle axis). Horizontal: work on a rotating spindle, tool on a cantilevered boring bar fed into the work [MC-G31 p.24]. Vertical: large heavy parts, diameter usually greater than length, clamped to a rotating worktable; tools on tool heads fed vertically (figure: cross-rail, tool head, side column, side tool head, worktable, base) [MC-G31 p.25].
  • Slides pp.1–23 are the same as [MC-G31] pp.1–23 (the between-centres slide p.19 has only the dog drawing, without the lathe-dog photo and text). Differences:
  • Horizontal boring can be set up in two ways [MC-G3 p.24]: (1) the work is fixtured to a rotating spindle and the tool is on a cantilevered boring bar fed into the work; (2) the tool is mounted on a boring bar supported and rotated between centres, and the work is fastened to a feeding mechanism that feeds it past the tool (Fig. 22.10: (a) boring bar fed into a rotating workpart — chuck, boring bar, feed motion, cutting tool; (b) work fed past a rotating boring bar — dog to rotate boring bar, bar between centres, table, clamps, feed motion) [MC-G3 pp.24–25].
  • Vertical boring machine: tool heads can be fed horizontally and vertically relative to the worktable ([MC-G31 p.25] says only "vertically") [MC-G3 p.26].
  • Aspects of turning from the handout [MC-GT]:
  • Centres: two types [MC-GT p.1]: the standard (dead) centre has no moving parts, and lubrication is needed between centre and work piece; the live centre is free to rotate with the work piece because it is mounted on a bearing (photos).
  • Aligning centres: if the centres are not aligned, any cut gives a taper; misaligning them is done on purpose when a taper is desired (figure) [MC-GT p.1].
  • Turning is the term for metal removal from the diameter of the work piece [MC-GT p.1].
  • Cut-off tools: always on centre, with the sides of the cutter perpendicular to the centre axis of the part (figures) [MC-GT p.1].
  • Drilling on a lathe: drills are mounted in the tailstock; the drill may first turn with the part until enough pressure tightens it in the holder; if it keeps rotating under pressure a "dog leg" may be used to stop it. Reamers are set up the same way [MC-GT p.2].
  • Hole-enlarging operations: boring and reaming; in both, the hole is drilled undersize and the boring tool or reamer brings the ID to its finished dimension [MC-GT p.2].
  • Boring tools must be positioned so that the side of the tool does not contact (rub) the part as the tool enters it (photo) [MC-GT p.2].
  • Tool post grinders: grind an angle into the part and/or grind a diameter (usually an OD) to its finished dimension; mounted in the tool-post "T" slot; own motor; wheel and part rotate in opposite directions [MC-GT p.2].
  • Knurling: creates a uniform roughness pattern on cylindrical surfaces where friction is desired (knobs, grip bars). Types: angular knurls (diamond-shaped ridges) and straight knurls (straight longitudinal ridges); photos show coarse, medium and fine patterns of each [MC-GT p.3].
Worked example: Example 01 (rough turning of gray cast iron)
  • Example 01, rough turning of gray cast iron [MC-1 pp.19–21 = MC-2 pp.6–8; MC-MID pp.8–10; MC-ES p.2]. Data: D = 50 mm, u_s = 0.065 kW/(cm³/min), κ = 20°, f = 0.4 mm/rev, d = 4 mm, V = 70 m/min.
    • MRR = V·f·d = 112,000 mm³/min = 112 cm³/min.
    • D_avg = 50 − 4 = 46 mm.
    • P = Q·u_s = 7.28 kW.
    • N = 2V/(π(D1 + D2)) with D2 = 42 mm, giving 485 rpm.
    • T = (7280)(60)/(2π·485) = 143 N·m.
    • a = 0.4 cos 20° = 0.376 mm.
    • L_m = 4/cos 20° = 4.257 mm.
  • Method variants of Example 01 in the mid-term notes and the section notes (same data and results):
  • pp.8– Ex (01) (= Example 01 [MC-1 pp.19–21]): D0 = 50 mm, U_s = 0.065 kW/(cm³/min), K = 20° lead angle, f = 0.4 mm/rev, d = 4 mm, V_c = 70 m/min; find (a) Q = MRR, (b) P_s spindle power, (c) spindle torque, (d) uncut chip thickness a and cutting-edge length L. Sol: d = (D0 − D1)/2 → 4 = (50 − D1)/2 → D1 = 42 mm [MC-MID p.8].
  • p.9 Ex 01 continued: MRR = A_chip·V_c with A_chip = a·L; a = f cos K = 0.4 cos 20 = 0.3758 mm; cos K = d/L → L = d/cos K = 4/cos 20 = 4.257 mm; Q = (0.3758)(4.257)(70 × 1000) = 112,000 mm³/min = 1.12 × 10⁻⁴ m³/min = 112 cm³/min; also A_chip = f·d = 0.4 × 4 = 1.6 mm². P_s = Q·U_s = 112 × 0.065 = 7.28 kW; P_s = T_s·ω → T_s = P_s/ω, ω = 2πN (a first attempt at N, "1521.67 rpm", is struck out) [MC-MID p.9].
  • p.10: N = V/(π(D0 + D1)/2) = 2V/(π(D0 + D1)) = 70 × 1000 × 2/(π(50 + 42)) = 484.38 ≈ 485 rpm; T_s = P_s/(2πN) = 7.28 kW/(2π × 485/60) = 0.14333 kN·m ≈ 143 N·m (Arabic: N must be converted to rev/s); a and L found; L = contact length (cutting-edge contact length) [MC-MID p.10].
  • p.2 Example (rough turning of gray cast iron): 50 mm work, U_s = 0.065 kW/(cm³/min), uncoated carbide tool (statement: "uncoated carbide tool" in the typed text), lead angle K = 20°, f = 0.4 mm/rev, d = 4 mm, V = 70 m/min; find (a) MRR, (b) power, (c) spindle torque, (d) uncut chip thickness and cutting-edge engagement length. Q = VFd = (70 × 10³)(0.4)(4) = 112 × 10³ mm³/min = 112 cm³/min; P = 112 × 0.065 = 7.28 kW; T = P/ω = P/(2πN/60); D2 = D1 − 2d = 50 − 8 = 42 mm; 70 × 10³ = π((50 + 42)/2)N → N = 484.3 ≈ 485 rpm; T = 7.28 × 10³/(2π × 485/60) = 143.3 N·m; a = f cos K = 0.4 cos 20 = 0.37 mm (engagement length not worked on the page) [MC-ES p.2].
  • A variant with D = 40 mm, d = 3 mm, f = 0.3 mm/rev, V = 60 m/min was set in the 2023–2024 final [MC-F24 pp.2–3]; see §9.4.

5.3 Facing

  • Facing machines the end of a work-piece perpendicular to the rotating axis. The tool moves along the radius of the work-piece to give the part length and a smooth face [MC-2 p.9].
  • Cutting force from power: F_c = 2T/D, i.e. F_c = P/(πND) [MC-2 p.12].
  • Radial force: generally less than 50 % of the cutting force in roughing, but it can equal the cutting force in finishing [MC-2 p.12].
  • p.11 Facing operation (sketch: work rotation, D1, depth of cut d, turning tool, feed direction radial). Arabic: we assume the strongest of all the forces is the cutting (tangential) force. Q = MRR = A_chip·V_c = d·f·V_c; V_c = πDN, and the largest diameter D0 is substituted (Arabic: V_c at the centre is zero, the largest force is at the largest diameter, so D0 is used in V_c) [MC-MID p.11].
Worked example: Example 2.9 (face turning of an aluminium tube flange)
  • Example 2.9, face turning of an aluminium tube flange [MC-2 pp.10–13; MC-MID pp.11–15; MC-ES pp.3–4]. Data: d = 8 mm, D_i/D_o = 100/200 mm, overhang L = 500 mm, N_max = 400 rpm, f_max = 0.25 mm/rev, lead angle 30°, u_s = 0.025 kW/(cm³/min), E = 50 GPa.
    • (a) Maximum speed is at the larger diameter: MRR = πDN·f·d = π(200)(400)(0.25)(8) = 502,400 mm³/min ≈ 502 cm³/min, and P = 12.6 kW.
    • (b) Cutting time over the length (D_o − D_i)/2: t_m = L/f_r = (D_o − D_i)/(2fN) = 100/(2 × 0.25 × 400) = 0.5 min = 30 s.
    • (c) Worst case: take F_r = F_c. Then F_c = P/(πND) = 12,600/[π(400/60)(0.2)] = 3000 N.
    • Tube deflection: δ = F_r L³/(3EI), with I = π(D_o⁴ − D_i⁴)/64 = 73.594 × 10⁶ mm⁴, gives δ = 0.034 mm.
    • Taper of the face: tan α_δ = x/D_o, with tan α_δ taken as δ/L, gives x = 200(0.034/500) = 0.0136 mm ("the taper error is 0.0136 mm"). See ⚠ F4–F6.
  • Method variants in the mid-term notes and the section notes:
  • pp.12–15 Ex. 2.9, face turning (tube flange) (= [MC-2 pp.10–13]): d = 8 mm, D_i = 100 mm, D_o = 200 mm, N = 400 rpm, f = 0.25 mm/rev, K = 30°, overhang 500 mm, E = 50 GPa = 50 × 10⁹ N/m², U_s = 0.025 kW/(cm³/min); find (a) P_max = P_s, (b) cutting time, (c) perpendicularity of the flange face with the part axis (Arabic: this is the error value; F_r causes the deflection (bending); F_c gives the torque) [MC-MID p.12].
    • L_m (machining length) = (D_o − D_i)/2 = (200 − 100)/2 = 50 mm; Q = d·f·V_c, V_c = πDN = π × 200 × 400 = 251,327.4123 mm/min (Arabic: we said take the larger D); Q = (8)(0.25)(251,327.4123) = 502,654.8246 mm³/min = 502.654 cm³/min; P_s = 0.025 × 502 = 12.55 kW; t_m = L_m/f_r, f_r = fN → T_m = (D_o − D_i)/(2fN) = 100/(2 × 0.25 × 400) = 0.5 min ≈ 30 s [MC-MID p.13].
    • Cutting force: P = F_c·V_c → F_c = P/(πDN) = 12.55 kW/(π × 0.2 m × 400/60) = 2.996 kN ≈ 3000 N (Arabic: N in rev/s and D in m to get watts). Torque T = P/ω = 12.55/(2π × 400/60) = 0.2996 kN·m = 299.6 N·m. Second method: T = F_c·D_o/2 → F_c = P/(D_o πN). Worst case F_r ≈ F_c (causes the deflection); δ = F L³/(3EI); I = (π/64)(D_o⁴ − D_i⁴) = (π/64)(200⁴ − 100⁴) = 73,631,077.82 mm⁴; δ = 3000 × 500³/(3 × 50 × 10⁹/(10³)² × 73,631,077.82) = 0.034 mm [MC-MID p.14].
    • tan θ = 0.034/500 → θ = 3.896 × 10⁻³°; sin θ = x/D_o → x = 200 sin(3.896 × 10⁻³°) = 0.0136 mm [MC-MID p.15].
  • pp.3–4 Example 2.9 (tube flange) (full typed statement: end face of a tube face turned on a lathe, d = 8 mm, inside/outside flange diameters 100 and 200 mm; tube held in a hydraulic chuck at the other end (Figure 2.40), extends 500 mm, aluminium; maximum speed 400 rpm; maximum feed 0.25 mm/rev; side cutting-edge (lead) angle 30°; determine (a) maximum power, (b) cutting time, (c) perpendicularity of the flange face to the part axis; U_s = 0.025 kW/(cm³/min), E = 50 GPa) [MC-ES p.3].
    • Q = MRR = VFd = (πD_oN)Fd = (π × 200 × 400)(0.25)(8) = 502,654 mm³/min = 502 cm³/min; power = 502 × 0.025 = 12.55 kW; cutting time = L/F_r = (D_o − D_in)/(2FN) = (200 − 100)/(2 × 0.25 × 400) = 0.5 min [MC-ES p.3].
    • (α_δ): F_t = 2T/D_o, T = P/ω = P/(2πN/60) = 12.6 × 10³/(2π × 400/60) = 300.8 N·m; F_t = 2 × 300.8/(200 × 10⁻³) = 3000 N; δ = F_t L³/(3EI), I = (π/64)(D_o⁴ − D_in⁴); δ = 3000 × 500³/(3 × 50 × 10³ × (π/64)(200⁴ − 100⁴)) = 0.034 mm; α_δ = tan⁻¹(δ/L) = tan⁻¹(0.034/500) = 3.8 × 10⁻³ (°); tan α_δ = x/D_o → tan(3.8 × 10⁻³) = x/200, "x =" left blank (⚠ F39) [MC-ES p.4].

5.4 Drilling and core drilling [MC-2 pp.14–20]

  • Drilling creates a round hole, usually with a rotating cylindrical tool with two cutting edges (drill, drill bit); the most common is the twist drill; the rotating drill feeds into the stationary work to form a hole of the drill diameter; done on a drill press (figure: through hole with point angle θ, approach A, work thickness t; blind hole with depth d) [MC-G41 p.2].
  • Cutting conditions in drilling [MC-G41 p.3]:
    • N = v/(πD) (v in mm/min, D drill diameter in mm);
    • fr = N f (f feed in mm/rev);
    • through hole: Tm = (t + A)/fr, with approach allowance A = 0.5 D tan(90 − θ/2) (t work thickness);
    • blind hole: Tm = (d + A)/fr;
    • R_MR = π D² fr / 4.
  • Drilling formulas of the Unit 1 lecture (the same relations appear in the mid-term and section notes):
  • Cutting speed: V = πDN. Feed rate: f_r = f·N. Feed per tooth: f_t = f/n_t, with n_t the number of flutes [MC-2 p.15; MC-MID p.16; MC-ES p.5].
  • Nominal width of cut: b = D/(2 sin ρ), where ρ is the half point angle of the drill [MC-2 p.15; MC-MID p.16; MC-ES p.5]. (Figure: point angle θ [MC-2 p.16].)
  • Uncut chip thickness: a = f_t sin ρ [MC-2 p.16–17; MC-MID p.16; MC-ES p.5].
  • MRR: Q = (πD²/4)·f_r [MC-2 p.16–17; MC-MID p.17; MC-ES p.5].
  • Drilling time for a hole of depth L: t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r, with L_e = D/(2 tan ρ) + ΔL [MC-2 p.16–17; MC-MID p.17; MC-ES p.5]. ΔL is the approach distance between the drill chisel edge and the entrance surface, plus the overtravel of the drill in through holes [MC-2 p.16–17; MC-MID p.17; MC-ES p.5].
  • Figures label the approach allowance A, work thickness t, and A1, A2, I, O and L [MC-2 p.16–17].
  • Core drilling enlarges a hole from D_i to D [MC-2 p.18]:
    • b = (D − D_i)/(2 sin ρ);
    • Q = [π(D² − D_i²)/4]·f_r.
    • The figure also shows step drilling.
  • Convention difference: the lecture [MC-G41 p.3] approach allowance A = 0.5 D tan(90 − θ/2) covers only the drill tip, and its through-hole time is (t + A)/f_r; [MC-2 pp.16–17] adds the approach and overtravel distance ΔL (⚠ F28).
  • pp.16–17 Drilling: sketch — N, D, feed direction, point angle θ ≈ 120°, approach allowance A, thickness t. Chip: f_t = f/n (n = number of cutting edges; Arabic: how many pieces cut), a uncut chip thickness, b nominal width of chip, ρ = 120/2 = 60°. sin ρ = (D/2)/b → b = D/(2 sin ρ); sin ρ = a/f_t → a = f_t sin ρ; V_c = πDN; f_r = f·N; A_chip = (D/2)·f_t [MC-MID p.16].
    • MRR = A_chip·V_c; for drilling Q = MRR = f_r·(π/4)D² (Arabic: as if removing layers of metal); "or Q = A_chip·V_c·n = (D/2)f_t·V_c·(2)" for a drill (n = number of cutting edges) (⚠ F37); core drilling (Arabic: if there is already a hole): MRR = f_r·(π/4)(D0² − D1²) [MC-MID p.17].
    • Time: approach distance ΔL1 (مسافة الاقتراب), overtravel ΔL2 (مسافة الابتعاد), approach allowance A with tan ρ = (D/2)/A → A = D/(2 tan ρ); L_m = L + A + ΔL1 + ΔL2; T_m = L_m/f_r [MC-MID p.17].
  • p.5 Drilling (figures: D, point angle θ, approach allowance A, thickness t; chip geometry with f_t, ρ, b, a): V = πDN (mm/min), D hole diameter (mm), N spindle speed (rpm); F_r = F·N (mm/min); F_t = feed per tooth = F/n_t, n_t number of flutes; a = F_t sin ρ, ρ half point angle; Q = (π/4)D²F_r (mm³/min); P = Q·U_s; t_m = (L + L_e)/F_r, L_e = D/(2 tan ρ) + ΔL, ΔL = approach + overtravel distance [MC-ES p.5].
  • Drill types, parts, point angles, deep and small holes, forces, speed and an example from the handout [MC-GD]:
  • Types of drill: twist drill (most common), gun drill, trepanner. Figure: (a) twist drill, (b) step drill, (c) straight-flute drill, (d) spade drill, (e) gun drill; and a row of operations — drilling, core drilling, step drilling, counterboring, countersinking, reaming, center drilling, gun drilling (high-pressure coolant) [MC-GD p.1].
  • Pilot holes: for large-diameter holes a smaller hole is sometimes drilled first to guide the large drill [MC-GD p.1].
  • Twist drill parts (figure, chisel-point drill) [MC-GD p.1]: tang, tang drive, taper shank, straight shank, shank diameter, shank length, neck, flutes, helix angle, flute length, body, overall length, point angle, drill diameter, lip relief angle, chisel edge angle, chisel edge, web, body diameter clearance, clearance diameter, margin, lip, land.
  • Drill point angle (figure) [MC-GD p.1]: 118° standard; 135° for harder materials (stainless steel, titanium), minimises burring; 90° for softer materials (plastic).
  • Trepanners: figure of a trepanning tool (shank, cutting tools) and a trepanning set-up (spindle, drill, tool, workpiece) [MC-GD p.1].
  • Deep holes: complications may occur when a hole is longer than 4 times the drill diameter. Problems: chip removal difficulty ("picking"), coolant dispensing to the cutting edge, tool deflection [MC-GD p.1].
  • Small holes: small drills 0.15–1 mm; micro-drilling 0.0025–0.5 mm [MC-GD p.1]. Microdrill figure: dia., "note back taper", point angle 118°–135°, clearance angle 8°–15°, shank [MC-GD p.2].
  • Pilot-hole notes (figures) [MC-GD p.2]: a pilot or lead hole makes drilling a large hole easier; the drill cuts exactly on centre if the hole is first started with a center drill; holes larger than 12.5 mm diameter require a pilot hole; there must be enough clearance between the back of the work-piece and the chuck face for the drill to come through without damaging the chuck.
  • Forces and torque [MC-GD p.2]: thrust force "acts perpendicular to the axis of the hole"; large forces can bend or break the drill (⚠ F30). The torque turning the drill is difficult to calculate.
  • Drill speed: V = πDN/1000 (V cutting speed, m/min — the velocity at which the drill edge moves along the work surface; D drill diameter, mm; N rpm) [MC-GD p.2].
  • Feeds for drills are listed in mm/rev; multiply by rpm for mm/min. On a hand-fed drill press the feed cannot be controlled accurately [MC-GD p.2].
  • Example (drilling aluminium) [MC-GD p.2]: HSS drill, D = 12.5 mm; recommended speed 60–90 m/min (from table), take v = 70 m/min → N = 1000 × 70/(π × 12.5) = 1782.5 rpm; recommended feed 0.15–0.25 mm/rev, take f = 0.2 → f_r = 0.2 × 1782.5 = 356.5 mm/min; MRR = (πD²/4) f N = [π(12.5)²/4] × 0.2 × 1782.5, printed 43,794 mm³/min (⚠ F31).
  • Drilling on a lathe [MC-GD p.3]: a straight-shank drill held in a Jacobs chuck (three-jaw; printed "tree jaws"); or a commercial drill holder (figure: taper-shank drill, drill holder, tailstock centre, tool holder, compound).
  • Reaming and reamers on a lathe: used to improve the dimensional accuracy or surface finish of an existing hole [MC-GD p.3]. Types: hand, rose, fluted, shell, expansion, adjustable, center reamers. Figures: (a) terminology for a helical reamer (chamfer angle, chamfer length, chamfer relief, helix angle, radial rake, margin width, land width, primary relief angle), (b) inserted-blade adjustable reamer (lock nut, body, blade, setscrew, adjusting nut); chucking reamer (taper shank, shank length); center reamer, included 60° or 90°; chucking reamer with parallel (straight) shank; long flute reamer; parallel shank hand reamer; chucking reamer with taper shank; hand taper pin reamer; machine taper pin reamer [MC-GD p.3]; shell reamer [MC-GD p.4].
  • Tapping and taps on lathes: used to make internal threads in work-piece holes. Types: tapered, bottoming, collapsible taps. Figure: tap, nut, chamfer angle, chamfer relief, land, flute, heel, cutting edge, rake angle, hook angle [MC-GD p.4].
  • Design considerations for drilling, reaming and tapping [MC-GD p.4]:
    • drill holes on flat surfaces perpendicular to the hole axis, to prevent drill deflection;
    • avoid interrupted hole surfaces;
    • the bottoms of blind holes should match standard drill point angles;
    • avoid blind holes where possible; if large-diameter holes are included, make a pre-existing hole in fabrication;
    • design the work-piece to minimise fixturing and repositioning during drilling;
    • provide extra hole depth for reaming or tapping blind or intersecting holes.
  • Summary: specialised cutting procedures exist for unusual materials and requirements; proper procedure, securing of the work-piece, and feeds and speeds must be considered to prevent damage and injuries [MC-GD p.4].
  • Operations related to drilling and drill-press types [MC-G41]:
  • Operations related to drilling (Fig. 22.14) [MC-G41 pp.4–5]:
    • (a) reaming — slightly enlarges a hole, gives better diameter tolerance and surface finish; tool = reamer, usually straight flutes;
    • (b) tapping — tap cuts internal threads in an existing hole;
    • (c) counterboring — stepped hole (larger diameter partially into the hole) to seat bolt heads below the surface;
    • (d) countersinking — like counterboring but the step is cone-shaped, for flat-head screws and bolts;
    • (e) centering (center drilling) — drills a starting hole to locate subsequent drilling; tool = center drill;
    • (f) spot facing — like milling; a flat machined surface in a localized area.
  • Drill press types: upright, radial, gang, multiple-spindle, CNC turret drill [MC-G41 p.6].
Worked example: Solved Problem 02 (drilling a magnesium alloy)
  • Solved Problem 02 [MC-2 pp.19–20; MC-MID pp.18–19; MC-ES p.6]. Data: 30 mm deep hole in magnesium alloy, u_s = 0.008 kW·min/cm³, 10 mm carbide drill, f = 0.3 mm/rev, V = 200 m/min, point angle 120°, approach = overtravel = 3 mm.
    • MRR = (area)(feed rate) = π(10)²/4[200,000/(π·10)] = 150 cm³/min.
    • t_m = (30 + 10/tan 60° + 3)/[(0.3)(6370)] = 0.02 min = 1.2 s (⚠ F8, F9).
    • P = 150 × 0.008 = 1.2 kW.
    • T = (1200)(60)/(2π·6370) = 1.8 N·m.
  • Method variants in the mid-term notes and the section notes:
  • pp.18–19 Ex. 02 (= Solved Problem 02 [MC-2 pp.19–20]): U_s = 0.008 kW·min/cm³, D = 10 mm, L = 30 mm, f = 0.3 mm/rev, V_c = 200 m/min, point angle 120°, ΔL1 = ΔL2 = 3 mm; find MRR, cutting time, torque. MRR = (π/4)(10)²·f_r, f_r = 0.3 × N, N = V_c/(πD) = 200 × 1000/(π × 10) rpm → MRR = 150,000 mm³/min ≈ 150 cm³/min [MC-MID p.18]. L_m = L + D/(2 tan ρ) + ΔL1 + ΔL2 = 30 + 10/(2 tan 60) + 3 + 3 = 38.88675 mm; t_m = L_m/(fN) = 38.88675/(0.3 × 200,000/(π × 10)) = 0.02 min ≈ 1.22 s; P = Q·U_s = 150 × 0.008 = 1.2 kW = 1.2 × 10³ W; T = P/(2πN) = 1200 × 60/(2π × 200,000/(π × 10)) = 1.8 N·m [MC-MID p.19]. (This uses the lecture formula with ΔL = 3 + 3, i.e. the resolution suggested under ⚠ F9.)
  • p.6 Example (Solved Problem 02): 30 mm deep hole, magnesium alloy, U_s = 0.008 kW·min/cm³, 10 mm carbide drill, f = 0.3 mm/rev, V = 200 m/min, point angle 120°, "approach and overtravel distance = 3 mm"; find (a) MRR, (b) cutting time, (c) torque. ρ = 60°, ΔL = 3 mm. MRR = (π/4)D²FN with N = V/(πD) → MRR = (D/4)FV = (10/4)(0.3)(200 × 10³) = 150 × 10³ mm³/min = 150 cm³/min; L_e = 10/(2 tan 60) + 3 = 5.88 mm; t_m = (30 + 5.88)/(0.3 × 200 × 10³/(π × 10)) = "1.9 × 10⁻³ min" (⚠ F39); T = P/ω = (MRR)U_s/(2πN/60) = 150 × 0.008 × 10³/(2π × 200 × 10³/(π × 10 × 60)) = 1.8 N·m [MC-ES p.6].

5.5 Milling

  • Milling: work fed past a rotating cylindrical tool with multiple edges; cutter axis perpendicular to the feed direction; tool = milling cutter, edges = teeth [MC-G41 p.7]. Two basic types: peripheral (plain) and face milling (Fig. 22.17) [MC-G41 p.8].
  • Peripheral milling types (Fig. 22.18) [MC-G41 pp.9–10]: (a) slab milling — cutter width extends beyond the work on both sides; (b) slotting (slot milling) — cutter narrower than the work, making a slot; with a very thin cutter, narrow slots or cutting the part in two = saw milling; (c) side milling — machines the side of the work; (d) straddle milling — side milling on both sides; (e) form milling — teeth with a special profile determining the slot shape.
  • In peripheral milling, rotation direction gives up milling (conventional) and down milling (climb) (Fig. 22.19, 20-tooth cutter; chip length, feed direction) [MC-G41 p.11].
  • Face milling: cutter axis perpendicular to the milled surface; Fig. 22.20: (a) conventional face milling, (b) partial face milling, (c) end milling, (d) profile milling, (e) pocket milling, (f) surface contouring [MC-G41 p.12]. Up vs down milling:
  • The uncut chip thickness varies continuously in milling. In up-milling it is small at the start of the cut and grows; in down-milling it is largest at the start [MC-3 p.2].
  • Comparison table [MC-Q p.8] (figure labels heat dissipation, cutting force and feed arrows):
Aspect Down milling Up milling
Cutter rotation direction Same as the feed direction Opposite to the feed direction
Chip thickness Starts thick and decreases gradually Starts thin and increases gradually
Tool life Long Short
Peripheral (slab and slot) milling: chip geometry, MRR and time

Peripheral milling: chip geometry [MC-3 p.3–5]

  • Instantaneous thickness: a_i = f_t cos κ sin ν_i, at engagement angle ν_i [MC-3 p.3; MC-MID p.21; MC-ES p.7].
  • Maximum: a_max = f_t cos κ sin ν_m [MC-3 p.3; MC-MID p.21; MC-ES p.7].
  • Average: a_avg = f_t cos κ sin(ν_m/2) [MC-3 p.3; MC-MID p.21; MC-ES p.7].
  • κ is the lead angle, the same as the lead angle in turning [MC-3 p.3].
  • Approximate equations [MC-3 p.4; MC-MID p.20]:
    • a_max = 2f_t√(d/D);
    • a_avg = f_t√(d/D);
    • chip length λ_c = √(D·d).
  • Engagement angle from depth: cos ν_m = 1 − 2d/D, i.e. (R − d)/R [MC-3 p.8, p.18; MC-MID p.20; MC-ES p.7].
  • MRR = f_r·b·d [MC-3 p.5; MC-MID p.21; MC-ES p.7].
  • Machining time: t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r, with L_e = L_a + L_o [MC-3 p.5; MC-MID p.22; MC-ES p.7]:
    • L_a = √(d(D − d)) + approach allowance;
    • L_o = √(d(D − d)) + overtravel allowance;
    • assume approach allowance = overtravel allowance = 5 mm.
  • Spindle speed and table feed as used in the examples: N = V/(πD) and f_r = n_t·f_t·N [MC-3 p.7, p.18, p.23; MC-G41 pp.13–14; MC-MID pp.24–25; MC-ES p.7].
  • Variants and extra details in the mid-term notes, the section notes and the handout [MC-G41]:
  • p.20 Slot milling operation: sketch of cutter in slot, ν_m. cos ν_m = (D/2 − d)/(D/2) (R − d over R) → cos ν_m = 1 − 2d/D, ν_m = cos⁻¹(1 − 2d/D); a_max = 2f_t√(d/D); a_avg = f_t√(d/D); chip length λ_c = √(D·d), or λ_c = (D/2)·ν_m·(π/180) (Arabic: as if finding the arc length, D/2 = half the diameter) [MC-MID p.20].
  • p.21 Milling chip thickness: a_i = f_t cos K sin ν_i; a_max = f_t cos K sin ν_m; a_avg = f_t cos K sin(ν_m/2) (sketch: a_i = 0 at entry, a_i = max at exit). MRR sketch: slab of width b, depth d moving at f_r: MRR = b·d·f_r, f_r = f·N = b·d·(f_t·N)·n (n = number of cutting edges) [MC-MID p.21].
  • p.22 T_m = L_tot/f_r. Heading "Asymmetrical cutting" (the sketch is a peripheral cutter entering the work): L_a = √((D/2)² − (D/2 − d)²) = √(D·d − d²), written as "√(d(D − 1))" in one line (⚠ F38), then L_tot = 2√(d(D − d)) + L_w + A + B (A approach allowance, B overtravel allowance) [MC-MID p.22].
  • p.23 Symmetrical cutting (Arabic: the work is on the same centreline as the tool): sketch with D/2, A_p at entry and D/2 at exit [MC-MID p.23].
  • p.7 Milling: a_max = F_t cos K sin ν_m, ν_m maximum engagement angle, ν_m = cos⁻¹((R − d)/R), d depth of cut, R cutter radius, K lead angle, cos K = 1 (straight teeth; Arabic note); F_t = feed per tooth = F_r/(n_t N), n_t number of milling teeth; Q = F_r·b·d, F_r = F·N (mm/min), b width of cut, d depth of cut; P = Q·U_s; V = πDN; t_m = (L + L_e)/F_r, L_e = L_a + L_o, L_a = √(d(D − d)) + approach distance, L_o = √(d(D − d)) + overtravel distance (figures: cutter with a_max, ν_m, D/2, approach, overtravel, L + L_e; L_a, L_w, L_o) [MC-ES p.7].
  • Cutting conditions in milling [MC-G41 pp.13–14]: N = v/(πD); fr = N nt f (nt number of teeth, f chip load = feed per tooth, mm/tooth); MRR = cross-sectional area of the cut × feed rate, R_MR = w d fr.
  • Slab milling time (Fig. 22.21, cutter entering the work): Tm = (L + A)/fr, A = √(d(D − d)) (d depth of cut, D cutter diameter) [MC-G41 p.14]. Face milling [MC-3 p.9–16]
  • General formulas [MC-3 p.9]:
    • a_i = f_t cos κ sin ν_i;
    • a_max = f_t cos κ sin ν_m;
    • a_avg = f_t cos κ sin(ν_m/2);
    • κ is the lead angle.
  • Symmetrical cutting, for both "cutter diameter > work width" and "cutter diameter < work width" [MC-3 p.11]:
    • a_i = f_t sin ν_i;
    • a_m = a_avg = f_t sin 90° = f_t;
    • chip length λ_c = ν_m (rad)·D/2;
    • the second figure marks ν_m = 180°.
  • Symmetrical machining time [MC-3 p.12]:
    • t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r, with L_e = 2L_c + A_p + O_t and L_c = D/2;
    • A_p is the approach allowance and O_t the overtravel allowance;
    • MRR = f_r·b·d.
  • Asymmetrical cutting, with ν_m in radians [MC-3 p.13]:
    • a_i = f_t sin ν_i;
    • a_m = f_t sin ν_m ≅ 2f_t√(b/D);
    • a_avg = f_t sin(ν_m/2) ≅ f_t√(b/D);
    • λ_c = ν_m (rad)·(D/2) = √(bD).
  • Asymmetrical machining time [MC-3 p.14]:
    • L_e = 2L_c + A_p + O_t, with L_c = √(b(D − b));
    • t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r;
    • MRR = f_r·b·d.
  • Chip thinning: the larger the cutting edge angle, the lower the chip thickness [MC-3 p.15]:
    • KAPR 90°: h = f_z;
    • KAPR 75°: h = 0.96f_z;
    • KAPR 45°: h = 0.75f_z (⚠ F13).
    • The figure also shows F_R, F_A and F_N on the insert.
  • Average chip thickness at programmed f_z = 0.0059 in (0.15 mm), by radial engagement [MC-3 p.16]:
    • 100 %: h_m = 0.1 mm (0.0039 in);
    • 50 %: 0.1 mm (0.0039 in);
    • 20 %: 0.07 mm (0.0028 in);
    • 10 %: 0.046 mm (0.0018 in).
  • Effective diameter [MC-3 p.18–21]:
    • round inserts: D_e = D − IC + √(IC² − (IC − 2d)²);
    • ball-nose end mill: D_e = 2√(d(D − d)).
    • General tool form: d_eff = d − 2r + 2√(a_p(2r − a_p)); ball nose: d_eff = 2√(a_p(d − a_p)) (schnittdaten.meusburger.com).
    • At a small axial doc the spindle speed is calculated on D_e [MC-3 p.18, p.21].
  • Face-milling cutter selection: the cutter diameter is chosen 20–40 % larger than the part width, and the cutter runs off the part's centreline [MC-3 p.23].
  • Approach and overtravel for face milling [MC-3 p.24]:
    • L_e|min = L_a − L_t = D/2 − ½√(D² − b²);
    • L_e|max = L_a + L_t = D/2 + D/2 = D.
    • The overtravel depends on the surface requirement: the minimum (negative) case is when the cutter stops within the part; the maximum applies if trailing marks must not show.
  • Face-milling approach in [MC-G41 p.15] (compare with [MC-3 p.24] above):
  • Face milling time (Fig. 22.22, approach and overtravel) [MC-G41 p.15]: (a) cutter centred over the work: A = 0.5(D − √(D² − w²)); if D = w, A = 0.5D; (b) cutter offset to one side: A = √(w(D − w)).
Worked examples (milling)
  • Solved Example 03, slot milling [MC-3 pp.6–8; MC-MID pp.24–27; MC-ES pp.8–9]. Data: groove 10 mm wide × 15 mm deep × 400 mm long in cast iron; side milling cutter D = 200 mm with 16 straight teeth; V = 80 m/min; a_max = 0.2 mm; 10 kW available.
    • u_s is taken from Table 2.1 as 0.07 kW·min/cm³, so MRR = P/u_s = 142.9 cm³/min.
    • In slotting, the radial depth d is along the cutter diameter and the axial width b equals the slot width. f_r = MRR/(d·b) = 952 mm/min.
    • N = 80,000/(3.14 × 200) = 128 rpm, giving f_t = 952/(16 × 128) = 0.465 mm/tooth.
    • The chip-thickness limit governs instead: cos ν_max = (100 − 15)/100, so ν = 32°, and f_t = 0.2/sin 32° = 0.377 mm/tooth. 0.38 mm/tooth is selected; it needs 8.2 kW, 82 % of the available power.
    • (b) Printed solution: L_a = 52.7 mm, overtravel ≈ 0, plus 10 mm total allowance. t_m = (400 + 52.7 + 10)/[(16)(0.38)(128)] = 0.595 min = 35.7 s.
    • The slide says "Please check this solution" and adds a handwritten alternative: L_A = √(15(200 − 15)) + 5 = 57.68 mm, L_B = L_A, t_m = (400 + 2 × 57.68)/774.14 = 0.665 min = 39.9 s (⚠ F12).
  • Method variants of Solved Example 03 in the mid-term notes and the section notes:

U_s = 0.07 kW·min/cm³ (from the table); MRR = P/U_s = 10/0.07 = 142.9 cm³/min = 142,900 mm³/min; MRR = f_r·b·d → f_r = 952.667 mm/min [MC-MID p.24]. L1 = √(d(D − d)) + A = √(15(200 − 15)) + 5 = 57.678 mm; L2 = 57.678 mm; L_w = 400 mm; L_tot = 2 × 57.678 + 400 = 515.357 mm; T_m = 515.357/772.0927 = 0.6674 min ≈ 40.044 s [MC-MID p.27] (⚠ F38) (same convention as the handwritten alternative on [MC-3 p.8], ⚠ F12).
  • pp.8–9 Example (slot milling) (typed statement = Solved Example 03: 10 mm wide groove across the full 400 mm length of a cast-iron part, depth 15 mm, 200 mm carbide brazed side milling cutter with 16 straight teeth, each insert cuts the full width, V = 80 m/min, maximum uncut chip thickness 0.2 mm; (a) maximum feed rate if the maximum available spindle power is 10 kW, (b) machining time). MRR = Power/U_s = 10/0.07 = 142.8 cm³/min (⚠ F39); MRR = b·d·F_r → 142.8 × 10³ = 10 × 15 × F_r → F_r = 952 mm/min; for the maximum feed a_max = F_t sin ν_m → F_t = a_max/sin(cos⁻¹((R − d)/R)) = 0.2/sin(cos⁻¹((100 − 15)/100)) = 0.377 mm/rev/tooth [MC-ES p.8]. t_m = (L + L_e)/F_r, L_e = L_a + L_o, L_a = L_o = √(15(200 − 15)) + 5 = 57.6 mm (assume approach = overtravel = 5 mm); F_r = F_t·n_t·N, N = 80 × 10³/(π × 200) = 127.3 ≈ 128 rpm; t_m = (400 + 57.6 × 2)/(0.38 × 16 × 128) = 0.66 min [MC-ES p.9].

Cutting temperature

In this section (5)
  1. 6.1 Heat generation and its effects
  2. 6.2 Measurement of cutting temperatures
  3. 6.3 Factors affecting the cutting temperature
  4. 6.4 Thermal and volumetric properties of materials
  5. 6.5 Analytical methods: Trigger and Cook equations

6.1 Heat generation and its effects

  • Course header: Theory of metal cutting, course code DPE 321, level 3rd, Mechanical Design & Production [MC-U21 p.1].
  • When metal is cut, energy is spent deforming the chip and overcoming friction between tool and work; almost all of it becomes heat, giving high temperatures in the deformation zones and surrounding regions of chip, tool and work (figure: shear zone, chip–tool interface, tool–work interface) [MC-U21 p.2; MC-RT p.1].
  • Heat is generated in: the primary shear zone (shearing); the tool–chip interface (friction); rubbing of the (dull/worn) tool tip against the machined surface [MC-U21 p.3; MC-RT p.1].
  • The temperature rise: adversely affects strength, hardness and wear resistance of the tool; damages the machined surface; uneven temperatures cause distortion; causes dimensional changes in the work [MC-U21 p.3; MC-RT p.1; MC-F24 p.3].
  • Tool–chip temperature distribution: FE contour plot (NT11 legend 0–810) [MC-U21 p.4].
  • The temperature pattern depends on specific heat, thermal conductivity, cutting speed, depth of cut, feed rate and cutting fluid (if any) [MC-U21 p.5]. Figure (isotherms, °C): chip 360–600, tool up to 700 (650/600 contours), workpiece 380, 130, 80, 30 [MC-U21 p.5].
  • The maximum temperature is about halfway up the tool face, with a steep gradient across the chip thickness. Some chips become red hot — a safety hazard needing safety guards [MC-U21 p.5].
  • Heat (thermal) capacity: a measurable quantity equal to the ratio of the heat added to an object to the resulting temperature change [MC-U21 p.5, p.13].
  • Cutting temperature [MC-G12 pp.44–46]:
    • High temperatures reduce tool life, produce hot chips (safety hazard to the operator), and can cause dimensional inaccuracy through thermal expansion of the work.
  • p.2 Temperature pattern depends on: specific heat, mechanical properties (strength, hardness…), cutting speed, feed rate, depth of cut, cutting fluid (⚠ F40; the lecture lists thermal conductivity, not mechanical properties [MC-U21 p.5]). Measurement: conventional thermocouple, metallurgical, infrared, other methods [MC-RT p.2].

6.2 Measurement of cutting temperatures

  • Measurement of cutting temperatures — four groups [MC-U21 p.6]: (1) conventional thermocouple methods, (2) metallurgical methods, (3) infrared methods, (4) other methods.
    • Thermocouple (figures) [MC-U21 p.7]: turning — work and tool both insulated, copper brush on the work, millivoltmeter between them (tool–work thermocouple); milling — embedded thermocouples in the work piece ("Figure 2 … [14]").
    • Metallurgical: metallic tool materials often undergo metallurgical transformations or hardness changes that correlate with temperature, so temperature distributions in tools can be mapped by sectioning the tools after cutting and doing metallographic or microscopic examination [MC-U21 p.8].
    • Infrared: estimate temperature by measuring the infrared radiation emitted from the cutting zone (photos: IR gun; thermal image 23 °C – 932 °C) [MC-U21 p.9].
    • Other [MC-U21 p.10]: thermosensitive paints on specimens; the colour of steel chips (degree of temperature-dependent oxidation); heat flux into an internally cooled tool estimated from the temperature rise of the cooling fluid, then tool interface temperatures by an inverse solution.
  • p.3 Thermocouple sketches: turning (insulated work and tool, copper brush, mV meter); milling (end mill, cutting speed V, N, thermocouples embedded in the work) [MC-RT p.3].
  • p.4 Metallurgical method: depends on the change of mechanical properties with temperature, by microscopic examination. Infrared (Arabic: a single ray gives a point; a set of rays gives an area, "2D"). Other: coating the specimen with thermosensitive paints, temperature estimated by colour; heat flux — measure the temperature rise of the cooling fluid (sketch: lathe, coolant tank, pump, d1) [MC-RT p.4].
  • An exam answer with the thermocouple sketches for turning and milling is in §9.4 [MC-F24 p.4].

6.3 Factors affecting the cutting temperature

  • pp.1–8 repeat [MC-U21] pp.11–18 (factors 1–3, thermal-property table, specific heat slides) [MC-U22 pp.1–8].
  • Factors affecting cutting temperature [MC-U21 pp.11–13]:
    1. Cutting speed and feed: T_int ∝ V^0.5 a^0.3. Higher speed and feed raise the rate of energy dissipation (plastic deformation and friction) and so of heat generation; speed has a greater influence than feed. Chip melting can occur machining Inconel 718 at speeds up to 1200 m/min, hardened 4340 steel above 3000 m/min, and 6061 Al above 700 m/min [MC-U21 p.11; MC-RT p.5; MC-F22 p.2].
    2. Material properties: harder work gives higher temperatures (higher forces and energy); at similar hardness, temperature rises with ductility (more energy absorbed in plastic deformation) [MC-U21 p.12; MC-RT p.5; MC-F22 p.2]. At about 300 m/min:
Work material Brinell hardness (HBN) Tool–chip temperature (°C)
Aluminum alloy 100 400
Brittle gray cast iron 200 750
Ductile mild steel 200 1000
  1. Thermal properties of the work (thermal conductivity K and heat capacity ρc): temperatures generally fall as these rise (heat conducted away faster, higher k; or temperature rises more slowly for a given heat input, higher ρc). C = E/ΔT (E total energy, ΔT temperature change); unit J/K or J/°C [MC-U21 p.13; MC-RT p.5; MC-F22 p.2].
  • Factor 4, nose radius [MC-U22 p.9; MC-RT p.6; MC-F22 pp.2–3]:
    • increasing the nose radius reduces the peak temperature, by reducing the maximum uncut chip thickness and spreading the frictional energy more evenly over the edge;
    • reducing the included (wedge) angle — by increasing the rake or relief angles — increases the peak temperature, by reducing the area through which heat can diffuse from the edge into the tool.
    • Figure: workpiece, chip, cutting tool, rake angle γ, edge radius r_n, clearance angle α, h1, h_min, stagnation point.
  • The student sketch of the nose-radius effect marks the uncut chip thickness as d1 and d2 [MC-RT p.6].

  • Specific heat capacity [MC-U21 p.15]: the heat energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance per unit mass; a physical property; the slide calls it "an example of an extensive property since its value is proportional to the size of the system" (⚠ F32). In SI (symbol c) it is the heat in joules to raise 1 gram by 1 kelvin; also J/kg·K; or cal/g·°C. Related: molar heat capacity J/mol·K; volumetric heat capacity J/m³·K. Heat capacity C = Q/ΔT (Q energy in J, ΔT in °C or K) [MC-U21 pp.15–16].
