6.5 Analytical methods: Trigger and Cook equations

  • Analytical (Nathan Cook, dimensional analysis with experimental data): T = (0.4U/ρC)·(v t0/K)^0.333, T = temperature rise at the tool–chip interface, U specific energy, v cutting speed, t0 chip thickness before cut, ρC volumetric specific heat, K thermal diffusivity of the work.
  • Experimental: most frequently the tool–chip thermocouple; Ken Trigger found T = K v^m (T measured interface temperature, v speed).
  • Analytical methods to compute cutting temperature:
    • (1) Trigger: speed–temperature relation T = K v^m; Trigger used the tool–chip thermocouple to relate temperature to cutting conditions such as speed and feed [MC-U22 p.10].
    • Chart "experimentally measured cutting temperatures against speed for three work materials" (°F vs ft/min): RC-130B titanium T = 479 v^0.182; 18-8 stainless steel T = 135 v^0.361; B1113 free-machining steel T = 86.2 v^0.348 [MC-U22 p.11].
    • (2) Cook (from experimental data for various work materials) predicts the mean temperature rise at the tool–chip interface: ΔT = (0.4U/ρC)·(v t0/K)^0.333 — ΔT in °C (°F); U specific energy, N·m/mm³ = J/mm³ (in·lb/in³); v cutting speed, m/s (in/s); t0 chip thickness before the cut, m (in); ρC volumetric specific heat of the work, J/mm³·°C (in·lb/in³·°F); K thermal diffusivity of the work, m²/s (in²/s) [MC-U22 p.14] (⚠ F34).
  • Solved Problem 01 (Trigger) [MC-U22 pp.11–12]: tool–chip thermocouple in turning, feed and depth constant: v = 120 m/min → 515 °C; 160 → 570 °C; 180 → 600 °C. Find T(v).
    • Handwritten solution: ln T = ln K + m ln v; using points 1 and 3: ln 515 − ln 600 = m(ln 120 − ln 180) → −0.153 = m(ln 120 − ln 180) → m = 0.377 ≈ 0.38; ln K = ln 515 − 0.38 ln 120 = 4.42 → K = e^4.42 = 83; T = 83 v^0.38 [MC-U22 p.12].
  • Mid-term exam question (figure only, no question text on the slide): cutting temperature (°C) vs cutting speed (m/min) for titanium (K1 = 9 mm²/s), stainless steel (K2 = 4 mm²/s) and free-machining steel (K3 = 12 mm²/s) [MC-U22 p.12]. It is the p.11 chart relabelled in °C and m/min (⚠ F33).
  • p.6 Trigger equation T = K v^m, relating temperature to cutting speed and feed rate; log T = log K + m log V, i.e. y = a + mx, slope m on log T vs log V [MC-RT p.6].
  • p.7 Ex. (Trigger data: V1 = 120 → 515 °C; V2 = 160 (written "16") → 570 °C; V3 = 180 → 600 °C): ln T = ln K + m ln V for each point; solving (1) with (3): ln 515 − ln 600 = m(ln 120 − ln 180) → m = 0.38; substituting in (1): K = 85 → T = 85 V^0.38 [MC-RT p.7] (lecture answer: T = 83 v^0.38 [MC-U22 p.12]; ⚠ F41).
  • The same Trigger problem was set in the finals: [MC-F23 p.3] (m = 0.38, K = 83.5) and [MC-F24 p.5] (m = 0.377, K = 85); see §9.4 and ⚠ F41.
  • Solved Problem 02 (Cook) = Example 3 [MC-U22 p.19; MC-G12 p.47; MC-RT p.8]: steel, v = 3.0 m/s, f = 0.25 mm, d = 4.0 mm; U = 2.2 N·m/mm³; ρ = 7.87 g/cm³; C = 0.460 J/g·°C; k = 0.046 J/s·mm·°C; ambient 20 °C. ρC = 7.87 × 0.46 = 3.62 × 10⁻³ J/mm³·°C; K = k/ρC = 0.046/[(7.87 × 10⁻³)(0.46)] = 12.7 mm²/s; t0 = f = 0.25 mm; T = (0.4 × 2.2/3.62 × 10⁻³)[3 × 10³ × 0.25/12.7]^0.333 = 0.2428 × 10³ × (59.06)^0.33 = 944.4 °C; final T = 20 + 944 = 964 °C (same as [MC-G12 p.47]) (⚠ F34).

Tool wear and tool life

In this section (8)
  1. 7.1 Introduction
  2. 7.2 Types of tool wear
  3. 7.3 Measurement of tool wear
  4. 7.4 Tool wear mechanisms
  5. 7.5 Tool-life testing and flank wear against time
  6. 7.6 Taylor tool-life equations
  7. 7.7 Example 9.1: Taylor parameters for a new carbide insert
  8. 7.8 Tool wear monitoring

7.1 Introduction

  • Contents: introduction; types of tool wear; measurement of tool wear; tool wear mechanisms; cutting tool materials; tool life testing; tool life equation; tool wear monitoring [MC-U23 p.2].
  • Introduction [MC-U23 p.3]: tool wear and failure mechanisms matter because they affect machining cost and quality; tool life is the most common criterion for rating tool performance and the machinability of materials; tool life is affected by tool wear; the goal is to predict tool life by understanding the failure mechanisms.

7.2 Types of tool wear

  • Types of tool wear:
    1. Flank wear: at the relief face; caused by rubbing of the tool on the work, giving abrasion of the edge (wear land); increases rubbing forces and so friction heating; increases deflection and gives inaccurate dimensions (figure: crater wear, flank wear bandwidth FW, notch wear, flank wear, nose radius wear, feed, depth of cut) [MC-U23 p.4].
    2. Crater wear: at the rake face; caused by the chip rubbing the rake face; due to temperature-activated diffusion or chemical wear mechanisms; crater formation may increase the effective rake angle and so reduce cutting forces, but an excessive crater weakens the tool and leads to fracture (figures: rake face wear, major/minor cutting edge, notch wear; cross-section ABC original vs AB′B″B‴C worn) [MC-U23 p.5].
    3. Notch wear: at the point of contact between tool and work (at the depth-of-cut line); when machining hard surfaces of work-hardened materials (stainless steels, nickel-based alloys); makes re-sharpening very difficult; may cause fracture, especially with ceramic tools (photo "VG (notch wear)") [MC-U23 p.6].
    4. Nose radius wear: due to abrasion and corrosion and/or oxidation of the edge; severe nose radius wear degrades surface finish (figure: theoretical vs real profile, r_ε, Ur_ε, Dr, a_pmax, a_pmin) [MC-U23 p.7].
    5. Thermal and mechanical cracking: due to cyclic loading of the tool when machining materials that give high tool–chip temperatures; perpendicular cracks from cyclic thermal loads (a), parallel cracks from cyclic mechanical loads (b); these lead to rapid fracture or chipping [MC-U23 p.8].
    6. Edge chipping (fritting): with brittle tool materials; when cutting work with hard abrasive particles (MMCs, Al–Si alloys); also from tool–work vibration; results in poor finish, increased flank wear, possible breakage (figure: rake face, notch wear, crater wear, flank wear, flank face, end clearance face, edge chipping) [MC-U23 p.9].
  • Student summary of the six types, with the sketches [MC-RT pp.9–11] (the crater point adds that the crater reduces the wedge angle, weakening the tool):
  • pp.9–11 Types of tool wear: (1) flank (relief face) wear — at the relief face; rubbing between tool edges and work; abrasion of the edge; increases rubbing, cutting force and friction heating; increases deflection and inaccurate dimensions. Sketch: crater wear, major cutting edge, notch wear, flank wear, minor cutting edge, edge chipping (fritting), nose radius wear. (2) Crater (rake face) wear — at the rake face; due to temperature diffusion and chemical wear mechanisms; crater formation increases the rake angle, reduces the cutting force and reduces the wedge angle, which weakens the tool and leads to fracture (sketch: rake angle increase, wedge angle decrease) [MC-RT p.9]. (3) Notch wear — at the point of contact between tool edges and work; when machining hard material; makes re-sharpening difficult; may fracture the tool, especially ceramic tools. (4) Nose radius wear — corrosion, oxidation and abrasion of the tool edges; degrades surface finish (theoretical vs real profile sketch). (5) Thermal and mechanical cracking — cyclic loading of the tool; perpendicular cracks from cyclic thermal loads; parallel cracks from cyclic mechanical loads (sketch) [MC-RT p.10]. (6) Edge chipping (fritting) — brittle tool materials; vibration between work and tool; poor surface finish and increased flank wear [MC-RT p.11].
  • Figure: mc2-tool-wear-curve.jpg shows flank wear against time (initial, steady, severe) [MC-U23 p.26]. Exam answers comparing flank and crater wear are in §9.4 [MC-F22 p.4; MC-F24 p.6].

7.3 Measurement of tool wear

  • Measurement of tool wear [MC-U23 p.10]: microscopes and stylus tracing instruments; a datum line on the cutting edge must be specified, from which both flank and crater wear are measured; video image processing of photographs at intervals records flank-wear progress; other techniques — gradually lapping down the tool from the top edge, and optical contour mapping.
  • Most standard tool-life tests use flank-wear criteria (ISO-style figure: flank wear land VB_C, VB_B, VB_B max, VB_A, VB_N, notch wear, zones C, B, A, N, b/4; crater KF front distance, KB width, KM centre distance, KT depth, section A-A, plane P_s) [MC-U23 p.11].
  • Flank wear measurement [MC-U23 p.12]: VB_avg and VB_max are measured; VB_max is the maximum width of the central section of the wear land. Volume worn off the flank: v_w = VB_avg² · b · tan θ / 2 (θ relief angle, b width of cut); v_w is proportional to the contact area A and the sliding length L_s; specific wear rate η = (1/A)(dv/dL_s).
  • Crater wear measurement [MC-U23 p.13]: crater width KB, depth KT and crater land width KF are measured; crater volume v_cr = 2b(KB − KF)KT/3; specific crater wear rate η_cr = (2/3)(dKT/dL_c), L_c tool–chip contact length.
  • On-line tool-wear sensing (optical, pneumatic, electric, displacement, force) has been proposed; force- and power-based methods seem the most practical; in turning the axial and radial forces are much more sensitive to flank wear than the tangential force, so the ratio axial (or radial)/tangential force correlates strongly with flank wear [MC-U23 p.14].
  • p.11 Measurement of tool wear: microscopic and stylus instruments; specify the datum line in the cutting edge for both flank and crater wear; video image — several photos of the edge at different intervals; other techniques such as lapping down; "direct: on-line tool-wear sensing methods based on optical, pneumatic and electrical measurements"; "indirect (off-line): based on force, displacement, torque, power and motor measurements" (⚠ F42); axial and radial forces in turning are much more sensitive to flank wear than the tangential load; the ratio of axial (or radial) to tangential force correlates strongly with tool wear [MC-RT p.11].

7.4 Tool wear mechanisms

  • Tool wear mechanisms depend on the materials, tool geometry and cutting conditions, especially cutting speed [MC-U23 p.15]:
    1. Adhesive wear: small tool particles adhere/weld to the chip by friction and are removed; mainly on the rake face, contributing to crater wear; rates usually low, not normally significant; but significant adhesive wear may accompany BUE (also caused by adhesion) and can chip the tool; mainly when cutting soft work at low speeds (figure: weld/adhesion points) [MC-U23 p.16].
    2. Abrasive wear: hard particles abrade the tool, mainly at the flank face; particles such as adhering sand in sand-cast parts, iron carbide in martensite, austenite and other hard phases in steels, free silicon in Al–Si alloys, fibres in MMCs; usually the primary cause of flank, notch and nose radius wear, so it often controls tool life at low-to-medium speeds (figure: two-body abrasive wear) [MC-U23 p.17].
    • Adhesive and abrasive wear: v = k_w N L_s / H (v volume worn away, k_w wear coefficient, N force normal to the sliding interface, L_s distance slid, H penetration hardness of the tool). Both are reduced by increasing tool hardness and reducing the cutting forces; hardness is severely affected by temperature (thermal softening); at higher speeds temperature-activated mechanisms dominate — diffusion, oxidation, chemical wear [MC-U23 p.18].
    1. Diffusion (solution) wear: a tool constituent diffuses into or forms a solid solution with the chip; weakens the surface, giving crater wear on the rake face; severe cratering leads to breakage. Depends on the solubility of the tool material in the work, the chip–tool contact area and the cutting temperature; reduced by a less soluble tool grade (figures: tool atoms, interphase, chip flow; tungsten diffusion into steel) [MC-U23 p.19].
    2. Oxidation wear: tool constituents (especially the binder) react with atmospheric oxygen; most often near the free surface of the part where the hot tool region is exposed; often gives severe depth-of-cut notch formation, recognised by discoloured tool material near the notch; oxidised wear debris or work particles give hard oxides that increase abrasive wear (figure: machining pure copper — WC-Co tool, Co binder promotes oxidation (CoO, Co₃O₄), poor wear resistance; WC-FeAl tool, FeAl does not, superior wear resistance) [MC-U23 p.20].
    3. Chemical (corrosion) wear: chemical reactions between tool constituents and the work or cutting fluid; produces flank and crater wear; flank wear dominates as speed rises; scars are smooth compared with other mechanisms; observed with highly reactive materials such as titanium alloys; the tool surface layer becomes a soft reaction product that wears rapidly by abrasion; reduced by changing the tool material (or coating) or the fluid additives. A thin hard, chemically inert coating can reduce abrasive, diffusion, oxidation and chemical wear (figure: uniform, pitting, intergranular, subsurface attack) [MC-U23 p.21].
  • Overall tool wear vs cutting speed (figure): adhesion dominates at low speed, abrasion across the range, oxidation at medium-high, diffusion rising steeply at high speed [MC-U23 p.22].
  • Student summary of the mechanisms [MC-RW2]:
  • p.1 Causes (Arabic: أسباب) of the tool wear mechanism: (1) the materials of the cutting tool and work piece, (2) tool geometry, (3) cutting conditions, especially cutting speed. (1) Adhesion wear: small tool particles adhere or weld to the chip material (sketch of surfaces A and B welding); occurs on the rake face and forms crater wear; adhesion wear rates are low; adhesion may cause BUE; occurs when cutting soft (ductile) materials at low speed [MC-RW2 p.1].
  • p.2 (2) Abrasive wear: hard material abrades and removes tool material; results in flank, notch and nose radius wear; so abrasive wear controls tool life at "low to high" speed (overwritten from "medium to high", ⚠ F44). Both abrasive and adhesion wear may be reduced by increasing hardness and reducing the cutting force. As speed increases, temperature and wear increase, and temperature-activated diffusion, chemical wear and oxidation increase [MC-RW2 p.2].
  • p.3 (3) Diffusion and solution wear: tool material forms a solid solution with the chip material; occurs on the rake face, forming the crater wear (Arabic: بوابة — sketch of the crater); depends on the solubility of the tool material in the work material, the chip–tool contact area and the cutting temperature; reduced by changing to a less soluble grade. (4) Oxidation wear: tool material (especially the binder) reacts with atmospheric oxygen (sketch: tool hard particles in binder); results in notch wear, with the tool material typically discoloured near the notch; oxidation forms hard oxides — "Al₂O₃ (for aluminium material), Fe₃O₄ (for steel)" — which increase abrasive wear (extra abrasive wear) [MC-RW2 p.3] (the oxide examples are not in [MC-U23 p.20]; ⚠ F44).
  • p.4 (5) Chemical (corrosion) wear: reaction between tool and work or cutting fluid; produces both flank and crater wear; scars smooth compared with other mechanisms; appears with highly reactive materials such as titanium alloy; coating the tool with a thin layer can reduce abrasive, diffusion, oxidation and chemical wear. Arabic closing note: God willing, these will be the most important repeated exam questions on tool wear mechanisms; they will not go beyond these four pages [MC-RW2 p.4].

7.5 Tool-life testing and flank wear against time

  • Tool life testing [MC-U23 pp.23–25]:
    • the maximum average flank wear criterion is used extensively; in the ISO turning test tool life ends when average flank wear VB reaches 0.5 mm under roughing conditions;
    • flank wear rate is low and repeatable, so tools failing by flank wear have long, consistent lives; other forms of wear are unavoidable; flank wear must be measured off-line with a microscope [MC-U23 p.24];
    • standard tests apply mainly to steel and iron work cut with HSS or WC tools; the baseline material in many tests is 1045 steel; they were developed to rank WC/HSS tool grades or the machinability of steels and irons [MC-U23 p.25].
  • Flank wear vs cutting time: initial wear, steady wear, severe wear (figure; see mc2-tool-wear-curve.jpg) [MC-U23 p.26].
  • p.12 Tool life testing: when the average flank wear VB reaches 0.5 mm the tool cannot be used (sketch VB = 0.5 mm; Arabic: "very important"); flank wear vs cutting time: initial wear, steady-state wear, severe wear [MC-RT p.12].

7.6 Taylor tool-life equations

  • Taylor tool life equation: V Tⁿ = C_t (T tool life in min, V cutting speed, C_t empirical constant); n determines the slope; on log T vs log V the slope is 1/n (figure) [MC-U23 pp.27–28]. Values of n: HSS 0.1–0.17; uncoated WC 0.2–0.25; TiC or TiN 0.3; coated WC 0.4; Al₂O₃-coated WC 0.3; solid ceramic 0.4–0.6 [MC-U23 p.27].
  • Extended Taylor equation: V Tⁿ f^a d^b = K_t, accounting for feed and depth of cut; values of K_t, n, a, b are sometimes tabulated in tooling catalogues; "in general n < a < b because cutting speed has a larger influence on tool life than feed and depth of cut" [MC-U23 p.29] (⚠ F35).
  • p.13 Taylor tool life curve: VTⁿ = C_t → log V + n log T = log C_t → x + ny = a → (1/n)x + y = a; slope 1/n on log T vs log V; log V = log C_t − n log T; n = (log V1 − log V4)/(log T4 − log T1) [MC-RT p.13].
  • Tool-life problems with a speed change (percentage change of life for −20 % and +30 % speed, using n = 0.237) are worked in §9.4 [MC-F23 pp.4–5; MC-F24 pp.7–8].

7.7 Example 9.1: Taylor parameters for a new carbide insert

  • Example 9.1 (Taylor parameters for a new carbide insert; alloy steel, ISO 3685; d = 2.54 mm, f = 0.18 mm/rev; tests at 90, 120, 150, 180 m/min) [MC-U23 pp.32–37; MC-RT pp.14–15]. Table 9.3 flank wear data (tool test: speed; time min → VB mm):
    • Test 1, 180 m/min: 1 → 0.14; 2 → 0.35; 3 → 0.49; 4 → 0.64.
    • Test 2, 150 m/min: 2 → 0.18; 4 → 0.3; 6 → 0.46; 8 → 0.66.
    • Test 3, 120 m/min: 2 → 0.11; 4 → 0.16; 6 → 0.23; 8 → 0.29; 12 → 0.37; 15 → 0.47; 20 → 0.71.
    • Test 4, 90 m/min: 6 → 0.11; 12 → 0.21; 25 → 0.27; 35 → 0.31; 40 → 0.37; 45 → 0.42; 50 → 0.5; 55 → 0.6; 60 → 0.78 [MC-U23 p.33].
    • Method of intercepts: tool life = intercept of each wear curve with the wear limit VB = 0.5 mm (Fig. 9.29) [MC-U23 p.34]. Table 9.4: 90 m/min → 50 min; 120 → 16; 150 → 6; 180 → 3 [MC-U23 p.35]. Fig. 9.30 linear plot and Fig. 9.31 log–log plot (straight line; C_t = V at T = 1) [MC-U23 p.35].
    • log V = log C_t − n log T; n = (log V1 − log V4)/(log T4 − log T1) = (log 90 − log 180)/(log 3 − log 50) = 0.25 (⚠ F36) [MC-U23 p.35].
    • C_t = V T1ⁿ = … = V T4ⁿ = (180)(3)^0.25 = 237 → V T^0.25 = 237 [MC-U23 p.36–37].
  • pp.14–15 Ex. (Table 9.4): 90 → 50 min, 120 → 16, 150 → 6, 180 → 3; plotted T (min) against V (m/min) (curve through points 1–4), and log T vs log V (straight line); n = (log 90 − log 180)/(log 3 − log 50) = 0.246 ≈ 0.25; C_t = (180)(3)^0.25 ≈ 237; VT^0.25 = 237 [MC-RT pp.14–15].

7.8 Tool wear monitoring

  • Tool wear monitoring [MC-U23 pp.30–31]: protects the machine from collision, missing tools, breakage or wear; direct methods measure wear/volumetric loss (radioactive, optical, laser scan micrometer, electrical resistance sensors); indirect methods relate wear to part quality, surface roughness, force or torque, motor power (current), acoustic emission, vibration; all use sophisticated signal processing; performance depends on transducer data quality and signal processing; multiple sensors often improve reliability (figure: CNC, processing unit, force amplifier, force transducer plate, turret, feed drive system, tool status and machine control signals).

Tool materials, surface finish and economics (partly covered)

  • Tool materials — Table 4 softening points (after Kramer, J. Eng. for Industry 109 (1987) 87–91): HSS 600 °C; cemented carbide (WC) 1100 °C; aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) 1400 °C; CBN 1500 °C; diamond 1500 °C. Coated cutting tools (carbide-coated tool: special lubricating film, AlCrTi anti-oxide film, Ti-Al wear-resistant film, high-strength carbide substrate) [MC-U23 p.23].
  • Taylor exponents n by tool material (HSS, uncoated and coated WC, ceramics) are listed in §7.6 [MC-U23 p.27].
  • Surface finish: the sources give only qualitative statements: severe nose-radius wear degrades the finish [MC-U23 p.7; MC-RT p.10; MC-F22 p.3] (theoretical vs real profile sketch), and the chip-type notes in §2.2. Machining economics and machinability ratings are not in the sources (see "Not covered by the sources").

9.1 Cutting questions and answers [MC-Q]

  • Q1 [MC-Q pp.1–2]: (1) types of chips (§2.2); (2) copying vs generation (§1.4); (3) advantages and disadvantages of machining (§1.2).
  • Q2 [MC-Q pp.2–4]: (1) advantages and disadvantages of taper turning, with a sketch (§5.2); (2) sketch the work-holding methods (§5.2); (3) "2 types of motion in turning" (§5.2, ⚠ F18).
  • Q3 [MC-Q pp.5–8]: (1) milling vs drilling (§5.1); (2) purpose of the quick-return mechanism, with a sketch (§5.6); (3) compare shaper, planer and slotter (§5.6); (4) classify peripheral milling by direction of rotation, up/down (§5.5).
  • The answers given in the file are summarised in the sections quoted.

9.2 Oral-exam multiple-choice questions [MC-GQO]

  1. Common features of machining: (a) a cutting tool forms a chip removed from the work; (b) relative motion between tool and work; (c) both (a) and (b) [MC-GQO p.1].
  2. Which is a machining operation: blanking / deep drawing / bending / drilling [MC-GQO p.1].
  3. Machine tools are used to: hold the workpiece / position the tool relative to the work / none / both (a) and (b) [MC-GQO p.1].
  4. Methods of holding the work in a lathe: chuck / collet / faceplate / all of the above [MC-GQO p.1].
  5. Operation that creates a round hole: drilling / casting / grinding / milling [MC-GQO p.2].
  6. Disadvantage of machining: wasteful of material / time consuming / high energy consumption / all of them [MC-GQO p.2].
  7. Cutting tools must be made of materials ___ than the work: harder / softer / softer / equal in hardness [MC-GQO p.2] (options b and c are identical as printed).
  8. Force (a) in the orthogonal-cutting figure (arrow along the shear plane, chip/tool/work, t0, tc, φ): normal / shear force / compressive / frictional [MC-GQO p.3].
  9. Work fed past a rotating cylindrical tool with multiple edges: drilling / milling / boring / grinding [MC-GQO p.3].
  10. The milling tool is called a ___ and its edges ___: tool–edges / cylinder–teeth / milling cutter – teeth / none [MC-GQO p.3].

9.3 Dr. El-Gohary's questions with student answers [MC-GQD]

  • p.1 "The orthogonal cutting model system": two sketches — 3-D (chip, tool, t0, tc, workpiece) and 2-D (chip, tc, t0, ls, φ, rake angle α, wedge angle, clearance angle γ, w.p., primary shear zone, secondary shear zone); faint text at the bottom repeats the tan φ and γ calculation of p.2 [MC-GQD p.1].
  • p.2 Ex.: orthogonal cutting, rake 10°, t0 = 0.50 mm, tc = 1.125 mm (the "given" list writes "1.125 in", ⚠ F26); find the shear-plane angle and shear strain. Solution: r = t0/tc = 0.5/1.125 = 0.444; tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α) = 0.444 cos 10/(1 − 0.444 sin 10) → φ = 25.4°; γ = tan(φ − α) + cot φ = tan(25.4 − 10) + cot 25.4 = 2.38 [MC-GQD p.2]. (Same data as Example 1.1 [MC-G1 p.5], which prints 2.386; see checks.)
  • p.3 Q: Effect of a higher shear plane angle? (ماذا تعني أن زاوية الـ shear كبيرة؟) Answer: a higher shear plane angle means a smaller shear plane, which means lower shear force, cutting force, power and temperature. Sketches compare a large φ (thin chip tc) with a small φ (thick chip) [MC-GQD p.3].
  • p.4 Ex. 2: turning stainless steel 200 HB, v = 200 m/min, f = 0.25 mm/rev, d = 7.5 mm, mechanical efficiency 90 %; power drawn? Use Table 21.2 for specific energy (Arabic margin: U_s is taken from the table, which will be given). U_s = 2.8 N·m/mm³ = 2.8 J/mm³; MRR = A_chip × V_c = f d V_c = 0.25 × 200 × 10³ × 7.5 = 375,000 mm³/min = 6250 mm³/s; P_c = U_s × MRR = 2.8 × 6250 = 17,500 W = 17.5 kW; P_g = P_c/η = 17.5/0.9 = 19.44 kW [MC-GQD p.4]. (Same as Example 2 [MC-G12 p.41].)
  • pp.5–6 Q: What types of milling and drilling? (support your answer by sketch). There are two basic types of milling, peripheral and face milling [MC-GQD p.5].
    • (A) peripheral milling, with sketches: (1) slab, (2) slotting, (3) side, (4) straddle, (5) form milling [MC-GQD p.5].
    • (B) face milling, with sketches: (1) end milling, (2) pocket milling, (3) partial (face) milling, (4) conventional face milling [MC-GQD p.6].
  • p.7 Types of drilling (i.e. operations related to drilling), with sketches: (1) reaming, (2) tapping, (3) counterboring, (4) countersinking, (5) spot facing [MC-GQD p.7].
  • p.8 "Figure 22.18": types of peripheral milling — slab, slotting, side, straddle, form — "with sketch"; in peripheral milling there are two forms, up milling and down milling (sketches: cutter rotation against / with the feed arrow) [MC-GQD p.8].

9.4.1 Final 2022–2023, Part (II) [MC-F23]
  • No. 4, true/false [MC-F23 pp.1–2] (the statements are not given; the answer notes are):
    • (1) True; the sketch marks the maximum temperature on the face of the cutting tool (Arabic: "here is the max temp, on the face of the cutting tool") [p.1]. Compare "about halfway up the tool face" [MC-U21 p.5].
    • (2) True; "heat flux" (Arabic: this is the heat-flux method), with a sketch of a lathe, tool, coolant pipes and pump [p.1]. Compare [MC-U21 p.10].
    • (3) False; "are higher for work mat. as … are increased" (the words in the gap are missing) [p.1].
    • (4) True; "ρC ↑, K ↑" [p.1].
    • (5) False; "when machined hard materials" [p.1].
    • (6) False; "increase the nose radius decreases the peak temp. as it reduces the uncut chip thickness" [p.1]. Compare [MC-U22 p.9].
    • (7) and (9): مذكور في (covered elsewhere; [MC-RW1 p.4] says items 7 and 9 are solved in the Final 11/1/2022, i.e. §9.4.3) [pp.1–2].
    • (8) True [p.2].
    • (10) True; "as the rake angle increases and reduces the cutting force" [p.2].
    • (11) False; "increase the generated cutting forces" [p.2].
    • (12)–(15): مذكور في "cutting fluid" (not in the set) [p.2].
  • No. 5 [MC-F23 pp.2–3]: (a) and (b) مذكور في "cutting fluid" [p.2].
    • 5(c), Trigger equation [p.3]: V1 = 120 m/min → T1 = 515 °C; V2 = 160 → 570 °C; V3 = 180 → 600 °C; find the Trigger equation T = K V^m. Solution: ln T = ln K + m ln V for the three points; equations (1) and (3): ln 515 − ln 600 = m(ln 120 − ln 180) → m = 0.38; then ln 515 = ln K + 0.38 ln 120 gives K = 83.5 (the last digit is written over) and T = 83.5 V^0.38. Sketch: log T against log V is a straight line with slope m and intercept a.
  • No. 6 [MC-F23 pp.4–5]: (a) "cutting fluid and wear mechanism" and (b) are مذكور في (RW1 p.4 says 6(a) is solved in Final 2024 and 6(b) in Final 11/1/2022) [p.4].
    • 6(c), Taylor tool-life equation [pp.4–5]. The data table is not reproduced (⚠ F47). The solution takes V1 = 100 m/min with T1 = 60 min and V4 = 190 m/min with T4 = 4 min. n = (log V1 − log V4)/(log T4 − log T1) = (log 100 − log 190)/(log 4 − log 60) = 0.237. C_t = V T^n = (60^0.237)(100) = 263.889, so V T^0.237 = 264.
    • Speed reduced by 20 %: V2 = 0.8 V, and V1/V2 = (T2/T1)^n gives T2 = 2.56 T, an increase of 156 % [p.4].
    • Speed increased by 30 %: V2 = 1.3 V, and V1/V2 = (T2/T1)^0.237 gives T2 = 0.33 T, a reduction of 67 % [p.5].
9.4.2 Final 2023–2024 [MC-F24]
  • No. 1 [MC-F24 pp.1–3] (turning and milling):
    • (a) Uncut chip thickness and cutting-edge engagement length, with the turning sketch (chuck, work-piece, tool, N, V, d, f, lead angle K, a, L): cos K = a/f, so a = f cos K; cos K = d/L, so L = d/cos K [p.1].
    • (b) Chip thinning phenomenon in face milling: four sketches at 100 %, 50 %, 20 % and 10 % radial engagement, each marking the average chip thickness a_avg. Arabic note: the smaller the engagement (contact), the smaller the average chip thickness [p.1]. Values are in [MC-3 p.16] (§5.5).
    • (c) Data: D0 = 40 mm, U_s = 0.065 kW/(cm³/min), K = 20°, f = 0.3 mm/rev, d = 3 mm, V = 60 m/min; find (a) MRR, (b) power, (c) torque, (d) a and L [p.2].
      • a = f cos K = 0.3 cos 20° = 0.282 mm; L = d/cos K = 3/cos 20° = 3.1925 mm; A_chip = a·L = (0.282)(3.1925) = 0.9 mm², or A_chip = f·d = (0.3)(3) = 0.9 mm² [p.2].
      • Q = MRR = A_chip·V_c = 0.9 × 60 × 1000 = 54,000 mm³/min = 5.4 × 10⁻⁵ m³/min = 54 cm³/min [p.2].
      • P = U_s·Q = 54 × 0.065 = 3.51 kW [p.2].
      • D1 from d = (D0 − D1)/2: 3 = (40 − D1)/2, so D1 = 34 mm; N = 2V/(π(D1 + D0)) = 2 × 60 × 1000/(π(40 + 34)) = 516.178 rpm [p.3].
      • T = P/ω = P/(2πN) = 3.51 × 10³/(2π(516.178)/60) = 64.94 N·m [p.3].
  • No. 2 [MC-F24 pp.3–5] (cutting temperature):
    • (a) Effects: (1) affects the strength, hardness and wear resistance of the cutting tool; (2) damages the machined surface; (3) temperature causes distortion; (4) temperature causes dimensional change in the work-piece; and (5, starred) the dissipated energy is converted into heat that raises the temperature in the cutting region, at (a) the tool–work-piece interface (rubbing), (b) the tool–chip interface (friction), (c) the primary shear zone (shearing); sketch labels: chip, tool–chip interface, tool–w.p. interface, shear zone [p.3].
    • (b) The conventional thermocouple method [p.4]: in turning, the chuck side and the tool are insulated, a copper brush touches the work and a millivoltmeter is connected between brush and tool; in milling, an end mill with cutting speed V and N and thermocouples embedded in the work-piece (sketch).
    • (c) Trigger equation with the same data as [MC-F23 p.3] (120 → 515 °C, 160 → 570 °C, 180 → 600 °C) [p.5]: equations (1) and (3) give m = 0.377; ln 515 = ln K + 0.377 ln 120 gives K = 85; T = 85 V^0.377 (⚠ F41).
  • No. 3 [MC-F24 pp.6–8] (tool wear):
    • (a) Flank wear vs crater wear [p.6]. Flank wear: (1) occurs at the relief face; (2) caused by rubbing between the work-piece and the cutting tool; (3) leads to abrasion; (4) increases the rubbing and the cutting force; (5) increases the deflection and gives inaccurate dimensions. Crater wear: (1) occurs at the rake face; (2) occurs due to temperature diffusion and the chemical wear mechanism; (3) crater formation increases the rake angle, decreases the cutting force and decreases the wedge angle, which weakens the tool and leads to fracture. Sketches: crater wear with the rake angle increased and the wedge angle decreased; a 3-D tool with crater wear, notch wear, flank wear, nose radius wear and edge chipping (fritting).
    • (b) Tool wear mechanism: مذكور في (covered elsewhere) [p.7].
    • (c) Taylor [pp.7–8]: (a) write the Taylor equation, V Tⁿ = C_t; (b) find the percentage increase in tool life if the cutting speed is reduced by 20 %. As in [MC-F23 p.4]: n = (log 100 − log 190)/(log 4 − log 60) = 0.237; C_t = (60^0.237)(100) = 263.889 (a first value, 178.41, is struck out), giving T V^0.237 = 263.889 (⚠ F50). With V2 = 0.8 V: T1/T2 = (V2/V1)^(1/n) (equivalently V1/V2 = (T2/T1)^n) gives T2 = 2.56 T, a 156 % increase. A first attempt, T2 = T/0.8 = 1.25 T, is struck out.
9.4.3 Final of 11/1/2022 [MC-F22]
  • No. 4, true/false [MC-F22 pp.1–2]:
    • (1) True; "by using heat flux", with the sketch of a lathe, tool, coolant pipes and pump [p.1].
    • (2) False; "are higher for harder mat." [p.1].
    • (3) True [p.1].
    • (4) False; "reduce the peak temp." [p.1].
    • (5) مذكور في (covered elsewhere; [MC-RW1 p.2] solves item 5 as False, see below) [p.1].
    • (6) True; Arabic gloss: increasing the crater increases the rake angle, which reduces the cutting force; the rest of the gloss, about the tool strength, is only partly legible (⚠ F49) [p.1].
    • (7) مذكور في (covered elsewhere; [MC-RW1 p.2] solves item 7 as True, see below) [p.2].
    • (8) True [p.2].
    • (9) False; "relief face" (i.e. the correct location is the relief face) [p.2].
    • (10) False [p.2].
  • No. 5-A, factors affecting the cutting temperature [MC-F22 pp.2–3]:
    • (A) Cutting speed and feed: (1) increasing them increases the energy dissipated (heat); (2) the cutting speed has a greater influence than the feed [p.2].
    • (B) Mechanical properties: (1) cutting temperatures are higher for hard materials as the force and energy increase; (2) for materials of the same hardness the temperature increases with ductility [p.2].
    • (C) Thermal properties of the material (thermal conductivity K and thermal capacity ρC): the answer reads "increases the thermal conductivity and thermal capacity of work piece increases the temp." (⚠ F45) [p.2].
    • (D) Nose radius: increasing the nose radius reduces the peak temperature by reducing the uncut chip thickness; "and reduce the wedge angle by increasing the rake angle" (the sentence is left without its effect, ⚠ F46) [p.3].
  • No. 5-B [MC-F22 p.3]: a heading "affect cutting temp." (with an arrow from the nose-radius note) and the answer "affect the dimensional accuracy as the nose radius wear can degrade the surface finish of the cutting edge"; sketches: work-piece with theoretical and real profile against the tool, and a tool with nose radius wear (⚠ F46).
  • No. 5-C [MC-F22 p.4]: solved in the Final 2024 (تم حلها في Final 2024).
  • No. 6-A, flank wear vs crater wear [MC-F22 p.4]. Flank wear: (1) occurs at the relief face; (2) leads to abrasion of the cutting edge; (3) caused by rubbing between the cutting tool and work-piece; (4) increases the rubbing and friction heat; (5) increases the deflection and gives inaccurate dimensions. Crater wear: (1) occurs at the rake face; (2) due to temperature diffusion and the chemical wear mechanism; (3) crater formation increases the rake angle, decreases the cutting force and reduces the wedge angle, which weakens the cutting tool and leads to fracture. Sketches as in [MC-F24 p.6] (crater wear, notch wear, flank wear, chipping wear, nose radius wear; rake angle increased, wedge angle decreased).
  • No. 6-B and 6-C [MC-F22 p.4]: 6-B is مذكور في (the target is not legible; [MC-RW1 p.3] solves "No. 6(B)"); 6-C is solved in the Final 2024.
  • Answers recorded in [MC-RW1] (same exam family):
  • p.1 Final 2024, No. 3(b): State the factors affecting the diffusion (solution) wear mechanism of the cutting tool. Answer: diffusion wear depends on (1) the solubility of the cutting-tool material in the work material, (2) the contact area of the tool–chip interface, (3) the cutting temperature (sketch: atoms moving between chip material B and tool material A) [MC-RW1 p.1].
  • p.2 Final 11/1/2022, No. 4 (true/false): (5) "Abrasive wear controls the tool life especially at high speed" — False, especially at low to medium speed. (7) "Oxidation wear can be recognized by discoloring the tool tip near the free surface of the work piece" — True (Arabic: the free surface meant is the flank surface; the notch and the discolouring occur in the region near the notch, i.e. at the free surface) [MC-RW1 p.2].
  • p.3 No. 6(B): At high cutting speed values, demonstrate which type of tool wear mechanism is dominating the tool wear process (Arabic gloss: المسيطرة). Answer: as cutting speed increases the temperature increases, wear increases, and the temperature-activated diffusion, chemical wear and oxidation increase. Sketch of tool wear vs cutting speed (low, medium, high speed; adhesion, abrasive, oxidation, diffusion bands): "from the graph we find that diffusion wear mechanism is dominating" (with oxidation) at high speed [MC-RW1 p.3].
  • p.4 2022–2023 final (31/12/2022) cross-references: No. 6(a) solved in Final 2024; No. 6(b) solved in Final 11/1/2022; No. 4 true/false items 9 and 7 solved in Final 11/1/2022 [MC-RW1 p.4].

9.6 Course and exam advice from a previous student [MC-IMP], and a cover page [MC-MS]

Study advice from a previous student, not course content; recorded because a TA may find it useful context.

  • The subject is described as the easiest subject of the term; 150 marks: 60 coursework (أعمال سنة) and 90 final [MC-IMP p.1].
  • Taught by Dr. Ahmed Shaker and Dr. Ahmed Ibrahim, both described as very good in explanation and dealing [MC-IMP p.1].
  • Dr. Ahmed Shaker's part is described as very easy and already studied in full in first-year Production (إنتاج سنة أولى) [MC-IMP p.1]; Dr. Ahmed Ibrahim's part has some things studied before and some new [MC-IMP p.2].
  • Advice: for Dr. Shaker's part study the lectures only; for Dr. Ibrahim's part make or use a summary (a colleague's "ملخصات" is recommended) [MC-IMP p.2].
  • Mid-term and final exams are described as regular/predictable, except that Dr. Ibrahim sometimes includes a true/false section; there are no sections (سكاشن) for this subject; for Dr. Ibrahim's part focus on previous years' exams (study the part first, then solve the exams); attend lectures because Dr. Ibrahim sometimes gives quizzes [MC-IMP p.3].
  • The single page is a cover: "شرح اخر مسألتين في محاضره (Milling)" (explanation of the last two problems in the lecture), "م/احمد الصعيدي", and a Google Drive folder link. No solution content is in the file; the linked folder was not opened (no network use) [MC-MS p.1].

Calculator candidates

  1. Turning: MRR, spindle/motor power, torque, chip thickness [MC-1 pp.14–15, pp.19–21; MC-2 p.8]
    • Inputs: D1 (mm), d (mm), f (mm/rev), V (m/min), κ (°), u_s (kW·min/cm³, Table 2.1), η.
    • Chain: D2 = D1 − 2d → N = 2V/(π(D1 + D2)) (rpm) → Q = V·f·d (mm³/min; ÷1000 for cm³/min) → P_s = Q·u_s (kW) → P_m = P_s/η → T = P_s/(2πN) (with N in rev/s) → a = f cos κ → L_m = d/cos κ.
    • Outputs: N, Q, P_s, P_m, T, a, L_m.
  2. Facing: time and maximum power [MC-2 pp.10–12]
    • Inputs: D_o, D_i (mm), d (mm), f (mm/rev), N (rpm), u_s.
    • Chain: Q_max = πD_o·N·f·d → P = Q·u_s → t_m = (D_o − D_i)/(2fN) → F_c = P/(πND_o).
  3. Drilling: MRR, time, torque [MC-2 pp.15–20]
    • Inputs: D (mm), point angle 2ρ (°), f (mm/rev), V (m/min), L (mm), ΔL (mm), u_s, n_t; optional D_i for core drilling.
    • Chain: N = V/(πD) → f_r = fN → Q = (π(D² − D_i²)/4)·f_r → L_e = D/(2 tan ρ) + ΔL → t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r → P = Q·u_s → T = P/(2πN) → b = (D − D_i)/(2 sin ρ), f_t = f/n_t, a = f_t sin ρ.
  4. Peripheral/slot milling: feed from power and chip limit, time [MC-3 pp.3–8]
    • Inputs: D (mm), n_t, V (m/min), d (radial, mm), b (axial, mm), a_max (mm), κ (°), P_avail (kW), u_s, L (mm), allowance (mm, default 5).
    • Chain: N = V/(πD) → cos ν_m = 1 − 2d/D → f_t,chip = a_max/(cos κ sin ν_m) → f_t,power = (P/u_s)/(d·b·n_t·N) → f_t = min(both) → f_r = n_t·f_t·N → MRR = f_r·b·d → L_e = 2(√(d(D − d)) + allowance) → t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r.
  5. Face milling: feed and time (symmetrical/asymmetrical) [MC-3 pp.9–14, pp.22–24]
    • Inputs: D, n_t, V, allowable a (mm), κ (°), b (mm), d (mm), L (mm), A_p, O_t.
    • Chain: N = V/(πD) → f_t = a/cos κ → f_r = n_t·f_t·N → L_c = D/2 (symmetrical) or √(b(D − b)) (asymmetrical) → L_e = 2L_c + A_p + O_t (or L_e,min = D/2 − ½√(D² − b²) per p.24) → t_m = (L + L_e)/f_r → MRR = f_r·b·d.
  6. Lathe slideway forces and face widths [MC-P pp.1–5]
    • Inputs: P_z, P_y, G (kgf or N), b, h, d (same length unit), α (°, with β = 90° − α), allowable pressure p, carriage length ℓ.
    • Chain: A, B, C from the three closed forms in §4.5 → widths A/(pℓ), B/(pℓ), C/(pℓ).
  7. Orthogonal cutting: shear angle, strain, forces, friction [MC-G1 pp.5–8; MC-G12 pp.39–41]
    • Inputs: t0, tc (mm), α (°), w (mm), Fc, Ft (N).
    • Chain: r = t0/tc → tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α) → γ = tan(φ − α) + cot φ; F = Fc sin α + Ft cos α; N = Fc cos α − Ft sin α; Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ; Fn = Fc sin φ + Ft cos φ; As = t0 w/sin φ; τ = Fs/As; μ = F/N = tan β; Merchant φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2 (β = 90° + α − 2φ).
    • Outputs: r, φ, γ, F, N, Fs, Fn, τ, β, μ.
  8. Cutting power and specific energy [MC-G1 pp.8–9; MC-G12 pp.36–42; MC-GQD p.4]
    • Inputs: v (m/min), t0 (mm), w or d (mm), Fc (N) or U (N·m/mm³), η.
    • Chain: R_MR = v·t0·w (mm³/min; ÷60 for mm³/s) → Pc = Fc·v (W) or Pc = U·R_MR → Pg = Pc/η → U = Fc/(t0 w). Optional worn-tool factor 1.0–1.25 and the t0 correction of Fig. 1.9.
  9. Cutting temperature: Trigger fit and Cook estimate [MC-U22 pp.10–19; MC-G12 pp.44–47; MC-F23 p.3; MC-F24 p.5]
    • Trigger inputs: pairs (V, T) (two or more). Chain: m = (ln T1 − ln T2)/(ln V1 − ln V2); K = T1/V1^m; T(V) = K V^m (least squares for three or more points).
    • Cook inputs: U (N·m/mm³), ρ (g/cm³), C (cal/g·°C or J/g·°C), k (J/s·mm·°C), v (m/s), t0 (mm), ambient temperature. Chain: ρC (J/mm³·°C, with ρ in g/mm³ and C × 4.186 J/cal) → K = k/(ρC) (mm²/s) → ΔT = (0.4U/ρC)(v t0/K)^0.333 with v in mm/s → T = ambient + ΔT.
  10. Taylor tool life: fit and speed-change effect [MC-U23 pp.27–37; MC-RT pp.13–15; MC-F23 pp.4–5; MC-F24 pp.7–8]
    • Fit inputs: pairs (V, T). Chain: n = (log V1 − log V4)/(log T4 − log T1) (or the slope of the log–log fit) → C_t = V·Tⁿ.
    • Speed-change inputs: n, percentage change p of speed. Chain: T2/T1 = (V1/V2)^(1/n) = (1 + p/100)^(−1/n) → percentage change of life = (T2/T1 − 1) × 100.
    • Extended equation V Tⁿ f^a dᵇ = K_t (solve for V or T when K_t, n, a, b are given, [MC-U23 p.29]).
  11. Machining time and MRR in the El-Gohary formulation [MC-G31 pp.10–12; MC-G41 pp.3, 13–15; MC-GD p.2]
    • Turning: N = v/(πD0), Df = D0 − 2d, f_r = N f, Tm = L/f_r = πD0 L/(f v), R_MR = v f d.
    • Drilling: A = 0.5 D tan(90° − θ/2), Tm = (t + A)/f_r (through hole) or (d + A)/f_r (blind hole), R_MR = πD² f_r/4; drill speed V = πDN/1000 (V in m/min, D in mm).
    • Milling: f_r = N n_t f, R_MR = w d f_r; slab A = √(d(D − d)); face milling centred A = 0.5(D − √(D² − w²)) or offset A = √(w(D − w)); Tm = (L + A)/f_r.
  12. Tool-wear volumes [MC-U23 pp.12–13]
    • Flank: v_w = VB_avg²·b·tan θ/2; specific wear rate η = (1/A)(dv/dL_s). Crater: v_cr = 2b(KB − KF)KT/3; η_cr = (2/3)(dKT/dL_c).
  13. Thermal property cross-check [MC-U21 pp.13–16]
    • Inputs: k (W/m·K), ρ (kg/m³), c (J/kg·K). Outputs: diffusivity k/(ρc) and effusivity √(kρc); heat capacity C = Q/ΔT; Q = m c ΔT. (Item 6's add-on: the cutting ratio r_cu = a1/a2 with a1 = s sin φ [MC-1 pp.16–18] is trivial; the orthogonal-cutting relations that were missing in pass 1 are now in item 7.)

⚠ Flags

Each flag gives what the source says, what I believe is correct, and a one-line check.

  • F1 [MC-1 p.21]: L_m = "(doc)s(κ) = (4 mm)s(20) = 4.257 mm". It should read sec κ, i.e. doc/cos κ. [MC-2 p.8] reprints the slide with "(doc)/cos(k)". Check: 4/cos 20° = 4.2567.
  • F2 [MC-1 p.20 = MC-2 p.7]: The solution calls u_s = 0.065 kW/(cm³/min) "the average value" from Table 2.1. The cast-iron range is 0.044–0.08, whose midpoint is 0.062; 0.065 is the value given in the problem statement. Check: (0.044 + 0.08)/2 = 0.062. The result, 7.28 kW, follows the stated 0.065 and stands.
  • F3 [MC-1 p.20]: N = 485 rpm is printed. 2(70,000)/(π·92) = 484.4 rpm, so this is a rounding issue only; T is 143.5 N·m either way.
  • F4 [MC-2 p.11]: The unit is printed "0.025 W·min/cm³". It should be kW·min/cm³ (the statement on p.10 has kW). Check: 502 × 0.025 = 12.55, which is in kW. Also, 502,400 uses π = 3.14; the exact value is 502,655 mm³/min.
  • F5 [MC-2 p.12]: I is printed "73.594×106 mm⁴"; it should be ×10⁶. With exact π the value is 73.63 × 10⁶ mm⁴. δ = 0.034 mm is unaffected.
  • F6 [MC-2 p.13], method, please confirm with the lecturer: The solution takes tan α_δ = δ/L. A cantilever with an end load has end slope F L²/(2EI) = 1.5δ/L. If the face tilt equals the tube-end slope, x = 200 × 1.5 × 0.034/500 = 0.0204 mm, not 0.0136 mm. Check: θ_end/(δ/L) = (FL²/2EI)/(FL²/3EI) = 1.5.
  • F7 [MC-G12 p.41, p.42; MC-GQD p.4]: Example 2 (stainless steel 200 HB) takes U = 2.8 N·m/mm³ "from Table 21.2", but Table 21.2 [MC-G12 p.42] lists stainless steels at 3.0–5.2 W·s/mm³ (1.1–1.9 hp·min/in³). The value 2.8 is the stainless-steel entry of Table 1.1 [MC-G1 p.9]. The results (17.5 kW cutting, 19.44 kW gross) follow the value used. Check: 2.8 lies outside 3.0–5.2; with 3.0 the powers would be 18.75 kW and 20.83 kW (not in the source).
  • F8 [MC-2 p.20]: MRR is printed "[p(10)²/4]"; it should be π(10)²/4. Check: 78.54 × 0.3 × 6366 = 150,000 mm³/min = 150 cm³/min ✔.
  • F9 [MC-2 p.20]: t_m uses L_e = D/tan ρ + ΔL, but the lecture formula [MC-2 p.16–17] is L_e = D/(2 tan ρ) + ΔL. Also, the statement gives approach = overtravel = 3 mm each, but the solution uses ΔL = 3 mm in total, while ΔL is defined as approach plus overtravel [MC-2 p.16].
    • Check with the lecture formula: ΔL = 3 gives (30 + 2.887 + 3)/1909.9 = 0.0188 min = 1.13 s; ΔL = 6 gives 0.0204 min = 1.22 s.
    • The printed 1.2 s matches only by coincidence (D/tan ρ with ΔL = 3 gives 1.22 s).
  • F10 [MC-3 p.17, p.20]: u_s is printed "0.08 KW·min/mm³". It should be kW·min/cm³: 0.08 per mm³ is 1000 times the Table 2.1 steel range. Check: Table 2.1 lists steels at 0.05–0.2 kW/(cm³/min). The value is not used, since only MRR is asked.
  • F11 [MC-3 p.7]: The text line reads "0.07 W·min/cm³", while the equation line has "KW" pasted over it. It should be kW·min/cm³. N = 128 rpm is printed; 80,000/(3.14 × 200) = 127.4, so 127 (rounding only).
  • F12 [MC-3 p.8], typos: "n_max = 32°" should be ν_max; "(128 mm/min)" should be rpm.
  • F12 [MC-3 p.8], two answers: The slide gives two answers for (b), and both are arithmetically right for their own assumptions.
    • The printed book solution: overtravel ≈ 0 and 10 mm total allowance, giving 35.7 s.
    • The handwritten "please check" solution follows the lecture convention [MC-3 p.5] (L_a = L_o = √(d(D − d)) + 5 mm), with exact N = 127.32 rpm and f_r = 774.1 mm/min, giving 39.9 s.
    • Please confirm which convention the exam expects. Check: (400 + 2 × 57.68)/774.13 = 0.6657 min = 39.94 s.
  • F13 [MC-3 p.15]: For KAPR 45° the figure prints h = 0.75f_z. It should be about 0.71f_z. Check: sin 45° = 0.707. The 75° value, 0.96 = sin 75°, is consistent; so is [MC-1 p.12], where 0.87h = cos 30°.
  • F14 [MC-3 p.18]: f_r = (3)(0.26)(1038) is printed as 747 mm/min. It should be 809.6 mm/min; 747 corresponds to f_t = 0.24. MRR then becomes 3 × 46 × 809.6 = 111,730 mm³/min, against the printed 103,136. The printed product (3)(46)(747) is itself 103,086, not 103,136. Check: 3 × 0.26 × 1038 = 809.64.
  • F15 [MC-3 p.21]: MRR = (6)(11)(2232 mm/min) = 147,312 mm³/min uses the spindle speed (2232 rpm) as the feed rate. With f_r = 1027 mm/min from the line above, MRR = 6 × 11 × 1027 = 67,782 mm³/min.
  • F16 [MC-3 p.11, p.13 vs p.9]: The symmetrical and asymmetrical face-milling formulas omit cos κ (a_i = f_t sin ν_i). The general face-milling slide [MC-3 p.9] has a_i = f_t cos κ sin ν_i, and Example 2.7 uses f_t = a/cos κ [MC-3 p.23]. pp.11/13 therefore implicitly assume κ = 0. This is a consistency note; check that p.9 with κ = 0 reduces to p.11.
  • F17 [MC-P p.2]: The elimination step assumes α + β = 90°, which holds only for a 90° V-way. It is satisfied in the exam problem (α = β = 45°), but the final A, B, C forms are not general.
    • Also, p.4 writes "B cos²α − P cos α"; it should be P_y cos α.
    • The moment equation's P_z·d/2 term is written "∓"; the derivation takes "−".
    • Check: solving the three equilibrium equations numerically with β = 90° − α reproduces the source's A, B, C exactly (verified for random inputs).
  • F18 [MC-Q p.4]: The question says "2 types of motion", but the answer lists four items. Item 2, "linear motion of the tool perpendicular to w.p axis (for cylindrical w.p)", should say parallel to the axis. Check: the turning figure [MC-1 p.14] shows the feed along the axis, and facing, the perpendicular case, is item 3 [MC-2 p.9].
  • F19 [MC-Q p.7]: In the feed-motion row, the English says "reciprocating motion" (of the W.P. for shaper and slotter, of the tool for planer). The Arabic under the same cells says الحركة العرضية (transverse motion), and "reciprocating" is already the cutting-motion row. I believe feed is the transverse motion, as the Arabic says. Check: compare the cutting-motion row directly above it.
  • F20 [MC-G1 p.7]: the first form of F_t is printed "S_t * w * sin(β − α)…"; it should be S·t0·w (the second form, Fs sin(β − α)/cos(φ + β − α), is correct).
  • F21 [MC-G1 p.7]: Example 1.3 prints "β = 2(45) + α − φ = 2(25) + 10 − 2(25.4)". The correct form is β = 2(45) + α − 2φ = 90 + 10 − 50.8 = 49.2°, so the answer is right. Check: it follows from φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2 and gives μ = tan 49.2° = 1.16.
  • F22 [MC-G1 p.8]: Example 1.4 uses F_c = 1557 N, while Example 1.2 (same data) gives 1559 N. Check: 1557 × 100/60 = 2595 W as printed; with 1559 it would be 2598 W (U = 1039.3 N/mm²).
  • F23 [MC-G1 p.5; MC-GQD p.2]: Example 1.1 prints γ = 2.386 ([MC-GQD p.2]: 2.38). With φ = 25.4° exactly, tan 15.4° + cot 25.4° = 2.381; with the unrounded φ = 25.37° it is 2.383. The printed tan φ = 0.4738 comes from r rounded to 0.444 (unrounded r gives 0.4743). Rounding only; φ = 25.4° stands.
  • F24 [MC-G1 p.10]: the Fig. 1.9 mm axis reads "… 0.88 0.1 1.25"; the 0.1 should be 1.0.
  • F25 [MC-G12 p.35]: "HPc = 0.745699872 kW; kW = 1.34 HPc" should read 1 hp = 0.7457 kW (1 kW = 1.34 hp). Check: 1/0.7457 = 1.341, as in [MC-1 p.15].
  • F26 (units), [MC-G12 p.15]: R_MR is printed "mm/min3"; it should be mm³/min. [MC-G12 p.20]: the book image of Example 21.1 prints t_c = 1.125 "in" with t0 = 0.50 mm ([MC-G1 p.5] has mm). [MC-GQD p.2]: the "given" list also writes "1.125 in".
  • F27 (tables differ) [MC-G1 p.9 = MC-U22 p.13; MC-G12 p.42; MC-1 p.15; MC-1 p.10]: the specific-energy tables do not agree for the same material. With 1 kW/(cm³/min) = 60 J/mm³ and 1 hp·min/in³ = 2.73 J/mm³: cast irons are 1.1–1.6 J/mm³ in Table 1.1, 1.6–5.5 in Table 21.2 and 2.6–4.8 in Table 2.1; steels are 1.6–2.8 (carbon steel, Table 1.1), 2.7–9.3 (Table 21.2) and 3.0–5.4 (Table 2.1, soft and R_c < 45). The footnotes differ (sharp tool at t0 = 0.25 mm; drive-motor values corrected for 80 % efficiency with × 1.25 for dull tools; [MC-1 p.10] 90 %). This is a difference of source and conditions, not an arithmetic error. Use the table the question supplies.
  • F28 [MC-G41 p.3 vs MC-2 pp.16–17], convention: [MC-G41] uses A = 0.5 D tan(90° − θ/2) and t_m = (t + A)/f_r; [MC-2] uses L_e = D/(2 tan ρ) + ΔL with ρ = θ/2. The tip terms are equal (D = 10 mm, θ = 120°: 2.887 mm in both). [MC-G41] has no separate overtravel term. Not an error; confirm which the exam expects.
  • F29 [MC-GT pp.2–3]: p.2 calls the angle that compensates for the tool being 5° above centre "the clearance angle" and the extra angle for spring-back "the relief angle", but p.3 calls the spring-back angle "the front clearance angle". Check (rounding, not a source error): 5° above centre per inch of diameter is (0.5 in) sin 5° = 0.0436 in ≈ 2.8/64 in, printed "approximately 3/64".
  • F30 [MC-GD p.2]: the thrust force is said to act "perpendicular to the axis of the hole". In drilling the thrust (feed) force acts along the drill axis (the feed is parallel to the axis, [MC-G41 p.2; MC-Q p.5]).
  • F31 [MC-GD p.2]: the MRR is printed 43,794 mm³/min; [π(12.5)²/4] × 0.2 × 1782.5 = 43,749 mm³/min (43,750 with the exact N).
  • F32 [MC-U21 pp.15–17]: p.15 calls specific heat an "extensive property … proportional to the size of the system", while p.16 says it does not change with sample size (it is intensive). p.15 "In SI units … 1 gram … 1 Kelvin": the SI unit is J/(kg·K), per kilogram (per gram is J/(g·K)). p.17 "4.18 J" and "0.39 J" omit "/g·°C". p.16 "Q = CmΔT" uses C for specific heat, while C = Q/ΔT on the same slide is heat capacity.
  • F33 [MC-U22 p.12]: the mid-term chart is the p.11 chart (°F, ft/min) relabelled "°C" and "m/min" with the same curves, so the axis numbers are not valid in the new units.
  • F34 [MC-U22 p.14, p.19]: the variable list gives t0 in m and K in m²/s, but the worked example uses mm, mm²/s and v in mm/s (consistent within the example, since v t0/K is dimensionless). p.19 prints the exponent as 0.333 in the formula and "0.33" in the substitution line.
  • F35 [MC-U23 p.29]: "n < a < b because cutting speed has a larger influence". In V Tⁿ f^a dᵇ = K_t, T ∝ V^(−1/n) f^(−a/n) d^(−b/n), so speed has the largest influence when 1 > a > b; a < b would make depth of cut more influential than feed. Please check the intended inequality with the lecturer.
  • F36 [MC-U23 p.35]: the general formula labels V1 with T1 (180 m/min, 3 min), but the substituted line pairs log 90 with log 3; the value 0.25 is unaffected because numerator and denominator both change sign.
  • F37 [MC-MID p.17]: the alternative drilling MRR "Q = A_chip·V_c·n = (D/2) f_t V_c (2)" uses the peripheral speed πDN for the whole lip; it gives πD²fN/2, twice the correct (π/4)D² f_r written on the same page (the mean speed along the lip is πDN/2).

Not covered by the sources

After pass 2 the following are still missing from the files supplied; add the lectures when available rather than filling them in from other books.

  • Cutting fluids. The finals refer to a cutting-fluid part: [MC-F23 pp.2–4] and [MC-F22 p.4] mark several questions "مذكور في … cutting fluid" (covered in the cutting-fluid file). [MC-G1 p.4] only says a fluid is often applied to cool and lubricate.
  • Machinability, surface finish and machining economics (optimum speed, cost per part, tool-change time). Only the qualitative effects of nose-radius wear on finish [MC-U23 p.7; MC-F22 p.3] appear.
  • Cutting-tool materials as a topic. [MC-U23 p.2] lists "cutting tool materials", but only the softening-point table, the coated-tool figure and the Taylor n values appear [MC-U23 pp.23, 27].
  • Derivation of the Merchant equation. [MC-G1 p.7] gives the result (φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2) and the idea (dS/dφ = 0) but no derivation.
  • Oblique cutting analysis beyond the force components and the comparison table [MC-G12 p.18, p.48] (chip-flow angle η and inclination are only named in the figure).
  • Formulas for reaming, boring, tapping, shaping, planing, broaching, sawing, screw threads, gears and high-speed machining. These are named in the contents [MC-G31 p.2] but have no slides in the set.
  • Wording of the true/false and other finals questions in [MC-F22], [MC-F23], [MC-F24]: only the answers are written. The data table of the Taylor problem in [MC-F23 p.4] and [MC-F24 p.7] is not given (see ⚠ F47).
  • The linked Google Drive folder of [MC-MS] (solutions of the last two milling problems) was not opened; no network was used.
  • Shear-plane velocity relations (chip velocity, shear velocity): only mentioned as labels in [MC-MID p.32].

About these notes

The vibration notes were written from three groups of files and are merged here under one outline. Each section shows what every group says; a group with nothing on the topic is left out. Every line ends with the tag of its source file and the PDF page. Flags are prefixed with the group letter (A-F1, B-F1, C-F1).

  • Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book.
  • Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files.
  • Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews.

Suspected errors in the sources are kept as printed and marked ⚠.

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

1.1 Definition of vibration and examples
  • Vibration: an oscillatory motion in which the system oscillates about a certain equilibrium position; it is characterised by small motion. Vibration can be considered the branch of engineering that deals with the repetitive motion of objects (a mechanical system) relative to a stationary frame of reference or nominal position, usually the equilibrium position [VA-CH p.7; VA-BK p.7].
  • Lecture definition: vibration is any motion that repeats itself after an interval of time. It is divided into free vibration and forced vibration. In the sketched record the cycles have unequal durations t1 ≠ t2 ≠ t3 (Arabic note: "the motion repeats itself after unequal periods of time") [VA-L1 p.1].
  • Sketched examples of vibration: an aeroplane wing carrying a motor, a simple pendulum (length l, mass M), a floating body in water, a spring–mass system, and an elastic beam with an end mass. Arabic note: these examples apply to both forced and free vibration [VA-L1 p.1].
  • Desired vibration: vibration of strings in musical instruments (e.g. guitar), rock drilling, concrete compactors, diggers, sorting sieves ("sorting seats"), vibratory conveyors [VA-CH p.7; VA-BK p.7].
  • Undesired vibration: ground motion from earthquakes; vibration of an aeroplane and its wings; vibration in machines; transport vehicles; robots; driving shafts; loose doors [VA-CH p.7; VA-BK p.7].
1.2 Physical explanation (energy interchange)
  • Vibration is the interplay between the potential energy and the kinetic energy of the system. A vibrating system must have a component that stores potential energy and releases it as kinetic energy (motion of a mass); the moving mass then gives the energy back to the storing element, and so on. So any vibrating system must have mass and elastic elements [VA-CH p.7; VA-BK p.7].
  • Mass–spring system (Fig. 2.1): the mass is in equilibrium at the static equilibrium position (S.E.P.). If it is displaced down and released, it vibrates about the S.E.P. The kinetic energy is greatest as the mass passes the S.E.P. and zero at the extreme upper and lower positions, where the potential energy is greatest [VA-CH p.7–8; VA-BK p.7–8].
1.3 Why vibration is studied (Arabic lecture notes, translated)
  • Vibration is a phenomenon found in every part of human life: we hear because the eardrum vibrates under sound waves, and we see through the vibration of light waves [VA-L1 p.9].
  • It explains failures that have no apparent cause from the design (strength) point of view. The lecture's example is a large bridge that collapsed about three months after opening because of vibration caused by wind; the collapse was later explained as resonance [VA-L1 p.9].
  • Vibration must be taken into account when designing structures and machines that vibrate in service, e.g. motors, aeroplanes and turbines [VA-L1 p.9].
1.4 Physical system; dynamic vs static
  • Physical system: a component (device), or a collection of components, in the natural world acting together to perform a specific desired objective [VA-CH p.8; VA-BK p.8].
  • Dynamic systems: their variables change with time. Static systems: their variables stay constant [VA-CH p.8; VA-BK p.8].
1.5 Basic elements of a vibrating system (Arabic lecture notes, translated)
  • Any vibrating system needs a means of storing kinetic energy and potential energy and a means of dissipating energy [VA-L1 p.9].
  • (1) Mass: the body or bodies in the system, which cannot be neglected when the system is studied. The mass is the source of kinetic energy [VA-L1 p.9].
  • (2) Springs: these need not be actual coil springs; they represent the elasticity of the parts of the system and are the source of potential energy. The sketches show an axial spring (carries a force) and a torsional spring (carries a torque) [VA-L1 p.9].
  • (3) Dampers (مخمدات الحركة): any source of energy loss that makes the motion die out and brings the parts back to equilibrium, e.g. the viscosity of a lubricant between parts (viscous damping). Dampers are an important part of a vibrating system: without them it could keep vibrating and might collapse in some cases [VA-L1 p.9].
1.6 Methods of studying physical systems
  • Empirical method: excitations are applied to the real system and its response is measured. If the performance (stability, accuracy, speed of response) is not satisfactory, parameters such as c, k and m are adjusted by cut and try. Despite its simplicity, it may not be usable when the system is (1) very complicated, (2) too expensive to test, or (3) dangerous to test (e.g. nuclear or chemical systems) [VA-CH p.8–9; VA-BK p.8–9].
  • Analytical method, in four stages [VA-CH p.9–10; VA-BK p.9–10]:
    1. Physical modelling: simplify the system so that it can be modelled mathematically with the physical laws. Different purposes need different models, e.g. an aeroplane is treated as a particle when studying its motion and as a rigid body when studying stresses. The components and parameters must be identified, and their (dynamic) properties are generally found by experiment.
    2. Mathematical modelling: derive the equations that describe the physical model using physical laws (Newton's laws, energy laws, heat laws). A system may have different mathematical models depending on the working range (linear or non-linear).
    3. Analysis, which is either quantitative (the response to a given excitation) or qualitative (general properties such as natural frequency, damping ratio and settling time; this matters because design techniques depend on it).
    4. Design: improve or optimise the performance by adjusting the system parameters.
  • Lecture version of the steps: (1) construct a mathematical model of the vibrating system; (2) derive the equation of motion of the model; (3) solve it; (4) interpret the results. Arabic note on step 4: this stage interprets the results and draws the recommendations needed for the system [VA-L1 p.10].
  • Mathematical modelling (Arabic notes, translated): it is the first step in studying any vibrating system. The actual physical problem is turned into a set of mathematical equations that can be solved. A model closer to reality is more complicated and harder to solve, but its results are closer to practice. The model is built from masses, springs and dampers [VA-L1 p.10].
  • Physical-model simplification (Arabic notes, translated): before deriving the equation of motion (the second step of the analysis), the physical model must be reduced to its simplest possible form. This requires knowing some details first, such as the number of degrees of freedom [VA-L1 p.13].
1.7 Types of study
  • Analysis: find the response when the excitation and the system characteristics are known. Deduction: find the excitation when the characteristics and the response are known. Synthesis: find the system characteristics when the excitation and the response are known [VA-CH p.10; VA-BK p.10].
1.8 Classification of vibration systems
  • By physical model: (a) discrete system — a finite number of DOF (lumped masses), described by ODEs, e.g. a car ("care") or a simple or compound pendulum; (b) continuous system — infinitely many DOF (distributed mass), described by PDEs, e.g. beams, buildings, strings [VA-CH p.11; VA-BK p.11].
  • By mathematical model: (a) linear — the superposition principle applies, i.e. the highest power of any variable in the equation of motion is one; the source's example is the simple pendulum; (b) non-linear — superposition does not apply (highest power > 1); the source's example is a simple beam [VA-CH p.11; VA-BK p.11] (⚠ A-F1).
  • By excitation (the source repeats the heading "According to the mathematical modeling"): (a) deterministically excited — the force can be described by a function F(t), e.g. a harmonic force; (b) non-deterministically excited — it cannot, e.g. a random force [VA-CH p.11; VA-BK p.11] (⚠ A-F2).
  • Lecture classification: any system that has mass and elasticity can vibrate freely, i.e. vibrate under an initial excitation only, with no external force acting. Vibrating systems are classified as (1) free or forced, (2) damped or undamped, (3) single or multi-DOF, (4) linear or non-linear, (5) deterministic or random [VA-L2 p.23].
  • Deterministic vibration results from a deterministic excitation, i.e. a force (or motion) whose magnitude is known at any time. Random vibration results from a non-deterministic (random) excitation, whose value (amplitude) cannot be predicted at a given time; examples: ground motion during earthquakes, road roughness, wind velocity [VA-L2 p.23].
  • Definitions: natural frequency (ωn ≡ fn) — the frequency at which an undamped system vibrates freely, without external force, after an initial excitation. Free vibrating system — one that vibrates freely, under its own mass only, without external force after the initial excitation. Amplitude (X̄) — the maximum displacement of the vibrating system from its static equilibrium position [VA-L2 p.26].
1.9 Degrees of freedom
  • DOF: the minimum number of independent coordinates ("generalized coordinates") needed to describe the motion of the system [VA-CH p.32; VA-BK p.32]. Lecture wording: the number of independent coordinates required to describe the motion of the vibrating system (Arabic: the independent coordinates needed to describe the motion of the masses in the system) [VA-L1 p.13].
  • Examples in the figures: SDOF — a simple pendulum, a mass on a horizontal spring with a bell-crank lever, a cantilever with an end mass; 2-DOF — two coupled pendulums, two discs on a shaft, two masses on springs in a vertical line; multi-DOF — three coupled pendulums, a triple pendulum, three discs on a shaft [VA-CH p.32–33; VA-BK p.32–33].
  • Lecture SDOF examples: a spring–mass system, a simple pendulum, a torsional disc, a pulley (I0 ≈ ½mR², treated as a disc) connected to a mass m by a rigid link with springs K1 and K2 (K2 fixed to the pulley at point A), and a rigid link pinned at O (moment of inertia I0, torsional spring Kt) connected to masses m1 and m2 on springs K1 and K2. Arabic note: in these examples one coordinate describes the motion of every part, so the system is SDOF; all masses can then be reduced to one equivalent mass Meq, all springs to Keq and all dampers to Ceq [VA-L1 p.13].
  • Lecture 2-DOF examples: two masses m1 and m2 on springs K1, K2 (and K3); a double pendulum (L1, θ1, L2, θ2); a link with Kt and I0 carrying a mass on springs K1 and K2; a mass on an elastic pendulum spring (θ(t), x(t)). Arabic note: two independent coordinates are needed, so the masses reduce to (M1)eq and (M2)eq only, and the springs to (K1)eq, or (K1)eq and (K2)eq, or (K1)eq, (K2)eq and (K3)eq, and no further; the same applies to dampers. The three-spring chain K3–m2–K2–m1–K1 cannot be combined any further; it is already the simplest form [VA-L1 p.14].
  • Worked simplification (crane): wire springs (Kwire)1 = K3 and (Kwire)2 = K4, the arm stiffness Ka, the base spring K1 = Kbase and damper Cbase = C, with M1 = Mb and m2 = W/g. They reduce to a 2-DOF model: m2 on (K2)eq above M1, which sits on K1 and C. How (K2)eq is found depends on the spring and damper connections [VA-L1 p.14].
