Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

1.1 Basic definitions and classification (book, Ch. 1)
  • Vibration: the motion of a particle, a body or a system of connected bodies displaced from a position of equilibrium [VB-AM p.18].
  • Most vibrations are undesirable in machines and structures: they increase stresses, cause energy losses, add wear, increase bearing loads, induce fatigue, create passenger discomfort in vehicles and absorb energy from the system; rotating machine parts need careful balancing to prevent vibration damage [VB-AM p.18].
  • Vibration occurs when a system is displaced from a position of stable equilibrium; it tends to return under restoring forces (elastic forces, e.g. mass on a spring; gravitational forces, e.g. simple pendulum) and keeps moving back and forth across the equilibrium position [VB-AM p.18].
  • System: a combination of elements intended to act together to accomplish an objective (e.g. an automobile: wheels, suspension, car body …) [VB-AM p.18].
  • Static element: output at any time depends only on the input at that time; dynamic element: present output depends on past inputs. A static system contains all (static) elements; a dynamic system contains at least one dynamic element [VB-AM p.18].
  • Dynamic state: a physical system undergoing a time-varying interchange or dissipation of energy among or within its storage or dissipative elements. The elements are in general passive (cannot generate net energy) [VB-AM p.18].
  • Lumped (discrete) system: finite number of storage elements → described by ordinary differential equations. Continuous system: elements dense in physical space → partial differential equations. The formulation depends on kinematic/geometric constraints and the physical laws [VB-AM p.18].
  • Three categories of vibration: free, forced and self-excited [VB-AM p.18].
    • Free vibration: occurs in the absence of external force [VB-AM p.18].
    • Forced vibration: caused by an external force acting on the system; the exciting force continuously supplies energy; may be deterministic (e.g. periodic, Fig. 1.1a) or random (Fig. 1.1b) [VB-AM p.18–19].
    • Self-excited vibrations: periodic and deterministic oscillations; under certain conditions the equilibrium becomes unstable and any disturbance grows until some effect limits the growth. Unlike forced vibration, the exciting force is independent of the vibrations and can persist even when the system is prevented from vibrating [VB-AM p.18–19] (⚠ B-F1).
  • Discrete (lumped-parameter) systems have a finite number of DOF; continuous (distributed) systems, e.g. with continuous elastic members, have an infinite number of DOF. Most mechanical and structural systems have elastic members and hence infinitely many DOF [VB-AM p.21].
  • Single-degree-of-freedom system: its motion is described by a single variable/coordinate; often used to approximate a more complex system. Excitations are of two types: initial excitations and externally applied forces; the resulting behaviour is the system response, generally described by displacements [VB-AM p.25].
1.2 Steps of vibration analysis (book)
  • The outputs depend on the initial conditions and external excitations. Steps: (1) mathematical modelling of the physical system, (2) formulation of governing equations, (3) mathematical solution of the governing equations, (4) physical interpretation of the results [VB-AM p.21–22] (⚠ B-F2).
  • (1) Modelling: determine the existence and nature of the system, its features and elements; simplifying assumptions are made. Implicit assumptions: (a) the system can be treated as a continuous piece of matter; (b) Newton's laws apply assuming the earth is an "internal frame"; (c) relativistic effects neglected. All components are taken as linear; the model may be linear or non-linear. All physical systems are generally non-linear; accurate models lead to non-linear ODEs that are hard or impossible to solve, so systems are linearised [VB-AM p.21–22] (⚠ B-F3).
  • Advantages of linear models: (1) response proportional to input; (2) superposition applies; (3) they closely approximate many dynamic systems; (4) response characteristics can be obtained from the form of the equations without a detailed solution; (5) a closed-form solution is often possible; (6) numerical techniques are well developed; (7) they are a basis for understanding non-linear behaviour. Most non-linear problems have no closed-form solution, so computer simulation is used. The model is only an approximation of the real system [VB-AM p.22].
  • (2) Formulation: apply the basic laws of nature and principles of dynamics to get the differential equations. A basic law of nature applies to all physical systems regardless of material; constitutive equations describe the materials; geometric constraints (kinematic relations between displacement, velocity, acceleration) are needed to complete the model and to form the boundary/initial conditions [VB-AM p.22].
  • (3) Solution methods: standard ODE methods, Laplace transformation, matrix methods, numerical methods. Exact analytical solutions exist for many linear systems but only a few non-linear ones; exact solutions are preferable to numerical/approximate ones [VB-AM p.22].
  • (4) Interpretation: compare predicted performance with experiment to validate the model (refine it if needed); may involve (a) general inferences, (b) design curves, (c) simple arithmetic to reach a conclusion for a specific problem, (d) recommendations on significance and required changes [VB-AM p.22–23].
1.3 Glossary of terms (book, compiled from ISO TC-108 / ANSI "Mechanical Vibration and Shock")
  • Acceleration: vector giving the time rate of change of velocity. Amplification factor: see magnification ratio. Amplification: amount of power or amplitude in an electric signal (transistors create/increase it) [VB-AM p.57].
  • Amplitude ratio (magnification factor): ratio of the maximum force developed in the spring of a mass–spring–dashpot system to the maximum exciting force. Amplitude: maximum distance from either side of the natural position the object can travel once released [VB-AM p.57].
  • Analytical mechanics (analytical dynamics, variational approach): considers the system as a whole rather than the components separately, which excludes reaction and constraint forces automatically [VB-AM p.57].
  • Angular (circular) frequency: frequency × 2π, in rad per unit time. Angular impulse of a constant torque T acting for time t = Tt. Angular (rotational) mechanical impedance: ratio of torque to angular velocity. Angular momentum: moment of the linear momentum about the rotation axis. Angular motion: see rotational particle motion [VB-AM p.57].
  • Anti-resonance: in forced oscillation, exists at a point when any small change in excitation frequency causes an increase in the response at that point [VB-AM p.57].
  • Auxiliary mass damper (damped vibration absorber): mass + spring + damper that reduces vibration by dissipating energy in the damper through relative motion between the mass and the structure it is attached to [VB-AM p.57].
  • Balancing: adjusting the mass distribution of a rotor so that journal vibration, or once-per-revolution bearing forces, are reduced or controlled [VB-AM p.57].
  • Basic law of nature: physical law that applies to all physical systems regardless of the material ("motional" [sic]) from which they are built [VB-AM p.57].
  • Beats: periodic variations from superposing two simple harmonic quantities of different frequencies f1, f2; periodic increase and decrease of amplitude at the beat frequency [VB-AM p.57].
  • Centrifugal force: reaction (at the rotation centre) to the arm tension on a body rotating at the end of an arm; the inertia force resisting change of direction. Centripetal acceleration: directed towards the centre of rotation. Centripetal force: centre-seeking force [VB-AM p.58].
  • Complex function: has real and imaginary parts. Complex vibration: components are sinusoids not harmonically related. Compliance: reciprocal of stiffness [VB-AM p.58].
  • Conservation of angular momentum / energy / linear momentum: total angular momentum about an axis is constant unless an external torque acts about it; energy can be neither created nor destroyed; total momentum in a direction is constant unless an external force acts in that direction [VB-AM p.58].
  • Conservative system: no mechanism for dissipating or adding energy. Continuous assumption: the system can be treated as a continuous piece of matter. Continuous (distributed-parameter) system: infinite number of DOF [VB-AM p.58].
  • Coulomb damping: due to dry friction when two surfaces slide against one another. Coupled modes: modes that influence one another through energy transfer. Electromechanical coupling factor: extent to which a transducer's electrical characteristics are modified by a coupled mechanical system and vice versa. Coupling: connection between equations of motion [VB-AM p.58].
  • Critical damping: minimum viscous damping that lets a displaced system return to its initial position without oscillation. Critical speed: speed of a rotating system corresponding to a resonant frequency. Critical velocity: minimum velocity at the highest point of a loop needed to complete a cycle. Critically damped system: motion on the border between underdamped and overdamped [VB-AM p.58].
  • Cycle: complete sequence of values of a periodic quantity during a period. D'Alembert's principle: the virtual [work] performed by the effective forces through infinitesimal virtual displacements compatible with the constraints is zero [VB-AM p.59].
  • Damped natural frequency: frequency of free vibration of a damped linear system; periodic in the limited sense that the time between zero crossings in the same direction is constant though amplitudes decrease; frequency = reciprocal of that interval [VB-AM p.59].
  • Damping ratio: actual damping / critical damping coefficient. Damping: the process of energy dissipation [VB-AM p.59].
  • Degrees of freedom: minimum number of independent coordinates needed to define completely the positions of all parts of the system at any instant; in general equal to the number of independent possible displacements [VB-AM p.59].
  • Dependent variables: describe the physical behaviour of the system. Deterministic excitation: excitation known at all instants. Discrete system: finite number of DOF [VB-AM p.59].
  • Displacement: net change in a particle's position from the position function; also: vector giving the change of position, usually from the mean position or position of rest (rotation vector, translation vector or both). Distributed systems: mass and elasticity treated as distributed parameters [VB-AM p.59].
  • Driving-point impedance: force/velocity with both measured at the same point and direction. Dry friction damping: see Coulomb damping. Duration of shock pulse: time for the acceleration to rise from a stated fraction of the maximum and decay back to it [VB-AM p.59].
  • Dynamic vibration absorber (tuned damper): auxiliary mass–spring system that tends to neutralise vibration of the structure it is attached to by vibrating out of phase with it, applying a counteracting force [VB-AM p.59].
  • Dynamically coupled: equation (or KE) contains cross products of velocity. Dynamics: study of moving objects [VB-AM p.59].
  • Elasticity: property that returns a material to its natural state after compression. Energy: capacity to do work [VB-AM p.60].
  • Equivalent system: one that may be substituted for another for analysis: (1) equivalent stiffness, (2) equivalent damping, (3) torsional system equivalent to a translational one, (4) electrical or acoustical system equivalent to a mechanical one, etc. [VB-AM p.60].
  • Equivalent viscous damping: assumed viscous damping giving the same energy dissipation per cycle at resonance as the actual damping [VB-AM p.60].
  • Excitation (stimulus): external force or other input causing a response. External forces: actions of other bodies on a rigid body. Flexibility matrix: inverse of the stiffness matrix. Force: push or pull (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic, contact) [VB-AM p.60].
  • Forced vibrations: occur in the presence of external excitation. Foundation (support): structure supporting the gravity load; fixed, or moving and exciting the supported system [VB-AM p.60].
  • Fraction of critical damping (damping ratio): c/cc. Free-body-diagram method: applies conservation laws to FBDs drawn at an arbitrary instant to derive the equations of motion. Free vibrations: in the absence of external excitation [VB-AM p.60].
  • Frequency: number of cycles per unit time, reciprocal of the period. Friction: force that always resists motion or impending motion. Fundamental frequency: lowest natural frequency. Fundamental mode: mode with the lowest natural frequency [VB-AM p.60].
  • Generalized coordinates: set of independent coordinates, equal in number to the DOF, that properly and completely define the configuration. Generalized forces: usually not actual forces but some component of a combination of them [VB-AM p.60].
  • Gravity acceleration: 9.8 m/s². Grid points: see mesh points. Harmonic excitation: "if the excitation force is periodic". Harmonic response: periodic response showing resonance at a frequency that is a multiple of the excitation frequency. Harmonic: sinusoidal quantity whose frequency is an integral multiple of a related periodic quantity [VB-AM p.61].
  • Holonomic coordinates: each independent of the others. Holonomic system: constraint equations contain only coordinates, or coordinates and time. Homogeneous differential equation: every term contains the unknown function or its derivative [VB-AM p.61].
  • Hysteretic ("hysteric") damping: energy dissipation each cycle due to the hysteresis loop. Impact: single collision of one moving mass with a second mass (moving or at rest) [VB-AM p.61].
  • Impedance: mechanical impedance = force-like quantity / velocity-like quantity (force, sound pressure, voltage, temperature / velocity, volume velocity, current, heat flow); reciprocal of mobility [VB-AM p.61].
  • Impulse: ∫F dt with F zero before t1 and after t2. Impulsive force: large magnitude, very short duration, finite time integral. Impulsive torque: torque acting for a very short time. Independent variables: those with which the dependent variable changes [VB-AM p.61].
  • Influence coefficient α12: static deflection at position 1 due to a unit force at position 2 acting alone. Internal forces: hold together the parts of a rigid body [VB-AM p.61].
  • Isolation: reduction in the capacity of a system to respond to excitation, by a resilient support; in steady-state forced vibration expressed as the complement of transmissibility. Jerk: time rate of change of acceleration (third derivative of displacement) [VB-AM p.61].
  • Kinematics: study of motion without its causes (geometry of motion). Kinetic coefficient of friction μ: Coulomb's law, friction force proportional to the normal force. Kinetic energy: ½mv² (work Ps done by force P over distance s from rest). Kinetics: study of motion and the forces causing it [VB-AM p.62].
  • Lagrange's method: uses the principle of virtual displacements and D'Alembert's principle to derive equations of motion. Lagrangian: KE − PE [VB-AM p.62].
  • Line spectrum: components at discrete frequencies. Linear damping: force proportional to velocity. Linear differential equation: no products of the solution function and/or its derivatives. Linear mechanical impedance: force / linear velocity. Linear (rectilinear) system: particles move only in straight lines [VB-AM p.62].
  • Logarithmic decrement: rate of amplitude decay expressed as the natural log of the amplitude ratio. Longitudinal wave: displacement normal to the wave front. Lumped-mass systems: modelled as distinct mass and elastic elements, possessing many DOF [VB-AM p.62].
  • Magnification factor (amplitude ratio, amplification factor): steady-state amplitude / pseudo-static deflection. Mass: found by comparison with a standard mass on a beam balance. Matrix iteration: numerical procedure giving natural frequencies and modes successively from the lowest. Mean square value: average of the squared values over a time interval [VB-AM p.62].
  • Mechanical shock: sudden, severe non-periodic excitation (foundation motion or applied force), usually causing significant relative displacements. Mechanical system: aggregate of matter with a defined configuration of mass, stiffness and damping. Mesh points: finite points replacing the solution domain in the finite difference method [VB-AM p.63].
  • Modal analysis: solving the simultaneous equations of motion by transforming them into independent equations with the modal matrix. Modal matrix: made of the modal (characteristic) vectors. Modal numbers: ordered integers relating the normal modes [VB-AM p.63].
  • Mode of vibration: characteristic pattern in which every particle moves simple-harmonically at the same frequency; several may coexist in an MDOF system. Modulation: variation of a parameter of a periodic oscillation (e.g. amplitude modulation). Momentum: mass × velocity [VB-AM p.63].
  • MDOF system: two or more coordinates needed. n-DOF system: n independent coordinates needed. Natural environments: conditions generated by forces of nature, experienced at rest and in operation [VB-AM p.63].
  • Natural frequencies: positive square roots of the eigenvalues, the circular frequencies at which the system can oscillate. Natural frequency: frequency of free vibration (for MDOF, of the normal modes). Natural modes: the eigenvectors (modal vectors). Natural motions: special independent free-vibration solutions in one natural mode [VB-AM p.63].
  • Natural vibration: motion about equilibrium after a disturbance applied once and removed (= free vibration). Negative damping: energy added rather than dissipated; can be unstable. Newtonian (vectorial) mechanics: equations in physical coordinates and forces, as vectors [VB-AM p.64].
  • Node: point in a principal-mode vibration with zero displacement at all times. Non-holonomic systems: constraints contain velocities. Non-linear damping: force not proportional to velocity. Non-linear system: governed by non-linear differential equations [VB-AM p.64].
  • Normal mode of vibration: uncoupled mode that can exist independently; in the eigenvalue formulation normal modes = eigenvectors, normal-mode frequencies = eigenvalues; "classical normal modes" (all elements at same frequency and phase) exist only without damping or with particular damping types [VB-AM p.64].
  • Normal modes / normalization: adjusting the natural-mode elements (normalization) gives normal modes; convenient choice reduces [m] to the identity so [k] becomes the diagonal matrix of ω². Number of DOF: coordinates needed to specify the state. Orthonormal: normalized modes [VB-AM p.64].
  • Oscillation: variation of a quantity alternately above and below a reference. Overdamped system: heavy damping, non-oscillatory motion. Partial node: point/line/surface in a standing wave with minimum non-zero amplitude (displacement, velocity, pressure partial node). Peak value: generally the maximum stress in the vibrating part [VB-AM p.64].
  • Peak-to-peak value: algebraic difference between extremes. Period: time for a full cycle. Periodic quantity: values recur for certain increments of the independent variable. Phase: fractional part of a period advanced from an arbitrary reference. Pickup: see transducer [VB-AM p.65].
  • Positive (negative) semi-definite matrix: coefficients of such a quadratic form. Positive definite system: [m] and [k] both positive definite → undamped free vibration. Positive semi-definite system: [m] positive definite, "[– k]" only positive semi-definite [VB-AM p.65].
  • Potential energy: energy of position = work to raise from a datum, mgh. Principle of virtual work: work of the applied forces through infinitesimal compatible virtual displacements is zero [VB-AM p.65].
  • Q (quality factor): measure of sharpness of resonance / frequency selectivity of an SDOF resonant system (mechanical or electrical); in a mechanical system = ½ × reciprocal of the damping ratio; used for lightly damped systems ("approximately equal to the following:" — the formula is missing in the source) [VB-AM p.65] (⚠ B-F17).
  • Quasi-sinusoid: a = A sin(2πft − θ) with A and/or f slowly varying functions of time, θ constant. Random excitation: force unknown but mean and standard deviation known. Random vibration: instantaneous magnitude specified only by probability distributions; contains no periodic or quasi-periodic constituents [VB-AM p.65].
  • Rayleigh method: estimates the fundamental frequency of a conservative system. Resonance frequency: frequency at which resonance exists [VB-AM p.65].
  • Resonance: condition where the amplitude increases without bound. Response: motion or other output from an excitation. Rigid body: does not deform under load. RMS value: square root of the mean square value. Rotational particle motion (angular, circular motion): motion around a circular path [VB-AM p.66].
  • Self-induced (self-excited) vibration: results from conversion, within the system, of non-oscillatory excitation to oscillatory excitation [VB-AM p.66].
  • Shock absorber: dissipates energy to modify the response to applied shock. Shock isolator (shock mount): resilient support isolating a system from shock motion. Shock motion: excitation by foundation motion. Shock pulse: disturbing force with rise and decay of acceleration in a very short time. Shock spectrum (response spectrum): maximum response of an SDOF system vs its own natural frequency for an applied shock (acceleration, velocity or displacement). Shock: transient phenomenon, sharp nearly sudden change in velocity [VB-AM p.66].
  • SHM: periodic oscillation about the equilibrium position. SDOF system: one coordinate defines the configuration. Spectrum: magnitudes of the frequency components of a quantity. Spring stiffness (spring constant): F = kx for a linear spring (dimension force per length) [VB-AM p.66].
  • Spring: flexible mechanical link between two particles. Static deflection: deflection due to gravity alone. Static friction: friction on a stationary body. Statically coupled: equation contains cross products of coordinates [VB-AM p.67].
  • Steady-state response: response after the transient has decayed. Steady-state vibration: every particle's velocity is a continuing periodic quantity. Stiffness: change of force (torque) / change of deflection (rotation). Strain energy: ½Sx² for an elastic body of stiffness S extended by x. Structural damping: energy loss in the material or at joints [VB-AM p.67].
  • Sub-harmonic response: harmonic response dominated by a sub-harmonic, often when the excitation frequency is a submultiple of the fundamental. Sub-harmonic: frequency is an integral submultiple of the fundamental. Synchronous: two harmonic oscillations of the same frequency [VB-AM p.67].
  • Torsional pendulum: torsional spring + mass. Torsional vibration: vibration of a rigid body about a reference axis, angular coordinate. Torsional spring: torque produces angular displacement between its ends [VB-AM p.67].
  • Transducer (pickup): converts shock/vibratory motion into an optical, mechanical or (mostly) electrical signal proportional to a motion parameter; generally converts input energy into another type of output energy. Transfer impedance: force at one point / velocity at another (or same point, different directions). Transient vibration: temporarily sustained vibration, forced, free or both [VB-AM p.67].
  • Transmissibility: non-dimensional ratio of response amplitude in steady-state forced vibration to excitation amplitude (forces, displacements, velocities or accelerations). Transverse wave: displacement parallel to the wave front [VB-AM p.68].
  • Tuned system: absorber natural frequency equals the frequency to be eliminated (forcing frequency). Uncoupled mode: can exist concurrently and independently. Undamped natural frequency: from elastic and inertia forces only. Underdamped system: harmonic displacement with exponentially decaying amplitude, damping below critical [VB-AM p.68].
  • Uniform mass damping: damping on each mass proportional to that mass. Uniform motion: uniform velocity. Unrestrained system: has a rigid-body mode with zero natural frequency. Unstretched length: spring length with no external force. Variance: mean of squared deviations from the mean [VB-AM p.68].
  • Vibration control: using vibration analysis to eliminate/reduce unwanted vibration or to protect against force/motion transmission. Vibration damper: auxiliary inertia element + viscous damper connected to a primary system. Vibration isolator (mount): resilient support isolating from steady-state excitation. Vibration machine: subjects a system to controlled reproducible vibration. Vibration meter: measures displacement, velocity or acceleration of a vibrating body [VB-AM p.68].
  • Vibration: oscillation of a parameter defining the motion of a mechanical system. Viscous damper (dashpot): resistive force on a body moving in a viscous fluid. Viscous damping: resisting force proportional to velocity magnitude, opposite in direction [VB-AM p.69].
  • Wave: disturbance propagated in a medium, a function of time at a point and of position at an instant. Weight: earth's attraction, measured by a calibrated spring balance. Work: average force × distance moved in its direction [VB-AM p.69].
1.4 "Vibrations Terms and Definitions" lists (VB-TD, VB-DE) and handwritten definitions (VB-DF)
  • VB-TD (2-page typed list, "نسخة من Vibrations Terms and Definitions") is the first part (A–V) of the list that VB-DE (4-page scanned print of the same list, title "Definition") gives in full; VB-DE pp.1–2 repeat VB-TD pp.1–2 word for word (VB-DE reads "produces" where VB-TD has the typo "produc!;!s"); VB-DE pp.3–4 add the terms from "Dynamic modulus" to "Vibration isolator" [VB-TD p.1–2] [VB-DE p.1–4]. Intro line: "The following are vibration related terms and definitions" [VB-TD p.1].
  • Acceleration: a vector quantity that specifies the rate of change of velocity [VB-TD p.1]. Accelerometer: a sensor whose electrical output is proportional to acceleration [VB-TD p.1]. Charge amplifier: the output voltage of the amplifier is proportional to the output charge from a piezoelectric transducer; advantage: the voltage output is not affected by the length of the connecting cable from the transducer [VB-TD p.1]. Critical damping: the minimum viscous damping that will allow a displaced system to return to its original position without oscillation [VB-TD p.1]. Displacement: a vector quantity that specifies the change of position of a body, usually measured from the rest position [VB-TD p.1]. Damping: "It means of dissipating vibration energy within a vibrating system" (sic) [VB-TD p.1]. Damping ratio: the ratio of actual damping to critical damping, at a resonant frequency [VB-TD p.1] (⚠ B-F84). Degree of freedom: in a mechanical system, the minimum number of independent coordinates required to completely define the position of all parts of the system at any instant of time [VB-TD p.1]. Dynamic mass: the ratio of applied force to resulting acceleration during simple harmonic motion [VB-TD p.1].
  • Vibrations meter: an instrument for measuring oscillatory displacement, velocity or acceleration [VB-TD p.2]. Vibration severity: a criterion for predicting the hazard related to specific machine vibration levels [VB-TD p.2]. Voltage preamplifier: a preamplifier which produces an output voltage proportional to the input voltage from a piezoelectric accelerometer; the input voltage depends upon cable capacitance [VB-TD p.2] (the list in VB-TD ends here, while the alphabetical entries between "Dynamic mass" and "Vibrations meter" are on VB-DE p.3–4).
  • Further terms in VB-DE: Dynamic modulus: the ratio of stress to strain under vibratory conditions [VB-DE p.3]. Excitation: an external force or motion applied to a system that causes the system to respond in some way [VB-DE p.3]. Force: "Retardation Agency which gives a mass an acceleration" (as printed) [VB-DE p.3] (⚠ B-F84). Impact: an excitation of a structure with a force pulse, e.g. using an impact hammer [VB-DE p.3]. Impulse: a well-defined pulse; periodic impulse is repeated impulses [VB-DE p.3]. Integrator: an electrical frequency filter used to convert a vibratory acceleration signal to one whose amplitude is proportional to velocity or displacement [VB-DE p.3]. Jerk: a vector quantity that specifies the time rate of change of acceleration [VB-DE p.3]. Mechanical impedance: the ratio of applied force to resulting velocity during simple harmonic excitation; also called driving-point impedance if force and velocity are measured at the same point, otherwise transfer impedance [VB-DE p.3]. Mobility: mechanical admittance, the inverse of mechanical impedance [VB-DE p.3]. Modal analysis: a process of determining the mode shapes and associated parameters, natural frequency and damping [VB-DE p.3]. Natural frequency: the frequency at which a resiliently mounted mass will vibrate when set into free vibration [VB-DE p.3].
  • Periodic vibration: an oscillatory motion whose amplitude pattern repeats after fixed increments of time [VB-DE p.4]. Random vibration: a vibration whose instantaneous amplitude is not specified at any instant of time; it can only be defined statistically by a probability distribution function giving the fraction of the total time that the amplitude lies within specified amplitude intervals [VB-DE p.4]. Resonance: conditions of peak vibratory response where a small change in excitation frequency causes a decrease in system response [VB-DE p.4]. Response: motion or other output resulting from an excitation, under specified conditions [VB-DE p.4]. Shock: rapid transient transmission of mechanical energy [VB-DE p.4]. Simple harmonic motion: a periodic motion whose displacement varies as a sinusoidal function of time [VB-DE p.4]. Stiffness: the ratio of the change in force to the corresponding change in displacement of an elastic element [VB-DE p.4]. Transmissibility: the ratio of the amplitude response of a system in steady-state vibration to the excitation amplitude [VB-DE p.4]. Velocity: a vector quantity that specifies the time rate of change of displacement [VB-DE p.4]. Vibration isolator: a resilient support that reduces transmissibility [VB-DE p.4].
  • VB-DF (2 scanned handwritten pages, "تعريفات ڤايبراشن") is the same handwritten oral-exam definition sheet as VB-T2 p.1–2: definitions 1–6 (degree of freedom, natural frequency, free vibration, logarithmic decrement δ = ln(xm/xm+1), resonance ωn = ω, mode shape) and 7–18 (magnification factor, physical system, vibration, amplitude, periodic motion, harmonic motion, transient response, periodic time, frequency, beating vibration, phase), with the boxed (X/δst)max = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) at the top; the wording is identical to 14.2 p.1–2 and is recorded there [VB-DF p.1–2] (see [VB-T2 p.1–2]).

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

1.1 Vibration, periodic motion, period and frequency
  • Vibration: any motion that repeats itself after intervals (حركة تكرر نفسها على فترات زمنية ليست بالضرورة أن تكون متساوية — the intervals need not be equal); sketch shows t1 ≠ t2 ≠ t3 ≠ t4 [VC-S1 p.1].
  • Examples: simple pendulum, car suspension system, human lungs [VC-S1 p.1].
  • Periodic motion: motion that repeats itself at equal time intervals (أي حركة بتكرر نفسها على فترات زمنية متساوية), t1 = t2 = t3 = τ; sketches of a square wave and a saw-tooth wave [VC-S1 p.1].
  • τ "periodic time" (sec): time needed to make one complete cycle; F "frequency" (Hz, cycle/s, s⁻¹): number of complete cycles in one second; τ = 1/F [VC-S1 p.1].
1.2 Degrees of freedom
  • Degree of freedom (D.O.F): the least number of motion variables needed to describe the motion of the system (أقل عدد من متغيرات الحركة اللازم لوصف حركة النظام) [VC-S1 p.5].
  • Sketched examples: mass on spring x(t) → single; simple pendulum θ → single; pendulum with a spring as the arm (θ and spring stretch) → two; two masses m1, m2 between springs K1, K2, K3 with x1(t), x2(t) → two; double pendulum θ1, θ2 → two [VC-S1 p.5].
1.3 Classification of vibrating systems
  • Tree: vibrating systems → single D.O.F (one equation of motion) or multi "two D.O.F" (equations of motion); each → free (no external force, the motion is under the effect of the initial force) or forced (an external "harmonic" force exists after the initial force); each → undamped (m–K) or damped (m–K–C), forced ones carry F(t) [VC-S1 p.5].
  • Classification list: 1. free or forced; 2. single or multi-degree of freedom; 3. damped or undamped; 4. linear or non-linear (Fs–δ plot: straight line K "linear"; hard spring curving above and soft spring curving below are "non-linear"); 5. random (amplitude cannot be computed at any time, e.g. earthquakes, الزلازل) or deterministic (amplitude easy to compute at any time) [VC-S1 p.6].
1.4 How to study a vibrating system
    1. Physical and mathematical model; 2. derive the equation(s) of motion for the model; 3. solve the derived equation(s); 4. interpret the obtained results [VC-S1 p.6].
1.5 Sheet 1 (Introduction — Fundamentals), Q1 and Q2
  • Sheet 1 Q1: define vibration, period, frequency, amplitude, free vibrating system and forced vibrating system [VC-SH1 p.1; VC-S2 p.7]. No written answer in the solution files; the definitions of §1.1 and §1.3 cover them [VC-S1 p.1, p.5].
  • Sheet 1 Q2: how many degrees of freedom are required to model the six shown systems [VC-SH1 pp.1–2; VC-S2 pp.7–8]. Student answers [VC-SH1S]:
    • Fig. 1 (rigid lever J0 pivoted at O, springs k1 at distance a above and k2 at b below): x1 = a sin θ, x2 = b sin θ → single DOF [VC-SH1S p.1].
    • Fig. 2 (m1 on a carriage m3 with springs k1…k5 and a rigid lever J0 at O): number of masses = 4, "DOF = 4 or 3"; the note says slipping is possible so there is no relation between x3 and x2 → no. of DOF = 4 [VC-SH1S p.1].
    • Fig. 3 (rigid bar J0 hinged at O with k1 at the free end and mass m hung by k2): masses = 2, "DOF = 2 or 1"; sin θ = x/L → x = L sin θ → "one degree of freedom" [VC-SH1S p.1] (⚠ C-F3).
    • Fig. 4 (disc J0 with k6, two rigid massless pulleys, m1 with k3, k4, k5, and m2 with k1, k2): masses = 3, "DOF = 3 or 2 or 1", boxed DOF = 3 [VC-SH1S p.1].
    • Fig. 5 (disc J0 linked by k1 to pulley JA carrying m2 on k2 and m1 on a rigid wire with k3): masses = 4, "DOF = 4 or 3 or 2 or 1"; x1 = R θA (rigid wire); θ0 ≠ θA because of the spring between them; final DOF = 3 [VC-SH1S p.2].
    • Fig. 6 (bar m on springs k1, k2 joined by a rigid link to a lever J0 pivoted at O with k3): masses = 2, "DOF = 2 or 1"; x = L sin θ → one degree of freedom [VC-SH1S p.2] (⚠ C-F3).
    • Q4 figures, DOF noted by the student: Fig. 1 "no. of masses = 5, DOF = 5 or 4" then "single degree of freedom"; Fig. 3 masses = 3 → single DOF; Fig. 4 masses = 3, "DOF = 3 or 2 or 1" → single DOF [VC-SH1S pp.3, 7].
1.6 Abdelrahman Mamdouh's introduction notes ([VC-AI])
  • Vibration (موضوع الاهتزاز): a to-and-fro (ترددية) motion that repeats itself regularly every period of time (the period τ) about the equilibrium position, "or" an exchange of kinetic and potential energy during the motion from one point to another (the Arabic is partly hard to read) [VC-AI p.1].
  • Elements of a vibrating system: (1) mass m; (2) spring K; (3) damper c; (4) force [VC-AI p.1].
  • Spring: the note says it is there to prevent the impact case a = (0 − V0)/0 = −∞ (so that F = ma would be infinite), with a sketch of a sinusoidal oscillation [VC-AI p.1].
  • Damper: "damper for damping vibrations" (لتحييد الاهتزازات), with a sketch of a decaying oscillation [VC-AI p.1].
  • Types: 1. free / forced; 2. damped / undamped; 3. linear / non-linear; 4. deterministic / random [VC-AI p.1].
  • Notes: (1) the elements that must be in a system are (m, K) — K is the element that stores potential energy (عنصر يخزن طاقة الوضع) and the mass stores kinetic energy (عنصر يخزن طاقة الحركة); (2) the elements that may be in a system are the damper and the force [VC-AI p.1].
1.7 ES summary: elements and degrees of freedom ([VC-ES])
  • Mechanical vibration — translation: 1 mass (kg), 2 spring k (N/m), 3 damper c (N·s/m), 4 force (sketch: m hanging from k and c, displacement x(t), force F(t)); rotation: 1 mass, 2 torsional spring Kt, 3 torsional damper Ct, 4 moment (sketches: pendulum with Kt and Ct at the pivot; disc rolling with centre displacement xG) [VC-ES p.1].
  • Degree of freedom: the number of variables needed to define the motion (Arabic heading, partly legible). Sketches: mass on spring x(t) = 1 DOF; simple pendulum θ = 1 DOF; pendulum with a spring arm (θ and x) = 2 DOF [VC-ES p.1].
  • The reverse side of p.1 shows through (mirror-writing, poor legibility): "Problems NO: Sheet 1: 1.6, 1.9, 1.21; Sheet 2: 2.7, 2.9, 2.10; Sheet 3: 3.1?, 3.9, 3.11; Sheet 4: 4.4, 4.5?; Sheet 5: 5.3, 5.4, 5.6" [VC-ES p.1].

  13. 2.4 Fourier series in Abdelrahman Mamdouh's notes ([VC-AF])

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

2.1 Periodic motion, period and frequency
  • Oscillatory motion is a repetitive motion about a certain reference. It is classified as simple harmonic, periodic or random [VA-CH p.15; VA-BK p.15].
  • Periodic motion: repeats itself at equal time intervals; the repetition time is the period τ, and x(t) = x(t + τ) [VA-CH p.18; VA-BK p.18; VA-L1 p.1]. The figures show a sine, a square wave and a triangular wave [VA-CH p.18; VA-BK p.18]. The lecture sketches rectified half-sine waves and sawtooth waves with t1 = t2 = t3 = τ. Arabic note: the periodic function need not be a displacement; it can be a force, e.g. the fourth example can represent the force of a forging hammer, which is periodic but not continuous [VA-L1 p.1].
  • Period τ: the time for one complete cycle; τ = 1/f [VA-L1 p.2]. With θ = ωt and θ = 2π at t = τ: τ = 2π/ω s [VA-CH p.16; VA-BK p.16].
  • Frequency f: the number of complete cycles per unit time; f = 1/τ = ω/2π cycles/s (Hz); ω = 2πf rad/s [VA-CH p.16; VA-BK p.16; VA-L1 p.2]. Example: τ = 0.1 s → f = 1/0.1 = 10 cycles/s (cps, Hz) [VA-L1 p.2].
  • Amplitude A: the maximum value of x(t), also called the peak amplitude Ap [VA-CH p.16; VA-BK p.16].
  • Random motion: can only be described by statistical techniques (figure of a random F(t)) [VA-CH p.27; VA-BK p.27].
2.2 Simple harmonic motion
  • Many mechanical systems behave as simple harmonic oscillators, e.g. a simple pendulum, a spring–mass system and a torsional system: x(t) = A sin ωt (or y(t) = A sin ωt), θ(t) = Θ sin ωt [VA-CH p.15; VA-BK p.15].
  • SHM is the projection on the vertical axis of a point P moving round a circle of radius A at constant angular velocity ω: x(t) = A sin θ = A sin ωt, where θ is the angular displacement (rad) and ω the angular velocity (rad/s) [VA-CH p.15; VA-BK p.15].
  • Lecture definition: harmonic motion is periodic motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement but in the opposite direction. Example: a link OA of length B rotating at ω: x(t) = B cos ωt, y(t) = B sin ωt; ẋ = −Bω sin ωt, ẏ = Bω cos ωt; ẍ = −Bω² cos ωt, ÿ = −Bω² sin ωt. So x ∝ ẍ and y ∝ ÿ, in opposite directions, which is why sin and cos are called "harmonic functions". For one cycle θ = 2π at t = τ, so ω = 2πf [VA-L1 p.2].
  • Velocity and acceleration: ẋ = Aω cos ωt = Aω sin(ωt + π/2); ẍ = −Aω² sin ωt = Aω² sin(ωt + π). Both are harmonic at the same frequency and lead the displacement by π/2 and π respectively (the source shows the rotating-vector and time plots) [VA-CH p.16; VA-BK p.16].
  • The potential energy ½kx² depends on displacement and the kinetic energy ½mẋ² on velocity, and the two are "perpendicular"; the energy-vs-x figure shows the oscillation as an interchange between PE and KE [VA-CH p.17; VA-BK p.17].
  • Vector representation: x⃗(t) = (B cos ωt) i + (B sin ωt) j (Arabic: the link OA can be treated as a vector whose components represent the two motions) [VA-L1 p.3].
  • Complex representation: x⃗(t) = a + ib = B cos ωt + i B sin ωt = B e^(iωt), with B = √(a² + b²) and ωt = tan⁻¹(b/a) [VA-L1 p.3].
  • Trigonometric and complex relations to revise (Arabic note: it is worth revising the trigonometric functions and their complex forms and how they relate): sin θ = θ − θ³/3! + θ⁵/5! − θ⁷/7! + …; cos θ = 1 − θ²/2! + θ⁴/4! − θ⁶/6! + …; e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ = 1 + iθ + (iθ)²/2! + (iθ)³/5! + … (as written); e^(−iθ) = cos θ − i sin θ = 1 − iθ + (iθ)²/2! − (iθ)³/3! + …; sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A−B)/2); sin nθ cos mθ = ½[sin(n+m)θ cos(n−m)θ] (as written) [VA-L1 p.3] (⚠ A-F3).
  • Questions posed in the lecture: what happens when B sin ωt + A sin ωt are added (same frequency), and when A sin(ω + δω)t + A sin ωt are added (very close frequencies, same amplitude) [VA-L1 p.3].
  • Example (SHM): A = 1 m, τ = 2 s → ω = 2π/τ = π rad/s; ẋmax = Aω = π = 3.14 m/s; ẍmax = Aω² = π² = 9.86 m/s². ẋmax occurs at ωt = 0, π, 2π, … i.e. t = 0, 1, 2, … s; ẍmax at ωt = π/2, 3π/2, … i.e. t = ½, 3/2, … s [VA-CH p.17; VA-BK p.17].
2.3 Fourier series
  • Harmonic motion is simpler to analyse than periodic motion. Many vibrations are periodic but not harmonic, so a way is needed to turn periodic motion into harmonic terms: any periodic x(t) can be written as a Fourier series, an infinite sum of sine and cosine terms [VA-L1 p.4; VA-CH p.18; VA-BK p.18].
  • Book form: x(t) = a0 + Σ an cos nωt + Σ bn sin nωt, with a0 = (1/τ)∫₀^τ x dt, an = (2/τ)∫₀^τ x sin ωt dt, bn = (2/τ)∫₀^τ x cos ωt dt (as printed), ω = 2πf = 2π/τ = fundamental angular frequency. The same form is given for a periodic exciting force F(t) [VA-CH p.18–19, 31; VA-BK p.18–19, 31] (⚠ A-F4). Figure: one-, two- and three-term approximations of a sawtooth wave [VA-CH p.18; VA-BK p.18].
  • Lecture form: x(t) = a0/2 + Σ(an cos nωt + bn sin nωt), with τ = 1/f = 2π/ω, a0 = (2/τ)∫₀^τ x dt = (ω/π)∫₀^(2π/ω) x dt, an = (2/τ)∫₀^τ x cos nωt dt, bn = (2/τ)∫₀^τ x sin nωt dt [VA-L1 p.4–5].
  • Shortcuts: even function x(t) = x(−t) → bn = 0 (e.g. cos); odd function x(t) = −x(−t) → an = 0 (e.g. sin) [VA-CH p.19; VA-BK p.19]; the lecture writes "odd functions: a0 = an = 0" [VA-L1 p.4]. A function symmetric about the ωt axis → a0 = 0 (∫₀^τ x dt = 0) [VA-CH p.19; VA-BK p.19].
  • Example 1, square wave (x = +1 for 0 ≤ ωt ≤ π, −1 for π ≤ ωt ≤ 2π): the function is odd → an = 0, and symmetric → a0 = 0. bn = (2/nπ)(1 − cos nπ) = 4/(πn) for odd n and 0 for even n. x(t) = (4/π)[sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + …] [VA-CH p.19–21; VA-BK p.19–21].
  • Example 2, triangular ("saw") wave of height 1 and period 2 (x = t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, x = −t + 2 for 1 ≤ t ≤ 2; τ = 2 s, ω = π): the function is even → bn = 0. an = (2/n²π²)(cos nπ − 1) = −4/(n²π²) for odd n and 0 for even n; a0 = 1/2. x(t) = 1/2 − (4/π²)[cos ωt + (1/3²) cos 3ωt + (1/5²) cos 5ωt + …] [VA-CH p.21–22; VA-BK p.21–22].
  • Example 3, triangular wave of height A (x = (2A/τ)t for 0 ≤ t ≤ τ/2; x = (2A/τ)(τ − t) for τ/2 ≤ t ≤ τ): even → bn = 0; a0 = A/2; an = (A/(π²n²))(2 cos nπ − 2) = −4A/(n²π²) for odd n and 0 for even n. x(t) = A/2 − (4A/π²)[cos ωt + (1/3²) cos 3ωt + (1/5²) cos 5ωt + …] [VA-CH p.23–25; VA-BK p.23–25].
  • Example 4, falling sawtooth (x = A − (A/τ)t for 0 ≤ t ≤ τ, also written (2A/τ)(−t + τ)): neither even nor odd. a0 = A/2; an = (A/(2π²n²))(1 − cos 2πn) = 0; bn = A/(nπ). Final result as printed: x(t) = A/2 − (A/π)[sin nωt + (1/2) sin 2ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + …] [VA-CH p.25–27; VA-BK p.25–27] (⚠ A-F5).
  • Example 5 (lecture), forging-hammer impact force modelled as a half-sine: x(t) = A sin ωt for 0 ≤ t ≤ τ/2 and 0 for τ/2 ≤ t ≤ τ, ω = 2π/τ. Arabic notes: the figure shows a force that is periodic but not continuous, and a periodic function need not be a displacement; it can be a velocity, an acceleration, a force, etc. The function is neither even nor odd, so a0, an and bn are all computed [VA-L1 p.5]:
    • a0 = (ω/π)∫₀^(π/ω) A sin ωt dt = 2A/π [VA-L1 p.6].
    • an = (Aω/2π)∫₀^(π/ω)[sin(1+n)ωt + sin(1−n)ωt] dt, using sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A−B)/2) → an = (A/2π){2/((1+n)(1−n)) − [cos(1+n)π/(1+n) + cos(1−n)π/(1−n)]}. For n = 1 this formula gives ∞ (Arabic: "this is not reasonable"), so n = 1 is substituted into the integral directly: a1 = 0. For even n: an = 2A/(π(1+n)(1−n)); for odd n (3, 5, …): an = 0 [VA-L1 p.6–7].
    • bn = (2/τ)∫₀^(τ/2) A sin ωt sin nωt dt = −(Aω/2π)∫[cos(1+n)ωt − cos(1−n)ωt] dt (using cos A − cos B = −2 sin((A+B)/2) sin((A−B)/2)) → b1 = A/2 and bn = 0 for n = 2, 3, 4, … [VA-L1 p.8].
    • Result: x(t) = A/π + Σ(n = 2, 4, 6, …) [2A/(π(1+n)(1−n))] cos nωt + (A/2) sin ωt. Four-term approximation: x(t) = A/π + (A/2) sin ωt − (2A/3π) cos 2ωt − (2A/15π) cos 4ωt (the handwriting first had sin, corrected to cos). Suggested check: τ = 2 s (ω = π), A = 10 N [VA-L1 p.8].
  • Problems (Fourier series of a triangular wave ±A, a rectangular pulse train, and a sawtooth of height 1.0 and period 2π): see §14 [VA-CH p.36; VA-BK p.36].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

2.1 Periodic and harmonic motion (book)
  • Periodic motion: motion repeated in equal intervals of time; simple harmonic motion is its simplest form: x = A cos ωt = A cos 2π t/τ, A = amplitude measured from the equilibrium position [VB-AM p.20].
  • Period τ (repetition time) = 2π/ω s/cycle; frequency f = 1/τ = ω/2π cycles/s or Hz; ω = circular frequency in rad/s; any periodic motion satisfies x(t) = x(t + τ) [VB-AM p.20].
  • Velocity and acceleration of a harmonic displacement are harmonic of the same frequency and lead the displacement by π/2 and π rad respectively [VB-AM p.20].
  • SHM definition: when the acceleration of a particle in rectilinear motion is always proportional to its displacement from a fixed point on the path and directed towards that point [VB-AM p.20].
2.2 Fourier series (book)
  • Many vibrations are periodic but not harmonic (e.g. the impact force of a forging hammer) [VB-AM p.20].
  • x(t) = a0/2 + Σ(n=1..∞) (an cos nωt + bn sin nωt), ω = 2π/τ = fundamental frequency [VB-AM p.20].
  • a0 = (2/τ)∫0^τ x(t) dt; an = (2/τ)∫0^τ x(t) cos nωt dt; bn = (2/τ)∫0^τ x(t) sin nωt dt [VB-AM p.20–21].
  • Exponential form: x(t) = Σ(n=−∞..∞) cn e^(inωt), cn = (1/τ)∫0^τ x(t) e^(−inωt) dt [VB-AM p.21].
  • an cos nωt, bn sin nωt = harmonics of order n; the n-th harmonic has period τ/n. Plotting an, bn as vertical lines against frequency nω gives the frequency spectrum [VB-AM p.21].
2.3 Harmonic analysis of periodic forces (book)
  • Harmonic functions: periodic functions whose Fourier coefficients are all zero except one [VB-AM p.40].
  • Even function F(t) = F(−t) (e.g. cos): all bm = 0. Odd function F(t) = −F(−t) (e.g. sin): a0 and an all zero [VB-AM p.40].
  • Periodic force of irregular form (graphical/tabulated values): numerical integration; divide period T into N equal intervals Δt = T/N: a0 = (2/N)ΣF(ti), an = (2/N)ΣF(ti) cos nωti, bn = (2/N)ΣF(ti) sin nωti (i = 1..N) [VB-AM p.40–41].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

2.1 Harmonic motion
  • Harmonic motion is a special case of periodic motion restricted to sine and cosine, in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement (تتناسب فيها العجلة مع الإزاحة) [VC-S1 p.2].
  • x(t) = A sin θ, A = amplitude (m), θ = angular displacement (rad); ω = θ/t → θ = ωt, ω = angular velocity (rad/s) [VC-S1 p.2].
  • Displacement x(t) = A sin ωt; velocity ẋ(t) = Aω cos ωt; acceleration ẍ(t) = −Aω² sin ωt [VC-S1 p.2].
  • For one complete cycle θ = 2π = ωτ, so ω = 2π/τ = 2πF [VC-S1 p.2].
  • In all vibration problems the treatment is with harmonic motion; a periodic function is converted to harmonic terms by Fourier expansion (Periodic →Fourier expansion→ Harmonic) [VC-S1 p.2].
2.2 Fourier series
  • x(t) = a0/2 + Σ(n=1..∞) an cos(nωt) + Σ(n=1..∞) bn sin(nωt) [VC-S1 p.2].
  • a0 = (2/t)∫0^t x(t) dt; an = (2/t)∫0^t x(t) cos(nωt) dt; bn = (2/t)∫0^t x(t) sin(nωt) dt (the source writes the period as "t") [VC-S1 p.3] (⚠ C-F1).
  • Even function (دالة زوجية, symmetric about the y-axis): x(−t) = x(t) → bn = 0 [VC-S1 p.3].
  • Odd function (دالة فردية, symmetric about the origin): x(−t) = −x(t) → an = a0 = 0 [VC-S1 p.3].
2.3 Harmonic motion in Abdelrahman Mamdouh's notes ([VC-AI])
  • If the motion is along one direction (x or y): x = A sin θ or x = A cos θ; ω = dθ/dt = θ/t so θ = ωt; x = A sin ωt or A cos ωt, A = amplitude [VC-AI p.6].
  • x = A sin ωt, ẋ = Aω cos ωt, ẍ = −ω²A sin ωt = −ω²x [VC-AI p.6].
  • If the motion is in both directions together (x and y), e.g. the motion of the vector OP on a circle: y = A sin ωt, x = A cos ωt; X⃗ = OP = a + ib = A(cos θ + i sin θ), with A = √(a² + b²) and θ = tan⁻¹(b/a); X⃗ = A(cos θ ± i sin θ) = A e^(±iθ) [VC-AI p.6].
2.4 Fourier series in Abdelrahman Mamdouh's notes ([VC-AF])
  • A periodic function is converted into harmonic terms by the Fourier series (sketch of one triangular pulse and its periodic repetition) [VC-AF p.1].
  • f(t) = a0 + Σ(n=1..∞)[an cos(2πn t/T) + bn sin(2πn t/T)], with a0 = (1/T)∫0^T f(t) dt; an = (2/T)∫0^T f(t) cos(2πn t/T) dt; bn = (2/T)∫0^T f(t) sin(2πn t/T) dt [VC-AF p.1]. (Here a0 is the mean value, whereas [VC-S1 p.2] writes a0/2 with a0 = (2/t)∫; both give the same series.)
  • Even function (symmetric about the y axis, f(t) = f(−t)) → bn = 0. Odd function (−f(t) = f(−t), symmetric about the origin) → an = 0. The note "symmetric function → a0 = 0" follows (zero mean) [VC-AF p.1].
  • Worked integrations (τ = period, ω = 2π/τ):
    • Triangular wave rising from 0 to A at τ/2 and falling back to 0 at τ [VC-AF pp.2–3]: x1(t) = 2At/τ for 0 < t < τ/2, x2(t) = −2At/τ + 2A for τ/2 < t < τ; the function is even, bn = 0, x(t) = a0 + Σ an cos nωt; a0 = (1/τ)[∫0^(τ/2)(2A/τ)t dt + ∫(τ/2)^τ (τ − t)(2A/τ) dt] = (1/τ)[Aτ/4 + τA/4] = A/2; an = (2/τ)[…] = (2A/(n²π²))(cos nπ − 1) → an = −4A/(n²π²) for n = 1, 3, 5, … and an = 0 for n = 2, 4, 6, …. The series itself is not written out.
    • Sawtooth falling from A at t = 0 to 0 at τ [VC-AF pp.4–5]: x(t) = −At/τ + A = (A/τ)(τ − t); a0 = A/2; an = (A/(2n²π²))(1 − cos 2nπ) as written → an = 0 for every n; bn = Aτ/(nτπ) = A/(nπ). Series: x(t) = A/2 + (A/π) sin ωt + (A/2π) sin 2ωt + (A/3π) sin 3ωt + … [VC-AF pp.4–5].
    • Rectangular pulse train, x = 1 for 0 < t < 2/k (the axis is marked "kπ" and "2/k") and 0 up to τ = 1 s, ω = 2π [VC-AF p.6]: a0 = 2/k; an = sin(4nπ/k)/(nπ); bn = (2/(nπ))[1 − cos(4nπ/k)] as written (⚠ C-F25).
    • Sawtooth rising x(t) = t, τ = 1 s, ω = 2π [VC-AF p.7]: a0 = 1/2; an = 0; bn = −2/(nπ) as written (⚠ C-F25).
    • Odd triangular wave with peaks ±A at t = τ/4 and 3τ/4: x1 = 4At/τ for −τ/4 < t < τ/4, x2 = −4At/τ + 2A for τ/4 < t < 3τ/4; odd and symmetric, so a0 = an = 0; bn = (2/τ)∫ x(t) sin nωt dt evaluated to bn = −(2A/(n²π²))[sin(−nπ/2) + sin(3nπ/2)]; bn = 0 for n = 2, 4, 6, …; bn = 4A/(n²π²) for n = 1, 5, 9, …; bn = −4A/(n²π²) for n = 3, 7, 11, … [VC-AF pp.8–9] (⚠ C-F25).

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

3.1 Classification of forces
  • Internal forces: (1) restoring forces (spring, buoyancy, gravity); (2) dissipative forces (dry friction, viscous friction, structural damping). External exciting forces: harmonic, periodic, non-periodic (arbitrary) [VA-CH p.28–32; VA-BK p.28–32].
3.2 Spring (restoring) force and stiffness
  • Within the elastic limit the force (or torque) is proportional to the deflection: F = Kx or T = Kθ. Stiffness K = F/x is the force needed to produce unit displacement in the direction of the force; units N/m (or N·m/rad). The force–deformation figure is linear up to the yield point A [VA-CH p.28; VA-BK p.28].
  • Stiffness table [VA-CH p.29; VA-BK p.29] (⚠ A-F6): see §15 Table A.
3.3 Equivalent stiffness from the modelling examples (lecture)
  • Ex. 1, cantilever of length L (E, I) with a tip mass M: δ = x(t) = mgL³/(3EI) = mg/Keq → Keq = 3EI/L³; for a rectangular section a × b, I = (1/12)ab³. The model is a mass on Keq (elasticity only) or on Keq and Ceq in parallel (elasticity and viscosity) [VA-L1 p.10].
  • Ex. 2, simply supported beam with a central mass: δ = mg/Keq = mgL³/(48EI) → Keq = 48EI/L³ [VA-L1 p.11].
  • Ex. 3, a cantilever (E1, I1, L1) and a simply supported beam (E2, I2, L2) carrying load F = mg: K1eq = 3E1I1/L1³ and K2eq = 48E2I2/L2³, drawn as springs in series (Keq1 above Keq2) [VA-L1 p.11].
  • Ex. 4, bar (E, A, L) under axial load F = mg: δ = FL/(EA) = F/Keq → Keq = EA/L [VA-L1 p.11].
  • Ex. 5, two cars m1, m2 joined by a bar (E, A, L) → a 2-DOF model m2–K–m1. With a coupling made of three parts (E1, L1, A1), (E2, L2, A2), (E3, A3, L3): K1 = E1A1/L1, K2 = E2A2/L2, K3 = … (not completed), drawn in series. Arabic note: x1 and x2 are the motions of the centres of the first and second cars, and m1, m2 are treated as masses concentrated at their centres of gravity [VA-L1 p.11].
  • Ex. 6, a shaft or rod (L, G, J) carrying a rotating part with polar mass moment of inertia I0 or J (a gear in a gearbox, a ship propeller, windmill or wind-turbine blades): θ = T/kt = TL/(JG) → kt = JG/L, where J = πd⁴/32 = (π/2)r⁴ is the polar moment of inertia of the shaft's area [VA-L1 p.12] (⚠ A-F7).
  • Ex. 7, ship propeller shaft of two parts (L1, J1, G1) and (L2, J2, G2): kt1 = J1G1/L1 and kt2 = J2G2/L2 in series, driving the propeller I0 with torque T [VA-L1 p.12].
  • Ex. 8, crane (body, arm, wire, weight W, base): model Mb on Kbase and Cbase, with the arm Ka and the wire springs (Kwire)1 and (Kwire)2 carrying W [VA-L1 p.12].
  • Ex. 9, forging hammer mh on an anvil mA, on an elastic pad (Cp, Kp), on a foundation block mf, on soil (Csoil, Ksoil): model mA–(Cp, kp)–mF–(Csoil, Ksoil). Arabic note: the forced and free vibration of this system must be distinguished; this is explained later [VA-L1 p.12].
3.4 Springs in parallel and in series (lecture)
  • Parallel: from the FBDs, mg = Keq x = (K1 + K2 + K3)x → Keq = K1 + K2 + K3. Arabic notes: the equivalent spring equals the sum of the springs; all springs share in resisting the load, and in most vibrating systems all the springs have the same displacement, equal to that of the equivalent spring [VA-L1 p.15].
  • Series: x = δ1 + δ2 + δ3; mg = Keq x = K1δ1 = K2δ2 = K3δ3, so δi = mg/Ki and x = mg/Keq → 1/Keq = 1/K1 + 1/K2 + 1/K3 [VA-L1 p.15].
  • Two springs in series only (a special case): Keq = K1K2/(K1 + K2). Arabic notes: in series the total displacement is the sum of the springs' displacements, and each spring carries the whole load and passes it to the next — the opposite of the parallel case [VA-L2 p.18].
  • Arabic note: in real applications the physical model is harder, both in deciding the type of connection and in finding the equivalent spring, so energy equivalence is used. (a) The spring is the source (storage) of potential energy in most vibrating systems, so the PE the equivalent spring stores must equal the PE stored in all the system's springs: (P.E.)eq = (P.E.)sys, with P.E. = ½kx² for axial springs (k in N/m, x in m) and ½ktθ² for torsional springs (kt in N·m/rad, θ in rad) [VA-L2 p.18].
  • (b) Equivalent stiffness of a tilted spring: displacements x and x′ are small, so the angle change α is very small and OA″ ≈ OA′. The spring's own deflection is x′, while x is the deflection of the equivalent spring along the force: ½Kx′² = ½Keq x² with x′ = x cos θ → Keq = K cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the line of action of the force (or weight) and the spring; θ and (180° − θ) give the same result because cos²θ = cos²(180° − θ) [VA-L2 p.19].
  • (c) Equivalent mass: the mass is the source of kinetic energy, so the KE of the equivalent mass must equal the KE of all the masses: (K.E.)sys = (K.E.)eq, with K.E. = ½mẋ² (translation) or ½Jθ̇² (rotation) [VA-L2 p.19].
  • Dampers combine like springs: Ceq = C1 + C2 + C3 + … in parallel and 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3 + … in series; in general (dissipative energy)sys ≡ (dissipative energy)eq (Arabic: this is explained with damped vibration) [VA-L2 p.22].
3.5 Equivalent-system examples (lecture)
  • Ex. 1, composite propeller shaft: a steel tube (OD 25 cm, ID 15 cm) around an aluminium core tube (OD 15 cm, ID 10 cm), L = 5 m, Gst = 80 GPa, GAl = 26 GPa; find the torsional spring constant. The two parts are torsional springs in parallel (same twist θ, and both share the torque T): Keq = (kt)st + (kt)Al with kt = GJ/L, J = πd⁴/32. (kt)st = 80 × 10⁹ × (π/32)(0.25⁴ − 0.15⁴)/5 = "5.34072 × 10⁵"; (kt)Al = 26 × 10⁹ × (π/32)(0.15⁴ − 0.1⁴)/5 = "0.207395 × 10⁵" N·m/rad; Keq = 5.54811 × 10⁶ N·m/rad [VA-L2 p.20] (⚠ A-F18).
  • Ex. 2, rocker arm referred to the x coordinate: a rigid rod pivoted at O (J0, torsional spring kt), with m1 on k1 at distance a above O and m2 on k2 at distance b below. Small θ: x = bθ, x1 = aθ = (a/b)x. KE: ½m2ẋ² + ½J0θ̇² + ½m1ẋ1² → Meq = m2 + (a/b)²m1 + J0/b² kg (Arabic note: be sure the result has units of mass (kg), otherwise the solution is wrong). PE: ½k2x² + ½ktθ² + ½k1x1² → Keq = k2 + kt/b² + (a/b)²k1 N/m [VA-L2 p.21].
  • Ex. 3, springs at angles around a load P: k5, k6, k7 in series → K1eq = k5k6k7/(k6k7 + k5k7 + k5k6); k8, k9 → K2eq = k8k9/(k8 + k9); k1, k2 → K3eq = k1k2/(k1 + k2); k3, k4 → K4eq = k3k4/(k3 + k4). In the direction of P: Keq = K1eq cos²θ1 + K2eq cos²θ2 + K3eq cos²θ3 + K4eq cos²θ4 [VA-L2 p.22].
3.6 Buoyant and gravity restoring forces
  • Buoyancy: displacing a floating body by x displaces liquid: F = ρgV = ρgA x = Keq x, so Keq = ρgA [VA-CH p.29; VA-BK p.29].
  • Gravity (pendulum): I0θ̈ + mgLθ = 0, Geq = mgL [VA-CH p.30; VA-BK p.30].
3.7 Dissipative forces (damping)
  • Dry (Coulomb) friction: from two dry surfaces sliding; FF = μR (μ = coefficient of friction, R = normal force) [VA-CH p.30; VA-BK p.30].
  • Viscous friction: the exact description is difficult, so an ideal model takes the damping force proportional to the relative velocity, Fd = c ẋ, where c is the coefficient of damping; it is drawn as a dashpot (figures of a plate on a fluid film of viscosity μ and thickness h, and a piston in a cylinder) [VA-CH p.30; VA-BK p.30].
  • Structural damping: caused by internal friction between the molecules of a structure; its exact description is complicated and unsuitable for vibration analysis, so a simplified model Fd = Ceq ẋ is used [VA-CH p.31; VA-BK p.31].
3.8 External exciting forces
  • Harmonic: F(t) = F0 cos ωt or F0 sin ωt (F0 = amplitude, ω = exciting frequency) [VA-CH p.31; VA-BK p.31].
  • Periodic: represented by a Fourier series (§2.3) [VA-CH p.31; VA-BK p.31].
  • Non-periodic (arbitrary): for linear systems superposition gives the total response; the force is represented by an infinite series of impulses and the response is found with the convolution integral [VA-CH p.32; VA-BK p.32].
3.9 Energy expressions
  • Kinetic energy is stored in a mass by its velocity (½mẋ²; ½Jθ̇² in rotation). Potential energy is stored as strain energy (½Kx²) or as work done in the gravitational field (pendulum U = mgl(1 − cos θ)) [VA-CH p.34; VA-BK p.34].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

3.1 Elements of a vibrating system (book)
  • A vibrating system consists of a spring (stores potential energy), a mass/inertia (stores kinetic energy) and a damper (energy gradually lost) (Fig. 1.2: spring k, damper c, mass m, excitation force F(t), displacement x from static equilibrium position) [VB-AM p.19–20].
  • Undamped system: potential energy and kinetic energy are transferred into each other alternately. Damped system: some energy is dissipated each cycle and must be replaced by an external source to keep a steady state [VB-AM p.19].
  • Stiffness of continuous elastic elements (rods, beams, shafts) is obtained from deflection considerations: rod (longitudinal) k = EA/l; cantilever beam (transverse, tip load) k = 3EI/l³; shaft (torsional) K = GJ/l [VB-AM p.23–24].
  • Springs in parallel: keq = Σ ki [VB-AM p.24].
  • Springs in series: the same force is developed in each spring (equal to the force on the mass); printed formula: 1/keq = 1/Σ(1/ki); text: "the reciprocal of the equivalent elastic constant is equal to the reciprocals of the elastic constants of the elements" [VB-AM p.24] (⚠ B-F4).
  • Mass/inertia element: assumed a rigid body; identified once the model is developed [VB-AM p.24].
  • Damping = the process of energy dissipation. A damper is considered to have neither mass nor elasticity. Three main forms: viscous, Coulomb (dry-friction), hysteresis damping [VB-AM p.25].
  • Viscous damper (dashpot): most common; damping force proportional to velocity [VB-AM p.25].
  • Coulomb (dry-friction) damping: sliding contact between dry or insufficiently lubricated surfaces; force constant in magnitude, opposite to the motion; energy dissipated as heat [VB-AM p.25].
  • Structural / hysteretic / material / solid damping: solid materials are not perfectly elastic; energy is absorbed and dissipated by internal friction between internal planes during deformation (visco-elastic solids) [VB-AM p.25].
  • Several dashpots in combination can be replaced by a single dashpot with an equivalent damping coefficient [VB-AM p.25].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

3.1 Elements of vibrating systems
    1. Mass: generates kinetic energy (تولد طاقة حركة) [VC-S1 p.3].
    1. Spring: stores the energy of motion as potential energy (يخزن طاقة الحركة في صورة طاقة وضع) [VC-S1 p.3].
  • 2.1) Axial spring: Fs = K δs; Fs spring force (N), K spring constant (N/mm), δs displacement (mm) [VC-S1 p.3].
  • 2.2) Torsional spring: M = Kt θ; M in N·mm, Kt spring constant (N·mm/rad), θ in rad [VC-S1 p.4].
    1. Dampers "energy absorber": dissipate the vibration energy and so return the system to its equilibrium position [VC-S1 p.4].
  • 3.1) Viscous damping (مقاومة مائع): fluid between two surfaces, or fluid around a cylinder (مساعد العربية — car shock absorber); Fd = C ẋ, Fd damping force (N), C damping constant (N·s/m), ẋ velocity (m/s) [VC-S1 p.4].
  • 3.2) Dry-friction damping: Fd = μN, μ coefficient of friction, N normal reaction; FBD of a block on a rough floor: Fs, μN, mẍ, N, mg [VC-S1 p.4].
  • 3.3) Solid-material or hysteretic damping: the motion is dissipated by friction of the material particles with each other (نتيجة احتكاك جزيئات المادة مع بعضها) [VC-S1 p.5].
3.2 Equivalent systems — known loading type (Section 2)
  • Construction of the physical and mathematical model; in the "equivalent systems" case the type of loading is known (في الحالة دي بنكون عارف نوع التحميل) [VC-S2 p.1].
  • Method: δmax of the elastic member = δ of the equivalent spring; for the spring FBD Fs = mg → K δsp = mg → δsp = mg/K [VC-S2 pp.1–2].
  • Cantilever with end mass (cross-section a × b): PL³/(3EI) = mg/K → K = 3EI/L³ [VC-S2 p.1].
  • Elastic bar/wire of length L carrying m axially: PL/(EA) = mg/K → K = EA/L [VC-S2 p.1].
  • Simply supported beam with m at mid-span: PL³/(48EI) = mg/K → K = 48EI/L³ [VC-S2 p.2].
  • Shaft with a disc and torque T: φshaft = φspring, TL/(GJ) = T/Kt → Kt = GJ/L; spring side T = Kt φsp, φsp = T/Kt [VC-S2 p.2].
  • Summary table (loading type → model) [VC-S2 p.3]:
# Loading type Model
1 Cantilever, end load P, length L K = 3EI/L³
2 Bar, axial load P, length L K = EA/L
3 Simply supported beam, central load P, span L K = 48EI/L³
4 Shaft, end torque T, length L Kt = GJ/L
  • E: modulus of elasticity (مقدار مقاومة المادة على الاستطالة تحت تأثير الأحمال — resistance of the material to elongation under load); G: modulus of rigidity (مقدار مقاومة المادة للتشوه — resistance to distortion) [VC-S2 p.3].
3.3 Springs and dampers in series and parallel
  • Here the type of connection is known (في الحالة دي بنكون عارف نوع التوصيل) [VC-S2 p.4].
  • Series springs K1, K2, K3 carrying m: mg = Keq x = K1x1 = K2x2 = K3x3, xi = mg/Ki, x = x1 + x2 + x3 → 1/Keq = 1/K1 + 1/K2 + 1/K3; the displacement is the sum of the displacements, and each spring carries the whole load alone and passes it on (كل spring بيشيل الحمل لوحدة وبعد كده ينقله) [VC-S2 p.4].
  • Parallel springs: mg = F1 + F2 + F3, Keq x = mg → Keq = K1 + K2 + K3; one common displacement and the springs share the load (الـ spring اتوزع عليهم الحمل) [VC-S2 p.5].
  • Dampers in series: 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3; in parallel: Ceq = C1 + C2 + C3 [VC-S2 p.5].
3.4 Complex systems — energy equivalence
  • When neither the loading type nor the connection type is known (لا أعرف نوع التحميل ولا نوع التوصيل) use energies [VC-S2 p.6].
  • Equivalent spring constant Keq: P.E.)sys = P.E.)eq; axial P.E. = ½Kx², torsional P.E. = ½Kt θ² [VC-S2 p.6; VC-S2 p.15].
  • Equivalent mass meq: K.E.)sys = K.E.)eq; translation K.E. = ½mẋ², rotation K.E. = ½J0 θ̇² (J0 = mass moment of inertia), general plane motion (G.P.M., translation + rotation) K.E. = ½mẋ² + ½J0 θ̇² [VC-S2 p.6].
3.5 Sheet 1 Q3 — equivalent spring stiffness
  • Fig. 1 — stepped bar A1, A2, A3 (lengths l1, l2, l3, same E) under axial F: segments 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 are series springs (each carries the load and passes it on), Ki = EiAi/li → 1/Keq = (1/E)(l1/A1 + l2/A2 + l3/A3) → Keq = E A1A2A3/(l1A2A3 + l2A1A3 + l3A1A2) [VC-S2 p.11; VC-SOL1 p.1; VC-SH1S p.2].
  • Fig. 2 — stepped shaft D1, D2, D3 (lengths l1, l2, l3) under torque T: torsional springs in series, Kti = GiJi/li, G = shear modulus of rigidity (MPa), Ji = polar moment of inertia = (π/32)Di⁴ → 1/Keq = (32/(πG))(l1/D1⁴ + l2/D2⁴ + l3/D3⁴) → Keq = πG D1⁴D2⁴D3⁴ / [32(l1D2⁴D3⁴ + l2D1⁴D3⁴ + l3D1⁴D2⁴)] [VC-S2 p.12].
  • Fig. 3 — spring network: two k in parallel → Keq1 = 2K; two k in series → Keq2 = K²/2K = K/2; right pair in parallel → Keq3 = 2K; Keq1 ∥ Keq2 → Keq4 = 5K/2; Keq4 in series with Keq3 → Keq5 = Keq4·Keq3/(Keq3 + Keq4) = 10K/9 [VC-S2 p.13; VC-SOL1 p.2; VC-SH1S p.2 (writes the unit N/m)].
3.6 Sheet 1 Q4 — equivalent mass and equivalent stiffness
  • Fig. 1 (block m with k1 on a pulley Jp of radius rp; rigid link 1 (mass m1, length l1) rotates with the pulley about O; rigid link 2 (mass m2) drives a cylinder mc, radius rc, rolling without slip, with k2):
    • Kinematics: θ1 = θp = x/rp; θp = x2/l1 → x2 = l1 x/rp, ẋ2 = l1 θ̇p; θc = x2/rc = x l1/(rp rc) [VC-S2 p.14; VC-SOL1 p.3; VC-SH1S p.4].
    • meq = m + Jp/rp² + J1/rp² + m2 l1²/rp² + Jc l1²/(rp² rc²) + mc l1²/rp², with J1 = m1 l1²/3 and Jc = mc rc²/2 [VC-S2 p.15]. The TA takes the cylinder about its contact point, Jc.c = ½mc rc² + mc rc² = (3/2)mc rc², and writes meq = m + Jp/rp² + m l1²/(3rp²) + m2 l1²/rp² + 3m l1²/(2rp²) [VC-SOL1 p.3] (⚠ C-F2). Student: Meq = M + Ip/rp² + I1/rp² + M2(L/rp)² + Ic(L/(rp rc))² + Mc(L/rp)², Ip = ½mp rp² (pulley as a disc), I1 = (1/12)m1L1² + m1(L1/2)² = (1/3)m1L1², and the note that the cylinder about the contact point gives ½Mc rc² + Mc rc² = (3/2)Mc rc² [VC-SH1S p.4].
    • Keq: ½K1x² + ½K2x2² = ½Keq x² → Keq = K1 + K2 l1²/rp² [VC-S2 p.15; VC-SOL1 p.4; VC-SH1S p.4].
  • Fig. 2 (lever J0 pivoted with torsional spring kt; m1 with k1 at distance a above the pivot, m2 with k2 at distance b below; x measured at m2):
    • Kinematics (small θ): sin θ = x/b → θ = x/b; θ = y/a = x/b → y = (a/b)x; ẋ = bθ̇, ẏ = aθ̇ [VC-S2 pp.16–17].
    • Keq: K1y² + K2x² + Kt θ² = Keq x² → Keq = (a²/b²)K1 + K2 + Kt/b² [VC-S2 p.16].
    • meq: m1ẏ² + m2ẋ² + I0θ̇² = meq ẋ² → meq = (a²m1 + b²m2 + I0)/b² [VC-S2 p.17].
  • Fig. 3 (cylinder m, radius r, rolling without slip, k1 at C; rigid link to a stepped pulley I0 at radius r2; k2 at radius r3; x at the link, x1 at r3):
    • θ = x1/r3 = x/r2 → x1 = r3 x/r2; θc = x/r [VC-S2 p.20; VC-SH1S p.6].
    • meq = I0/r2² + Ic/r² + m [VC-S2 p.20]; student: meq = m + Ic/r² + I0/r2² with Ic = ½mr², I0 = ½m0 r2² [VC-SH1S p.6].
    • Keq = K1 + K2 r3²/r2² [VC-S2 p.21; VC-SH1S p.6].
  • Fig. 4 (bell-crank lever J0 at O, 90° arms l1 (to m on k1, displacement x) and l2 (to a sphere ms, radius rs, rolling without slip, with k2)):
    • Kinematics: θc = x/l1; xs = θc l2 = x l2/l1; θs = xs/rs = x l2/(l1 rs) [VC-S2 pp.18–19; VC-SH1S p.7].
    • meq = m + J0/l1² + Js l2²/(l1² rs²) + ms l2²/l1² [VC-S2 p.19]; student: meq = m + I0(1/L1)² + Is(L2/(r2 L1))² + ms(L2/L1)², Is = (2/5)ms r², I0 given [VC-SH1S p.7] (⚠ C-F4); TA: sphere Is0 = (2/5)m rs² + m rs² about the contact point → meq = m + J0/l1² + (7/5)m(l1/l2)² [VC-SOL1 p.5] (⚠ C-F5).
    • Keq = K1 + K2 l2²/l1² [VC-S2 p.19; VC-SOL1 p.5; VC-SH1S p.7].
    • Student note: x ≠ xs because L2 ≠ L1; if L2 = L1 then x = xs; sketch example L1 = 20, L2 = 10 at 30°: displacements 20 sin 30 and 10 sin 30 [VC-SH1S p.7].
3.7 Abdelrahman Mamdouh's introduction and problems ([VC-AI], [VC-AP])
  • Mass moments of inertia (ΣMO = JOθ̈) [VC-AI p.2]: 1) point mass at distance L: JO = mL²; 2) disc about its centre: JO = ½mr²; 3) bar of length L about its centre: JO = Jcg = (1/12)mL²; 4) bar hinged at its end (l = L/2): JO = Jcg + ml² = (1/12)mL² + mL²/4 = (1/3)mL²; 5) disc rolling on a plane about the contact point: JO = Jcg + Mr² = ½Mr² + Mr²; 6) sphere: Jcg = (2/5)Mr², JO (about the contact point) = (2/5)Mr² + Mr² [VC-AI p.2].
  • Force F = mg; P.E. = ± mgh; K.E. translation = ½mv² = ½mẋ²; K.E. rotation and general plane motion = ½JOθ̇² [VC-AI p.2].
  • Translational spring: F = Kx, U = ½Kx², K = spring constant, stiffness or rate [N/m]. Rotational spring: T = Ktθ, U = ½Ktθ² [N·m/rad] [VC-AI p.3].
  • Keq of mechanical elements [VC-AI pp.3–4]:
    • Rod in tension/compression (E, A, L): Keq = EA/L (E modulus of elasticity N/m², A cross-section area m²).
    • Rod in torsion (G, J, L): Kt,eq = GJ/L; G modulus of rigidity = E/(2(1 + ν)); J polar moment of area = (π/32)d⁴.
    • Cantilever (E, I, L, end load F): Keq = 3EI/L³; I second moment of area; circular section I = (π/64)d⁴; rectangle Ixx = bh³/12 (h height).
    • Simply supported beam, central load: Keq = 48EI/L³.
  • Parallel connection: same deformation, Feq = F1 + F2 + F3, Keq Δeq = K1Δ1 + K2Δ2 + K3Δ3, Δeq = Δ1 = Δ2 = Δ3 → Keq = K1 + K2 + K3 + … [VC-AI p.4].
  • Series connection: same force, different deformations, Δeq = Δ1 + Δ2 + Δ3, Feq/Keq = F1/K1 + F2/K2 + F3/K3, Feq = F1 = F2 = F3 → 1/Keq = 1/K1 + 1/K2 + 1/K3 + … [VC-AI p.4].
  • Damper element [VC-AI p.5]: translational F = cẋ (N·s/m), dissipated-energy function De = ½cẋ²; rotational T = cθ̇ (N·m·s/rad), De = ½cθ̇². Dampers connect like springs.
  • Spring/damper deflection rule [VC-AI p.5]: if both ends move in the same direction, Δ = x1 − x2 (or x2 − x1) and v = ẋ1 − ẋ2 (or ẋ2 − ẋ1) (the note "the choice is free", حر الاختيار, is partly legible); if the ends move in opposite directions, Δ = x1 + x2 and v = ẋ1 + ẋ2. For a pendulum arm a: x = a sin θ ≈ aθ [VC-AI p.5].
  • Problems on equivalent stiffness and mass ([VC-AP]):
    • Lever (length l, force F at the top) with springs K1 at l1 and K2 at l2 [VC-AP p.1]: x = lθ, x1 = l1θ = (l1/l)x, x2 = l2θ = (l2/l)x, θ = x/l. P.E.: ½K1x1² + ½K2x2² = ½Keq x² → Keq = K1(l1/l)² + K2(l2/l)². Another solution by moments: Fl cos θ − K1x1l1 cos θ − K2x2l2 cos θ = I0θ̈ = 0 with sin θ = θ, cos θ = 1 → Fl = K1x1l1 + K2x2l2 = Keq x l → Keq = K1(l1/l)² + K2(l2/l)² (same result) [VC-AP p.1].
    • Three masses m1, m2, m3 on a bar hinged at the left at distances l1, l2, l3 (velocities ẋ1, ẋ2, ẋ3 upward) [VC-AP p.2]: choosing ẋ = ẋ1: ẋ2 = (l2/l1)ẋ, ẋ3 = (l3/l1)ẋ; K.E.system = K.E.eq → meq = m1 + m2(l2/l1)² + m3(l3/l1)². Choosing ẋ = ẋ2: ẋ1 = (l1/l2)ẋ, ẋ3 = (l3/l2)ẋ → meq = m1(l1/l2)² + m2 + m3(l3/l2)².
    • Rack and pinion (pinion J0, radius R; rack mass m, velocity ẋ) [VC-AP p.3]: x = Rθ, ẋ = Rθ̇, θ̇ = ẋ/R. 1) equivalent translational mass: ½J0θ̇² + ½mẋ² = ½meq ẋ² → meq = J0/R² + m. 2) equivalent rotational mass: ½J0θ̇² + ½mẋ² = ½Jeq θ̇² → Jeq = J0 + mR².
    • Torsional-and-translational springs on a lever [VC-AP p.4]: Kt1, Kt2 at the pivot, K1 and K2 attached at l1 (x1 = l1θ), K3 at l2 (x2 = l2θ): ½Kt1θ² + ½Kt2θ² + ½K3x2² + ½K1x1² + ½K2x1² = ½Kt,eq θ² → Kt,eq = Kt1 + Kt2 + K3l2² + K1l1² + K2l1².
    • Bar hinged at the top, length l, with k1 = k at l1 = l/3, k2 = 2k at l2 = 2l/3 and k3 = 3k at the bottom (force F, displacement x) [VC-AP p.5]: x1 = l1θ = x/3, x2 = l2θ = 2x/3, x = lθ; ½K3x² + ½K1x1² + ½K2x2² = ½Keq x² → 3k + k/9 + 2k(4/9) = Keq → Keq = 4k.
    • Disc with torsional-and-linear springs [VC-AP p.6]: K1, K2, K3 are torsional springs in series along the shaft → 1/K7 = 1/K1 + 1/K2 + 1/K3, K7 = K1K2K3/(K2K3 + K1K3 + K1K2); K5 and K6 act at radius R (x = Rθ); ½K7θ² + ½K4θ² + ½K5x² + ½K6x² = ½Kt,eq θ² → Kt,eq = K1K2K3/(K2K3 + K1K3 + K1K2) + K4 + K5R² + K6R².
3.8 ES summary: inertia and energy terms ([VC-ES])
  • Spring: linear spring force Kx with displacement x(t); torsional spring moment Ktθ with θ(t). Damper: Cẋ (translation) and Ctθ̇ (rotation) [VC-ES p.2].
  • Note (partly legible, with a warning triangle): the weight is neglected when the mass hangs vertically from a spring (spring force Kx shown, mass and pulley sketches crossed out) [VC-ES p.2].
  • Inertia terms: 1 translation mẍ; 2 rotation about the centre IGθ̈; 3 general plane motion (rolling disc): mẍG and IGθ̈, or equivalently Ioθ̈ about the contact point; 4 pendulum: Ioθ̈ about the hinge [VC-ES p.3].
  • Mass moment of inertia (I, J): disc IG = ½mr², Io = IG + mr² = ½mr² + mr² = (3/2)mr² (about the contact point); point mass on a massless rod: Io = mL²; rod: IG = (1/12)mL², Io = IG + m(L/2)² (hinged at the end) [VC-ES p.3].
  • Kinetic energy T (undamped) [VC-ES p.4]: translation T = ½mẋ²; rotation about the centre T = ½IGθ̇²; rolling disc T = ½Ioθ̇² (about the contact point); pendulum T = ½Ioθ̇².
  • Potential energy U [VC-ES p.5]: spring U = ½kx (printed; x² is meant, see ⚠ C-F35); gravity U = ± mgΔh (up +, down −); pendulum of length L: Δh = L − L cos θ = L(1 − cos θ), U = mgL(1 − cos θ). An Arabic note (partly legible) says that when the mass moves horizontally with a spring the potential energy of the weight is not counted [VC-ES p.5].
