Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

  • Deriving the equation of motion is the second step in studying a vibrating system [VA-L2 p.24].
  • Newton's 2nd law (lecture): ΣF = Mẍ (translation) or ΣM = Jθ̈ (rotation), where ΣF is the sum of all forces except the inertia force, Mẍ is the inertia force, ΣM is the sum of the moments of all loads except the inertia moment, and Jθ̈ is the inertia moment [VA-L2 p.24].
  • Energy method (lecture): applicable to conservative (undamped) systems only: d/dt[(K.E.) + (P.E.)] = 0 gives the equation of motion, since (K.E.) + (P.E.) = constant. Arabic note: the total PE + KE is constant (energy is neither lost nor created); with damping, energy is lost, so the method cannot be applied [VA-L2 p.24].
  • Rayleigh method: since KE + PE is constant, PE = 0 when KE is maximum and PE is maximum when KE = 0, so (K.E.)max = (P.E.)max. It gives ωn only, not the equation of motion [VA-L2 p.24].
  • Newton's method: usable for any vibrating system — free or forced, damped or undamped, single or multi-DOF. Rotation: Jθ̈ = ΣT; translation: mẍ = ΣF [VA-CH p.33; VA-BK p.33].
  • Energy method: for a conservative system the total energy is constant, so for a free undamped SDOF system T + U = constant and d/dt(T + U) = 0 (T = kinetic energy, U = potential energy) [VA-CH p.33; VA-BK p.33].
  • Lagrange method: the general form of the energy law, usable for any system (free or forced, damped or undamped, SDOF or MDOF): d/dt(∂T/∂q̇r) − ∂T/∂qr + ∂D/∂q̇r + ∂U/∂qr = Qqr. Here T = KE and U = PE of the whole system, D = dissipative energy = ½Cq̇r², C = damping coefficient, qr = generalized coordinate, q̇r = dqr/dt = generalized velocity, and Qqr = generalized external force associated with qr [VA-CH p.34–35; VA-BK p.34–35].
  • Example: m1 and m2 joined by spring k, with force F2 on m2: q1 = x1, q2 = x2, Qq1 = 0, Qq2 = F2 [VA-CH p.35; VA-BK p.35].
  • Measuring x from the static equilibrium position removes the spring's static force kΔ and the weight mg from the equation of motion [VA-CH p.39; VA-BK p.39].
  • Worked SDOF derivations by both methods: see §5.4 [VA-CH p.41–59; VA-BK p.41–59].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

4.1 Energy method (book)
  • In undamped free vibration no energy is dissipated; KE T is stored in the mass (velocity), PE U as strain energy. T + U = constant, d/dt(T + U) = 0 [VB-AM p.27–28].
  • T1 + U1 = T2 + U2; take 1 = passing through static equilibrium (U1 = 0 reference) and 2 = maximum displacement (T2 = 0) → T1 = U2; for harmonic motion Tmax = Umax, useful to get the natural frequency directly [VB-AM p.28].
4.2 Analytical dynamics: Lagrange, virtual work, D'Alembert, Hamilton (book)
  • Two approaches: vectorial dynamics (Newton's second law, forces and motions) and analytical dynamics (system as a whole, scalar kinetic and potential energies). Lagrange's equations: ODEs in generalized coordinates based on the energies and instantaneous work [VB-AM p.53].
  • Generalized coordinates: coordinates describing the motion in each DOF (Cartesian, polar, cylindrical, spherical) with motion along each independent of the others; may lack simple meaning (e.g. Fourier coefficients of a string deflection, each term a DOF). For N particles, 3N Cartesian coordinates relate to generalized coordinates qi (n = 3N): xi = xi(q1…qn, t), yi = …, zi = … [VB-AM p.53–54].
  • Virtual work: statement of static or dynamic equilibrium. Virtual displacement δr: imaginary, infinitesimal, occurs without passage of time, obeys differential calculus; consistent with constraints φj(x1, y1, z1…, t) = 0 (j = 1..k) if the constraint equations remain satisfied. δW = Σ Fi·δri; in equilibrium the virtual work of all forces (applied + constraint) over any consistent virtual displacement is zero [VB-AM p.54].
  • D'Alembert's principle: virtual work extended to dynamics by including inertia forces (dynamic equilibrium); generalized form: the virtual work of the effective forces through virtual displacements compatible with the constraints is zero [VB-AM p.54–55].
  • Lagrange's equation: d/dt(∂T/∂q̇i) − ∂T/∂qi + ∂V/∂qi = Qi (Qi = generalized force); with Lagrangian L = T − V: d/dt(∂L/∂q̇i) − ∂L/∂qi = Qi [VB-AM p.55].
  • Variational principles view the motion as a whole: search for the path in configuration space giving a stationary value of an integral, with fixed initial and final points; best known = Hamilton's principle [VB-AM p.55].
  • Hamilton's principle (derived from the generalized D'Alembert principle): ∫t0^t1 (δT + δW)dt = 0, or ∫δ(T − V)dt = 0, δ∫L dt = 0, L = T − V. Usual form (conservative systems, forces derivable from V(q, t)): the actual path of a holonomic system from t0 to t1 makes I = ∫t0^t1 L dt stationary for path variations vanishing at the end points [VB-AM p.55].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

4.1 Methods (Section 3)
    1. Newton's law: translation ΣF = mẍ, with the forces Fsp (spring), Fd (damper), mg (not always taken — ليها تعامل خاص) and the external harmonic F(t); rotation ΣM = Iθ̈ (ΣM = moment, I = mass moment of inertia) [VC-S3 p.1].
    1. Energy method: d/dt (K.E. + P.E.) = 0, used for the undamped case only (يستخدم في حالة الـ undamped فقط) [VC-S3 p.1].
    1. Virtual displacement — not required (مش علينا) [VC-S3 p.1].
4.2 Static deflection and the weight
  • Static: mg = K δst. Dynamic FBD: spring force K(x + δst) up, mg down → mg − Kx − Kδst = mẍ → mẍ + Kx = 0 [VC-S3 p.2].
  • Important notes: (1) when the mass m causes δst (vertical hanging), mg and δst are not taken into account; sketch: unstretched position, then the position after hanging the mass [VC-S3 p.4]. (2) If a rod hangs vertically there is no δst, so mg is taken into account (e.g. pendulum rod with a horizontal spring) [VC-S3 p.5]. (3) If a rod is horizontal (δst present), mg and δst are not taken: the spring force K(x + δst) and mg cancel down to Kx [VC-S3 p.5].
4.3 Sheet 2 Problem 1 — equations of motion (Section 3 solutions)
  • Sheet 2 P1: for Figs. 1–7 write the equation of motion and derive the natural frequency using (1) Newton's method and (2) the principle of energy conservation [VC-SH2 p.1].
  • The same Problem 1–4 solutions (identical steps and answers) are repeated in [VC-S34 pp.20–34]; the lines below cite [VC-S3] only.
  • Fig. 1 (bar of length L pivoted at A, L/3 from the top, torsional spring Kt at A, two springs K at the top end and two springs K at the bottom end): x = (L/3)θ, y = (2L/3)θ; ΣMA = Jθ̈: −2Kx(L/3) − Ktθ − mg(L/6)θ − 2Ky(2L/3) = Jθ̈ → Jθ̈ + ((10/9)KL² + (1/6)mgL + Kt)θ = 0; with J = mL²: mL²θ̈ + ((10/9)KL² + (1/6)mgL + Kt)θ = 0, ωn = √[((10/9)KL² + (1/6)mgL + Kt)/(mL²)] [VC-S3 pp.8–9] (⚠ C-F6).
  • Fig. 2 (rod m2 of length L hinged at O with a bob m1 at its end): x1 = (L/2)θ, x2 = Lθ; ΣMO = Jθ̈: −m2g x1 − m1g x2 = Jθ̈ → Jθ̈ + (m1gL + ½m2gL)θ = 0, ωn = √[(m1gL + ½m2gL)/J] [VC-S3 p.10].
  • Fig. 3 (disc m, J0, radius R, rolling on an incline with springs K1, K2 attached at distance a from the centre, on the far side from the contact point P): θ small, θ = x/(R + a); ΣMP = J0θ̈: −Fs1(a + R) − Fs2(a + R) = J0θ̈ → J0θ̈ + [K1(a + R)² + K2(a + R)²]θ = 0 → θ̈ + [(K1 + K2)(a + R)²/J0]θ = 0, ωn = √[(K1 + K2)(a + R)²/J0] [VC-S3 p.11].
  • Fig. 4 (massless beam E, I, L hinged at O with mass m at the tip, springs K1 above and K2 below at L/2): x = (L/2)θ; ΣMO = Jθ̈: −K1x(L/2) − K2x(L/2) = Jθ̈ → Jθ̈ + (L²/4)(K1 + K2)θ = 0, ωn = (L/2)√[(K1 + K2)/J] [VC-S3 p.12].
  • Fig. 5(a) simple pendulum: −mgx = Jθ̈, x = Lθ, −mgLθ = mL²θ̈ → θ̈ + (g/L)θ = 0, ωn = √(g/L) [VC-S3 p.13; VC-S3 p.4].
  • Fig. 5(b) pendulum with a horizontal spring K at distance a below O: x = Lθ, x1 = aθ, −mgLθ − Ka²θ = mL²θ̈ → θ̈ + [(mgL + Ka²)/(mL²)]θ = 0, ωn = √[(mgL + Ka²)/(mL²)] [VC-S3 p.13].
  • Fig. 5(c) inverted pendulum (m on top, hinge O at the bottom, spring K at height a): mgLθ − Ka²θ = mL²θ̈ → θ̈ + [(Ka² − mgL)/(mL²)]θ = 0, ωn = √[(Ka² − mgL)/(mL²)], with Ka² > mgL for stability [VC-S3 p.14].
  • Fig. 6 (bar hinged at O with K1 at l1, K2 at l2, and the mass m hung through K3 at the tip l3): energy ½Keq1 l3²θ² = ½K1 l1²θ² + ½K2 l2²θ² → Keq1 = (K1 l1² + K2 l2²)/l3²; Keq1 in series with K3 → Keq = (K1K3 l1² + K2K3 l2²)/(K3 l3² + K1 l1² + K2 l2²); ωn = √(Keq/m) = √[(K1K3 l1² + K2K3 l2²)/(m(K1 l1² + K2 l2² + K3 l3²))]; the source writes the equation as θ̈ + (same ratio)θ = 0 [VC-S3 pp.15–16].
  • Fig. 7 (same bar with m at the tip on K2 below): Keq1 = (K1 l1² + K2 l2²)/l3², in parallel with K2 → Keq = [K1 l1² + (l2² + l3²)K2]/l3²; ωn = √{[K1 l1² + (l2² + l3²)K2]/(m l3²)}; θ̈ + {[K1 l1² + (l2² + l3²)K2]/(m l3²)}θ = 0 [VC-S3 pp.17–18].
  • Sheet 2 Problem 1 figures as printed [VC-SH2 pp.1–2]: Fig. 1 vertical bar labelled m, pivot A (with torsional spring kt) at l/3 from the top and 2l/3 from the bottom, a pair of horizontal springs k at each end; Fig. 2 pendulum O with rod m2 (weight m2g at mid-length) and bob m1 at length l; Fig. 3 disc m, J0, radius R, centre O, on an incline between springs k1 (lower) and k2 (upper), attached at a point a from the centre; Fig. 4 massless beam E, I, L carrying m at its tip, springs k1 above and k2 below at L/2 from the tip; Fig. 5 (a) simple pendulum, massless bar, length l, (b) the same with a horizontal spring k at distance a below the hinge, (c) inverted pendulum, massless bar, hinge at the bottom, spring k at height a; Fig. 6 bar hinged at P with k1 (at l1, to ground below), k2 (at l2, to ceiling above) and m hung by k3 from the tip Q (l3); Fig. 7 same bar with m at the tip resting on k2 to ground and k2 to the ceiling at l2 (both upper and lower springs are labelled k2) [VC-SH2 pp.1–2].
4.4 Lagrange's equation (Section 7)
  • d/dt(∂T/∂q̇i) − ∂T/∂qi + ∂D/∂q̇i + ∂U/∂qi = Qqi [VC-S7 p.3].
  • T kinetic energy (belongs to the masses, خاصة بالكتل): translation T = ½mẋ²; rotation T = ½J0θ̇² (J0 mass moment of inertia); general plane motion T = ½mẋ² + ½J0θ̇²; ∂T/∂qi is always zero because T is a function of the velocities, not the displacements (دائماً بتساوي الصفر لأن T دالة في السرعة وليس الإزاحات) [VC-S7 p.3].
  • D dissipative energy (belongs to the damping elements): D = ½CV² [VC-S7 p.3].
  • U potential energy (belongs to the springs): axial U = ½Kx², torsional U = ½Ktθ² [VC-S7 p.3].
  • Qqi external forces; qi coordinates or degrees of freedom [VC-S7 p.3].
  • Newton's law for 2-DOF: translation ΣF = mẍ; rotation ΣM = J0θ̈ (moment about the point of rotation, J0 mass moment of inertia) [VC-S7 p.2].
4.5 ES summary: Newton and energy methods ([VC-ES])
  • (1) Newton: ΣF = mẍ (translation), ΣMo = Ioθ̈ (rotation) — "for all types of problems" (Arabic, جميع الأنواع). (2) Energy: d/dt (T + U) = 0, "for free undamped" only. The 1 S.D.F cases are free undamped, free damped and forced; 2-DOF cases are listed after them [VC-ES p.2].
  • Worked example (pendulum of length L with a horizontal spring k at distance a below the hinge O; mass m at L; θ(t)) [VC-ES pp.6–7]:
    • Newton: ΣMo = Ioθ̈: −kx a cos θ − mgL sin θ = Ioθ̈ with x = a sin θ → Ioθ̈ + k a sin θ a cos θ + mgL sin θ = 0; sin θ = θ, cos θ = 1 → Ioθ̈ + (ka² + mgL)θ = 0, with Io = Ieq (meq) and (ka² + mgL) = Keq [VC-ES p.6].
    • Energy: T = ½Ioθ̇², U = ½kx² + mgL(1 − cos θ) = ½ka² sin²θ + mgL(1 − cos θ); d/dt(½Ioθ̇² + ½ka² sin²θ + mgL(1 − cos θ)) = 0 → Ioθ̈θ̇ + ka² sin θ cos θ θ̇ + mgL sin θ θ̇ = 0 → Ioθ̈ + ka²θ + mgLθ = 0 → Ioθ̈ + (ka² + mgL)θ = 0, meq = Ieq = Io, Keq = ka² + mgL [VC-ES p.7].
4.6 Solutions from [VC-SOLU]
  • Rod m2 of length l hinged at O with a bob m1 at its end (same as Sheet 2 P1 Fig. 2, §4.3) [VC-SOLU p.1]: y = (l/2) sin θ = (l/2)θ, x = l sin θ = lθ; Io = (1/12)m2l² + m2(l/2)² + m1l² = ⅓m2l² + m1l² = (⅓m2 + m1)l². Newton: ΣMo = Ioθ̈: −m2g y − m1g x = Ioθ̈ → (⅓m2 + m1)l²θ̈ + (m2g l/2 + m1g l)θ = 0 → (⅓m2 + m1)l²θ̈ + gl(m2/2 + m1)θ = 0. Energy: K.E. = ½Ioθ̇² = ½(⅓m2 + m1)l²θ̇²; P.E. = m2g a + m1g b with a = (l/2)(1 − cos θ), b = l(1 − cos θ); d/dt(K.E. + P.E.) = 0 with sin θ = θ, cos θ = 1 gives the same equation (⅓m2 + m1)l²θ̈ + gl(m2/2 + m1)θ = 0 [VC-SOLU p.1].
  • Simple pendulum (sin θ ≈ θ) by Newton and energy: ωn = √(g/l), ml²θ̈ + mglθ = 0 (same working as [VC-AU p.5]; an Arabic note says sin θ = θ or cos θ = 1 must not be substituted before differentiating in the energy method) [VC-SOLU p.2].
  • "Sheet Power": bar hinged at O with K1 at l1, K2 at l2 and the mass m hung by K3 at l3 (same as Sheet 2 P1 Fig. 6) [VC-SOLU p.3]: ΣMo = Ioθ̈ = 0: K1l1²θ + K2l2²θ + K3l3²θ − K3l3x = 0 → (K1l1² + K2l2² + K3l3²)θ = K3l3x (1); mass: ΣF = mẍ → mẍ + K3x = K3l3θ (2); from (1) θ = K3l3x/(K1l1² + K2l2² + K3l3²) (3); substituting (3) in (2): mẍ + K3x − [K3²l3²/(K1l1² + K2l2² + K3l3²)]x = 0 → m(K1l1² + K2l2² + K3l3²)ẍ + (K3K1l1² + K2K3l2²)x = 0 [VC-SOLU p.3]. This agrees with the Keq/ωn of [VC-S3 pp.15–16].
  • Problem (3), projectile and block (Sheet 2 P2; data m1 = 10 kg, m2 = 0.1 kg, v0 = 500 m/s, x0 = 0, ẋ0 = v1; K = 3000 N/m) [VC-SOLU p.4]: (m1 + m2)ẍ + Kx = 0 → (10 + 0.1)ẍ + 3000x = 0; ωn = √(3000/10.1) = 17.235 rad/s; momentum m2v0 = (m1 + m2)v1 → 0.1 × 500 = 10.1v1 → v1 = 4.95 m/s; τ = 2π/ωn = 0.3646 s; x(t) = A cos ωnt + B sin ωnt, x(0) = 0 → A = 0; ẋ(0) = Bωn = 4.95 → B = 4.95/ωn = 0.287 → x(t) = 0.287 sin ωnt; ẋ = Bωn cos ωnt = 0 → ωnt = π/2 → t = (π/2)(1/ωn) = τ/4 = 0.09115 s, x = 0.287 sin(ωnt) = 0.287 m. Energy method: ½(m1 + m2)v1² = ½KX² → X = √(mv²/K) = 0.287 m [VC-SOLU p.4].
4.7 Sheet 2 Problem 1 — Sherif's solutions ([VC-SH2S])
  • Fig. 1 (bar, pivot A at L/3, torsional spring Kt at A, springs K at both ends) [VC-SH2S p.1]: x = (L/3)tan θ = (L/3)θ, y = (2L/3)θ (cos θ = 1); IO = (1/12)mL², IA = (1/12)mL² + m(L/6)² = (1/9)mL². ΣMA = IAθ̈: IAθ̈ = −2Kx(L/3) − Ktθ − mgθ(L/6) − 2Ky(2L/3) = −2K(L²/9)θ − Ktθ − mg(L/6)θ − 2K(4L²/9)θ → IAθ̈ + ((2/9)KL² + Kt + (L/6)mg + (8/9)KL²)θ = 0 (the two spring terms are boxed as (10/9)KL²); ωn = √[((2/9)KL² + Kt + (L/6)mg + (8/9)KL²)/IA] (⚠ C-F6: this solution uses IA = mL²/9, unlike [VC-S3 p.9]).
  • Fig. 2 (rod m2 of length L, bob m1 at the end) [VC-SH2S p.2]: ΣMO = Jθ̈ (Io): Iθ̈ = −m2gθ(L/2) − m1gθ(L) → Iθ̈ + θ(m1gL + ½m2gL) = 0; ωn = √[(m1gL + ½m2gL)/Io,tot] with Io,tot = Io,sphere + Io,rod = msL² + ⅓mrL² (sphere lumped: Icg = (2/5)mr² neglected as 0; rod Io = (1/12)mrL² + mr(L/2)² = ⅓mrL²).
  • Fig. 3 (sphere m, J0, radius R, springs K1, K2 at a from the centre, on an incline) [VC-SH2S p.3]: tan θ = x/(a + R) → θ = x/(a + R), x = (a + R)θ; ΣMC = Icθ̈ (C the contact point): Icθ̈ = −Fs2(a + R) − Fs1(a + R) → Icθ̈ + K1(a + R)²θ + K2(a + R)²θ = 0; ωn = √[(K1(a + R)² + K2(a + R)²)/Ic] with Ic = (2/5)mR² + mR² = (7/5)mR² (a sphere is assumed; the sheet gives J0, see ⚠ C-F41).
  • Fig. 5 [VC-SH2S p.4]: (a) simple pendulum: Ioθ̈ = −mgθL → θ̈ + (mgL/Io)θ = 0, ωn = √(mgL/Io), Io = mL² (the (2/5)mr² term is crossed out); (b) with horizontal spring at a: x = a sin θ = aθ; Ioθ̈ = −mgθL − Kxa → Ioθ̈ + (mgL + Ka²)θ = 0, ωn = √[(mgL + Ka²)/Io]; (c) inverted: Ioθ̈ = Kxa·(…) + mgθL as printed → Ioθ̈ + (Ka² − mgL)θ = 0, ωn = √[(Ka² − mgL)/Io], condition of stability Ka² − mgL > 0, i.e. Ka² > mgL.
  • Fig. 6 (bar hinged at P with K1 at L1, K2 at L2 and m hung by K3 at L3) [VC-SH2S pp.8–9]: x3 = L3θ; ΣMP = 0: −K1(L1θ)L1 − K2L2(θL2) − K3(L3θ − x)L3 = 0 → (K1L1² + K2L2² + K3L3²)θ = K3L3x, θ = K3L3x/(K1L1² + K2L2² + K3L3²) (1); mass: ΣF = Mẍ: Mẍ = K3(L3θ − x) → Mẍ + K3x = K3L3θ (2); substituting: (K1L1² + K2L2² + K3L3²)Mẍ + (K1L1² + K2L2² + K3L3² … − K3²L3²)x = 0 as printed, labelled Meq and Keq; ωn = √(Keq/Meq) (⚠ C-F42) — the same result as [VC-SOLU p.3] and [VC-S3 pp.15–16] once the missing factor K3 is restored.
  • Fig. 4 (massless beam E, I, L with m at the tip and K1 above, K2 below at L/2) [VC-SH2S p.10]: x = (L/2)θ; Ioθ̈ = −K2x(L/2) − K1x(L/2) → Ioθ̈ + [K2(L/2)² + K1(L/2)²]θ = 0, ωn = √{[K2(L/2)² + K1(L/2)²]/Io}; Io = (1/12)mL² + m(L/2)² = ⅓mL² (⚠ C-F42); an "another solution" by P.E.eq = P.E.sys with ½Keq x² = ½K1… is started and not finished [VC-SH2S p.10].

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

5.1 Introduction and mass–spring system
  • Every system with mass and elasticity can vibrate freely. Free vibration results from initial conditions with no external excitation; the first thing of interest is the natural frequency, obtained from the equation of motion. Damping makes the amplitude decay with time [VA-CH p.38; VA-BK p.38].
  • Static equilibrium (FBD 1): KΔ = mg (K = spring stiffness, Δ = static deflection under the weight). Dynamic motion (FBD 2), x measured from the S.E.P.: mẍ = mg − k(x + Δ) → mẍ + kx = 0 [VA-CH p.38–39; VA-BK p.38–39].
  • Solution: (mD² + k)x = 0, D = d/dt → D1,2 = ±i√(k/m); x = c1 e^(i√(k/m) t) + c2 e^(−i√(k/m) t). Using e^(±iθ) = cos θ ± i sin θ: x = A sin √(k/m) t + B cos √(k/m) t. With ωn = √(K/m) (natural frequency): ẍ + ωn x = 0 (as printed); x = A sin ωn t + B cos ωn t = X sin(ωn t + φ), where the constants come from x(0) and ẋ(0); τ = 2π/ωn. The response is SHM of amplitude X and phase φ [VA-CH p.39–40; VA-BK p.39–40] (⚠ A-F8).
  • Lecture derivation: dynamic FBD ΣF↓ = mẍ: mg − K(x + δst) = mẍ → mẍ + Kx = mg − Kδst; the static FBD gives mg = Kδst, so mẍ + Kx = 0, ẍ + (K/m)x = 0, ẍ + ωn²x = 0 (translation). For rotation: Jθ̈ + Ktθ = 0, θ̈ + ωn²θ = 0. The sketch marks the unstretched position, the static equilibrium position (δst below it), the maximum-compressed and maximum-tension positions, and the response over one complete cycle [VA-L2 p.25].
  • ωn = √(K/M) = √(Kt/J) rad/s, where K ≡ Keq (N/m), M ≡ Meq (kg), Kt = (Kt)eq (N·m/rad) and J = Jeq, the equivalent polar mass moment of inertia (kg·m²). Remember ωn = 2πfn = 2π/τn (fn = natural frequency in cps = Hz; τn = natural period in s) [VA-L2 p.26].
  • Solution: ẍ + ωn²x = 0 is a 2nd-order homogeneous ODE. With the operator D = d/dt: (D² + ωn²)x = 0, x ≠ 0 → D² + ωn² = 0 (the characteristic equation) → D1,2 = ±iωn [VA-L2 p.27].
  • General root cases: (1) real and distinct D1 ≠ D2 → x = C1e^(D1t) + C2e^(D2t); (2) complex D1,2 = a ± ib → x = e^(at)(C1 cos D1t + C2 sin D2t) (as written, with "b" marked above); (3) real and repeated D1 = D2 = D → x = e^(Dt)(C1 + tC2). Here case 2 applies with a = 0, b = ωn → x = C1 cos ωnt + C2 sin ωnt [VA-L2 p.27] (⚠ A-F19).
  • Initial conditions x(0) = x0, ẋ(0) = ẋ0 → C1 = x0, C2 = ẋ0/ωn. Response: x(t) = x0 cos ωnt + (ẋ0/ωn) sin ωnt = X̄ cos(ωnt ± α) with α = tan⁻¹(∓B/A); = X̄ sin(ωnt ± φ) with φ = tan⁻¹(±A/B); A = x0, B = ẋ0/ωn; X̄ = √(A² + B²) = √(x0² + (ẋ0/ωn)²) is the amplitude and α, φ are phase angles [VA-L2 p.27–28].
  • Phase angle: the angle between two synchronous motions (same frequency, whatever the amplitudes), e.g. A sin ωt and B cos ωt, which differ by π/2 (sin θ = cos(θ − π/2), cos θ = sin(θ + π/2)). Figure: x1 = A cos ωnt plus x2 = B sin ωnt equals x = X̄ cos(ωnt + α1), α1 = tan⁻¹(−B/A), all with period τn = 2π/ωn. Arabic note: the resultant amplitude is a constant (independent of time), and its frequency equals that of each original motion [VA-L2 p.28].
  • Note: ωn = √(K/M) and mg = Kδst (static FBD) → K/m = g/δst → ωn = √(g/δst). This holds only for vertical suspension [VA-L2 p.28].
5.2 Lecture examples (free undamped)
  • Ex. 1, effect of the spring's mass: spring K (length L) of mass ms, uniformly distributed, carrying m. An element dy at distance y from the fixed end has mass ms dy/L and displacement xel = x·y/L (velocity ẋ·y/L). (K.E.)spring = ∫₀^L ½(ms dy/L)(y/L)²ẋ² = msẋ²/(2L³)·[y³/3]₀^L = msẋ²/6 = ½(ms/3)ẋ² → mseq = ms/3, Meq = m + ms/3, ωn = √(Keq/Meq) = √(3K/(ms + 3m)) [VA-L2 p.29].
  • Ex. 2, mass m between springs k1 and k2 on a surface inclined at θ: mẍ = −k1x − k2x → mẍ + (k1 + k2)x = 0, ωn = √((k1 + k2)/m) rad/s, fn = (1/2π)√((k1 + k2)/m) cps (Hz). Arabic notes: the inclination does not affect the equation of motion or ωn, but it does affect the static deflection δst of each spring. So: (1) all four cases drawn (inclined with k1 only or k1 + k2, vertical k1 and k2 in parallel, a single spring k1 + k2) are equivalent; (2) (δst)1 = (δst)2 ≠ (δst)3; (3) ωn = √(g/(δst)3) is valid only for cases 3 and 4, not 1 and 2; (4) the lecture poses the question of (ωn)1 and (ωn)2 for a horizontal mass on one spring K (length L) versus a mass between two half-length springs (L/2 each) — left unanswered. Pendulums with a spring k at a and length L (hanging, inverted, horizontal) are sketched [VA-L2 p.30].
  • Ex. 3 (marked "not necessary"), cantilever of total mass mL with a tip mass M: assume the static deflection shape y = ½ymax[3(x/L)² − (x/L)³] = (ymax/2L³)(3x²L − x³), with dmb = (dx/L)(mL) = m dx. (K.E.)beam = (ẏmax²/8L⁶)∫₀^L(9x⁴L² − 6x⁵L + x⁶)m dx = (mẏmax²/8L⁶)(9L⁷/5 − L⁷ + L⁷/7) = 0.11786 mLẏmax² = ½Mef ẏmax² → Mef = Meq = 0.2357 mL. Meq = (M + 0.2357 mL) kg, Keq = 3EI/L³, ωn = √(Keq/Meq) [VA-L2 p.31] (⚠ A-F20).
  • Ex. 4 (also typed as "Example (1-1)" in the "Solved Examples" handout): k/m = 4.0 s⁻²; the mass is displaced 2 cm down from equilibrium and given 8 cm/s upward. ωn = 2 rad/s, x0 = 0.02 m, ẋ0 = −0.08 m/s. X̄ = √(0.02² + (0.08/2)²) = 0.04472 m = 4.472 cm; α = tan⁻¹((+0.08/2)/0.02) = +63.435° = +1.10715 rad; x = X̄ cos(ωnt + α). Maximum acceleration: dẍ/dt = ωn³X̄ sin(ωnt + α) = 0 → ωnt + α = 0 (gives t < 0, rejected) or π → t = (π − 1.10715)/2 = 1.01722 s; ẍ = −(4 × 0.04472) cos π = +0.1789 m/s². Summary: x = 0.04472 cos(ωnt + 1.10715), ẋ = −0.08944 sin(ωnt + 1.10715), ẍ = −0.1789 cos(ωnt + 1.10715) (hand plot of x, ẋ, ẍ with ẋ(0) = −0.08 m/s). Arabic note: the maxima can be read straight from these equations, since each equals its amplitude [VA-L2 p.32, 34].
  • Typed handout plots for this example: Figure 1, system response (displacement in cm, velocity in cm/s, acceleration in cm/s²) against time 0–10 s; Figure 2, displacement response and its two terms against angle (rad) and time; Figure 3, displacement, velocity and acceleration against angle and time [VA-L2 p.33, 35].
5.3 Experiments based on free vibration
  • Stiffness of an unknown spring: time about 20 complete oscillations, τ = t/20, then ωn = 2π/τ = √(k/m) gives k [VA-CH p.41; VA-BK p.41].
  • g from a simple pendulum: τ = t/20; τ = 2π/ωn = 2π√(L/g) → τ² = (2π)²L/g, so τ² ∝ L. Plot τ² against L; the slope tan θ = (2π)²/g gives g, to be compared with 9.81 m/s² [VA-CH p.42; VA-BK p.42].
  • J of an unknown disc on a rod of known properties: τ = t/20, ωn = 2π/τ = √(k/J), with k from the rod's properties [VA-CH p.44; VA-BK p.44].
  • Radius of gyration of a rod swung as a compound pendulum, compared with the theoretical value "K² = L³/3" [VA-CH p.45; VA-BK p.45] (⚠ A-F9).
5.4 Worked natural-frequency examples (book, Ch. 3)
  • Simple pendulum (Newton): I0θ̈ = −mgL sin θ, I0 = mL² → mL²θ̈ + mgL sin θ = 0. This is non-linear; for small θ (5°–7°), sin θ = θ − θ³/3! + … ≈ θ, so θ̈ + (g/L)θ = 0 and ωn = √(g/L). Energy method: T = ½m(Lθ̇)², U = mgL(1 − cos θ) → mL²θ̈ + mgL sin θ = 0 [VA-CH p.41–43; VA-BK p.41–43].
  • Torsional vibration: steel rod d = 0.5 cm, L = 2 m, G = 80 × 10⁹ N/m², 10 oscillations in 30.2 s; find J. k = GIp/L, Ip = πd⁴/32; Jθ̈ + Kθ = 0 → ωn = √(K/J), J = K/ωn²; f = 10/30.2 Hz, ωn = 20π/30.2 rad/s → J = 0.567 kg·m² [VA-CH p.43–44; VA-BK p.43–44].
  • Compound pendulum (h = distance from the pivot to the CG): IAθ̈ + mghθ = 0 with IA = IC.G + mh² = mk² + mh² (k = radius of gyration) → ωn = √(gh/(k² + h²)) [VA-CH p.45; VA-BK p.45].
  • h for maximum ωn of a disc (radius r) pivoted at a distance h from its centre: (Mr²/2 + Mh²)θ̈ + Mghθ = 0, ωn² = gh/(r²/2 + h²). Setting dωn/dh = 0 gives r²/2 + h² − 2h² = 0 → h = r/√2, and ωn,max = √(g/(√2 r)) = (1/2)^(1/4) √(g/r) [VA-CH p.46; VA-BK p.46].
  • Inverted pendulum (mass m at height L above pivot O, spring k at distance a, x = aθ): mL²θ̈ + (Ka² − mgL)θ = 0 → ωn = √((Ka² − mgL)/(mL²)); the energy method (U = ½Ka²θ² − mgL(1 − cos θ)) gives the same [VA-CH p.47; VA-BK p.47].
  • Disc (I, m, r) rolling without slip with a spring k at its centre: IAθ̈ = −kxr, (I + mr²)θ̈ + Kr²θ = 0 → ωn = √(K/(I/r² + m)); the energy method gives the same [VA-CH p.48; VA-BK p.48].
  • Disc (radius R, hub r) rolling on an incline with the spring attached at the hub, xs = (R + r)θ, IA = (3/2)mR²: (3/2)mR²θ̈ + K(R + r)²θ = 0 → ωn = √(2K(R + r)²/(3mR²)) [VA-CH p.49; VA-BK p.49].
  • Rolling disc (radius r) with two springs K attached at height a above the centre, y = (r + a)θ: (3/2)mr²θ̈ + 2K(r + a)²θ = 0 → ωn = √(4K(r + a)²/(3mr²)) [VA-CH p.50; VA-BK p.50].
  • Disc J0 with two springs k initially stretched by δ, x = rθ: J0θ̈ = −k(x + δ)r − k(x − δ)r = −2krx, written "= −2krθ²" → "ωn = √(2Kr/J0)" [VA-CH p.51; VA-BK p.51] (⚠ A-F10). The preload δ cancels [VA-CH p.51; VA-BK p.51].
  • Disc hanging in a rope loop with spring k (y = 2x = 2rθ, IA = (3/2)mr²): (3/2)mr²θ̈ + 4kr²θ = 0 → ωn = √(8K/(3m)); the energy method gives the same [VA-CH p.52; VA-BK p.52].
  • Massless rod pivoted at one end, spring k at a, disc (M1, I) at distance b, and M2 hanging from a rope on the disc (x = rθ, φ = rθ/b, x1 = 2rθ, keq = (a/b)²k): (I + M1r² + 4M2r²)θ̈ + (a²/b²)r²kθ = 0 → ωn = √((a²K/b²)/(I/r² + M1 + 4M2)) [VA-CH p.53–54; VA-BK p.53–54].
  • Pulley system, two springs k (2T = kx, y = 2x): mÿ = −2T = −kx → 2mẍ + kx = 0, ωn = √(k/(2m)) [VA-CH p.54; VA-BK p.54].
  • Pulley system with springs Ka and Kb (2T = KaXa = KbXb, X = 2Xa + 2Xb → Xa = X/(2(Ka + Kb)/Kb)): mẌ + ½KaXa = 0 → Ẍ + (1/4)(KaKb/(m(Ka + Kb)))X = 0, ωn = √(KaKb/(4m(Ka + Kb))) [VA-CH p.55; VA-BK p.55].
  • Inclined axis carrying a wheel with an unbalance weight W at radius r (axis at α to the vertical, total inertia J): Jθ̈ = −W sin α (r sin θ) → ωn = √(Wr sin α/J), f = (1/2π)√(Wr sin α/J) [VA-CH p.56; VA-BK p.56].
  • Two masses sliding in a tube that rotates horizontally at constant ω, each held by an unstretched spring of free length r0: m(ẍ + r0ω²) = m(r0 + x)ω² − Kx (as printed) → mẍ + kx − mxω² = 0, ωn = √((K − mω²)/m) = √(K/m − ω²) [VA-CH p.56; VA-BK p.56].
  • Fluid in a U-tube manometer (column length l, area A, specific weight γ): mẍ = −γ(2x)A with m = γlA/g → ẍ + (2g/l)x = 0, ωn = √(2g/l) [VA-CH p.57; VA-BK p.57].
  • Piece of a disc (I, pivot at distance h, CG at distance a): (mh² + I)θ̈ + mg(a − h)θ = 0; energy method T = ½IAθ̇², U = mg(a − h)(1 − cos θ) [VA-CH p.57; VA-BK p.57].
  • Hemispherical shell (radius R, CG at rc from the centre) rocking without slip: [Ic + m(R − rc)²]θ̈ + mgrcθ = 0 with rc = 2R/π → ωn = √(g/((π − 2)R)) [VA-CH p.58; VA-BK p.58] (⚠ A-F11).
  • Sphere of radius r rolling without slip inside a sphere of radius R (Rθ = rφ): translation T1 = ½(W/g)(R − r)²θ̇², U1 = W(R − r)(1 − cos θ); rotation at (φ̇ − θ̇) = (R/r − 1)θ̇, T2 = ½(Wr²/(2g))(R/r − 1)²θ̇² (as written, with I = Wr²/(2g)), U2 = 0 → (3/2)((R − r)/g)θ̈ + θ = 0, ωn = √(2g/(3(R − r))) [VA-CH p.59; VA-BK p.59].
5.5 Problems (free undamped)
  • See §14 [VA-CH p.77–80; VA-BK p.77–80].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

5.1 Undamped translational SDOF (book)
  • Model: single mass on a linearly elastic massless spring, constrained to move vertically, coordinate x(t) → one DOF (Fig. 1.8) [VB-AM p.25].
  • m ẍ + kx = 0 → ẍ + ωn² x = 0, ωn = √(k/m); initial conditions x(0) = x0, ẋ(0) = v0 [VB-AM p.26].
  • General solution x(t) = A1 e^(iωn t) + A2 e^(−iωn t) (A1, A2 complex) = (X/2)[e^(i(ωn t−φ)) + e^(−i(ωn t−φ))] = X cos(ωn t − φ) → "harmonic oscillator" [VB-AM p.26].
  • Amplitude X and phase φ depend on the initial excitations; ωn depends only on system parameters, hence "natural frequency" [VB-AM p.26].
  • X = √(x0² + (v0/ωn)²); φ = tan⁻¹[v0/(x0 ωn)] [VB-AM p.26].
  • Period τ (time for one cycle, or between two consecutive peaks) = 2π/ωn = 2π√(m/k); fn = 1/τ = (1/2π)√(k/m) in cps = Hz [VB-AM p.26].
5.2 Undamped torsional SDOF (book)
  • Disc on a shaft of negligible mass (Fig. 1.9). Twisting torque Mt = GJ/l (per unit twist), J = πd⁴/32 for a circular shaft, G = shear modulus, l = length; kt = T/θ = GJ/l [VB-AM p.27] (⚠ B-F5).
  • IG θ̈ + kt θ = 0, ωn = (kt/IG)^½; θ(t) = θ0 cos ωn t + (θ̇0/ωn) sin ωn t [VB-AM p.27].
5.3 Stability (book)
  • Mass and stiffness enter the characteristic equation, so they affect the stability of an undamped SDOF system; proper selection avoids instability. A stable system executes bounded oscillations about the equilibrium position [VB-AM p.28].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

5.1 Free, single, linear, undamped system (Section 3)
  • Translation: mẍ + Kx = 0, i.e. ẍ + (K/m)x = 0 — a linear, ordinary, 2nd-order differential equation; K = equivalent stiffness, m = equivalent mass; solved with the differential operator to get the response [VC-S3 p.2].
  • x(t) = C1 cos(√(K/m) t) + C2 sin(√(K/m) t); ωn = √(K/m) = 2πFn = 2π/τn (rad/s) [VC-S3 p.3].
  • Natural frequency ωn (the source spells it "neutral frequency"): the frequency at which the system moves in the undamped, unforced case [VC-S3 p.3].
  • Initial conditions give C1, C2: x(0) = x0, ẋ(0) = ẋ0 → C1 = x0, C2 = ẋ0/ωn → x(t) = x0 cos ωnt + (ẋ0/ωn) sin ωnt [VC-S3 p.3].
  • The response may be written with cos or sin only: x(t) = X̄ cos(ωnt ± α), α = tan⁻¹(∓C2/C1); x(t) = X̄ sin(ωnt ± φ), φ = tan⁻¹(±C1/C2); amplitude X̄ = √(C1² + C2²) = √(x0² + (ẋ0/ωn)²) [VC-S3 p.3].
  • φ and α are phase angles: the angle between two motions of the same frequency, regardless of the amplitude [VC-S3 p.3].
  • Vertical hanging only (في حالة التعليق الرأسي فقط): mg = Kδst → K/m = g/δst → ωn = √(K/m) = √(g/δst) [VC-S3 p.4].
  • Rotation (simple pendulum): ΣM0 = J0θ̈, −mgx = J0θ̈, x = L sin θ ≈ Lθ (θ small), −mgLθ = mL²θ̈ → θ̈ + (g/L)θ = 0, ωn = √(g/L) [VC-S3 p.4].
5.2 Example 1 (Section 3) — four springs
  • Given m = 1 kg, K1 = K2 = K3 = K4 = 1 N/m (K1 ∥ K2 above the mass, K3 in series with K4 below); required ωn, F, τ and the response for x0 = 0, ẋ0 = 1 m/s [VC-S3 p.6].
  • Keq1 = K1 + K2 = 2 N/m; Keq2 = K3K4/(K3 + K4) = ½ N/m; Keq = 2 + ½ = 5/2 N/m; ωn = √(5/2) rad/s; F = √(5/2)/(2π) Hz; τ = 2π/√(5/2) s [VC-S3 p.6].
  • x(t) = C1 cos ωnt + C2 sin ωnt; x(0) = 0 → C1 = 0; ẋ(0) = 1 → C2 = 1/ωn = √(2/5); x(t) = √(2/5) sin(√(5/2) t) [VC-S3 pp.6–7].
5.3 Sheet 2 Problems 2–4 (Section 3 solutions)
  • Sheet 2 P2: a 0.1 kg projectile is fired into a 10 kg block initially at rest with no force in the spring (Fig. 8); (a) equation of motion of block + projectile, (b) natural frequency and period, (c) maximum horizontal displacement and the time at which it occurs [VC-SH2 p.1].
    • Given mb = 0.1 kg, m = 10 kg, K = 3×10³ N/m, Vb = 500 m/s, x0 = 0 [VC-S3 p.19].
    • (a) −Kx = (m + mb)ẍ → ẍ + [K/(m + mb)]x = 0 [VC-S3 p.19].
    • (b) ωn = √(3×10³/10.1) = 17.234 rad/s; τn = 2π/17.234 = 0.3646 s [VC-S3 p.20].
    • (c) Momentum: (m + mb)ẋ0 = mbVb → 10.1ẋ0 = 0.1×500 → ẋ0 = 4.95 m/s; ẋ(t) = (ẋ0/ωn)ωn cos ωnt = 0 → ωnt = 90×π/180 → "tmax = 1.572 sec"; x = (4.95/17.234) sin(17.234×1.572×180/π) → xmax = 0.26584 m [VC-S3 p.20] (⚠ C-F7).
  • Sheet 2 P3: natural frequency of the system of Fig. 9; W is applied at the tip of beam 1 (cantilever L1, E1, I1) and at the midpoint of beam 2 (simply supported L2, E2, I2) [VC-SH2 p.1].
    • K1 = 3E1I1/L1³, K2 = 48E2I2/L2³, parallel → Keq = K1 + K2, written as Keq = 3E1I1/L1³ + 48E2I2/L2²; ωn = √(Keq/meq) = √[(3E1I1/L1³ + 48E2I2/L2²)/m] [VC-S3 p.21] (⚠ C-F8).
  • Sheet 2 P4: k/m = 4 s⁻²; the mass is deflected 2 cm down from equilibrium and given an upward velocity of 8 cm/s; find amplitude, maximum acceleration and the time at which it occurs [VC-SH2 p.1].
    • Given k/m = 4 s⁻², x0 = 0.02 m, ẋ0 = 0.08 m/s; x(t) = X̄ cos(ωnt + α); X̄ = √[(0.02)² + (0.08/2)²] = 0.04472 m; ẋ = −ωnX̄ sin(ωnt + α), ẍ = −ωn²X̄ cos(ωnt + α), α = tan⁻¹(−ẋ0/(x0ωn)) (written tan⁻¹(−x0/(ẋ0/ωn)) in the source); "to find tmax, set ẋ(t) = 0" — the page ends there, so maximum acceleration and its time are not completed in this file [VC-S3 p.22].
  • Sheet 2 P5 (Fig. 10): pulley P approximated as a uniform disk of mass mP and radius R, the mass of pulley C neglected; block A (mass mA) hangs from the rope on P, the other rope end runs horizontally round pulley C, which is held by spring k to the wall; write the equation of motion, the natural frequency and the natural period [VC-SH2 p.3].
    • Solution [VC-S34 pp.35–36]: pulley C: 2T = ½Kx (spring force Fs = Kx/2 on C) → T = ¼Kx; mass A: −TA = mAẍ → TA = −mAẍ; pulley P: ΣMo = Jθ̈, +TA R − T R = Jθ̈ → −mAẍR − ¼KxR = Jθ̈; with x = Rθ, ẋ = Rθ̇, ẍ = Rθ̈: (J + mAR²)θ̈ + ¼KR²θ = 0 → θ̈ + [¼KR²/(J + mAR²)]θ = 0; ωn = √[¼KR²/(J + mAR²)]; τn = 2π/ωn = 2π/√[¼KR²/(J + mAR²)] [VC-S34 pp.35–36]. (J of the uniform-disk pulley is left as J in the solution.)
5.4 Abdelrahman Mamdouh's free-undamped notes ([VC-AU])
  • Free undamped system: no external force F(t) = 0, no damper C = 0 [VC-AU p.1].
  • Newton method: ΣF = mẍ (translation), ΣMO = IOθ̈ (rotation). Energy method: K.E. translation ½mẋ², rotation and G.P.M. ½IOθ̇²; P.E. = ± mgh (only when the mass moves vertically and the spring is not present to carry it — the Arabic condition is partly legible) and spring P.E. = ½Kx²; d/dt(K.E. + P.E.) = 0 [VC-AU p.1].
  • Three hanging springs a, b, c: a unstretched; b static with static deflection δ; c dynamic with displacement x from the static position. Static: ΣF = 0, mg − Kδ = 0 → mg = Kδ (1). Dynamic: ΣF = mẍ, spring force Ks = K(δ + x): mg − K(δ + x) = mẍ → −Kx = mẍ → mẍ + Kx = 0 (2) [VC-AU p.2].
  • Harmonic function: x = X0 sin(ωt + φ) (3), ẋ = X0ω cos(ωt + φ), ẍ = −X0ω² sin(ωt + φ) (4); substituting (3) and (4) in (2): −mω² + K = 0 → K = mω² → ωn = √(Keq/meq), the natural frequency [VC-AU pp.2–3].
  • Initial conditions at t = 0: x = A, ẋ = B: A = X0 sin φ (5), B = X0ωn cos φ (6); (6) ÷ (5) gives (1/ωn) tan φ = A/B → φ = tan⁻¹(Aωn/B); X0 is then obtained from (5). Also ωn = 2πF = 2π/τ and τ = 1/F [VC-AU p.3].
  • Exponential solution: mẍ + Kx = 0 → mλ² + K = 0, λ = ± √(−K/m) = ± iωn; x(t) = C1 e^(iωt) ± C2 e^(−iωt), with e^(iαt) = cos αt + i sin αt and e^(−iαt) = cos αt − i sin αt; can be written x(t) = A0 cos ωnt + B sin ωnt [VC-AU p.4].
  • With x(0) = x0, ẋ(0) = ẋ0 the constants A0 and B are found by substitution (the Arabic note "لو قيمة" — the expressions are not written). Writing A0 = A cos φ, B = A sin φ gives x(t) = A cos(ωnt − φ); or, with B = A cos φ, A0 = A sin φ, x(t) = A sin(ωnt + φ); A = √(A0² + B²), φ = tan⁻¹(B/A0) (from tan φ = A sin φ/A cos φ = B/A0) [VC-AU p.4] (⚠ C-F26).
  • Simple pendulum example, sin θ ≈ θ [VC-AU p.5]: Newton: ΣMO = JOθ̈, JO = ml², −mglθ = JOθ̈ → JOθ̈ + mglθ = 0 → (ml²)θ̈ + (mgl)θ = 0, ωn = √(mgl/ml²) = √(g/l). Energy: K.E. = ½JOθ̇² = ½(ml²)θ̇²; P.E. = mgΔy = mg(l − l cos θ) (sin θ ≈ θ or cos θ = 1 is not used before differentiating); d/dt(½ml²θ̇² + mgl − mgl cos θ) = 0 → 2·½ml²θ̇θ̈ + mgl sin θ θ̇ = 0 → (ml²θ̈ + mgl sin θ)θ̇ = 0 → ml²θ̈ + mglθ = 0 with sin θ = θ.
5.5 Sheet 2 Problems 2, 3, 5 — Sherif's solutions ([VC-SH2S])
  • P2 (projectile and block) [VC-SH2S pp.11–12]: (a) ΣF = mẍ: −Kẋ… → (10 + 0.1)ẍ + Kx = 0 → ẍ + (3×10³/10.1)x = 0; (b) ωn = √(3000/10.1) = 17.235 rad/s, τn = 2π/ωn = 0.3646 s; (c) system SDOF free undamped, x0 = 0 (starts from rest) so x(t) = (ẋ0/ωn) sin ωnt; momentum: (m + mb)ẋ0 = mbvb → 10.1ẋ0 = 0.1×500 → ẋ0 = 4.95 m/s; ẋ(t) = ẋ0 cos ωnt = 0 → cos ωnt = 0 → ωnt = 90°·π/180 = 1.57 → t = 1.57/17.235 = 0.0912 s; the sine evaluated there is written 0.1097 m (as read; ⚠ C-F7), while a side note gives the amplitude √(0² + (ẋ0/ωn)²) = 0.28 m and says x(t)max = ẋ0/ωn is the amplitude [VC-SH2S pp.11–12].
  • P3 (two beams) [VC-SH2S p.13]: W applied at the tip of beam 1 (cantilever, I1, E1, L1) and at the mid-point of beam 2 (simply supported, I2, E2, L2); K1 = 3E1I1/L1³, K2 = 48E2I2/L2³; both carry the same load, i.e. parallel connection: Keq = K1 + K2 = 3E1I1/L1³ + 48E2I2/L2³, m = W/g; ωn = √(Keq/meq) = √[(3E1I1/L1³ + 48E2I2/L2³)/meq] (exponent 3 on L2, correcting [VC-S3 p.21], ⚠ C-F8).
  • P4 [VC-SH2S p.14]: only a heading; Arabic note "solved completely in the doctor's lecture".
  • P5 (pulleys P and C, block A) [VC-SH2S pp.15–16]: x = Rθ, ẋ = Rθ̇, ẍ = Rθ̈; pulley C: 2T = Kx/2 → T = ¼Kx (with y = θ0 r, x = 2θ0 r → y = x/2, so the spring force on C is K·x/2, from the geometry of the rigid links and the pulley's instantaneous centre); mass A: −TA = mAẍ; pulley P: ΣMo = Ioθ̈: Ioθ̈ + TR − TAR = 0 → Ioθ̈ + ¼KxR + mAẍR = 0 → (Io + mAR²)θ̈ + ¼KR²θ = 0; ωn = √[¼KR²/(Io + mAR²)], τn = 2π/ωn; a side note gives Io = ½mr² for the disk [VC-SH2S p.15].

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

6.1 Equation of motion and roots
  • Mass–damper–spring: mẍ = −cẋ − kx → mẍ + cẋ + kx = 0, a second-order linear ODE ("non-homogeneous, where the free end is zero", as written) [VA-CH p.60; VA-BK p.60].
  • (D² + (c/m)D + k/m)x = 0 → D1,2 = −c/2m ± √((c/2m)² − k/m); x(t) = e^(−(c/2m)t)(A e^(√((c/2m)² − k/m) t) + B e^(−√(…) t)), with A and B from x(0) and ẋ(0) [VA-CH p.60–61; VA-BK p.60–61].
  • The sign of the "radical value" (c/2m)² − k/m sets the root locations and whether the system vibrates (figure: responses for different root positions in the complex plane) [VA-CH p.61–62; VA-BK p.61–62]:
    • (A) positive: two real roots, exponential response, no oscillation → overdamped [VA-CH p.62; VA-BK p.62].
    • (B) negative: complex-conjugate roots, oscillation (growing, constant or decaying depending on root location) → underdamped [VA-CH p.62; VA-BK p.62].
    • (C) zero: equal real roots, no oscillation → critically damped [VA-CH p.63; VA-BK p.63].
6.2 Critical damping and damping ratio
  • (cc/2m)² = K/m = ωn² → cc = 2mωn = 2√(km). ζ = c/cc = c/(2mωn) = c/(2√(km)); k/m = ωn², c/m = 2ζωn → ẍ + 2ζωnẋ + ωn²x = 0. D1,2 = −ζωn ± √(ζ² − 1) ωn = −ζωn ± i√(1 − ζ²) ωn [VA-CH p.63; VA-BK p.63].
  • Root locus: a semicircle of radius ωn in the left half-plane. ζ = 0 gives ±iωn; for 0 < ζ < 1 the roots are complex conjugates that move together as ζ rises; at ζ = 1 they meet at −ωn; for ζ > 1 they separate along the real axis [VA-CH p.64; VA-BK p.64].
  • Cases: critically damped ζ = 1, underdamped ζ < 1, overdamped ζ > 1. General solution x(t) = e^(−ζωn t)(A e^(√(ζ²−1) ωn t) + B e^(−√(ζ²−1) ωn t)) [VA-CH p.64; VA-BK p.64].
6.3 Critically damped
  • With ζ = 1 the solution x = e^(−ωn t)(A + B) = D e^(−ωn t) has only one constant for two initial conditions, so it is modified to x(t) = e^(−ωn t)(A + Bt). xmax is found from ẋ = 0 → t1, xmax = x(t1). There is no oscillation: the response decays exponentially [VA-CH p.64–65; VA-BK p.64–65].
6.4 Underdamped
  • x(t) = e^(−ζωn t)[C sin √(1−ζ²) ωn t + D cos √(1−ζ²) ωn t] = X e^(−ζωn t) sin(√(1−ζ²) ωn t + φ), with X and φ from the initial conditions [VA-CH p.65; VA-BK p.65].
  • Damped frequency ωd = √(1 − ζ²) ωn; τd = 2π/ωd = 2π/(√(1 − ζ²) ωn). ωd and ζ are properties of the system [VA-CH p.66; VA-BK p.66].
  • Logarithmic decrement: the ratio of successive amplitudes is constant, X1/X2 = X2/X3 = … Proof: X2 is taken at t1 + τd; since √(1−ζ²) ωn τd = 2π the sine terms are equal, so X1/X2 = e^(ζωn τd). Then δ = ln(X1/X2) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) and ζ = δ/√((2π)² + δ²) (printed as √((2π)² − δ²) on p.67) [VA-CH p.66–67; VA-BK p.66–67] (⚠ A-F12). Figure: δ against ζ, exact curve and the straight line δ ≈ 2πζ [VA-CH p.67; VA-BK p.67].
  • Over n cycles: X1/Xn+1 = e^(nδ) → δ = (1/n) ln(X1/Xn+1) [VA-CH p.67; VA-BK p.67]. The problems page's support box gives δ = ln(X0/Xn) = 2nπξ/√(1 − ξ²) [VA-CH p.82; VA-BK p.82].
6.5 Overdamped
  • ζ > 1: two real roots; x(t) = e^(−ζωn t)(A e^(√(ζ²−1) ωn t) + B e^(−√(ζ²−1) ωn t)), decaying exponentially without oscillation ("called a periodic motion" as printed, i.e. aperiodic). Figures compare the overdamped and underdamped responses [VA-CH p.68; VA-BK p.68].
6.6 Worked examples (free damped)
  • m = 0.907 kg, K = 7.0 N/cm = 700 N/m: cc = 2√(Km) = 2√(700 × 0.907) N·s/m (numerical value left blank) [VA-CH p.68; VA-BK p.68] (⚠ A-F13).
  • Dashpot calibration: a ½ lb force gives a constant 1.2 in/s → c = Fd/ẋ = (1/2)/1.2 = 1/2.4 lb·s/in (the asked-for ζ is not computed) [VA-CH p.69; VA-BK p.69].
  • Response with x(0) = 0, ẋ(0) = v0 [VA-CH p.69–70; VA-BK p.69–70]:
    • ζ = 2 (overdamped): A = −B = v0/(2ωn√(ζ² − 1)); x(t) = (v0 e^(−ζωn t)/(2ωn√(ζ² − 1)))(e^(√(ζ²−1) ωn t) − e^(−√(ζ²−1) ωn t)).
    • ζ = 0.5 (underdamped): φ = 0, X = v0/(√(1 − ζ²) ωn); x(t) = (v0/(√(1 − ζ²) ωn)) e^(−ζωn t) sin √(1 − ζ²) ωn t.
    • ζ = 1 (critical): A = 0, B = v0; x(t) = v0 t e^(−ωn t).
  • m = 2.267 kg, K = 17.5 N/cm, Xn/Xn+1 = 1/0.98: (a) ωn = √(K/m) = 27.784; (b) δ = ln(1/0.92) (as printed) = 0.020; (c) ζ = 0.003215; (d) c = 2ζmωn = 0.545; ωd = 27.78 [VA-CH p.70–71; VA-BK p.70–71] (⚠ A-F14).
  • m = 4.534 kg, K = 35 N/cm, c = 0.1243 N·s/cm: (a) ζ = c/(2√(Km)) = 0.1243 × 100/(2√(4.534 × 35 × 100)) = 0.049; (b) δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = 0.3; (c) Xn/Xn+1 = e^δ = 1.34 [VA-CH p.71; VA-BK p.71].
  • m = 17.5 kg, K = 70.0 N/cm, C = 70.0 N·s/cm (rewritten as 0.7 N/(cm/s)): ζ = 0.7 × 100/(2√(7 × 100 × 17.5)); ωn = √(70 × 100/17.9); ωd, δ and the amplitude ratio are left blank [VA-CH p.71–72; VA-BK p.71–72] (⚠ A-F15).
  • Railway buffer: two parallel oil cylinders, each giving 50 kN at 0.3 m/s and each with a spring of 65.5 kN/m (negligible initial compression); train mass 205 000 kg at 1.52 m/s. C = 50/0.3 kN·s/m, C′ = 2C = 333.3 × 10³ N·s/m; ζ = C′/(2√(K′m)) = 333.3 × 10³/(2√(2 × 65.5 × 10³ × 205 000)) = 1.017 ≈ 1; ωn = √(K′/m) = 0.799 rad/s → treated as critically damped. x(0) = 0, ẋ(0) = 1.52 → A = 0, B = 1.52; x(t) = 1.52 t e^(−0.799t); ẋ = 0 at t = 1/ωn = 1.25 s → xmax = 0.6998 m (the distance travelled before first coming to rest) [VA-CH p.72–73; VA-BK p.72–73].
  • Mass dropped from height h onto a spring–damper: x(0) = 0, ẋ(0) = √(2gh); x = e^(−ζωn t)(A sin ωd t + B cos ωd t) → B = 0, A = √(2gh)/ωd; x(t) = (√(2gh)/ωd) e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t [VA-CH p.73–74; VA-BK p.73–74].
  • Rod pivoted at O (mass m at L, damper C at a, spring K at L): ma²θ̈ + Ca²θ̇ + KL²θ = 0 (as printed; see ⚠ A-F16) → θ̈ + (C/m)θ̇ + (KL²/(ma²))θ = 0; ωn = √(KL²/(ma²)); Cc = 2mωn = 2√(KmL²/a²); ωd = √(ωn² − (ζωn)²) = √(KL²/(ma²) − (C/2m)²) [VA-CH p.74; VA-BK p.74] (⚠ A-F16).
  • Gun barrel: m = 500 kg, recoil spring 200 kN/m, critical damping (return in the least time without oscillation), recoil 1.25 m. (a) C = Cc = 2√(KM) = 2√(200 × 10³ × 500) = 2 × 10⁴ N·s/m. (b) x = e^(−ωn t)(A + Bt), x(0) = 0 → A = 0; ẋ = B e^(−ωn t)(1 − ωn t); xmax at t = 1/ωn, xmax = B/(eωn) → B = eωn xmax; ωn = √(200 × 10³/500) = 20 rad/s; "B = e × 20 × 1.25 = 62 m/s". (c) time to recoil 1 m: "1 = 68 e^(−20t)", t not completed [VA-CH p.75–76; VA-BK p.75–76] (⚠ A-F17).
6.7 Lecture problems (free damped) — typed statements, response plots and handwritten solutions
  • Solution form used throughout (underdamped): x(t) = e^(−ζωn t)[x0 cos ωd t + ((ẋ0 + ζωn x0)/ωd) sin ωd t] = X̄d e^(−ζωn t) cos(ωd t ± φ). Critically damped: x = e^(−ωn t)[x0 + (ẋ0 + ωn x0)t]. Overdamped: x = e^(−ζωn t)[x0 cosh ω′d t + ((ẋ0 + ζωn x0)/ω′d) sinh ω′d t], with ω′d = ωn√(ζ² − 1) [VA-LP p.2–3].
  • Ex. 1: a machine of weight 500 N on a foundation with keq = 50 kN/m and ceq = 400 N·s/m; x0 = 8 mm, ẋ0 = −31.392 mm/s. (a) equation of motion; (b) plot the response; (c) plot it again for ceq = 3192.754 N·s/m (ζ = 1) and 5427.6818 N·s/m (ζ = 1.7) (typed Fig. 3: ζ = 0.125, 1, 1.7) [VA-LP p.1]. Solution: m = 500/9.81; mẍ + cẋ + kx = 0; c/m = 7.848 = 2ζωn; k/m = ωn² = 981 → ωn = 31.32 rad/s; ζ = 0.1252836781 < 1 (underdamped); ωd = 31.073 rad/s; C1 = x0 = 0.008 m; C2 = (ẋ0 + ζωn x0)/ωd "= 0.009 ≈ zero" → x(t) = e^(−3.92388t)[0.008 cos(31.073t)], i.e. X̄d = 0.008 = x0 [VA-LP p.2]. ζ = 1: x(t) = e^(−31.32t)[0.008 + "2.4744"t]. ζ = 1.7: x(t) = e^(−53.244t)[0.008 cosh(43t) + "0.098" sinh(43t)], ω′d = ωn√(ζ² − 1) = 43.057. Sketch of the three responses (ζ > 1, ζ = 1, ζ < 1) with τd = 2π/ωd "= 2π/31.32 = 0.2 s" [VA-LP p.3] (⚠ A-F21).
  • Ex. 2: a 2000 kg locomotive car at 10 m/s is stopped at the end of the track by a spring–damper, k = 40 N/mm, c = 8.94427 N·s/mm (handwritten: assume the car does not rebound from / stays connected to the spring–damper). (a) maximum displacement after engaging the buffer; (b) time to reach it; (c) repeat for c = 17.88854 × 10³ and 35.7771 × 10³ N·s/m (typed Fig. 4: ζ = 0.5, 1, 2) [VA-LP p.4]. Solution: ẍ + 4.47ẋ + 20x = 0; ωn = √20 = 2√5 = 4.47 rad/s; ζ = 0.49999 ≈ 0.5 (underdamped); ωd = √15 = 3.8729 rad/s; with x0 = 0: x(t) = e^(−√5 t)[2.58 sin(3.87t)], X̄d = 2.58, τd = 2π/√15 = 1.6223 s. Setting ẋ = 0: e^(−√5 t)[−√5 sin 3.87t + 3.87 cos 3.87t] = 0; "e^(−√5 t) = 0 → t = 318.31 s" (rejected), or √5 sin 3.87t = 3.87 cos 3.87t → t = 0.27 s → x = 1.22 m [VA-LP p.5–6] (⚠ A-F22). Part (c) is only shown in the typed figure [VA-LP p.4].
  • Ex. 3: a boy on a bicycle modelled with W = 800 N, k = 50 000 N/m, c = 1000 N·s/m; the road level drops suddenly (the concrete blocks settled differently; sketch: 5 cm step, lengths 10 m, 15 m, 10 m) at a speed of 5 m/s (18 km/h). Find the vertical displacement, assuming no vertical vibration before the step, and repeat for critical damping and for over-damping (c = 8000 N·s/m). Typed Fig. 5: (a) ζ = 1 (c = 4038.55 N·s/m), 1.981 (c = 8000), 0.2476 (c = 1000); (b) responses with x0 and ẋ0, x0 only, ẋ0 only [VA-LP p.7]. Handwritten case 1 (x0 = 0.05 m, ẋ0 = 0): ẍ + 12.2625ẋ + 613.125x = 0; ωn = 24.76 rad/s; ζ = 0.2476 (underdamped); ωd = 23.9889 ≈ 24 rad/s; ζωn x0/ωd = 0.2476(24.76)(0.05)/24 = 0.01277; "X̄d = √(C1² + C2²) = 0.05"; φ = tan⁻¹(−0.01277/0.05) = −0.25 rad → x(t) = 0.05 e^(−6.13t) cos(24t − 0.25); ẋ = 0 gives the maximum at t = 0, X̄d = X̄ = 0.05 m [VA-LP p.8–9] (⚠ A-F23).
  • Ex. 4: masses m1 = 72 g and m2 = 45 g on two rigid massless rods hinged at O, with a spring k at b = 3 cm and a damper c = 5 N·s/m at a = 4 cm; l1 = 10 cm, l2 = 8 cm. Find k so that the amplitude falls to one tenth after three complete cycles (typed Fig. 6, ζ = 0.1213; handwritten: from the response x = x0 e^(−ζωn t) cos ωd t, read τd → ωd and X1/X2 → δ → ζ, then ωn) [VA-LP p.10]. Solution: δ = (1/3) ln 10 = 0.7675; ζ = 1/√(1 + (2π/δ)²) = 0.121254; J0 = m1l1² + m2l2² = 0.001008 kg·m²; θ̈(m1l1² + m2l2²) + ca²θ̇ + kb²θ = 0; ca²/J0 = 2ζωn → 5(0.04)²/0.001008 = 2(0.121254)ωn → ωn = 32.726 rad/s; k = ωn² J0/b² = 1199.56 ≈ 1200 N/m [VA-LP p.11–12].
  • Ex. 5: an underdamped shock absorber for a 200 kg motorcycle (two springs k/2 and a damper c); after a road bump gives an initial vertical velocity, the damped period is 2 s and the amplitude falls to one fourth in half a cycle. Find k, c, and the minimum initial velocity for a maximum displacement of 250 mm (typed Fig. 7: responses for the design, ζ = 1 and ζ = 1.5) [VA-LP p.13]. Solution: ωd = 2π/τ = π = 3.14 rad/s; δ = 2 ln 4 = 2.7726 (reduction over half a cycle); ζ = 0.4037 (underdamped); ωn = 3.433 rad/s; c = 200(2)(0.40371)(3.433) = 554.36 N·s/m; k = mωn² = 200(3.433)² = 2358 N/m. With x0 = 0: x = e^(−ζωn t)(ẋ0/ωd) sin ωd t; ẋ = 0 → tan ωd t = ωd/(ζωn) = 2.26676 → "3.433 t = 1.15532 → t = 0.3365 s"; 0.25 = e^(−1.385)[(ẋ0/3.433) sin(3.433 × 0.3365)] → "ẋ0 = 3.747 m/s" (crossed out, no final answer) [VA-LP p.14–15] (⚠ A-F24).
  • Ex. 6: a cannon whose barrel and recoil mechanism have a mass of 500 kg, with a recoil spring of 10 000 N/m and critical damping (to return in the shortest time without oscillation); the gun recoils 0.4 m (maximum allowable displacement). Find (1) the critical damping coefficient, (2) the initial velocity (handwritten: assuming zero initial displacement), (3) the time to return to 0.1 m from the initial position (typed Fig. 8: response for ζ = 1) [VA-LP p.16]. Solution: ωn = √(10000/500) = 2√5 = 4.47 rad/s; cc = 2√(km) = 4472.135955 N·s/m; x(t) = e^(−ωn t)[ẋ0 t]; ẋ = 0 → t = 1/ωn = √5/10 s; 0.4 = e^(−2√5(√5/10))[ẋ0 √5/10] → ẋ0 = 4.8626 m/s; 0.1 = "e^(−2√5(√5/10))"[4.8626 t] → t = 0.825 s [VA-LP p.17].
6.8 Coulomb (dry-friction) damping
  • Only the force law FF = μR is given (§3.6); these files have no Coulomb-damped response [VA-CH p.30; VA-BK p.30].
6.9 Problems (free damped)
  • See §14 [VA-CH p.81–82; VA-BK p.81–82].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

6.1 Viscous damping (book)
  • Damping force F = c ẋ, opposite to velocity; c = damping constant (coefficient of viscous damping). ẍ + (c/m)ẋ + (k/m)x = 0 (Fig. 1.10: spring force k(Δ + x), damper force cẋ, weight mg) [VB-AM p.28–29].
  • Try x = Ce^(st) → s² + (c/m)s + k/m = 0 → s1,2 = −c/2m ± √((c/2m)² − k/m) [VB-AM p.29].
  • (c/2m)² − k/m = 0 → c = 2mωn, repeated roots s = −c/2m, x = (A + Bt)e^(−(c/2m)t); critical damping constant Cc = 2mωn [VB-AM p.29].
  • s1,2 = (−ζ ± √(ζ² − 1)) ωn; damping factor ζ = c/Cc = c/(2mωn) [VB-AM p.29].
  • ζ < 1 (underdamped): "roots both imaginary"; x(t) = X e^(−ζωn t) sin(ωd t + φ), ωd = √(1 − ζ²) ωn (damped circular frequency, always less than ωn) (Fig. 1.11) [VB-AM p.29–30] (⚠ B-F6).
  • ζ = 1 (critically damped): x(t) = (A + Bt)e^(−ωn t): linear function × decaying exponential, decays without oscillation (Fig. 1.12) [VB-AM p.30].
  • ζ > 1 (overdamped): x(t) = C1 e^((−ζ + √(ζ²−1))ωn t) + C2 e^((−ζ − √(ζ²−1))ωn t), non-oscillatory (Fig. 1.13) [VB-AM p.30].
6.2 Logarithmic decrement (book)
  • Represents the rate at which the amplitude of free damped vibration decreases; defined as the natural log of the ratio of any two successive amplitudes [VB-AM p.30].
  • xi/xi+1 = Xe^(−ζωn ti)/Xe^(−ζωn(ti+τd)) = e^(ζωn τd) = constant; δ = ln(xi/xi+1) = ζωn τd; with τd = 2π/ωd = 2π/(ωn√(1−ζ²)): δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) [VB-AM p.31].
6.3 Torsional viscous damping (book)
  • I θ̈ + ct θ̇ + kt θ = 0 (I = disc mass moment of inertia, kt = restoring torque per unit angular displacement) [VB-AM p.31].
6.4 Coulomb damping (book)
  • Damping force = normal force × coefficient of dry friction, independent of velocity; mass sliding on a horizontal surface with friction coefficient f (Fig. 1.14) [VB-AM p.31].
  • m ẍ = −kx − Fd "if ẍ > 0"; m ẍ = −kx + Fd "if ẍ < 0"; the equations and solutions are discontinuous at the end points of the motion [VB-AM p.31] (⚠ B-F7).
  • For motion to the left (ẋ < 0): x = A sin ωt + B cos ωt + Fd/k [VB-AM p.31].
  • Solution for motion to the left starting from x = x0, ẋ = 0 (extreme right): x = (x0 − Fd/k) cos ωt + Fd/k (ẋ < 0); holds until ẋ is again zero; the displacement is then to the left of neutral with magnitude 2Fd/k less than x0 [VB-AM p.32].
  • Constant amplitude loss of 4Fd/k per cycle; motion is a linearly decaying harmonic function made of half-sine waves offset successively by Fd/k up or down depending on the direction of motion; period τ = 2π/ωn (Fig. 1.15) [VB-AM p.32].
6.5 Hysteretic (structural) damping (book)
  • Solid materials, in particular metals, are not perfectly elastic and exhibit hysteretic (structural) damping, due to friction between internal planes that slip during deformation; the area of the hysteresis loop = energy loss per loading cycle [VB-AM p.32].
  • ΔU = πβkX², β = dimensionless structural damping coefficient, k = equivalent spring constant, X = displacement amplitude (π included for convenience); energy loss is a non-linear function of displacement [VB-AM p.32].
  • Equivalent viscous damping constant: ce = βk/ω = β√(mk) [VB-AM p.32] (⚠ B-F8).

6.2 Single, free, linear, damped ("decay") system (Section 3&4)
  • Model: m hung from a spring K and a damper C in parallel; FBD forces Fd = Cẋ and Fs = Kx upward, inertia mẍ [VC-S34 p.6].
  • ΣFx = mẍ: −Fs − Fd = mẍ → meq ẍ + Ceq ẋ + Keq x = 0 → ẍ + (C/m)ẋ + (K/m)x = 0 (equation of motion) [VC-S34 p.6].
  • With K/m = ωn² and C/m = 2ζωn: ẍ + 2ζωnẋ + ωn²x = 0; ζ "damping factor" = C/Cc = C/(2mωn) = C/(2√(Km)); Cc = critical damping factor [VC-S34 p.6].
  • Roots: D1,2 = −ζωn ± ωn√(ζ² − 1) [VC-S34 p.6].
  • Cases of ζ: = 1 critical damping; > 1 over damping; < 1 under damping; = 0 undamping [VC-S34 p.6].
  • ζ = 1 (critical): x(t) = e^(−ωnt)(x0 + (ẋ0 + ωnx0)t); sketch: non-vibrating curve that decays without crossing, against the undamped sine [VC-S34 p.7].
  • ζ < 1 (underdamped): x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)(x0 cos ωdt + ((ẋ0 + ζωnx0)/ωd) sin ωdt); ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) (ωd frequency of the damped system, ωn frequency of the undamped system), ωn > ωd; ωd = 2π/τd = 2πFd; sketch of the decaying oscillation against the undamped one [VC-S34 p.7].
  • ζ > 1 (overdamped): x(t) = C1 e^((−ζωn + ωn√(ζ²−1))t) + C2 e^((−ζωn − ωn√(ζ²−1))t); C1 = [ẋ0 + (ζωn + ωn√(ζ²−1))x0]/(2ωn√(ζ²−1)); C2 = [(ωn√(ζ²−1) − ζωn)x0 − ẋ0]/(2ωn√(ζ²−1)); sketch: rises once then decays, no oscillation [VC-S34 p.8].
  • Important relations: ωn = √(K/m) (undamped); ζ = C/Cc = C/(2√(Km)) = C/(2mωn); Cc = 2√(Km) = 2mωn; ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 2π/τd = 2πFd; ωd < ωn [VC-S34 p.8].
  • Logarithmic decrement δ — a measure of how much the motion decays (قياس مقدار تحلل الحركة); sketch of successive peaks X1, X2 … Xm+1 with τd between peaks [VC-S34 p.9].
    • Over m cycles: ln(X1/Xm+1) = mδ = 2πmζ/√(1 − ζ²), m = cycle number [VC-S34 p.9].
    • Between two successive amplitudes (بين اتنين Amp. متتاليين): δ = ln(X1/X2) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) [VC-S34 p.9].
  • Specific damping capacity "s.d.c": the ratio of the energy lost in one cycle to the total energy (النسبة بين الطاقة المفقودة في الدورة الواحدة إلى الطاقة الكلية المفقودة); s.d.c = 2δ = 4πζ/√(1 − ζ²) [VC-S34 p.9].
  • Energy dissipated in one cycle: Ed = CπX̄²ωd [VC-S34 p.9].
  • Loss factor η (the ratio lost per 1 rad to the total lost): η = s.d.c/(2π) = δ/π [VC-S34 p.9].
6.3 Damped examples (Section 3&4)
  • Example (1) [VC-S34 p.10] — same data as Sheet 2 P13(a): m = 200 kg, τd = 2 s, x0 = 0, X1/X3/2 = 4; required K, C, ζ. ωd = 2π/τd = π rad/s; ln(X1/X1.5) = mδ = 2πmζ/√(1 − ζ²) with m = ½: ln 4 = ½δ = 2π·½ζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.4037; ωn = π/√(1 − 0.4037²) = 3.4338 rad/s; K = ωn²m = (3.4338)²·200 = 2358.196 N/m; C = 2ζ√(Km) = 2·0.4037·√(2358.196·200) = 554.49 N·s/m [VC-S34 p.10].
  • Example (1) "on single, free, damped, linear systems" [VC-S34 p.11]: rod mr of length 4r hinged at O (2r below the sphere, spring K at distance r below O), sphere ms of radius r on top (centre 3r above O); required ωn. x = rθ; ΣMo = Ioθ̈: 3mgrθ − Kr²θ = Ioθ̈; Io = Irod + Isp = (1/12)mr(4r)² + (2/5)ms r² + ms(3r)²; Ioθ̈ + (Kr² − 3mgr)θ = 0; ωn = √[(Kr² − 3mgr)/Io] (m here is the sphere mass ms) [VC-S34 p.11].
  • Example (2) [VC-S34 p.12]: disc ms of radius r with a welded rod mr of length 3r; damper C at the rod tip (3r), damper C1 at the top of the disc (radius r), spring K at the side of the disc (radius r); required ωn and ζ. ΣMo = Ioθ̈: −3Crθ̇(3r) − C1r²θ̇ − Kr²θ = Ioθ̈ → Ioθ̈ + (9Cr² + C1r²)θ̇ + Kr²θ = 0; ωn = √(Kr²/Io); 2ζωn = c/m → ζ = c/(2√(Km)) = (9Cr² + C1r²)/(2√(Kr² Io)) [VC-S34 p.12].

6.5 Abdelrahman Mamdouh's free-damped notes ([VC-AD])
  • Equation of motion, Newton (mass on wheels with K and C): ΣF = mẍ, mẍ = −Fs − Fd = −Kx − Cẋ → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = 0; general form meq ẍ + Ceq ẋ + Keq x = 0 [VC-AD p.1].
  • Bar of mass m, length L hinged at the top, spring K at L/2 and damper C at the bottom end; I0 = mL²/3, x1 = (L/2)θ, ẋ2 = Lθ̇: −Kx1(L/2) cos θ − Cẋ2 L cos θ − mg(L/2) sin θ = I0θ̈ → (mL²/3)θ̈ + CL²θ̇ + (KL²/4 + mgL/2)θ = 0; meq = mL²/3, Ceq = CL², Keq = KL²/4 + mgL/2 (an intermediate line prints "K L⁴/4", see ⚠ C-F27) [VC-AD p.1].
  • Disc M, radius R, rolling in a box with a spring K at the centre and a damper C at the top of the disc: I0 = IG + MR² = ½MR² + MR² = (3/2)MR²; x = Rθ, ẋ1 = 2Rθ̇; −KxR − Cẋ1(2R) = I0θ̈ → (3/2)MR²θ̈ + (4CR²)θ̇ + (KR²)θ = 0 [VC-AD p.2].
  • Response: mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = 0 is a 2nd-order ordinary homogeneous differential equation; auxiliary equation (ẍ → λ², ẋ → λ, x → 1): mλ² + Cλ + K = 0, λ1,2 = (−C ± √(C² − 4mK))/(2m) [VC-AD p.2].
  • Four possible root types: 1) complex, λ = real ± i imaginary; 2) complex without real part, λ = ± i imaginary; 3) real repeated, λ1 = λ2; 4) real different. The discriminant (C² − 4Km) decides the type: C² < 4Km → complex; C² = 4Km → real repeated; C² > 4Km → real different; C = 0 → complex without real part [VC-AD p.3].
  • Consequences: Cc² = 4Km → Cc = 2√(Km); ωn = √(K/m); damping ratio ζ = C/Cc: ζ = 0 (C = 0) complex without real; 0 < ζ < 1 (C < Cc) complex; ζ = 1 (C = Cc) real repeated; ζ > 1 (C > Cc) real different [VC-AD p.3].
  • Roots in terms of ζ: λ1,2 = −C/(2m) ± √(C² − Cc²)/(2m) = −ζωn ± ωn√(ζ² − 1), using C/(2m) = ζωn and √(C² − Cc²)/(2m) = ωn√(ζ² − 1) (worked out at the side of p.4) [VC-AD p.4].
  • ζ = 0, C = 0, undamped: λ1,2 = ± iωn; x(t) = A cos ωnt + B sin ωnt (sinusoid sketch) [VC-AD p.4].
  • ζ = 1, C = Cc, critically damped: λ1,2 = −ωn (real repeated); x(t) = A e^(−ωnt) + B t e^(−ωnt); sketch decays without oscillating [VC-AD p.4].
  • 0 < ζ < 1, C < Cc, underdamped: λ1,2 = −ζωn ± iωn√(1 − ζ²) = −ζωn ± iωd, ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²); x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)[A cos ωdt + B sin ωdt] = C e^(−ζωnt) sin(ωdt + φ); sketch of a decaying oscillation [VC-AD p.5].
  • Side note on the conversion A cos θ + B sin θ = C sin(θ + φ) = C cos(θ − φ), C = √(A² + B²): for the cos(θ − φ) case A = C cos φ, B = C sin φ, φ = tan⁻¹(B/A) (coefficient of sin over coefficient of cos); for the sin(θ + φ) case A = C sin φ, B = C cos φ, φ = tan⁻¹(A/B) (coefficient of cos over coefficient of sin) [VC-AD p.5].
  • ζ > 1, C > Cc, overdamped: λ1 = −ζωn + ωn√(ζ² − 1), λ2 = −ζωn − ωn√(ζ² − 1) (real different); x(t) = A e^(λ1t) + B e^(λ2t); sketch decays slowly without oscillating [VC-AD p.5].
  • "Laws" page [VC-AD p.6]: meq ẍ + Ceq ẋ + Keq x = 0; (1) ωn = √(K/m); (2) Cc = 2√(Km); (3) ζ = C/Cc; (4) C/(2m) = ζωn; (5) √(C² − 4Km)/(2m) = ωn√(ζ² − 1); (6) ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) for underdamped [0 < ζ < 1]; (7) x(t) = A cos ωnt + B sin ωnt = C cos(ωnt − φ) = C sin(ωnt + φ), φ = tan⁻¹(B/A) for the cos form and φ = tan⁻¹(A/B) for the sin form, C = √(A² + B²), at ζ = 0; (8) x(t) = A e^(−ωnt) + B t e^(−ωnt) at ζ = 1; (9) x(t) = C e^(−ζωnt) sin(ωdt + φ) = C e^(−ζωnt) cos(ωdt − φ), φ = tan⁻¹(A/B) (sin form) or tan⁻¹(B/A) (cos form), C = √(A² + B²), at 0 < ζ < 1; (10) x(t) = A e^(λ1t) + B e^(λ2t) at ζ > 1; (11) λ1,2 = −ζωn ± ωn√(ζ² − 1).
  • Logarithmic decrement [VC-AD pp.7–8]: underdamped x(t) = e^(−ζωnt) X sin(ωdt + φ); peaks x1 at t1 and x2 at t2 = t1 + τd, ωd = 2πfd = 2π/τd, τd = 2π/ωd. x1/x2 = e^(−ζωnt1) sin(ωdt1 + φ)/[e^(−ζωn(t1+τd)) sin(ωd(t1 + 2π/ωd) + φ)] = e^(ζωnτd) = e^(2πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) = e^δ, so δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = ln(x1/x2) [VC-AD pp.7–8].
  • Over cycles: x1/x3 = (x1/x2)(x2/x3) = e^δ e^δ = e^(2δ) → δ = ½ ln(x1/x3); general δ = (1/(n − 1)) ln(x1/xn), where n = (number of cycles) + 1 [VC-AD p.8].
  • Example: the 1st peak is reduced by 75 % in 3 cycles: n = 3 + 1 = 4, δ = (1/(4 − 1)) ln(x1/x4) = (1/3) ln(x1/x4), x4 = (1 − 75 %)x1, x1/x4 = 1/(1 − 0.75) = 1/0.25 = 4 [VC-AD p.8].
  • Example: the 1st peak is reduced to 75 % in 3 cycles: n = 4, x4 = 75 % x1, x1/x4 = 1/0.75 = 4/3, δ = (1/3) ln(x1/x4) (the source stops before evaluating) [VC-AD p.8].
6.6 Sheet 2 damped problems — Sherif's solutions ([VC-SH2S])
  • P7 (cannon recoil) [VC-SH2S pp.16–19]: ζ = 1 given; ωn = √(10000/500) = 4.472 rad/s; Cc = 2mωn = 2(500)(4.472) = 4472 N·s/m = C; equation Mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = 0 → ẍ + 8.944ẋ + 20x = 0; x(t) = e^(−ωnt)[x0 + (ẋ0 + ωnx0)t], C1 = x0, C2 = ẋ0 + ωnx0; x0 = 0 → x(t) = ẋ0 t e^(−ωnt); ẋ = 0 → t = 1/ωn = 1/4.472 = 0.224 s; xmax = 0.4 m = ẋ0(0.224)e^(−4.472×0.224) → ẋ0 = 4.863 m/s; time to 0.1 m: 0.1 = e^(−4.472t)(4.863t) → t = 0.023 s (only the first root, ⚠ C-F10). The page about the pulley geometry on p.16 belongs to P5.
  • P8, Fig. 12 (rod m1, length l, sphere m2 at L; spring k and damper c at the sphere) [VC-SH2S pp.19–23]: ΣM = Ioθ̈: Ioθ̈ = −Kx(L) − Cẋ(L) + m1g(l/2)θ + m2gLθ, x = Lθ → Ioθ̈ + KL²θ + CL²θ̇ − m1g(l/2)θ − m2gLθ = 0 with Io = Is,o + Irod,o = msL² + ⅓mrl² (Is = (2/5)mr² neglected; rod (1/12)mrl² + mr(l/2)² = ⅓mrl²); θ̈ + [CL²/(msL² + ⅓mrl²)]θ̇ + [KL²/(…) − m1g(L/2)/(…) − m2gL/(…)]θ = 0 [VC-SH2S pp.19–21]. Response for C < Ccr with x(0) = x0, ẋ(0) = 0: ζ = C/Cr (the page writes "> 1 under damping case", ⚠ C-F43), x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)(x0 cos ωdt + (ζωnx0/ωd) sin ωdt). Stability: IoD² + CeqD + Keq = 0 with Ceq = CL², Io = msL² + ⅓mrl², Keq = KL² − m1g(l/2) − m2gL; D1,2 = (−Ceq ± √(Ceq² − 4IoKeq))/(2Io); for stability Ceq > 0, Io > 0, Keq > 0; the first two hold, so KL² > ½m1lg + m2gL (written with L in the boxed line) [VC-SH2S pp.21–22].
  • P8, Fig. 13 (rigid massless bar of length L; damper C and spring K at L1, spring K carrying m at the tip) [VC-SH2S pp.5–7]: ΣMo = Ioθ̈: Ioθ̈ = −Kx(L) − Kx1(L1) − Cẋ1(L1); x = Lθ, x1 = L1θ → Ioθ̈ + CL1²θ̇ + (KL² + KL1²)θ = 0; Ieq = Io; ωn = √[K(L² + L1²)/Io]; ζ = C/Cc = Ceq/(2meqωn) = CL1²/(2Io√[K(L1² + L²)/Io]); ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²); τn = 2π/ωn; τd = 2π/ωd; the sheet asks "find the logarithmic decrement δ" and the page ends there (the tip mass m is not used as a separate coordinate, compare ⚠ C-F11).
  • P9 (stepped pulley, Fig. 14; Jo = 5 kg·m², fn = 5 Hz, m = 10 kg, r1 = 0.1 m, r2 = 0.25 m, 10 cycles, amplitude reduced by 80 %) [VC-SH2S pp.23–27]: mass: mẍ = −T − Kx; pulley: Ioθ̈ = T r2 − Cẏ r1 → (Io + mr2²)θ̈ + C r1²θ̇ + K r2²θ = 0; (5 + 10(0.25)²)θ̈ + (0.1)²Cθ̇ + (0.25)²Kθ = 0 → 5.625θ̈ + 0.01Cθ̇ + 0.0625Kθ = 0. δ = (1/m) ln(x1/x1+m) = (1/10) ln(10/2) = 0.16094 (x11 = 10 − 80/100 × 10 = 2); δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.02561; ζ = C/Cr = Ceq/(2meqωn) with ωn = 2π(5) = 31.42 rad/s: 0.02561 = 0.01C/(2·5.625·31.42) → C = 905.25 N·s/m; ωn = √(Keq/meq): 31.42 = √(K(0.25)²/5.625) → K = 88 849.476 N/m; ωd = 31.42√(1 − 0.02561²) = 31.416 rad/s, τd = 2π/ωd = 0.2 s; specific damping capacity = 4πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = 4π(0.02561)/√(1 − 0.02561²) = 0.32193 [VC-SH2S pp.23–26].
  • P10 (stepped cylinder, Fig. 15; 20 kg, IG = 0.0045 kg·m², r = 45 mm, K = 300 N/m, C = 120 N·s/m) [VC-SH2S pp.27–28]: ΣMo = Ioθ̈ about the contact point O: Ioθ̈ = −Cẋ(r) − Kx(r), x = rθ → Ioθ̈ + Cr²θ̇ + Kr²θ = 0; Io = 0.0045 + mr² = 0.0045 + 20(0.045)² = 0.045 kg·m²; 0.045θ̈ + 0.243θ̇ + 0.6075θ = 0; ωn = √(0.6075/0.045) = 3.674 rad/s; ζ = 0.243/(2 × 0.045 × 3.674) = 0.735; ωd = 3.674√(1 − 0.735²) = 2.4912 rad/s; δ = 2π(0.735)/√(1 − 0.735²) = 6.8107; s.d.c = 2δ = 13.6214.
  • P11 (railroad car; m = 2000 kg, v = 10 m/s, K = 40 N/mm = 40×10³ N/m, C = 8.9443 N·s/mm = 8.9443×10³ N·s/m) [VC-SH2S pp.29–31]: Keq = K/2 + K/2 = K; Mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = 0; ωn = √(40×10³/2000) = 2√5 rad/s; ζ = C/(2mωn) = 8.9443×10³/(2 × 2000 × 2√5) = 0.5 < 1 (underdamped); x0 = 0, ẋ0 = 10 m/s → x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)(ẋ0/ωd) sin ωdt with ωd = 2√5√(1 − 0.5²) = √15 rad/s; setting ẋ = 0 the page writes −√5 e^(−√5t)(2.5825 sin √15t) + e^(−√5t)(10 cos √15t) = 0 and gives tmax = 36.7385 s and xmax = 3.325×10⁻³⁶ m (⚠ C-F12).

(b) x0 = 0: x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)(ẋ0/ωd) sin ωdt; ẋ = 0 → tan ωdt = ωd/(ζωn) → ωdt = tan⁻¹(3.14/(0.403 × 3.431)) = 66.2338° = 66.2338π/180 → tmax = 0.3677 s; xmax = 250/1000 = e^(−0.403·3.431·0.3677)(ẋ0/3.14) sin(3.14 × 0.3677 × 180/π (degrees)) → ẋ0 = 1.427 m/s [VC-SH2S pp.33–35].
