Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

7.1 Equation of motion and the two parts of the solution (book Ch. 4)
  • Harmonic excitation often exists in mechanical systems and always occurs because of rotating unbalance in rotary machines. It is studied through the response of an SDOF system (m, C, K) to F(t) = F0 sin ωt, with F0 the amplitude and ω the exciting frequency. From the free-body diagram: m ẍ + c ẋ + K x = F(t) = F0 sin ωt, a second-order, linear, non-homogeneous ODE whose solution has two parts, x(t) = x_c.f + x_p.I [VA-BK p.85]. (The heading "4.1 Introduction" of the chapter is empty; PDF p.84 carries only the heading [VA-BK p.84]. Printed page = PDF page − 8 for Ch. 4–5.)
  • x_c.f, the complementary function (solution of the homogeneous equation), is the transient solution. It is the free-vibration solution of the last chapter and depends on ζ = C/(2√(Km)); the transient response lasts a limited time, after which the system settles into the steady-state solution. It depends on the system parameters m, k, c [VA-BK p.86].
  • x_p.I, the particular integral, is the steady-state solution. It depends on the type of exciting force; for a harmonic force it is the same function as the force but with a different amplitude and a phase: x_p.I(t) = X sin(ωt − φ), where X is the amplitude, ω the angular frequency of the force and φ the phase angle between x_p.I(t) and F(t). Figures: F(t) and x_p(t) against ωt showing the phase φ, and the combined motion = transient + steady-state motion [VA-BK p.86].
7.2 Steady-state amplitude and phase
  • To find X and φ, x_p.I is substituted in the equation of motion; the resulting vector equation is solved graphically with the force polygon (vectors F0, KX, CωX and mω²X at angle ωt) [VA-BK p.87].
  • From the polygon: F0² = (KX − Mω²X)² + (CωX)², i.e. F0 = X√((K − Mω²)² + (Cω)²) [VA-BK p.87].
  • X = (F0/K) / √([1 − (ω/ωn)²]² + [2ζ(ω/ωn)]²); tan φ = Cω/(K − Mω²) = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/[1 − (ω/ωn)²] [VA-BK p.87] (⚠ A-F25).
  • F0/K is the static displacement X0 (the deflection under the static force F(t) = F0). Dimensionless form: X/X0 = 1/√([1 − (ω/ωn)²]² + [2ζ(ω/ωn)]²), called the magnification factor or amplification factor; φ = tan⁻¹{2ζ(ω/ωn)/[1 − (ω/ωn)²]} [VA-BK p.87, 88].
  • Figures on p.88: X/X0 against ω/ωn for ζ = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00 (peaks near ω/ωn = 1, marked P1 and P2 on the ζ = 0.05 curve), and φ against ω/ωn for the same ζ (all curves pass through π/2 at ω/ωn = 1; ζ = 0 jumps from 0 to π), and X/X0 for ζ = 0 (positive below ω/ωn = 1, negative above it) [VA-BK p.88].
7.3 Characteristics of the forced response
  • (1) ζ = 0 (no damping): X/X0 = 1/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), tan φ = 0, φ = 0° or 180°. For ω/ωn < 1, X/X0 is positive and φ = 0; for ω/ωn > 1, X/X0 is negative and φ = "1" (as printed; 180° is meant, ⚠ A-F26). For simplicity the negative part of the drawing is plotted in the positive part with a dotted line [VA-BK p.88].
  • (2) Resonance: when ω = ωn (ω/ωn = 1), X_res/X0 = 1/(2ζ) and φ = 90°. The peak amplitude occurs at resonance or very near it, especially for lightly damped systems (ζ ≪), so resonance must be avoided [VA-BK p.89].
  • Experimental use: resonance can be used to find ζ — increase ω until φ = 90°, measure X_res, then ζ = X0/(2 X_res) [VA-BK p.89].
  • (3) Peak amplitude: setting d(X/X0)/d(ω/ωn) = 0 gives ωp/ωn = √(1 − 2ζ²) and Xp/X0 = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)). A peak exists only for ζ < 1/√2 = 0.707; at ζ = 0, ωp = ωn, and as ζ increases ωp < ωn until ωp = 0 at ζ = 0.707; beyond that there is no peak Xp and the curve falls directly [VA-BK p.89].
7.4 Worked examples (forced harmonic)
  • Ex. A (machine part): m = 2 kg in a viscous medium; a harmonic force of 2.5 kgf gives a resonant amplitude "1.5 cm" (the solution uses X_res = 1.25 cm) with period 0.2 s. Find the damping coefficient. Solution: ω = ωn = 2π/τres = 2π/0.2 = 10π rad/s; K = mωn² = 2(10π)² N/m; X_res/X0 = X_res/(F0/K) = 1/(2ζ) → ζ = F0/(2K X_res) = 2.5 × 9.81/(2 × 2(10π)² × 1.25/100) = 0.49698; C = 2mωnζ = 62.45 "N·s/cm" [VA-BK p.90] (⚠ A-F27).
  • Ex. B: weight on a spring of stiffness 0.54 kN/m with a viscous damper; free-vibration period "1.8 s" (the solution uses τd = 1.2 s in one line and 1.8 s afterwards), ratio of consecutive amplitudes 4.2 to 1.0; find the amplitude and phase when F(t) = 2 cos 3t acts (the solution uses F = 9 sin 3t). Solution: K = 0.54 kN/m; Xn/Xn+1 = 4.2 (written 4.2/10); δ = ln(4.2) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.223; τd = 2π/(√(1 − ζ²) ωn) = 1.8 s → ωn = 3.58 rad/s; K = mωn² = 540 (written N/m²). Forced case: F0 = 9, ω = 3; X = (F0/K)/√([1 − (3/3.58)²]² + [2 × 0.223 × 3/3.58]²) = 9/540/… = 0.0349 m = 34.9 mm (the printed lines show "3/358" and "3/3.52"); tan φ = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) → φ = 51.54° [VA-BK p.90–91] (⚠ A-F28).
7.5 Forced vibration with periodic exciting forces (book §4.4)
  • Equation of motion m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F(t) with F(t) periodic (period η in the source; τ elsewhere; figure of a periodic F(t), period T) [VA-BK p.115].
  • Expand F(t) in a Fourier series: F(t) = a0 + Σ ai cos iωt + Σ bi sin iωt, with a0 = (1/η)∫₀^η F(t) dt, ai = (2/η)∫₀^η F(t) cos iωt dt, bi = (2/η)∫₀^η F(t) sin iωt dt; ω = 2πf = 2π/η is the fundamental (basic) frequency of the excitation [VA-BK p.115].
  • Since the system is linear, superposition is used: solve m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = a0 (x0 = a0/k; the source leaves "x0 =" blank, ⚠ A-F42), then each term separately [VA-BK p.115–116]:
    • m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = a1 cos ωt → x_a1 = X_a1 cos(ωt − φ_a1), X_a1 = (a1/k)/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²), φ_a1 = tan⁻¹{2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²)}.
    • m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = a2 cos 2ωt → x_a2 = X_a2 cos(2ωt + φ_a2) (as printed), X_a2 = (a2/k)/√((1 − (2ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ·2ω/ωn)²), φ_a2 = tan⁻¹{2ζ(2ω/ωn)/(1 − (2ω/ωn)²)}; and so on.
    • m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = b1 sin ωt → x_b1 = X_b1 sin(ωt − φ_b1), X_b1 = (b1/k)/√(…), φ_b1 = φ_a1; m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = b2 sin 2ωt → x_b2 = X_b2 sin(2ωt + φ_b2) (as printed), X_b2 = (b2/k)/√((1 − (2ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ 2ω/ωn)²), φ_b2 = φ_a2.
    • Total: x(t) = x0 + x_a1 + x_a2 + … + x_b1 + x_b2 + … (superposition, linear system).
  • Ex. (electric relay): a relay imparts to the upper end of a system (k1 in series to mass m, which stands on C and K2 in parallel) a periodic displacement x(t), a square wave of amplitude ±a (two relays with currents i1, i2 alternate). Derive the response y(t) by Fourier analysis. Solution: m ÿ + c ẏ + (k1 + k2) y = k1 x; ωn = √((k1 + k2)/M), 2ζωn = C/M. x(t) has period η, is odd and symmetric, so a0 = ai = 0 and x(t) = Σ bi sin iωt with bi = (2/η)∫x sin iωt dt = (2/η)[∫₀^(η/2) a sin iωt dt − ∫_(η/2)^η a sin iωt dt] = (4a/η)∫₀^(η/2) sin iωt dt = (−2a/πi)[cos iπ − 1] = 4a/(πi) for i = 1, 3, 5, … and 0 for i = 0, 2, 4, …; x(t) = (4a/π) sin ωt + (4a/3π) sin 3ωt + (4a/5π) sin 5ωt + …. The force F(t) = k1 x(t) = F01 sin ωt + F03 sin 3ωt + F05 sin 5ωt + …, with F01 = 4ak1/π, F03 = 4ak1/3π, …. By superposition y(t) = y1 + y2 + y3 + …, where M ÿ1 + c ẏ1 + (k1 + k2)y1 = F01 sin ωt, y1 = Y1 sin(ωt − φ1), Y1 = (F01/(k1 + k2))/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²), tan φ1 = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/√(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² (as printed); likewise M ÿ3 + c ẏ3 + (k1 + k2)y3 = F03 sin 3ωt, y3 = Y3 sin(3ωt − φ1), Y3 = (F03/(k1 + k2))/√((1 − (3ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²) (as printed) [VA-BK p.117–119] (⚠ A-F43).
  • Ex. (cam and follower): the cam and follower impart to the lower end of the system a periodic displacement x(t) (two shapes: a triangular wave of height A, and a falling sawtooth); derive y(t) by Fourier analysis using one of them. FBD: m_eq ÿ + k_eq y = k_eq x (no damper) [VA-BK p.119–120].
    • First function (triangular): x = x1 + x2 with x1 = (2A/τ)t for 0 ≤ t ≤ τ/2 and x2 = −(2A/τ)t + 2A = (2A/τ)(−t + τ) for τ/2 ≤ t ≤ τ; ω = 2π/τ; x(t) = x(−t), so the function is even and bn = 0 and x(t) = a0 + Σ an cos nωt. a0 = (1/τ)[∫₀^(τ/2)(2A/τ)t dt + ∫_(τ/2)^τ(2A/τ)(−t + τ) dt] = A/2. an = (2/τ)∫x cos nωt dt (integrated by parts) = (4A/(τ²n²ω²))(2 cos nω(τ/2) − 1 − cos nωτ) = (A/(π²n²))(2 cos nπ − 2) = −4A/(n²π²) for n odd, 0 for n even. x(t) = A/2 − (4A/π²)[cos ωt + (1/3²) cos 3ωt + (1/5²) cos 5ωt + …] [VA-BK p.120–122].
    • Then m_eq ÿ + k_eq y = ½Ak_eq − (4Ak_eq/π²)[cos ωt + (1/3²) cos 3ωt + …] = F0 − F1 cos ωt + F3 cos 3ωt + F5 cos 5ωt + … (as printed) with F0 = ½Ak_eq, F1 = −4Ak_eq/π², F3 = −4Ak_eq/(3π)², F5 = −4Ak_eq/(5π)². Superposition: y = y0 + y1 + y3 + y5 + …, y0 = A/2, y1 = Y1 cos(ωt − φ1) with Y1 = (F1/k_eq)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = (−4A/π²)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), φ1 = 0; y3 = Y3 cos(3ωt − φ3), Y3 = (−4A/(3π)²)/(1 − (3ω/ωn)²), φ3 = 0; y5 = Y5 cos(5ωt − φ5), Y5 = (−4A/(5π)²)/(1 − (5ω/ωn)²), φ5 = 0; ωn = √(k_eq/m_eq) [VA-BK p.122–123].
    • Second function (falling sawtooth): x(t) = −(A/τ)t + A = (2A/τ)(−t + τ) (as printed) for 0 ≤ t ≤ τ; x(t) ≠ x(−t), so x = a0 + Σ an cos nωt + Σ bn sin nωt. a0 = A/2; an = (A/(2π²n²))(1 − cos 2πn) = 0 (printed with the factor 2A/(…)); bn = (2A/(τ²nω))(τ − (1/nω) sin 2πn) = 2A/(τnω) = A/(nπ). Hence x(t) = A/2 + Σ (A/nπ) sin nωt = A/2 + (A/π)[sin ωt + ½ sin 2ωt + ⅓ sin 3ωt + …] (⚠ A-F5 and F44) [VA-BK p.123–125].
    • m_eq ÿ + k_eq y = ½Ak_eq + (Ak_eq/π)[sin ωt + ½ sin 2ωt + ⅓ sin 3ωt + …] = F0 + F1 sin ωt + F2 sin 2ωt + F3 sin 3ωt + … with F0 = ½Ak_eq, F1 = Ak_eq/π, F2 = Ak_eq/2π, F3 = Ak_eq/3π. Response y = y0 + y1 + y2 + y3 + …, y0 = A/2; yn = Yn sin(nωt − φn) with Y1 = (A/π)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), Y2 = (A/2π)/(1 − (2ω/ωn)²), Y3 = (A/3π)/(1 − (3ω/ωn)²), φ1 = φ2 = φ3 = 0; ωn = √(k_eq/m_eq) [VA-BK p.125–126].
7.6 Forced vibration with non-periodic ("arbitrary") forces (book §4.5)
  • When a system is suddenly excited by a non-periodic force, the response is not steady: it ends when the excitation ends, and the system then continues in free motion at its natural frequency under the initial conditions produced by the transient excitation. This is called transient vibration: it does not take the system to a steady state, and the system vibrates at ωn. Figures: a half-sine pulse (peak F0, duration t0), a rectangular pulse (F0 for 0 to t0) and a velocity record v(t) with ±vmax and time 2t0 [VA-BK p.126–127].
  • Non-periodic forces can in most cases be expressed by a series of impulsive forces (figure of F(τ) split into strips of width Δτ), so the response to an impulsive force must be studied first [VA-BK p.127].
7.7 Impulsive excitation (§4.5.1)
  • An impulsive force is a pulse whose application time t0 tends to a very small interval ε, so its magnitude tends to infinity. The area under F(t) is the strength or impulse F̂ of the force: F(t) = lim(ε→0) F̂/ε for 0 ≤ t ≤ ε and 0 otherwise; F̂ = ∫₀^ε F(t) dt, which stays finite [VA-BK p.127–128].
  • When F̂ = 1 the impulsive force is the Dirac delta function δ(t). Delta at t = ζ (the source uses ζ for the time variable): (1) δ(t − ζ) = 0 for t ≠ ζ, and larger than any assumed value at t = ζ; (2) ∫₀^∞ δ(t − ζ) dt = 1 for 0 < ζ < ∞; (3) multiplying δ(t − ζ) by any time function F(t) gives zero everywhere except at t = ζ, where ∫₀^∞ F(t) δ(t − ζ) dt = F/ζ (as printed; F(ζ) is meant, ⚠ A-F45) [VA-BK p.128].
  • An impulse acting on a system: the pulse force equals the rate of change of momentum, F(t) = m dv/dt → ∫₀^ε F dt = m ∫ dv = m(v(ε) − v(0)); with v(ε) = ẋ(0), v(0) = 0 and ∫F dt = F̂: F̂ = m ẋ(0) → ẋ(0) = F̂/m. So the impulse is treated as initial conditions only: the system vibrates freely with x(0) = 0, ẋ(0) = F̂/m [VA-BK p.128–129].
  • ζ = 0: x(t) = A sin ωn t + B cos ωn t; x(0) = B = 0, ẋ(0) = Aωn = F̂/m → A = F̂/(mωn); x(t) = (F̂/(mωn)) sin ωn t, the response to an impulse of strength F̂ applied at t = 0 [VA-BK p.129].
  • ζ < 1: x(t) = X e^(ζωn t) sin(√(1 − ζ²) ωn t + φ) = X e^(ζωn t) sin(ωd t + φ) (printed with a positive exponent; decay is meant, ⚠ A-F46); x(0) = X sin φ = 0 → φ = 0; ẋ(0) = F̂/m = Xωd → X = F̂/(mωd); x(t) = (F̂/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t, the response to an impulse F̂ at t = 0 with ζ < 1 [VA-BK p.129–130].
7.8 Arbitrary excitation (§4.5.2)
  • Let g(t) be the response at time t to a unit impulse (F̂ = 1) applied at t = 0 (figures: system, force pulse F·Δt = 1, decaying response x(t) = g(t) with period 2π/ωd): g(t) = (1/(mωn)) sin ωn t for ζ = 0, and g(t) = (1/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t for ζ < 1 [VA-BK p.130].
  • For a unit impulse applied at t = ξ: g(t − ξ) = (1/(mωn)) sin ωn(t − ξ) for ζ = 0, and (1/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn(t−ξ)) sin ωd(t − ξ) for ζ < 1 [VA-BK p.130].
7.9 Convolution (Duhamel) integral (§4.5.2, continued)
  • An impulse of strength F(ξ) applied for the interval Δξ is F(ξ)Δξ; the response at time t to it, applied at t = ξ, is F(ξ)Δξ g(t − ξ) [VA-BK p.131].
  • Assuming the arbitrary force is a series of impulses and the system is linear, superposition gives the response as the integral of all impulse responses: x(t) = ∫₀^t F(ξ) g(t − ξ) dξ for t ≤ t*, called the convolution integral. For t > t* (excitation finished) the system vibrates freely with the initial conditions x(t*), ẋ(t*) [VA-BK p.131].
  • Ex. (step function of height F0), undamped: g(t − ξ) = (1/mωn) sin ωn(t − ξ); x(t) = (F0/mωn)∫₀^t sin ωn(t − ξ) dξ = (F0/mωn²)[1 − cos ωn t] = (F0/K)(1 − cos ωn t); xmax = 2F0/K when cos ωn t = −1 (figure: oscillation between 0 and 2F0/k about F0/k) [VA-BK p.132].
  • Same step, damped: g(t − ξ) = e^(−ζωn(t−ξ)) sin ωd(t − ξ)/(mωd); x(t) = (F0/mωd) I with I = ∫₀^t e^(−ζωn(t−ξ)) sin ωd(t − ξ) dξ. Integrating by parts twice: I(1 + ζ²ωn²/ωd²) = (1/ωd)[1 − e^(−ζωn t)(cos ωd t + (ζωn/ωd) sin ωd t)], i.e. I(ωn²/ωd²) = (1/ωd)[1 − e^(−ζωn t)(cos ωd t + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωd t)]. Hence x(t) = (F0/mωn²)[1 − e^(−ζωn t)(cos ωd t + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωd t)]. Writing the bracket as A cos(ωd t − φ) with A cos φ = 1, A sin φ = ζ/√(1 − ζ²): tan φ = ζ/√(1 − ζ²), A = 1/√(1 − ζ²), so x(t) = (F0/k)[1 − (e^(−ζωn t)/√(1 − ζ²)) cos(ωd t − φ)] (figure: decaying oscillation about F0/k, first peak below 2F0/k) [VA-BK p.133–134].
  • Ex. (half-sine pulse): find the response of the system to F(t) = F0 sin(πt/T) for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, T = π/ω (so F(t) = F0 sin ωt), and the peak response [VA-BK p.134]. Undamped: x(t) = (1/mωn)∫₀^t F(η) sin ωn(t − η) dη = (F0/mωn)∫₀^t sin ωη sin ωn(t − η) dη; with sin α sin β = ½[cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)]: x = (F0/2mωn)∫₀^t [cos{(ω + ωn)η − ωn t} − cos{(ω − ωn)η + ωn t}] dη = (F0/2mωn)[(sin ωt + sin ωn t)/(ω + ωn) − (sin ωt − sin ωn t)/(ω − ωn)] = (F0/2mωn)·(−2ωn sin ωt + 2ω sin ωn t)/(ω² − ωn²). The final line is printed x(t) = (F0/k)[sin ωt + (ω/ωn) sin ωn t]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) (⚠ A-F47) [VA-BK p.135].
  • Peak: set ẋ = 0: ẋ(t) = (F0ω/k)[cos ωt − cos ωn t]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = 0 → cos ω tm − cos ωn tm = 0 → −2 sin((ω + ωn)tm/2) sin((ω − ωn)tm/2) = 0. Two families: tm1 = 2iπ/(ω + ωn) and tm2 = 2iπ/(ω − ωn), i = 1, 2, 3, …. Then x(tm1) = (F0/K) sin(2iπ (ω/ωn)/(1 + ω/ωn))/(1 − ω/ωn) and x(tm2) = (F0/K) sin(2iπ (ω/ωn)/(1 − ω/ωn))/(1 + ω/ωn); since x(tm1) > x(tm2), x(tmax) = x(tm1) (as stated) [VA-BK p.136].
  • The peak time must occur during the pulse: 2iπ/(ωn + ω) < π/ω < T, so i < ½(1 + ωn/ω). With ω = π/T and ωn = 2π/T (pulse duration equal to the natural period), ω/ωn = ½; the source writes "i < ½(1 + ωn/ω) < ½(1 + ½) < 3/4", so tm = 2iπ/(ω + ωn), i < 3/4 (⚠ A-F48) [VA-BK p.136–137].
7.10 Chapter 4 problems (forced SDOF)
  • See §14.5 [VA-BK p.138–142].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

7.1 Types of excitation and response (book)
  • External forces may be harmonic, non-harmonic but periodic, non-periodic with a defined form, or random; response to them = forced response; to harmonic excitation = harmonic response; to suddenly applied non-periodic excitation = transient response. Sources of harmonic excitation: unbalance in rotating machines, forces from reciprocating machines, motion of the machine itself [VB-AM p.32–33].
7.2 Damped SDOF under F0 sin ωt (book)
  • Model Fig. 1.16; ẍ + (c/m)ẋ + (k/m)x = (F0/m) sin ωt [VB-AM p.33].
  • x = xh + xp; xh (complementary function) = transient response, dies out with damping; xp (particular integral) = steady-state solution, exists long after the transient disappears [VB-AM p.33].
  • xp = A1 sin ωt + A2 cos ωt with r = ω/ωn, ζ = c/Cc = c/(2mω), X0 = F0/k: A1 = (1 − r²)X0/[(1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²], A2 = −(2rζ)X0/[(1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²] [VB-AM p.33] (⚠ B-F9).
  • xp = X0/√((1−r²)² + (2rζ)²) · sin(ωt − φ), φ = tan⁻¹[2rζ/(1 − r²)]; compact form xp = X0 β sin(ωt − φ), magnification factor β = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²) (Figs 1.17 MF = X/X0 vs r for ζ = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.707, 2; 1.18 φ vs r for ζ = 0, 0.07, 0.2, 0.75, 1) [VB-AM p.34] (⚠ B-F10).
  • β is maximum at r = √(1 − 2ζ²); βmax = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) [VB-AM p.35].
  • Undamped: xp(t) = (F0/k)/[1 − (ω/ωn)²] · sin ωt; X/δst = 1/[1 − (ω/ωn)²], δst = F0/k = static deflection; X/δst = ratio of dynamic to static amplitude = magnification factor, amplification factor or amplitude ratio [VB-AM p.35].
7.3 Resonance and beats (book)
  • Resonance: r = ω/ωn = 1 (forcing frequency equals natural frequency); "the displacement x(t) goes to infinity for any value of time t"; the amplitude grows with time (Fig. 1.19, envelope lines, τ = 2π/ωn) and eventually becomes infinite, at which point the spring fails [VB-AM p.35] (⚠ B-F11).
  • Beating: undamped forced SDOF with ω close but not equal to ωn; amplitude builds up and diminishes in a regular pattern; noticed in audio/sound vibration and in electric power generation when a generator is started [VB-AM p.36].
7.4 Quality factor and bandwidth (book)
  • Q factor = amplitude ratio at resonance (analogy with electrical engineering): Q = 1/(2ζ) [VB-AM p.37].
  • Half-power points R1, R2: where the amplification factor falls to Q/√2; power absorbed by the damper ΔW = πcωX². Bandwidth = difference between the frequencies at R1 and R2 (Fig. 1.21). Q = 1/(2ζ) = ωn/(ω2 − ω1); Q can be used to estimate the equivalent viscous damping [VB-AM p.37–38].
7.5 Forced response with Coulomb and hysteresis damping (book)
  • Coulomb: X = X0/√((1 − r²)² + (4F/(πXk))²) → X = X0 √(1 − (4F/(πF0))²)/(1 − r²); real only if 4F < πF0, i.e. F < (π/4)F0 [VB-AM p.39].
  • Hysteresis: steady-state motion is harmonic; amplitude found with an equivalent viscous damping constant from equating energies: X = X0/√((1 − r²)² + β²) [VB-AM p.39].
7.6 General (periodic / non-periodic) forcing (book)
  • General forcing may be periodic or non-periodic (e.g. ground vibration in an earthquake, a vehicle hitting a pothole). Non-periodic excitations are called transient (not steady state) [VB-AM p.39].
  • Periodic force with period T: F(t) = a0/2 + Σ an cos nωt + Σ bn sin nωt, ω = 2π/T; or F(t) = F0 + Σ Fn sin(ωn t + φn), F0 = a0/2, Fn = √(an² + bn²), ωn = nω, φn = tan⁻¹(an/bn) [VB-AM p.40].
  • Response to a general periodic force (Fig. 1.23): xp(t) = a0/(2k) + Σ (an/k)/√((1 − rn²)² + (2ξrn)²) cos(nωt − ψn) + Σ (bn/k)/√((1 − rn²)² + (2ξrn)²) sin(nωt − ψn); the first two or three terms usually suffice; if a harmonic nω is close to "ω", r ≈ 1 and resonance can occur [VB-AM p.41] (⚠ B-F12).
  • Transient vibration: response to a suddenly applied non-periodic excitation; steady-state oscillations are generally not produced [VB-AM p.41].
  • Impulse F̂ = ∫F(t)dt (lb·s or N·s). Rectangular pulse F = F̂/ε at t = a over ε (Fig. 1.24); as ε → 0 the force → ∞ but F̂ stays defined. F̂ = 1 → unit impulse = Dirac ("Direc") delta δ(t − a): δ(t − a) = 0 for t ≠ a; ∫0^∞ δ(t − a)dt = 1; ∫0^∞ δ(t − a)F(t)dt = F(a) (0 < a < ∞); impulsive force F(t) = F̂ δ(t − a) [VB-AM p.42].
  • Impulse response: x(t) = F̂ H(t), impulse response function H(t) = (1/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t; for a force at t = τ: H(t − τ) = (1/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn(t−τ)) sin ωd(t − τ) [VB-AM p.42].
  • Arbitrary input: x(t) = ∫0^t F(τ) H(t − τ) dτ = convolution integral = Duhamel's integral = superposition integral [VB-AM p.43].
  • Laplace transform method: handles periodic and non-periodic forces, discontinuous functions, and includes the initial conditions automatically; relies on tables of transform pairs. x̄(s) = [F̄(s) + (ms + c)x(0) + m ẋ(0)]/(ms² + cs + k); x(t) = L⁻¹{x̄(s)} [VB-AM p.43].
7.7 Forced vibration with Coulomb damping (VB-RU, textbook §3.8, start only, book p.293)
  • SDOF with Coulomb (dry-friction) damping under F(t) = F0 sin ωt (Fig. 3.22): mẍ + kx ± µN = F(t) = F0 sin ωt (3.85), where the friction force µN = µmg is positive (negative) when the mass moves left to right (right to left) [VB-RU p.7].
  • The exact solution of (3.85) is quite involved. If the dry-friction force is large the motion of the mass will be discontinuous; if it is small compared with the applied-force amplitude F0 the steady state is expected to be nearly harmonic, and an approximate solution can be found with an equivalent viscous-damping ratio obtained by equating the energy dissipated by dry friction to that dissipated by an equivalent viscous damper in a full cycle. With motion amplitude X, the friction force µN dissipates µNX in a quarter cycle, so per full cycle ΔW = 4µNX (3.86); the file ends here [VB-RU p.7].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

7.1 Harmonically excited systems (Section 6)
  • Harmonically excited vibration: the motion of a system vibrating under the effect of its weight and elasticity with an external force acting on it (هي الحركة الناتجة من اهتزاز النظام تحت تأثير وزنه والمرونة وبوجود قوة خارجية تؤثر على النظام); standard model m, K, C with F(t) and x(t) [VC-S6 p.1].
  • Types of harmonic excitation: 1. simple harmonic F(t) = F0 sin ωt or F0 cos ωt; 2. general harmonic F(t) = F1 sin ωt + F2 cos ωt = F0 e^(iωt), F0 = amplitude of excitation (N) = √(F1² + F2²) [VC-S6 p.1].
  • Sources of harmonic excitation: 1. reciprocating machines (sketch: m on K and C driven by a follower on a cam keyed to a shaft); 2. rotating unbalance (motors) — see §8; 3. support or base motion ("rough road") — see §9 [VC-S6 pp.2–4].
7.2 Single, undamped, linear, harmonically excited system (Section 6)
  • F(t) = F0 cos ωt; FBD: Kx up, F(t) and mẍ down; F(t) − Kx = mẍ → mẍ + Kx = F(t) = F0 cos ωt — 2nd-order, linear, ordinary, differential, non-homogeneous [VC-S6 p.5].
  • Solution x(t) = xh(t) + xp(t): total response = homogeneous ("free") response + particular (dynamic or steady-state) response; when the total is not asked for, the steady state is what is required (في حالة لم يطلب الـ Total يبقى المقصود هنا الـ steady state) [VC-S6 p.5].
  • Steady state: xp(t) = X̄p cos ωt; X̄p = dynamic, steady-state or particular amplitude (m) = F0/(K − mω²) = (F0/K)/(1 − (m/K)ω²) = δst)0/(1 − r²); δst)0 = F0/K = deflection due to the amplitude of excitation; r = ω/ωn frequency ratio [VC-S6 p.6].
  • Amplification factor (معامل التكبير, amplitude ratio): Mp = X̄p/δst)0 = 1/(1 − r²); m equivalent mass (kg), K equivalent spring constant (N/m), ω excitation frequency (rad/s), ωn natural frequency of the system (rad/s) [VC-S6 p.6].
  • Homogeneous part: xh(t) = (x0 − X̄p) cos ωnt + (ẋ0/ωn) sin ωnt; total x(t) = (x0 − X̄p) cos ωnt + (ẋ0/ωn) sin ωnt + X̄p cos ωt, X̄p = (F0/K)/(1 − r²) = F0/(K − mω²) [VC-S6 p.7].
  • Sketch of Mp vs r (undamped): starts at 1, rises to +∞ as r → 1, and beyond r = 1 is negative and tends to 0 [VC-S6 p.7].
7.3 Resonance (الرنين) (Section 6)
  • A forced-vibration case with r = 1, ω (frequency of excitation) = ωn (natural frequency of the system); it may lead to collapse of the system because of the high amplitude (قد تؤدي إلى انهيار النظام في حالة الـ Amp. العالي) [VC-S6 p.8].
  • xp(t) = [(F0/K)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²)] cos ωt → ∞ as ω → ωn; by L'Hôpital (differentiate with respect to ω): xp(t) = (F0/K) lim t sin ωt/(2ω/ωn²) → xp(t) = xtotal(t) = (F0/2K) t ωn sin ωnt; sketch: oscillation of period τn inside a linearly growing envelope [VC-S6 p.8].
7.4 Beating phenomenon (التخبيط) (Section 6)
  • A forced-vibration case in which ω approaches ωn; a beat is the motion between two zero amplitudes (هي الحركة بين اتنين "Zero Amplitude"); sketch of a fast oscillation inside a slow envelope of height (F0/m)/(2εω) [VC-S6 p.9].
  • ωn − ω = 2ε; x(t) = [((F0/m)/(2εω)) sin εt] sin ωt, the bracket being the amplitude; τ = 2π/ε; τbeat = τ/2 = (2π/ε)/2 = π/ε — a beat is heard every τbeat (هنسمع تخبيطة كل زمن τbeat); ωbeat = 2π/τb = 2ε rad/s; fb = ωb/2π = ε/π beat/s [VC-S6 pp.9–10].
7.5 Single, damped, linear, harmonically excited system (Section 6)
  • F(t) = F0 cos ωt; F(t) − Cẋ − Kx = mẍ → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = F0 cos ωt (2nd-order, linear, ordinary, differential, non-homogeneous); x(t) = xh (homogeneous or free) + xp (particular, dynamic or steady-state) [VC-S6 p.11 (repeated p.12)].
  • Steady state: xp(t) = X̄p cos(ωt − φp), φ = phase angle due to the damper [VC-S6 p.11].
  • X̄p = F0/√((K − mω²)² + (Cω)²) = (F0/K)/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (Cω/K)²); with C/m = 2ζωn, Cω/K = 2ζmωnω/K = 2ζω/ωn = 2ζr → X̄p = (F0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), F0/K = δst)0 [VC-S6 p.13].
  • φp = tan⁻¹[Cω/(K − mω²)] = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)] [VC-S6 p.13].
  • Amplification factor Mp = dynamic amplitude/static amplitude = X̄p/δst)0 = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) [VC-S6 p.13].
  • Symbols: m equivalent mass (kg), K (N/m), C (N·s/m), ω (rad/s), ωn = √(K/m), ζ damping ratio = C/Cc = C/(2mωn) = C/(2√(Km)), δst)0 static amplitude = F0/K [VC-S6 p.14].
  • Homogeneous: xh(t) = e^(−ζωnt)[A cos ωdt + B sin ωdt], A = x0 − X̄p cos φp, B = [ẋ0 + ζωn(x0 − X̄p cos φp)]/ωd [VC-S6 p.14] (⚠ C-F13).
  • Total: x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)[A cos ωdt + B sin ωdt] + X̄p cos(ωt − φp); sketches: xh(t) dies out by t0, xp(t) continues, and x(t) = transient response (الاستجابة السريعة) before t0 + steady-state response after t0 [VC-S6 p.15].
  • Mp–r curves: all start at Mp = 1 at r = 0; ζ = 0 goes to ∞ at r = 1; ζ = 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 give finite peaks that fall as ζ grows; ζ = 1 and ζ = 1.5 fall steadily; all tend to 0 at large r. φ–r curves: all pass through 90° at r = 1 (ω = ωn); ζ = 0 gives 0° below and 180° above r = 1; larger ζ makes the curves flatter [VC-S6 p.16].
  • Notes on the figure: (1) ζ = 0 (undamped): r < 1, φp = 0 — response and excitation "in plane" (in phase); r > 1, φp = 180° — "out of plane"; (2) ζ > 0 (damped): r < 1, 0 < φp < 90° — response lags excitation by φp; r > 1, 90° < φp < 180° — "response lead excitation by φp"; (3) at resonance (ω = ωn) φp = 90° [VC-S6 pp.17–19] (⚠ C-F14).
  • Energy dissipated due to damping (forced): Wd)forced = πCωX̄p, with X̄p = (F0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); at resonance (r = 1, ω = ωn) X̄p = (F0/K)/(2ζ) and ω → ωn in Wd [VC-S6 p.20] (⚠ C-F15).
7.6 Forced-vibration examples (Section 6)
  • Total response [VC-S6 pp.26–28]: m = 10 kg, C = 20 N·s/m, K = 4000 N/m, x0 = 0.01 m, ẋ0 = 0; (a) F(t) = F0 cos ωt with F0 = 100 N, ω = 10 rad/s; (b) free vibration F(t) = 0.
    • ωn = √(4000/10) = 20 rad/s; ζ = 20/(2√(4000·10)) = 0.05; r = 10/20 = 0.5; ωd = 20√(1 − 0.05²) = 19.975 rad/s [VC-S6 p.26].
    • X̄p = (100/4000)/√((1 − 0.5²)² + (2·0.05·0.5)²) = 0.0336 m; φp = tan⁻¹[2·0.05·0.5/(1 − 0.5²)] = 3.814°; A = 0.01 − 0.0336 cos 3.814° = −0.0235; B = [0 + 0.05·20(0.01 − 0.0336 cos 3.814°)]/19.975 = −1.176×10⁻³; x(t) = e^(−t)(−0.0235 cos 19.975t − 1.176×10⁻³ sin 19.975t) + 0.0336 cos(10t − 3.814°) [VC-S6 p.27].
    • (b) x(t) = e^(−ζωnt)(A cos ωdt + B sin ωdt), A = x0 = 0.01, B = (ẋ0 + ζωnx0)/ωd = 0.05·20·0.01/19.975 = 5×10⁻⁴ → x(t) = e^(−t)(0.01 cos 19.975t + 5×10⁻⁴ sin 19.975t) [VC-S6 p.28].
  • Stepped pulley with forced mass [VC-S6 pp.30–32]: K1 = 1000 N/m, K2 = 500 N/m, C1 = 500 N·s/m, m = 10 kg, r = 5 cm, Jo = 1 kg·m², F0 = 50 N, ω = 20 rad/s; pulley Jo with radii r and 2r, K2 horizontal at radius r, m hung from radius 2r on K1 and C1, F(t) = F0 sin ωt on m; x = 2rθ, x1 = rθ.
    • Mass: F(t) − K1x − C1ẋ − T = mẍ → T = F0 sin ωt − K1x − C1ẋ − mẍ; pulley: T(2r) − K2x1(r) = Joθ̈ → [Jo + 4r²m]θ̈ + 4r²C1θ̇ + [K2r² + 4r²K1]θ = 2rF0 sin ωt [VC-S6 pp.30–31].
    • Jeq = 1 + 4(0.05)²·10 = 1.1 kg·m²; Ceq = 4(0.05)²·500 = 5 N·s·m/rad; Keq = 500(0.05)² + 4(0.05)²·1000 = 11.25 N·m/rad; M0 = 2rF0 = 2·0.05·50 = 5 N·m [VC-S6 p.31].
    • X̄p = 5/√((11.25 − 1.1·20²)² + (5·20)²) = 0.01136 "m"; φp = tan⁻¹[5·20/(11.25 − 1.1·20²)] = −13.1287°; xp(t) = 0.01136 cos(20t + 13.1287°) [VC-S6 p.32] (⚠ C-F16).
  • Bar with end springs and a harmonic moment at the hinge [VC-S6 pp.33–35]: uniform rigid bar m = 10 kg, L = 1 m, hinge O at L/4 from the left end; K = 5000 N/m at each end, C = 1000 N·s/m at L/4 right of O, M0 cos ωt at O, M0 = 100 N·m, N = 1000 rpm; x = (3L/4)θ, y = (L/4)θ.
    • M0 cos ωt − Ky(L/4) − Cẏ(L/4) − Kx(3L/4) = Joθ̈ → Joθ̈ + (L²/16)Cθ̇ + (5/8)L²Kθ = M0 cos ωt [VC-S6 p.34].
    • Jeq = (1/12)mL² + m(L/4)² = 1.45833 kg·m²; Ceq = L²C/16 = 62.5 N·s·m/rad; Keq = (5/8)L²K = 3125 N·m/rad; ω = 2π·1000/60 = 104.72 rad/s; 1.45833θ̈ + 62.5θ̇ + 3125θ = 100 cos 104.72t [VC-S6 p.34].
    • θp(t) = θ̄p cos(ωt − φp) (as xp for translation); θ̄p = M0/√((K − Jω²)² + (Cω)²) = 6.927×10⁻³ rad; φp = tan⁻¹[Cω/(K − Jeqω²)] = −26.96°; θp(t) = 6.927×10⁻³ cos(104.72t + 26.96°) [VC-S6 p.35] (⚠ C-F16).
  • Bar with force at mid-length — two arrangements [VC-S6 pp.36–39]: uniform slender bar m hinged at O (left end), F0 sin ωt at the middle G.
    • Case 1 (K at 3L/4, C at the tip L): y = (3L/4)θ, x = Lθ; F0 sin ωt(L/2) − Ky(3L/4) − Cẋ(L) = Joθ̈ → Joθ̈ + CL²θ̇ + (9/16)L²Kθ = (L/2)F0 sin ωt; Jeq = (1/12)mL² + m(L/2)² = (1/3)mL², Ceq = CL², Keq = (9/16)L²K, M0 = (L/2)F0; θ̄p)1 = (L/2)F0/√[((9/16)L²K − (mL²/3)ω²)² + (CL²ω)²], φp)1 = tan⁻¹[CL²ω/((9/16)L²K − (mL²/3)ω²)] [VC-S6 pp.36–37].
    • Case 2 (C at 3L/4, K at the tip): F0 sin ωt(L/2) − Cẏ(3L/4) − Kx(L) = Joθ̈ → Joθ̈ + (9/16)L²Cθ̇ + KL²θ = (L/2)F0 sin ωt; Jeq = (1/3)mL², Ceq = (9/16)L²C, Keq = KL², M0 = (L/2)F0; θ̄p)2 = (L/2)F0/√[(KL² − (1/3)mL²ω²)² + ((9/16)L²Cω)²], φp)2 = tan⁻¹[(9/16)L²Cω/(KL² − mL²ω²/3)] [VC-S6 pp.38–39].
    • Which arrangement is desirable? "Usually C smaller than K; if C negligible θ̄p)1 < θ̄p)2, so case 1 desirable" [VC-S6 p.39] (⚠ C-F17).
7.7 Abdelrahman Mamdouh's forced-vibration notes ([VC-AFV])
  • Newton: F(t) − Kx − Cẋ = mẍ → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = F(t); general form meq ẍ + Ceq ẋ + Keq x = F(t) [VC-AFV p.1].
  • Types of F(t): impulse, step (constant), harmonic (F(t) = F sin ωt or F cos ωt), random [VC-AFV p.1].
  • Harmonic force: meq ẍ + Ceq ẋ + Keq x = F0 sin ωt (non-homogeneous equation); x(t) = xh(t) + xp(t), where xh depends on ζ as in free damped vibration; xp(t) = Xp sin(ωt − φ), ω = forced frequency, F0 = force amplitude [VC-AFV p.1].
  • Dimensional form: Xp = F0/√((K − mω²)² + (Cω)²) (steady-state amplitude); φ = tan⁻¹[Cω/(K − mω²)] (phase angle) [VC-AFV p.2].
  • Non-dimensional form: Xp = (F0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); φ = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)]; δstatic = F0/K (static deflection); r = ω/ωn (frequency ratio); M = Xp/δstatic = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) (amplitude ratio, magnitude ratio) [VC-AFV p.2].
  • Resonance (الرنين) [VC-AFV p.4]: undamped case ζ = 0: Xp = (F0/K)/(1 − r²); for ω = ωn (r = 1) Xp = (F0/K)/(1 − 1) = ∞, the resonance case, and M = Xp/δst = ∞. Damped case at r = 1: Xp = δst/(2ζ), Mp = Xp/δst = 1/(2ζ); as ζ increases (ترداد) Mp decreases (تقل).
7.8 Chapter 4 — forced vibration with harmonic exciting force ([VC-A4])
  • Section 4.1 "Introduction" is a heading only (the page is blank under it) [VC-A4 p.2].
  • Harmonic excitation often exists in mechanical systems and always occurs because of rotating unbalance in rotary machines; it is studied through the response of an SDOF system to F(t) = F0 sin ωt (F0 amplitude, ω excitation frequency) [VC-A4 p.3].
  • Equation of motion from the FBD: mẍ + cẋ + Kx = F(t) = F0 sin ωt — an ordinary differential equation of second order, linear and non-homogeneous; x(t) = xc.f + xp.I, where xc.f is the complementary function (solution of the homogeneous equation, the transient solution) and xp.I the particular integral (the steady-state solution) [VC-A4 p.3].
  • Transient part: depends on the value of C/(2√(Km)) as in the previous chapter; it lasts a limited time, after which the system settles at the steady-state solution; it depends on m, k, c [VC-A4 p.4].
  • Steady-state part: same function as the excitation with a different amplitude and a phase: xp.I(t) = X sin(ωt − φ); X amplitude, ω angular frequency of the excitation, φ phase angle between xp.I(t) and F(t) [VC-A4 p.4].
  • Substituting in the equation of motion gives the force polygon (mω²X, cωX, KX, F0, phase φ): F0² = (KX − mω²X)² + (cωX)², F0 = X√((K − mω²)² + (cω)²); X = (F0/K)/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²); tan φ = Cω/(K − mω²) = (2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) [VC-A4 p.5].
  • X0 = F0/K is the static displacement (static force F(t) = F0); dimensionless form X/X0 = 1/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²), called the magnification (or amplification) factor; phase φ = tan⁻¹[(2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²)] [VC-A4 pp.5–6].
  • Curves shown: X/X0 against ω/ωn for ζ = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00 (peaks grow as ζ falls) and φ against ω/ωn (all pass through 90° at ω/ωn = 1) [VC-A4 p.6].
  • Case (1) ζ = 0: X/X0 = 1/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), tan φ = 0, φ = 0° or 180°; for ω/ωn < 1, X/X0 positive and φ = 0; for ω/ωn > 1, X/X0 negative and (the source writes) φ = 1 (meaning 180°, see ⚠ C-F28). The negative part of the drawing is drawn in the positive part with a dotted line for simplicity [VC-A4 p.6].
  • Case (2) resonance: ω = ωn, so ω/ωn = 1, Xres/X0 = 1/(2ζ) and φ = 90°. The peak amplitude occurs at resonance or very near it, especially for low damping (ζ << ), so resonance must be avoided [VC-A4 p.7].
  • Resonance can be used experimentally to find ζ: increase ω until φ = 90°, measure Xres, then ζ = X0/(2Xres) [VC-A4 p.7].
  • Case (3) peak amplitude: d(X/X0)/d(ω/ωn) = 0 gives ωp/ωn = √(1 − 2ζ²) and Xp/X0 = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)); a peak exists only while ζ < √(1/2) = 0.707; at ζ = 0, ωp = ωn, and as ζ increases ωp < ωn until ωp = 0 at ζ = 0.707; beyond that there is no peak and the curve collapses directly [VC-A4 p.7].
  • Example A (machine part) [VC-A4 p.8]: m = 2 kg in a viscous medium; harmonic force F0 = 2.5 kgf gives a resonant amplitude of (statement 1.5 cm; solution uses Xres = 1.25 cm) with period 0.2 s; required the damping coefficient. ω = ωn = 2π/τres = 2π/0.2 = 10π rad/s; K = mωn² = 2(10π)² N/m; Xres/X0 = Xres/(F0/K) = 1/(2ζ) → ζ = F0/(2K Xres) = 2.5×9.81/(2·2(10π)²·1.25/100) = 0.49698; C = 2mωnζ = 62.45 N·s/cm (⚠ C-F29).
  • Example B (weight on a spring) [VC-A4 pp.8–9]: K = 0.54 kN/m, damped period 1.8 s (the data line prints τd = 1.2 s), consecutive amplitude ratio 4.2 to 1.0; find the amplitude and the phase when F(t) = 2 cos 3t acts. δ = ln(Xn/Xn+1) = ln(4.2/1) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.223; τd = 2π/(√(1 − ζ²)ωn) = 1.8 s → ωn = 3.58 rad/s; K = mωn² = 540 N/m; forced case F = F0 sin ωt = 9 sin 3t, F0 = 9, ω = 3 (the solution does not use the statement's 2 cos 3t, see ⚠ C-F29); X = (F0/K)/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²) = (9/540)/√((1 − (3/3.58)²)² + (2·0.223·3/3.52)²) = 0.0349 m = 34.9 mm; tan φ = (2·0.223·3/3.58)/(1 − (3/3.52)²) → φ = 51.54° (3.52 and 3.58 are both printed).
7.9 Chapter 4 — forced vibration with periodic exciting forces ([VC-A4])
  • F(t) periodic (sketch with period τ): mẍ + cẋ + kx = F(t); expand F(t) = a0 + Σ ai cos iωt + Σ bi sin iωt, with a0 = (1/τ)∫0^τ F(t) dt, ai = (2/τ)∫0^τ F(t) cos iωt dt, bi = (2/τ)∫0^τ F(t) sin iωt dt; ω = 2πf = 2π/τ is the fundamental (basic) frequency of the exciting force [VC-A4 p.33].
  • Superposition (linear system): mẍ + cẋ + kx = a0 gives x0; mẍ + cẋ + kx = a1 cos ωt gives xa1 = Xa1 cos(ωt − φa1), Xa1 = (a1/k)/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²), φa1 = tan⁻¹[(2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²)]; for a2 cos 2ωt: xa2 = Xa2 cos(2ωt + φa2) (sign as printed), Xa2 = (a2/k)/√((1 − (2ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ·2ω/ωn)²), φa2 = tan⁻¹[(2ζ·2ω/ωn)/(1 − (2ω/ωn)²)]; for b1 sin ωt: xb1 = Xb1 sin(ωt − φb1), φb1 = φa1; for b2 sin 2ωt: xb2 = Xb2 sin(2ωt + φb2), φb2 = φa2; total x(t) = x0 + xa1 + xa2 + … + xb1 + xb2 + … [VC-A4 pp.33–34].
  • Example (electric relay) [VC-A4 pp.35–37]: two relays impart a square-wave displacement x(t) = ±a of period τ to the upper end of a spring k1; the mass m sits on k2 and a damper C with displacement y(t). Equation mÿ + cẏ + (k1 + k2)y = k1x; ωn = √((k1 + k2)/M), 2ζωn = C/M. x(t) = a0 + Σ ai cos iωt + Σ bi sin iωt; x is odd and symmetric so a0 = ai = 0 and x(t) = Σ bi sin iωt. bi = (2/τ)[∫0^(τ/2) a sin iωt dt − ∫(τ/2)^τ a sin iωt dt] = (4a/τ)∫0^(τ/2) sin iωt dt = (−2a/(πi))[cos iπ − 1] = 4a/(πi) for i = 1, 3, 5, … and 0 for i = 0, 2, 4, …; x(t) = (4a/π) sin ωt + (4a/3π) sin 3ωt + (4a/5π) sin 5ωt + … ; F(t) = k1x(t) = F01 sin ωt + F03 sin 3ωt + F05 sin 5ωt + …, F01 = 4ak1/π, F03 = 4ak1/3π, …; y(t) = y1 + y2 + y3 + …, with Mÿ1 + cẏ1 + (k1 + k2)y1 = F01 sin ωt, y1 = Y1 sin(ωt − φ1), Y1 = [F01/(k1 + k2)]/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²), tan φ1 = (2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); likewise Mÿ3 + cẏ3 + (k1 + k2)y3 = F03 sin 3ωt, y3 = Y3 sin(3ωt − φ1) (the source keeps the subscript 1 on φ), Y3 = [F03/(k1 + k2)]/√((1 − (3ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ·3ω/ωn)²) [VC-A4 pp.36–38].
  • Example (cam and follower) [VC-A4 pp.37–44]: the cam displaces the lower end of a spring keq under meq with x(t) = the triangular (or the falling-sawtooth) wave of amplitude A and period τ; the response y(t) is to be found for one of them. Free-body diagram: meq ÿ + keq y = keq x (undamped).
    • Triangular wave (0 → A at τ/2 → 0 at τ): x1 = 2At/τ (0 ≤ t ≤ τ/2), x2 = (2A/τ)(−t + τ) (τ/2 ≤ t ≤ τ), ω = 2π/τ; x(t) = x(−t), so even and bn = 0; a0 = A/2; an = (2/τ)∫… = (A/(π²n²))(2 cos nπ − 1 − cos 2πn) = (A/(π²n²))(2 cos nπ − 2) = −4A/(n²π²) for n = 1, 3, …, 0 for n even; x(t) = A/2 − (4A/π²)[cos ωt + (1/3²) cos 3ωt + (1/5²) cos 5ωt + …] [VC-A4 pp.38–41].
    • Then meq ÿ + keq y = keq x = ½Akeq − (4Akeq/π²)[cos ωt + (1/3²) cos 3ωt + …] = F0 − F1 cos ωt + F3 cos 3ωt + F5 cos 5ωt … (as printed), with F0 = ½Akeq, F1 = −4Akeq/π², F3 = −4Akeq/(3π)², F5 = −4Akeq/(5π)². By superposition y = y0 + y1 + y3 + y5 + …, y0 = A/2, y1 = Y1 cos(ωt − φ1) with Y1 = (F1/keq)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = (−4A/π²)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), φ1 = 0; y3 = Y3 cos(3ωt − φ3), Y3 = [−4A/(3π)²]/(1 − (3ω/ωn)²), φ3 = 0; y5 likewise with 5π and 5ω; ωn = √(keq/meq) [VC-A4 pp.40–42].
    • Falling sawtooth x2 = −At/τ + A = (2A/τ)(−t + τ)... as printed [(A/τ)(−t + τ) is what the integrals use], 0 ≤ t ≤ τ; x(t) ≠ x(−t), so x = a0 + Σ an cos nωt + Σ bn sin nωt; a0 = A/2; an = (A/(2π²n²))(1 − cos 2πn) = 0; bn = A/(nπ); x(t) = A/2 + Σ (A/nπ) sin nωt = A/2 + (A/π)[sin ωt + ½ sin 2ωt + ⅓ sin 3ωt + …]; meq ÿ + keq y = ½Akeq + (Akeq/π)[…] = F0 + F1 sin ωt + F2 sin 2ωt + F3 sin 3ωt + …, F0 = ½Akeq, F1 = Akeq/π, F2 = Akeq/2π, F3 = Akeq/3π; y = y0 + y1 + y2 + y3 + …, y0 = A/2, y1 = Y1 sin(ωt − φ1), Y1 = (F1/keq)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = (A/π)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), φ1 = 0, y2 = Y2 sin(2ωt − φ2) with Y2 = (A/2π)/(1 − (2ω/ωn)²), y3 with Y3 = (A/3π)/(1 − (3ω/ωn)²); ωn = √(keq/meq) [VC-A4 pp.41–44].
7.10 Chapter 4 — non-periodic (impulsive and arbitrary) excitation ([VC-A4])
  • When a system is suddenly excited by a non-periodic force the response is not steady: when the excitation ends, the system continues in free motion at its natural frequency under its initial conditions, called transient vibration because it does not bring the system to a steady state [VC-A4 p.44]. Sketches of a half-sine pulse, a rectangular pulse and a triangular pulse are shown; non-periodic forces can in most cases be expressed as a series of impulsive forces, so the response to an impulse is studied first [VC-A4 p.45].
  • Impulsive excitation: F(t) is a pulsating force applied for a very short time ε, so its magnitude tends to infinity; the area under F(t) is the strength or impulse: F̂ = ∫0^ε F(t) dt; F(t) = lim(ε→0) F̂/ε for 0 ≤ t ≤ ε and 0 for t > ε [VC-A4 p.45].
  • If the strength is unity, F̂ = 1, the force is the Dirac delta function δ(t); the delta at t = ζ (written ζ and also ξ in the source) has properties: 1) δ(t − ζ) = 0 for t ≠ ζ and larger than any assumed value at t = ζ; 2) ∫0^∞ δ(t − ζ) dt = 1 for 0 < ζ < ∞; 3) ∫0^∞ F(t)δ(t − ζ) dt = F/ζ for 0 < ζ < ∞ (as printed, see ⚠ C-F30) [VC-A4 pp.45–46].
  • The pulse force equals the rate of change of momentum: F(t) = m dv/dt; ∫0^ε F dt = m∫ dv = m(v(ε) − v(0)), with v(ε) = ẋ(0), v(0) = 0, ∫F dt = F̂ → F̂ = mẋ(0), ẋ(0) = F̂/m. The impulsive force is therefore treated as initial conditions only: free vibration with x(0) = 0, ẋ(0) = F̂/m [VC-A4 pp.46–47].
  • ζ = 0: x(t) = A sin ωnt + B cos ωnt; x(0) = B = 0, ẋ(0) = Aωn = F̂/m → A = F̂/(mωn); x(t) = (F̂/(mωn)) sin ωnt, the response to an impulse F̂ applied at t = 0 [VC-A4 p.47].
  • ζ < 1: x(t) = X e^(ζωnt) sin(√(1 − ζ²) ωnt + φ) = X e^(ζωnt) sin(ωdt + φ) (positive exponent as printed, ⚠ C-F30); x(0) = X sin φ = 0 → φ = 0; ẋ(0) = F̂/m = Xωd → X = F̂/(mωd); x(t) = (F̂/(mωd)) e^(−ζωnt) sin ωdt, the response for an impulse F̂ at t = 0, ζ < 1 [VC-A4 pp.47–48].
  • Arbitrary excitation: the response to a unit impulse F̂ = 1 at t = 0 is g(t) = (1/(mωn)) sin ωnt (ζ = 0) and g(t) = (1/(mωd)) e^(−ζωnt) sin ωdt (ζ < 1) (sketch of the system, the unit impulse and the decaying response); the response to a unit impulse applied at t = ξ is g(t − ξ) = (1/(mωn)) sin ωn(t − ξ) (ζ = 0), (1/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn(t−ξ)) sin ωd(t − ξ) (ζ < 1) [VC-A4 p.48].
  • An impulse F(ξ)Δξ applied at t = ξ gives the response F(ξ)Δξ g(t − ξ); assuming the arbitrary force is a series of impulses and the system is linear (superposition) the response is x(t) = ∫0^t F(ξ) g(t − ξ) dξ for t ≤ t* — the convolution integral; for t > t* the force has finished and the system vibrates freely with the initial conditions x(t*), ẋ(t*) [VC-A4 p.49].
  • Example (step function F0) [VC-A4 pp.50–52]: undamped: x(t) = (F0/(mωn))∫0^t sin ωn(t − ξ) dξ = (F0/(mωn²)) cos ωn(t − ξ)|0^t = (F0/(mωn²))[1 − cos ωnt] = (F0/K)(1 − cos ωnt); xmax = 2F0/K when cos ωnt = −1 (sketch: oscillation between 0 and 2F0/K about F0/K). Damped: g(t) = (e^(−ζωnt)/(mωd)) sin ωdt, x(t) = (F0/(mωd))∫0^t e^(−ζωn(t−ξ)) sin ωd(t − ξ) dξ; with I = ∫…, integrating by parts twice gives I(ωn²/ωd²) = (1/ωd)[1 − e^(−ζωnt)(cos ωdt + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωdt)], so x(t) = (F0/(mωn²))[1 − e^(−ζωnt)(cos ωdt + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωdt)]; writing cos ωdt + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωdt = A cos(ωdt − φ) with A cos φ = 1, A sin φ = ζ/√(1 − ζ²), tan φ = ζ/√(1 − ζ²), A = 1/√(1 − ζ²): x(t) = (F0/(mωn²))[1 − (e^(−ζωnt)/√(1 − ζ²)) cos(ωdt − φ)] = (F0/k)[1 − (e^(−ζωnt)/√(1 − ζ²)) cos(ωdt − φ)] (sketch approaching F0/k with the first peak near 2F0/k).
  • Example (half-sine pulse) [VC-A4 pp.52–55]: F(t) = F0 sin(πt/T) for 0 ≤ t ≤ T with T = π/ω, i.e. F(t) = F0 sin ωt; response (undamped) and peak response. x(t) = (1/(mωn))∫0^t F(η) sin ωn(t − η) dη = (F0/(mωn))∫0^t sin ωη sin ωn(t − η) dη; using sin α sin β = ½[cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)], x(t) = (F0/(2mωn))[sin((ω + ωn)η − ωnt)/(ω + ωn) − sin((ω − ωn)η + ωnt)/(ω − ωn)]0^t = (F0/k)[sin ωt + (ω/ωn) sin ωnt]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) (as printed, see ⚠ C-F30) [VC-A4 pp.52–53].
    • Maximum: ẋ = 0: ẋ(t) = (F0ω/k)[cos ωt − cos ωnt]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = 0 → cos ωtm − cos ωntm = 0; with cos α − cos β = −2 sin((α + β)/2) sin((α − β)/2): sin((ω + ωn)tm/2) = 0 → tm1 = 2iπ/(ω + ωn), or sin((ω − ωn)tm/2) = 0 → tm2 = 2iπ/(ω − ωn), i = 1, 2, 3, …; x(tm1) = (F0/K)[sin(2iπω/(ω + ωn)) − (ω/ωn) sin(2iπωn/(ω + ωn))]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = (F0/(K(1 − ω/ωn))) sin(2iπ(ω/ωn)/(1 + ω/ωn)); x(tm2) = (F0/(K(1 + ω/ωn))) sin(2iπ(ω/ωn)/(1 − ω/ωn)); x(tm1) > x(tm2) so x(tmax) = x(tm1) [VC-A4 pp.53–54].
    • The maximum must occur during the pulse: 2iπ/(ωn + ω) < π/ω < T → i < ½(1 + ωn/ω); with ω = π/T, T = 1/f, ωn = 2πf … the source states ω/ωn = ½ and then "i < ½(1 + ½) < ¾", giving tm = 2iπ/(ω + ωn), i < 3/4 (⚠ C-F30) [VC-A4 pp.54–55].
7.11 Ayman's part-D notes: peak of Mp, resonance, unbalance ([VC-AAy])
  • Peak of the magnification factor: dMp/dr = d/dr[1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)] = 0 (Mp is maximum where dMp/dr = 0) → −½·[2(1 − r²)(−2r) + 4ζ²(2r)]/[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]^(3/2) = 0 → 2r³ − 2r + 4ζ²r = 2r(r² − 1 + 2ζ²) = 0 → r = 0 or r = √(1 − 2ζ²); the negative root r = −√(1 − 2ζ²) is rejected because r = ω/ωn is positive (Arabic note) [VC-AAy p.1].
  • With r = √(1 − 2ζ²): Mp,max = 1/√((1 − (1 − 2ζ²))² + (2ζ)²(1 − 2ζ²)) = 1/√(4ζ⁴ + 4ζ² − 8ζ⁴) = 1/(2√(ζ²(1 + ζ² − 2ζ²))) → Mp,max = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)); "at resonance" (r ≈ 1) Mp,max = 1/(2ζ) [VC-AAy p.2].

Rotating and reciprocating unbalance

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

8.1 Rotating unbalance (book §4.2.1.1)
  • Rotating unbalance in rotary machines is the general source of excited vibration. Model: a machine of mass M constrained to move horizontally, on springs k/2 + k/2 and a damper C, excited by an unbalance (eccentric) mass m at eccentric radius e rotating at constant ω [VA-BK p.92].
  • With x(t) measured from static equilibrium: M ẍ = ΣF = −C ẋ − K x + m ω² e sin ωt → M ẍ + C ẋ + K x = m ω² e sin ωt = F0 sin ωt, where F0 = m ω² e; steady state x(t) = X sin(ωt − φ) [VA-BK p.92].
  • From the force polygon: X = (F0/K)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ ω/ωn)²]^½ = (mω²e/K)/[…]^½, i.e. M X/(m e) = (ω/ωn)²/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ ω/ωn)²]^½, with tan φ = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) [VA-BK p.92–93].
  • Characteristics [VA-BK p.93]:
    • (1) Resonance: ω/ωn = 1, M X_res/(m e) = 1/(2ζ), φ = 90°.
    • (2) Maximum peak: d(MX/me)/d(ω/ωn) = 0 → ωp/ωn = 1/√(1 − 2ζ²) (that is, ωp/ωn ≥ 1, the peak lies above ωn); it exists only for ζ < 0.707, and M Xp/(m e) = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)).
    • (3) No damping: ζ = 0, φ = 180° (as printed), MX/(me) = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); for ω/ωn > 1 this is negative, so the curve is drawn dotted in the upper part.
    • Figure: MX/(me) against frequency ratio ω/ωn (0–5) for ζ = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.375, 0.5 and 1.0 (all curves tend to 1 at high frequency), with the phase-angle curves (0–180°) as an inset [VA-BK p.93].
  • Ex. (grinding machine): a precise grinding machine of mass 65 kg is mounted on three springs and a dashpot. The free-vibration amplitude falls from 36 mm to 6 mm in two complete cycles and the period of each cycle is 0.33 s; unbalance 0.2 kg at (e = 0.05 m) at 200 rev/min. Find (1) ζ, (2) ωd/ωn, (3) the stiffness of each spring, (4) the amplitude at that speed. Solution: δ = (1/n) ln(X1/Xn+1) = ½ ln(36/6) = 0.8959 = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.14; ωd/ωn = √(1 − ζ²) = 0.99; ωn = ωd/0.99 = 19.05 rad/s = √(K/65) → K = 23.589 kN/m, so each spring = K/3 = 7.862 kN/m; MX/(me) = (ω/ωn)²/[…]^½ → X = 0.5 cm [VA-BK p.94] (⚠ A-F29).
  • Ex. (motor on a table): an electric motor is mounted at the centre of a light frame table; motor weight plus effective table mass = 40 kg; armature and rotating parts 10 kg with eccentricity 15 mm; the table deflects 3 mm under the motor; in free vibration a displacement of 32 mm is damped to 1 mm in one second. Find the amplitude. Solution (data as written there: M = 40 kg, m = 10 kg, e = 15 cm, δst = 3 cm, X1 = 32, Xn+1 = 1, nτd = 1 s): ln(X1/Xn+1) = 2πnζ/√(1 − ζ²) = ζωn·nτd = ζωn; ωn = √(K/M) = √(g/δst) = √(9.81/0.003) = 57.19 rad/s; ln 32 = 57.18 ζ → ζ = 0.06; ω = 875 × 2π/60 = 91.629 rad/s (875 rev/min is not in the statement); MX/(me) formula → X = 6.09 cm [VA-BK p.95] (⚠ A-F30).
8.2 Whirling of rotating shafts (book §4.2.1.4)
  • Rotating shafts tend to bend outward, or whirl, at certain speeds. Whirling is the rotation of the plane formed by the bent shaft and the line joining the bearing centres. It occurs from different causes: unbalanced mass, gyroscopic force or friction of the fluid inside the bearings [VA-BK p.101].
  • It is a self-excited motion: the centre of mass G does not coincide with the centre of geometry S, so a centrifugal force is generated when the shaft rotates. The whirl velocity may or may not equal the shaft velocity in magnitude and direction; the simplest case, treated here, is where they coincide and is called synchronous whirl [VA-BK p.101].
  • Model: a disc of mass m on a shaft between two bearings (span L); G lies at distance e (the rotor eccentricity) from S; the bearing centreline meets the disc plane at O; the shaft deflection is r = OS; ρ = OG. Required: r(ω) [VA-BK p.102]. Forces on the disc [VA-BK p.102]:
    • Elastic force Fs = K r, in the direction SO, with K = 48EI/L³ and I = πd⁴/64.
    • Damping force Fd = c ω r, orthogonal to OS, with ω = 2πN/60 (N in rev/min).
    • Centrifugal force Fc = ρ m ω², in the direction OG.
  • Force balance: K r = m ω² ρ cos α and c ω r = m ω² ρ sin α, with ρ sin α = e sin φ and ρ cos α = r + e cos φ [VA-BK p.102]. Substituting: K r = m ω²(r + e cos φ), i.e. K r − m ω² r = m ω² e cos φ, and c ω r = m ω² e sin φ [VA-BK p.103].
  • tan φ = cωr/(Kr − mω²r) = (cω/K)/(1 − mω²/k) = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); sin φ = cω/√((cω)² + (k − mω²)²). Substituting: r/e = (ω/ωn)²/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ ω/ωn)²) [VA-BK p.103] (⚠ A-F31).
  • Characteristics [VA-BK p.103–104]:
    • (1) Peak amplitude: d(r/e)/d(ω/ωn) = 0 → ωρ/ωn = 1/√(1 − 2ζ²) ≥ 1, r_max/e = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)).
    • (2) No damping (ζ = 0): r/e = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), φ = 0. (A) ω/ωn < 1: r/e is positive, meaning S lies between O and G. (B) ω/ωn > 1: r/e is negative, meaning S lies between O and S (as printed; G is presumably meant, ⚠ A-F32).
    • (3) Resonance: ω/ωn = 1, r/e = 1/(2ζ) (= ∞ for ζ = 0), φ = 90°; resonance must be avoided.
    • (4) Load at the bearing: (a) if the damping force is transmitted to the casing, F/bearing = K r/2; (b) if the damping force is transmitted to the bearing, F/bearing = √((Kr/2)² + (cωr/2)²) = (Kr/2)√(1 + (2ζ ω/ωn)²).
    • (5) Unsafe range of rotating speed: the bending stress is σb = Mb y/Izz = (K r L/4)(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = C r, a linear relation with constant C; for design choose σb < σmax, find rmax from this relation, and the unsafe range is ω1/ωn < ω/ωn < ω2/ωn.
  • Ex. (turbine wheel): a 27 kg turbine wheel with 0.5 mm eccentricity is mounted centrally on a 30 mm diameter shaft, 300 mm between bearings; find the stress from the unbalance at 3600 rev/min, E = 21 × 10¹⁰ N/m². Solution: K = 48EI/L³, I = π(0.03)⁴/64 = 3.97 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴, K = 48 × 21 × 10¹⁰ × 3.97 × 10⁻⁸/(0.3)³ = 1.483 × 10⁷ N/m; ωn = √(K/M) = 741 rad/s; ω = 3600 × 2π/60 = 377 rad/s; ζ = 0: r/e = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = 0.349, r = 0.5 × 0.349 = 0.174 mm; σb = Mb y/Izz = (KrL/4)(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = 142 N/mm² [VA-BK p.105] (⚠ A-F33).
  • Ex. (turbocharger): the rotor has mass 10 kg, keyed to the centre of a 25 mm diameter steel shaft (E = 21 × 10¹⁰ N/m²), 400 mm between bearings. Find (a) the critical speed in rev/min, (b) the shaft amplitude at 3500 rev/min if the eccentricity is 0.015 mm, (c) the vibrating force transmitted to each bearing at this speed and at 500 rev/min. Solution: K = 48EI/L³ = 48E(πd⁴/64)/L³; ωcr = ωn = √(K/M) = "459.5" rad/s; Ncr = 60ωcr/2π = 5247.8 rev/min; (b) r/e = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = 0.8 → r = 0.012 mm; (c) F/bearing = Kr/2 = 18.14 "KN" (the 500 rev/min case is not worked) [VA-BK p.106] (⚠ A-F34).
  • Ex. (gas turbine): rotor weight 120 N at the midspan of a simply supported steel shaft 70 cm long, 40 mm diameter, eccentricity 0.025 mm, working speed 3500 rev/min, "E = 2 × 10¹⁰ N/m²" in the statement. Find (a) the critical speed, (b) the maximum rotor amplitude and the maximum dynamic force on each bearing, (c) if the turbine is brought up to the critical speed with no internal deflection, the time to pass the critical speed so that the shaft's dynamic bending stress equals that at its normal working speed. Solution: M = 120/9.81 kg; K = 48EI/L³ with E = 21 × 10¹⁰ = 3.673 × 10⁶ N/m; ωn = √(K/M) = 549.4 rad/s = ωcr; (b) r/e = 0.8, r = "0.02 cm"; (c) σnormal = σresonance, r = r_resonance = "0.002 cm", r_resonance/e = ωn t/2 → t = 2.91 × 10⁻⁴ s [VA-BK p.107] (⚠ A-F35).
  • Ex. (shaft with a third bearing): a steel shaft (E = 21 × 10¹⁰ N/m²) of "25 cm" diameter in two short bearings "750 cm" apart carries a turbine rotor of weight 100 N midway; a third bearing of stiffness 2.4 × 10⁵ N/m sits in a recess in the rotor, immersed in oil to give damping 1.1 kN·s/m; the rotor's centre of gravity is 0.25 cm from the shaft axis and the shaft turns at 900 rev/min. Find (a) the dynamic force at each bearing, (b) the range of speed in which it is unsafe to run if the dynamic bending stress must not exceed 28 MN/m². Solution: D = 0.25 m, L = 0.75 m, M = 1.0/9.21 kg (as printed); Ks = 48EI/L³, K = 2.4 × 10⁵; Keq = K + Ks = 6.98 × 10⁵ N/m; ωn = √(Keq/M) = 261.6 rad/s; ζ = C/(2√(Keq M)) = 0.206; r/e = (ω/ωn)²/√(…) = 0.147, r = 0.037 m; F(bearing I, II) = Ks r/2 = 8.48 N; F(III) = √((cωr)² + (Kr)²); σb = (KrL/4)(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = 28 × 10⁶ → r = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m, ω1 = 300.9, ω2 = 227 [VA-BK p.108] (⚠ A-F36).
8.3 Reciprocating unbalance
  • (nothing in this set) — only rotating unbalance (§8.1) and whirling (§8.2) are treated [VA-BK p.92–108].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

8.1 Rotating unbalance (book)
  • Unbalance in rotating systems is a common source of vibration excitation. M = total machine mass including eccentric mass m rotating at ω with eccentricity e: xp(t) = (me/M) βr sin(ωt − φ), βr = r²/√((1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²) [VB-AM p.38].
  • Steady-state vibration from unbalance is proportional to the unbalance m and its distance e from the rotation centre, and increases with the square of the speed; the maximum displacement lags the maximum force by φ [VB-AM p.38].
8.2 Damped system under rotating unbalance (VB-RU, textbook §3.7, book pp.287–291)
  • Unbalance in rotating machinery is one of the main causes of vibration. Simplified model (Fig. 3.19): total machine mass M with two eccentric masses m/2 rotating in opposite directions at constant angular velocity ω (eccentricity e); the centrifugal force (mω²e)/2 of each mass excites M. Two equal masses turning in opposite directions are used so that the horizontal components cancel while the vertical components add along the axis of symmetry A–A [VB-RU p.1–2].
  • Measuring the angular position from the horizontal, the total vertical excitation is F(t) = meω² sin ωt; equation of motion Mẍ + cẋ + kx = meω² sin ωt (3.78) [VB-RU p.2].
  • Solution as for Eq. (3.60) with m → M and F0 → meω²: xp(t) = X sin(ωt − φ) = Im[(me/M)(ω/ωn)² H(iω) e^(i(ωt − φ))] (3.79), ωn = √(k/M); X = meω²/[(k − Mω²)² + (cω)²]^½ = (me/M)(ω/ωn)²|H(iω)|; φ = tan⁻¹[cω/(k − Mω²)] (3.80) [VB-RU p.2–3].
  • With ζ = c/cc, cc = 2Mωn: MX/(me) = r²/[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]^½ = r²|H(iω)|; φ = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)] (3.81). MX/(me) versus r for various ζ is Fig. 3.17; φ versus r is as in Fig. 3.11(b) [VB-RU p.3].
  • Observations: (1) all curves start at zero amplitude; the amplitude near resonance (ω = ωn) is markedly affected by damping, so if the machine is to run near resonance, damping should be introduced purposefully to avoid dangerous amplitudes; (2) at very high speeds MX/(me) is almost unity and the effect of damping is negligible; (3) for 0 < ζ < 1/√2 the maximum of MX/(me) occurs where d(MX/me)/dr = 0 (3.82), i.e. r = 1/√(1 − 2ζ²) > 1, with (MX/me)max = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) (3.83), so the peaks lie to the right of r = 1; (4) for ζ > 1/√2 the ratio has no maximum, growing from 0 at r = 0 to 1 as r → ∞; (5) the force transmitted to the foundation is F(t) = kx + cẋ, with magnitude F = meω²[(1 + 4ζ²r²)/((1 − r²)² + 4ζ²r²)]^½ (3.84) (derived in the book's Problem 3.73) [VB-RU p.3–4].
  • Example 3.6 (deflection of an electric motor due to rotating unbalance, Fig. 3.20: motor of mass M on an elastic foundation k, c, unbalanced mass m at eccentricity e): deflection at resonance 0.15 m; unbalanced mass = 8% of the rotor mass (m = 0.08M); ζ = 0.025. Find (a) the eccentricity e; (b) the peak deflection as the frequency ratio varies from resonance; (c) the additional mass to add uniformly to the motor to reduce the resonance deflection to 0.1 m (eccentric mass unaltered) [VB-RU p.4].
    • (a) At r = 1: MX/(me) = 1/(2ζ) = 1/(2 × 0.025) = 20 → e = MX/(20m) = M(0.15)/[20(0.08M)] = 0.09375 m [VB-RU p.4–5]. (b) (MX/me)max = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) = 1/[2(0.025)√(1 − 0.025²)] = 20.0063 → Xmax = 20.0063 me/M = 20.0063(0.08M)(0.09375)/M = 0.150047 m [VB-RU p.5]. (c) (M + Ma)(0.1)/[(0.08M)(0.09375)] = 20 → Ma = 0.5M: increase the motor mass by 50% to reduce the resonance deflection from 0.15 m to 0.10 m [VB-RU p.5].
  • Example 3.7 (Francis water turbine, Fig. 3.21: water flows from A into blades B and down into tail race C; rotor–stator radial clearance 5 mm; shaft length l = 2 m clamped at the bearings, rotor at the end): rotor mass 250 kg, unbalance me = 5 kg·mm, speed range 600 to 6000 rpm; find the shaft diameter so that the rotor always clears the stator, damping negligible [VB-RU p.5–6].
    • With c = 0: X = meω²/(k − Mω²) = meω²/[k(1 − r²)] (E.1); me = 5 kg·mm, M = 250 kg, limit X = 5 mm; 600 rpm = 20π rad/s, 6000 rpm = 200π rad/s; ωn = √(k/M) = √(k/250) = 0.063245√k rad/s (k in N/m) (E.2) [VB-RU p.5–6].
    • For ω = 20π: 0.005 = (5.0 × 10⁻³)(20π)²/{k[1 − (20π)²/(0.004k)]} = 2π²/(k − 10⁵π²) → k = 10.04 × 10⁴π² N/m (E.3); for ω = 200π: 0.005 = 200π²/(k − 10⁷π²) → k = 10.04 × 10⁶π² N/m (E.4) [VB-RU p.6–7].
    • From Fig. 3.17 the shaft amplitude is minimised by making r = ω/ωn very large, i.e. ωn small compared with ω, so k must be small: choose k = 10.04 × 10⁴π² N/m. Cantilever shaft stiffness k = 3EI/l³ = (3E/l³)(πd⁴/64) (E.5); d⁴ = 64kl³/(3πE) = (64)(10.04 × 10⁴π²)(2³)/[3π(2.07 × 10¹¹)] = 2.6005 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴ → d = 0.1270 m = 127 mm (E.6) [VB-RU p.7] (⚠ B-F70).

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

8.1 Rotating unbalance (Section 6)
  • Source 2 of harmonic excitation, rotating unbalance (motors): unbalanced mass m at eccentricity e rotating at ω inside a machine M guided vertically on rollers, mounted on C and K, displacement y(t); centrifugal force F = mω²e with vertical component mω²e sin ωt and horizontal component mω²e cos θ, θ = ωt [VC-S6 p.2].
  • ΣF = Mÿ: mω²e sin ωt − Cẏ − Ky = Mÿ → Mÿ + Cẏ + Ky = mω²e sin ωt; F(t) = mω²e sin ωt; F0 = mω²e (amplitude of excitation); m unbalanced mass (kg), ω excitation frequency (rad/s) [VC-S6 p.3].
  • Steady-state amplitude: Xp = meω²/√((K − Mω²)² + (Cω)²) = (meω²/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); M equivalent mass (kg), K equivalent stiffness (N/m), C equivalent damping constant (N·s/m), r = ω/ωn [VC-S6 p.3].
8.2 Unbalance examples (Section 6)
  • Unbalanced rotating machine — transmissibility and K [VC-S6 pp.21–22]: M = 380 kg, δst = 0.8 cm, m = 2 kg, N = 800 rpm, e = 1 cm, X1/X5 = 20.
    • ln(X1/Xm+1) = 2πmζ/√(1 − ζ²) with m = 4: ln 20 = 8πζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.11835; ω = 2πN/60 = 83.776 rad/s; ωn = √(g/δst) = √(9.81/0.008) = 35.0178 rad/s [VC-S6 p.21].
    • ωn = √(g/δst) = √(K/M) → K = ωn²M = (35.0178)²·380 = 465973.6 N/m; r = 83.776/35.0178 = 2.392; F0 = meω² = 2·0.01·(83.776)² = 140.37 N; FTR = FT/F0 = √{[1 + (2·0.11835·2.392)²]/[(1 − 2.392²)² + (2·0.11835·2.392)²]} = 0.24165 [VC-S6 p.22].
  • Fan on a hinged plate (US units) [VC-S6 pp.42–44]: rigid plate of weight 100 lb hinged at P and supported on a dashpot at the opposite edge Q; a 50 lb fan rotating at 750 rpm is mounted on the plate through a spring K = 200 lb/in; fan CG 0.1 in from its axis of rotation; spring at 5 in from P, plate CG at 20 in, Q at 40 in; find the steady-state motion of edge Q.
    • x = 5θ, y = 40θ, ẏ = 40θ̇; fan (rotating unbalance): xp(t) = X̄p cos ωt, X̄p = meω²/|K − mω²| = (50/386.4)(0.1)ω²/|200 − (50/386.4)ω²|, ω = 2π·750/60 = 78.54 rad/s → X̄p = 0.13343 in, xp(t) = 0.13343 cos 78.54t [VC-S6 pp.42–43].
    • Plate: ΣMP = JPθ̈: JPθ̈ = −K(x − xp(t))(5) − Cẏ(40) → JPθ̈ + 1600Cθ̇ + 25Kθ = 0.66715K cos 78.54t → with K = 200 lb/in: JPθ̈ + 1600Cθ̇ + 5000θ = 133.43 cos 78.54t [VC-S6 p.43].
    • JP = [(1/12)mL² + md²]plate + m(5)²fan = (1/12)(100/386.4)(40)² + (100/386.4)(20)² + (50/386.4)(5)² = 141.2612 lb·in·s²; 141.2612θ̈ + 1600Cθ̇ + 5000θ = 133.43 cos 78.54t, with C = 1 marked under the C [VC-S6 pp.43–44].
    • θ̄p = M0/√((K − mω²)² + (Cω)²) = 133.43/√((5000 − 141.2612·78.54²)² + (1·78.54)²) = 1.54×10⁻⁴; φp = tan⁻¹[78.54·1600/(5000 − 141.2612·78.54²)] = −8.25296°; θp(t) = 1.54×10⁻⁴ cos(78.54t + 8.25296°); at Q: y = 40θp(t) = 6.16×10⁻³ cos(78.54t + 8.25296°) [VC-S6 p.44] (⚠ C-F16, C-F19).
8.3 Chapter 4 — rotating unbalance and shaft whirl ([VC-A4])
  • Rotating unbalance in rotary machines is the general source of excited vibration. Model: a mass M whose motion is constrained in the horizontal direction (on rollers), mounted on K/2 + K/2 and a damper C, excited by an eccentric mass m at eccentric radius e rotating at constant ω; displacement x(t) from static equilibrium [VC-A4 p.10].
  • Mẍ = ΣF = −Cẋ − Kx + mω²e sin ωt → Mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = mω²e sin ωt = F0 sin ωt, F0 = mω²e; steady state x(t) = X sin(ωt − φ); from the force polygon X = (F0/K)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2) = (mω²e/K)/[…]^(1/2) [VC-A4 pp.10–11].
  • MX/(me) = (ω/ωn)²/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2); tan φ = (2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) [VC-A4 p.11].
  • Characteristics [VC-A4 p.11]: (1) resonance ω/ωn = 1: MXres/(me) = 1/(2ζ), φ = 90°. (2) Maximum peak: d(MX/me)/d(ω/ωn) = 0 → ωp/ωn = 1/√(1 − 2ζ²) ≥ 1 (the peak lies above resonance) and MXp/(me) = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)); the source says the last peak occurs at ζ = √(1/2) = 0.707. (3) No damping ζ = 0: φ = 180°, MX/(me) = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); for ω/ωn > 1 the ratio is negative, so the curve is drawn dotted in the upper part. The plotted curves (with a phase inset) show MX/me → 1 at high frequency for all ζ [VC-A4 pp.11–12].
  • Example (grinding machine) [VC-A4 p.12]: M = 65 kg on three springs and a dashpot; free-vibration amplitude falls from 36 mm to 6 mm in two complete cycles, period of each cycle 0.33 s; unbalance m = 0.2 kg (e = 0.05 m in the data line), speed 200 rpm; find (1) ζ, (2) ωd/ωn, (3) stiffness of each spring, (4) the amplitude. (1) δ = (1/n) ln(X1/Xn+1) = ½ ln 6 = 0.8959 = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) → ζ = 0.14; (2) ωd = √(1 − ζ²) ωn → ωd/ωn = 0.99; (3) ωn = ωd/0.99 = 19.05 rad/s = √(K/65) → K = 23.589 kN/m; each spring K/3 = 7.862 kN/m; (4) MX/(me) = (ω/ωn)²/√(…) gives X = 0.5 cm (⚠ C-F31).
  • Example (motor on a light frame table) [VC-A4 p.13]: M = 40 kg (motor + effective table mass), rotating parts m = 10 kg, e = 15 (mm in the statement, cm in the solution), δst = 3 (mm in the statement, cm in the solution but 0.003 m is used), free vibration 32 → 1 (mm in the statement, cm in the solution) in one second (n τd = 1 s). ωn = √(g/δst) = √(9.81/0.003) = 57.19 rad/s; ln(X1/Xn+1) = (2π n/√(1 − ζ²)ωn)·ζωn = nτdζωn = ζωn → ln 32 = 57.18ζ → ζ = 0.06; ω = 875×2π/60 = 91.629 rad/s (875 rpm is not in the statement); MX/(me) from the unbalance formula → X = 6.09 cm (⚠ C-F31).
  • Whirling of a rotating shaft [VC-A4 pp.19–26]: rotating shafts tend to bend outwards, or whirl, at certain speeds. Whirling is the rotation of the plane formed by the bent shaft and the centreline connecting the bearing centres; causes: unbalanced mass, gyroscopic force or friction of the fluid inside the bearings. Whirl is a self-excited motion: the centre of mass G does not coincide with the geometric centre S, so a centrifugal force appears when the shaft rotates. The whirl velocity may equal the shaft velocity in magnitude and direction or not; the simplest case, where they coincide, is called synchronous whirl [VC-A4 p.19].
    • Disc of mass m with G at distance e from S (rotor eccentricity); the bearing centreline meets the disc plane at O; the shaft deflection is r = OS; find r(ω). Forces: elastic Fs = K r in the direction SO, K = 48EI/L³ (centrally loaded shaft), I = πd⁴/64; damping Fd = cωr orthogonal to OS, ω = 2πN/60 (N rpm); centrifugal Fc = mω²ρ (ρ = OG) along OG [VC-A4 pp.20–21].
    • Force analysis: Kr = mω²ρ cos α; cωr = mω²ρ sin α, with ρ sin α = e sin φ and ρ cos α = r + e cos φ → Kr − mω²r = mω²e cos φ; cωr = mω²e sin φ; tan φ = cωr/(Kr − mω²r) = (2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); sin φ = cω/√((cω)² + (K − mω²)²); substituting: cωr = mω²e cω/√((cω)² + (K − mω²)²) → r/e = (ω/ωn)²/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²) [VC-A4 pp.20–21].
    • Characteristics [VC-A4 pp.21–22]: (1) peak amplitude: d(r/e)/d(ω/ωn) = 0 → ωρ/ωn = 1/√(1 − 2ζ²) ≥ 1, rmax/e = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)). (2) Undamped: r/e = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), φ = 0; (A) ω/ωn < 1: r/e positive, S lies between O and G; (B) ω/ωn > 1: r/e negative, "S lies between O, S" (as printed; presumably O and G is meant, see ⚠ C-F32). (3) Resonance: ω/ωn = 1, r/e = 1/(2ζ) (∞ for ζ = 0), φ = 90°, so avoid resonance. (4) Load at the bearing: (a) if the damping force is transmitted to the casing, F/bearing = Kr/2; (b) if transmitted to the bearing, F/bearing = √((Kr/2)² + (cωr/2)²) = (Kr/2)√(1 + (2ζω/ωn)²). (5) Unsafe speed range: σb = Mb y/Izz = (KrL/4)(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = Cr, a linear relation with constant C; for design choose σb < σmax, find rmax from it, and the unsafe range is ω1/ωn < ω/ωn < ω2/ωn.
  • Example (turbine wheel) [VC-A4 p.23]: 27 kg wheel, e = 0.5 mm, shaft d = 30 mm, L = 300 mm between bearings, wheel central, 3600 rpm, E = 21×10¹⁰ N/m²; find the stress. K = 48EI/L³, I = πd⁴/64 = π(0.03)⁴/64 = 3.97×10⁻⁸ m⁴, K = 48·21×10¹⁰·3.97×10⁻⁸/0.3³ = 1.483×10⁷ N/m; ωn = √(K/M) = 741 rad/s; ω = 3600·2π/60 = 377 rad/s; r/e = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = 0.349 (ζ = 0), R = 0.5×0.349 = 0.174 mm; σb = (Mb y/Izz) = (KrL/4)(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = 142 N/mm² (the denominator is printed πd²/64, ⚠ C-F31).
  • Example (turbocharger rotor) [VC-A4 p.24]: 10 kg rotor keyed to the centre of a 25 mm steel shaft (E = 21×10¹⁰), length 400 mm; (a) critical speed in rpm, (b) shaft amplitude at 3500 rpm if e = 0.015 mm, (c) force transmitted to each bearing at this speed and at 500 rpm. (a) K = 48E(πd⁴/64)/L³, ωcr = ωn = √(K/M) = 459.5 rad/s, Ncr = 60ωcr/2π = 5247.8 rpm; (b) r/e = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) = 0.8 → r = 0.012 mm; (c) F/bearing = Kr/2 = 18.14 kN (the 500 rpm case is not worked) (⚠ C-F31).
  • Example (gas turbine rotor) [VC-A4 p.25]: rotor of weight 120 N at the midspan of a simply supported steel shaft 70 cm long, 40 mm diameter, e = 0.025 mm, working speed 3500 rpm, E as printed 2×10¹⁰ (21×10¹⁰ is used); (a) critical speed, (b) maximum amplitude and maximum dynamic force per bearing, (c) if the turbine is brought up to the critical speed with no internal deflection, the time to pass the critical speed such that the dynamic bending stress equals that at working speed. M = 120/9.81 kg, K = 48EI/L³ = 3.673×10⁶ N/m, ωn = √(K/M) = 549.4 rad/s = ωcr (a); (b) r/e = 0.8 → r = 0.02 cm; (c) σnormal = σresonance, r = rresonance = 0.002 cm, rresonance/e = (ωn/2) t → t = 2.91×10⁻⁴ s; the bearing force in (b) is not computed (⚠ C-F31).
  • Example (shaft with a damped third bearing) [VC-A4 p.26]: steel shaft E = 21×10¹⁰ N/m², "25 cm" diameter (D = 0.25 m in the solution), bearings "750 cm" apart (L = 0.75 m used), rotor weight 100 N at mid-span (M written 1.0/9.21 kg), a third bearing of stiffness 2.4×10⁵ N/m in the rotor recess in oil with damping coefficient 1.1 kN·s/m; CG 0.25 cm from the shaft axis; 900 rpm; find (a) the dynamic force at each bearing, (b) the unsafe speed range if the dynamic bending stress is not to exceed 28 MN/m². Ks = 48EI/L³, K = 2.4×10⁵, Keq = K + Ks = 6.98×10⁵ N/m; ωn = √(Keq/M) = 261.6 rad/s; ζ = C/(2√(Keq M)) = 0.206; r/e = (ω/ωn)²/√(…) = 0.147, r = 0.037 m; F(bearings I, II) = Ks r/2 = 8.48 N; FIII = √((cωr)² + (Kr)²); σb = (Mb y/Izz) = (KrL/4)(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = 28×10⁶ with r = 5×10⁻⁴ m, ω1 = 300.9, ω2 = 227 (rad/s) (⚠ C-F31).
8.4 Ayman's rotating-unbalance notes ([VC-AAy])
  • Model: M on rollers with spring and damper, eccentric mass m at e rotating at ω; forces mew² sin ωt (vertical) and mew² cos ωt (horizontal). ΣF = Mẍ → Mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = mew² sin ωt, F0 = mew²; Xp = (F0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), K = Mωn² → Xp = (me r²/M)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); β = MXp/(me) = r²/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) (amplitude ratio); φp = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)] [VC-AAy p.3].
  • Transmitted force: FT(t) = Cẋ + Kx = Xp√(K² + (Cω)²) sin(ωt + φT − φp); |FT| = Xp√(K² + (Cω)²) = (F0/K)√(K² + (Cω)²)/√((K − Mω²)² + (Cω)²) = F0√(1 + (2ζr)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) = mω²e√(1 + (2ζr)²)/√(…); transmissibility = |FT|/(mω²e) = √[(1 + (2ζr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)] [VC-AAy p.3].
  • At resonance (r = ω/ωn = 1): Xp = me r²/(2Mζ) (r = 1), φp = 90°, β = 1/(2ζ). βmax: dβ/dr = 0 → r = 1/√(1 − 2ζ²), βmax = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)); the last peak of β occurs at ζ = 1/√2, where r = ∞ and βmax = 1 [VC-AAy p.4].
