Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

9.1 Moving support (book §4.2.1.2)
  • The system is excited by the motion of its support: y(t) is the support displacement and x(t) the mass motion (mass m on spring k and damper c standing on the moving base). Equation of motion: m ẍ = −C(ẋ − ẏ) − K(x − y) → m ẍ + C ẋ + K x = C ẏ + K y [VA-BK p.96].
  • For harmonic support motion y = Y sin ωt: m ẍ + C ẋ + K x = CωY cos ωt + KY sin ωt = F0 sin(ωt + ψ), with F0 = √((KY)² + (CωY)²) = KY√(1 + (2ζ ω/ωn)²) and tan ψ = CωY/(KY) = 2ζ(ω/ωn) [VA-BK p.96].
  • Steady state assumed as x(t) = X sin(ωt + ψ − φ). Using the force polygon: X = (F0/K)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^½ = Y[1 + (2ζω/ωn)²]^½/[…]^½, so X/Y = [1 + (2ζω/ωn)²]^½/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^½, with tan φ = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) [VA-BK p.96–97].
  • X/Y is called the transmissibility = amplitude of transmitted motion / amplitude of excited motion. Its properties are studied with vibration isolation [VA-BK p.97].
  • Ex. (corrugated road): a load of mass 250 kg on a spring of stiffness "k = 4000 N/m" and a damper giving ζ = 0.20 rides on a wheel moving horizontally at v = 25 m/s over a corrugated road of the form y = Y sin(2πx/L), Y = 25 cm, L = 20 m. Find the amplitude of the load and the critical horizontal speed Vcr. Solution (m = 250 kg, K = 40 kN/m, V = 25 m/s; "in the case of no damping"): the period of the road excitation is η = L/V = 20/25 s and ω = 2π/η = 7.8 rad/s; X/Y = 1/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) → X = 0.4 m. The critical speed is at the peak of the load motion, i.e. resonance ωcr = ωn: Vcr = 1/ηcr = L/(2π/ωn) = Lωn/2π = 40 m/s [VA-BK p.97–98] (⚠ A-F37).
9.2 Vibration isolation (book §4.2.1.3)
  • Vibration forces generated by machines and motors often cannot be avoided, so a machine can be isolated from the fixed foundation by mounting it on springs and dampers or viscous-elastic material (rubber, plastic, …) to reduce the force transmitted from the machine to the foundation. The purpose of designing a mechanical isolator between machine and foundation is to select the values of k and c [VA-BK p.98].
  • Model: a machine (springs k/2 + k/2, damper c) with the exciting force F(t) = F0 sin ωt from rotating unbalance; m ẍ + c ẋ + K x = F0 sin ωt; x(t) = X sin(ωt − φ) [VA-BK p.99].
  • The force transmitted to the foundation through the springs and dampers is FT = Fs + Fd = kx + cẋ = kX sin(ωt − φ) + cωX cos(ωt − φ) = FT0 sin(ωt + ψ − φ) (force polygon with mω²X, cωX, kX, FT) [VA-BK p.99].
  • Amplitude of the transmitted force: FT0 = √((kX)² + (cωX)²) = kX√(1 + (2ζ ω/ωn)²), and with X = (F0/K)/[…]^½: FT0 = F0√(1 + (2ζω/ωn)²)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^½ [VA-BK p.99–100].
  • Transmissibility TR = FT0/F0 = amplitude of transmitted force / amplitude of excited force = [(1 + (2ζω/ωn)²)/((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²)]^½ [VA-BK p.100].
  • Properties (same for moving support) [VA-BK p.100–101]:
    • (2) TR = 1, i.e. FT0 = F0, when ω/ωn = 0 and when ω/ωn = √2.
    • (3) In the interval 0 < ω/ωn < √2, TR > 1, which is undesired and must be avoided; TR decreases with increasing ζ. In 0 < ω/ωn < 1, for any ζ, TR increases with ω/ωn; in 1 < ω/ωn < √2, TR decreases with increasing ω/ωn.
    • (4) For ω/ωn > √2, TR < 1, which is desired, but TR increases with increasing ζ. Although increasing ζ usually decreases vibration, for ω/ωn > √2 in this application increasing the damping must be avoided because it increases the transmitted vibration.
    • Figure: |TR| against ω/ωn (0–5) for ζ = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.375, 0.50, 1.0, all curves crossing at ω/ωn = √2, with the phase angle ψ (0–180°) as an inset [VA-BK p.100].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

9.1 Transmissibility and isolation (book)
  • Forces of vibrating machines are transmitted to the support structure (undesirable effects, e.g. noise); machines are mounted on designed flexible supports = vibration isolators (isolators) [VB-AM p.36].
  • Amplitude of vibration reduces with increasing k and c; proper selection of k and c is needed to reduce the transmitted force [VB-AM p.36].
  • FT = k xp + c ẋp = X0 β √(k² + (cω)²) sin(ωt − φ̄), φ̄ = φ − φt, φt = tan⁻¹(cω/k) = tan⁻¹(2rζ); FT = F0 βt sin(ωt − φ̄), βt = √(1 + (2rζ)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²) [VB-AM p.36].
  • Transmissibility βt = ratio of the maximum transmitted force to the amplitude of the applied force (Fig. 1.20, ζ = 0, 0.2, 0.75, 1.0) [VB-AM p.36–37].
  • r < √2: βt > 1 (transmitted force larger than applied); transmitted force reduced by increasing ζ. r = √2: every curve passes through βt = 1. r > √2: βt < 1 and tends to zero as r increases; here the transmitted force increases with increasing ζ. Hence isolation is best achieved by an isolator of spring elements only, with r > √2 and no damping element [VB-AM p.36].
9.2 Base excitation (book)
  • Vehicles on a moving support/base: base motion causes forces transmitted to the equipment. Base y = Y0 sin ωt (Fig. 1.22) [VB-AM p.38].
  • xp(t) = Y0 βb sin(ωt − φ + φb), φ = tan⁻¹[2rζ/(1 − r²)]; displacement transmissibility βb = √(1 + (2rζ)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²) [VB-AM p.39].
  • Relative motion z = x − y = Y0 r²/√((1 − r²)² + (2rζ)²) · sin(ωt − φ) [VB-AM p.39].
9.3 Machine on a resilient foundation (VB-RU, Example 3.5, book p.287)
  • Example 3.5: a heavy machine of weight 3000 N on a resilient foundation; static deflection of the foundation 7.5 cm; the machine vibrates with amplitude 1 cm when the base of the foundation is subjected to harmonic oscillation at the undamped natural frequency of the system with amplitude 0.25 cm. Find (a) the damping constant of the foundation, (b) the dynamic force amplitude on the base, (c) the amplitude of the displacement of the machine relative to the base [VB-RU p.1].
  • (a) k = weight/δst = 3000/0.075 = 40,000 N/m. At resonance (ω = ωn, r = 1), Eq. (3.68): X/Y = 0.010/0.0025 = 4 = {[1 + (2ζ)²]/(2ζ)²}^½ (E.1) → ζ = 0.1291; c = ζ·cc = ζ·2√(km) = 0.1291 × 2 × √[40,000 × (3000/9.81)] = 903.0512 N·s/m (E.2; the square root is lost in the source typography) [VB-RU p.1].
  • (b) At r = 1 (Eq. 3.74): FT = Yk[(1 + 4ζ²)/(4ζ²)]^½ = kX = 40,000 × 0.01 = 400 N (E.3) [VB-RU p.1].
  • (c) Relative displacement at r = 1 (Eq. 3.77): Z = Y/(2ζ) = 0.0025/(2 × 0.1291) = 0.00968 m (E.4). Since X = 0.01 m, Y = 0.0025 m and Z = 0.00968 m, Z ≠ X − Y because of the phase differences between x, y and z [VB-RU p.1].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

9.1 Support (base) motion (Section 6)
  • Source 3 of harmonic excitation, support or base motion ("rough road"): m on K and C riding a wheel over a sinusoidal road y(t) = Y sin ωt, ẏ = ωY cos ωt; Fs = K(x − y), Fd = C(ẋ − ẏ) [VC-S6 p.4].
  • −Fs − Fd = mẍ → −C(ẋ − ẏ) − K(x − y) = mẍ → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = Cẏ + Ky = ωYC cos ωt + KY sin ωt; F0 = √((ωYC)² + (KY)²), φ = tan⁻¹[Cω/(K − mω²)] = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)]; mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = F0 cos(ωt − φ) [VC-S6 p.4] (⚠ C-F18).
9.2 Transmitted force and force transmissibility (Section 6)
  • Transmitted force: the amount of force transmitted to the support (هي مقدار القوة التي تنتقل إلى الـ support); support force Cẋ + Kx with xp(t) = X̄p cos(ωt − φp), ẋp(t) = −ωX̄p sin(ωt − φp): KX̄p cos(ωt − φp) − CωX̄p sin(ωt − φp) = FT cos((ωt − φp) + αp) [VC-S6 p.19].
  • F̄T = √((KX̄p)² + (CωX̄p)²) = F0√{[1 + (2ζr)²]/[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]}; αp = tan⁻¹(2ζr) [VC-S6 p.19].
  • Force transmissibility F.T.R = FT/F0 — how much the support is affected by the excitation (الـ support اتأثر أد ايه من الـ excitation) [VC-S6 p.19]. Worked use: §8.2 [VC-S6 p.22].
9.3 Base-excitation examples (Section 6)
  • Vehicle on a rough road [VC-S6 pp.23–25]: m = 1200 kg, K = 400 kN/m, ζ = 0.5, V = 20 km/h, road y(t) = Y0 sin ωt with Y0 = 0.05 m and wavelength λ = 6 m; required X̄p.
    • ω = 2πf = 2πV/λ (V = λf) = 2π·20×10³/(60·60·6) = 5.818 rad/s; mẍ = −K(x − y) − C(ẋ − ẏ) → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = CY0ω cos ωt + KY0 sin ωt; ωn = √(4×10⁵/1200) = 18.257 rad/s; r = 5.818/18.257 = 0.3187 [VC-S6 p.24].
    • C = 2mζωn = 2·1200·0.5·18.257 = 21908.4 N·s/m; F0 = √((CY0ω)² + (KY0)²) = √((21908.4·0.05·5.818)² + (4×10⁵·0.05)²) = 20990.88 N; X̄p = (20990.88/4×10⁵)/√((1 − 0.3187²)² + (2·0.5·0.3187)²) = 0.055 m [VC-S6 p.25].
  • Damper-driven mass [VC-S6 p.29]: m on wheels with K and C2 to the wall and C1 connecting m to an end moving as y(t) = Y cos ωt; required X̄p. mẍ = −C2ẋ − Kx − C1(ẋ − ẏ) → mẍ + (C1 + C2)ẋ + Kx = C1ẏ; ẏ = −Yω sin ωt = Yω sin(ωt + π) → mẍ + Ceqẋ + Kx = C1Yω sin(ωt + π); F0 = C1Yω; ζ = (C1 + C2)/(2√(Km)); r = ω/ωn; X̄p = (F0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) [VC-S6 p.29].
  • Bar with a moving spring end [VC-S6 pp.40–41]: uniform bar m pivoted at O (L/4 from the left end) and supported at the ends by two springs; the end P of spring PQ at the right end moves as x(t) = X0 sin ωt; damper C at L/4 right of O; L = 1 m, K = 1000 N/m, C = 500 N·s/m, m = 10 kg, X0 = 1 cm, ω = 10 rad/s; find the steady-state angular displacement.
    • y = (L/4)θ, x = (3L/4)θ; Joθ̈ = −Ky(L/4) − Cẏ(L/4) − K(x − x(t))(3L/4) → Joθ̈ + (L²/16)Cθ̇ + (5/8)L²Kθ = (3/4)LKX0 sin ωt [VC-S6 p.41].
    • Jo = (1/12)mL² + m(L/4)² = (7/48)mL² = 1.4583 kg·m²; Ceq = 31.25 N·s·m/rad; Keq = 625 N·m/rad; M0 = (3/4)(1)(1000)(0.01) = 7.5 N·m; 1.4583θ̈ + 31.25θ̇ + 625θ = 7.5 sin 10t; θ̄p = 7.5/√((625 − 1.4583·10²)² + (31.25·10)²) = 0.01311 rad [VC-S6 p.41].
9.4 Transmitted force in Abdelrahman Mamdouh's notes ([VC-AFV])
  • FT(t) = Cẋp + Kxp (1), with xp(t) = Xp sin(ωt − φ) (2) and ẋp(t) = ωXp cos(ωt − φ) (3); substituting: FT(t) = CωXp cos(ωt − φ) + KXp sin(ωt − φ) = |FT| sin(ωt − φ + α) [VC-AFV p.3].
  • |FT| = √((CωXp)² + (KXp)²) = Xp√((Cω)² + K²) = F0√(K² + (Cω)²)/√((K − mω²)² + (Cω)²) (dimensional form); |FT| = F0√[(1 + (2ζr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)] (non-dimensional form), the amplitude of the transmitted force; transmissibility T.R = |FT|/F0 (the page ends at "|FT|/F") [VC-AFV p.3]. The phase α is left undefined in the source.
9.5 Chapter 4 — moving support and vibration isolation ([VC-A4])
  • Moving support: the system is excited by the motion of the support y(t); x(t) is the mass motion. mẍ = −C(ẋ − ẏ) − K(x − y) → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = Cẏ + Ky; for y = Y sin ωt: mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = CωY cos ωt + KY sin ωt = F0 sin(ωt + ψ) [VC-A4 p.14].
  • Force polygon: F0 = √((KY)² + (CωY)²) = KY√(1 + (2ζω/ωn)²); tan ψ = CωY/(KY) = 2ζω/ωn; steady state assumed X(t) = X sin(ωt + ψ − φ) [VC-A4 p.14].
  • X = (F0/K)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2) = Y[1 + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2); X/Y = [1 + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2); tan φ = (2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²). X/Y is the transmissibility = amplitude of transmitted motion / amplitude of excited motion; its properties are studied later with vibration isolation [VC-A4 pp.14–15].
  • Example (load on a wheel over a corrugated road) [VC-A4 pp.15–16]: m = 250 kg on a spring k = 4000 N/m (the solution uses K = 40 kN/m) and a damper with ζ = 0.20, wheel horizontal speed v = 25 m/s, road amplitude Y = 25 cm, wavelength L = 20 m; find the load amplitude and the critical speed Vcr. Solution (no damping): τ = L/V = 20/25 = 0.8 s, ω = 2π/τ = 7.8 rad/s; X/Y = 1/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) → X = 0.4 m; the critical speed is at resonance, ωcr = ωn: Vcr = L/τcr = L/(2π/ωn) = Lωn/2π = 40 m/s (⚠ C-F33).
  • Vibration isolation: vibration forces of machines often cannot be avoided, so machines are isolated from the fixed foundation by springs and dampers or visco-elastic material (rubber, plastic …) to reduce the force transmitted; the purpose of the isolator design is to select k and c [VC-A4 p.16].
  • Machine with rotating-unbalance source F(t) = F0 sin ωt: mẍ + cẋ + Kx = F0 sin ωt, x(t) = X sin(ωt − φ); transmitted force FT = Fs + Fd = kx + cẋ = kX sin(ωt − φ) + cωX cos(ωt − φ) = FTo sin(ωt + ψ − φ), with FTo = √((kX)² + (cωX)²) = kX√(1 + (2ζω/ωn)²), X = (F0/K)/[…]^(1/2) [VC-A4 pp.17–18]. Force polygon with mω²X, cωX, kX, F, FT and phase φ shown on p.17.
  • FTo = F0√(1 + (2ζω/ωn)²)/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]^(1/2); transmissibility TR = FTo/F0 = {[1 + (2ζω/ωn)²]/[(1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²]}^(1/2) (same for moving support) [VC-A4 p.18].
  • Properties [VC-A4 pp.18–19]: (1) TR = FTo/F0 = amplitude of transmitted force / amplitude of excited force; (2) TR = 1 (FTo = F0) when ω/ωn = 0 and when ω/ωn = √2; (3) for 0 < ω/ωn < √2, TR > 1, which is undesired and must be avoided; TR reduces as ζ increases, and for 0 < ω/ωn < 1 TR increases with increasing ω/ωn, while for 1 < ω/ωn < √2 TR reduces with increasing ω/ωn; (4) for ω/ωn > √2, TR < 1, which is desired, but TR increases with increasing ζ, which must be avoided — although normally increasing damping decreases vibration, for ω/ωn > √2 increasing damping increases the transmitted force. The plotted curves (ζ = 0.05 to 1.0 with a phase inset) all cross TR = 1 at ω/ωn = √2 [VC-A4 pp.18–19].
9.6 Ayman's support-motion notes ([VC-AAy])
  • Support motion y(t) = Y0 sin ωt: mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = Cẏ + Ky, ẏ = Y0ω cos ωt → mẍ + Cẋ + Kx = CY0ω cos ωt + KY0 sin ωt = Y0√((Cω)² + K²) sin(ωt + α); F0 = Y0√(K² + (Cω)²); α = tan⁻¹(Cω/K) = tan⁻¹(2ζr) [VC-AAy p.5].
  • Response x(t) = Xp sin(ωt + α − φp) = Xp sin(ωt − (φp − α)); Xp = Y0√(1 + (2ζr)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); φp = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)]; tan(φp − α) = (tan φp − tan α)/(1 + tan φp tan α) = 2ζr³/(1 − r² + (2ζr)²) [VC-AAy p.5]; φp − α = tan⁻¹[2ζr³/(1 − r² + (2ζr)²)] [VC-AAy p.6].
  • Transmitted force: FT(t) = C(ẋ − ẏ) + K(x − y) = −mẍ, with xp(t) = Xp sin(ωt + α − φp) → FT = mXpω² sin(ωt + α − φp); |FT| = mXpω² = mY0ω²√(1 + (2ζr)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); using mω² = Kr²: |FT| = KY0r²√(1 + (2ζr)²)/√(…); transmissibility |FT|/(KY0) = r²√[(1 + (2ζr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)] = TRF [VC-AAy p.6].
  • Displacement transmissibility TR = Xp/Y0 = amplitude of system motion / amplitude of support motion = √(1 + (2ζr)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); TRmax at r = (1/2ζ)√(√(1 + 2ζ²) − 1) (written twice, see ⚠ C-F36); Xp,max = TR|max × Y0 [VC-AAy p.7].
  • Relative motion: z = x − y (x = z + y): mẍ + Cż + Kz = 0 → m(z̈ + ÿ) + Cż + Kz = 0 → mz̈ + Cż + Kz = −mÿ = mω²Y0 sin ωt; F0 = mω²Y0; z(t) = Zp sin(ωt − φp), Zp = (mω²Y0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) = Y0r²/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); φp = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 − r²)] [VC-AAy pp.8–9] (p.9 is the same page photographed again).
9.7 Vehicle pitch-and-bounce road excitation ([VC-R2D])
  • A two-degree-of-freedom base-excited example (bounce x and pitch θ, front and rear wheels seeing the same sinusoidal road with a phase lag 2π(L1 + L2)/λ) is worked in §11.8 [VC-R2D pp.1–3]; a two-storey base-excited system is in §11.9 [VC-R2D pp.4–5].

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

10.1 Seismic instrument (book §4.3)
  • A vibrometer or seismometer unit is a container holding a seismic mass m carried by a spring k inside the container, with damping c provided by a liquid around the mass. The container is fixed to the body whose vibration x(t) = X sin ωt (drawn as the surface motion y = A sin ωt) is to be measured [VA-BK p.109].
  • Motion of the seismic mass (y = seismic-mass displacement in the source's notation): m ÿ + c(ẏ − ẋ) + K(y − x) = 0 (as printed). With z(t) = y(t) − x(t), the relative displacement between mass and container (z is the measured displacement, x the actual one): m z̈ + c ż + K z = −m ẍ = m ω² X sin ωt; steady state z_p.I = Z sin(ωt − φ) [VA-BK p.109].
  • Z/X = (ω/ωn)²/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ ω/ωn)²) = M.F. (magnification factor); tan φ = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) [VA-BK p.109] (⚠ A-F38).
  • Figure: |Z/Y| against ω/ωn (0–5) for ζ = 0 to 1.0, with the shaded regions marked "Accelerometer" (small ω/ωn) and "Seismometer" (ω/ωn above about 2.5), and the phase-angle inset. The ratio Z/X depends on ω/ωn and ζ, and the theory of vibration-measuring units depends on the range of the frequency ratio (ω/ωn ≫ or ≪): two kinds of unit result [VA-BK p.110].
10.2 Vibrometer or seismometer (§4.3.1)
  • Principle: make ω/ωn very large by using a large mass and small stiffness (ωn ≪); then Z/X ≅ 1 and the mass m stays stationary while the container moves with the vibrating body [VA-BK p.110].
  • Properties [VA-BK p.110–111]: (1) ωn is very small (m is large), so its large size is a defect of the seismometer. (2) Percentage error e = X_actual − X_measured = Z/M.F − Z = Z(1/M.F − 1); e% = (e/X_actual) × 100 = M.F(1/M.F − 1) × 100 = 100(1 − M.F). (3) Useful range ω/ωn > 2.5 for ζ = 0.7.
10.3 Accelerometer (§4.3.2)
  • Principle: when ωn is large relative to the measured frequency ω (ω/ωn ≪ 1), the measured displacement is proportional to the acceleration of the measured motion: Z/X ≅ (ω/ωn)², Z = ω²X/ωn² ≅ acceleration/ωn², so Z ∝ acceleration with 1/ωn² the proportionality constant. X_measured = (ωn/ω)² Z, X_actual = Z/M.F [VA-BK p.111].
  • Properties [VA-BK p.112]: (1) the mass m is small (ωn ≫), so the accelerometer is distinguished by its small size, opposite to the vibrometer; most vibration measurements, even of earthquakes, are done with accelerometers, and velocity and displacement are obtained by integration. (2) Percentage error e = X_actual − X_measured = Z/M.F − (ωn²/ω²)Z = Z(1/M.F − ωn²/ω²); e% = (e/Z_actual) × 100 = 100(1 − (ωn²/ω²) M.F). (3) Useful range ω/ωn < 0.4 for ζ = 0.7. (4) Materials with piezoelectric properties, such as crystals, are used to measure accelerations of high frequency and are distinguished by their small size.
  • Ex. 1 (vibrometer error): a vibrometer with m = 2.5 kg, k = 60 N/m and ζ = 0.22; find the frequency range for which the percentage error does not exceed 5%. Solution: e% = (1 − M.F) × 100, 5 = (1 − M.F) × 100 → M.F = 0.95; putting M.F = (ω/ωn)²/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²) and squaring: 1 − 2(ω/ωn)² + (ω/ωn)⁴ + 4ζ²(ω/ωn)² = (1/M.F)²(ω/ωn)⁴ → (ω/ωn)⁴(1 − 1/M.F²) + (ω/ωn)²(4ζ² − 2) + 1 = 0 → (ω/ωn)⁴ + 16.71(ω/ωn)² − 9.25 = 0 → (ω/ωn)² = [−16.71 ± √(16.71² + 4 × 9.25)]/2 = 0.53 or −17.24 → ω/ωn = 0.728 [VA-BK p.112–113] (⚠ A-F39).
  • Ex. 2: a vibrometer of natural frequency 5 Hz and ζ = 0.6; find the minimum frequency for a measurement accurate to ±2%. Solution starts: e% = (1 + M.F) × 100 (as printed), 2 = (1 − M.F) × 100 → M.F = 0.98, M.F = (ω/ωn)²/√(…); the solution stops here [VA-BK p.113] (⚠ A-F40).
  • Ex. 3: a vibrometer fixed on the case of a motor turning at 1600 rev/min; the seismic mass vibrates with amplitude 1.5 mm relative to the case; the vibrometer's natural frequency is 10 cycles/s. Find the amplitude of the motor. Solution: ζ = 0, Z/X = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); ωn = 2πf = 20π, ω = 1600 × 2π/60 = 160π/3; Z/X = 1.5/X = (160/60)²/(1 − (160/60)²) = 64/(−55); X = −55 × 0.5/64 cm = 1.289 cm [VA-BK p.114] (⚠ A-F41).

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

10.1 Vibrometer and accelerometer — Chapter 4 section 4.3 ([VC-A4])
  • A vibrometer (seismometer) unit has a container (case) holding a seismic mass m carried by a spring k with damping c from a liquid; the case is placed on the body whose motion x(t) = X sin ωt is to be measured [VC-A4 p.27].
  • The seismic mass y(t): mÿ + c(ẏ − ẋ) + K(y − x) = 0. With the relative displacement z(t) = y(t) − x(t) (the measured displacement; x is the actual displacement): mz̈ + cż + Kz = −mẍ = mω²X sin ωt; steady state zP.I = Z sin(ωt − φ); Z/X = (ω/ωn)²/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²) = M.F (magnification factor), tan φ = (2ζω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²) [VC-A4 p.27].
  • The chart of Z/X against ω/ωn (and phase angle, for ζ = 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.70, 1.0) shows the ratio depends on ω/ωn and ζ; the theory of the instruments depends on the range of ω/ωn, ω/ωn >> 1 or ω/ωn << 1, giving two kinds of units (the shaded zones marked "Seismometer" and "Accelerometer") [VC-A4 p.28].
  • 4.3.1 Vibrometer or seismometer [VC-A4 pp.28–29]: makes ω/ωn very large by using a large mass and a small stiffness, so ωn << ω; then Z/X ≅ 1 and the mass stays stationary while the container moves with the vibrating body. Properties: (1) ωn very small (m large), so its large size is a defect; (2) percentage error e = Xactual − Xmeasured: e = Z/M.F − Z = Z(1/M.F − 1); e% = (e/Xactual)×100 = M.F(1/M.F − 1)×100 = 100(1 − M.F); (3) useful range ω/ωn > 2.5 for ζ = 0.7.
  • 4.3.2 Accelerometer [VC-A4 pp.29–30]: when ωn is large relative to the measured frequency ω (ω/ωn << 1), the measured displacement is proportional to the acceleration of the measured motion. Z/X = (ω/ωn)²/(M.F·√(…)) → Z/X ≅ (ω/ωn)², Z ≅ ω²X/ωn² ≅ acceleration/ωn², so Z ∝ acceleration with 1/ωn² the proportional constant; Xmeasured = (ωn/ω)²Z, Xactual = Z/M.F. Properties: (1) the mass m is small (ωn >>), so the accelerometer is small in size, unlike the vibrometer; most vibration measurements (even earthquakes) are carried out with accelerometers, and velocity and displacement are obtained by integration; (2) percentage error e = Xactual − Xmeasured = Z/M.F − (ωn²/ω²)Z = Z(1/M.F − ωn²/ω²); e% = 100(1 − (ωn²/ω²)M.F); (3) useful range ω/ωn < 0.4 for ζ = 0.7; (4) materials with piezoelectric properties such as crystals are used for accelerations of high frequency and are distinguished by small size.
  • Example (vibrometer error 5 %) [VC-A4 pp.30–31]: m = 2.5 kg, k = 60 N/m, ζ = 0.22; find the frequency domain for an error not exceeding 5 %. e% = (1 − M.F)×100 → 5 = (1 − M.F)×100, M.F = 0.95 (the source writes "5 = (1 − M.F)/100"); M.F = (ω/ωn)²/√((1 − (ω/ωn)²)² + (2ζω/ωn)²) → (ω/ωn)⁴(1 − 1/M.F²) + (ω/ωn)²(4ζ² − 2) + 1 = 0 → (ω/ωn)⁴ + 16.71(ω/ωn)² − 9.25 = 0 → (ω/ωn)² = [−16.71 ± √(16.71² + 4×9.25)]/2 = (−16.71 ± 17.71)/2 = 0.53, −17.24 → ω/ωn = 0.728 (⚠ C-F34).
  • Example (vibrometer accuracy 2 %) [VC-A4 p.31]: natural frequency 5 Hz, ζ = 0.6; find the minimum frequency for an accuracy of ±2 %. The page writes e% = (1 + MF)×100 and 2 = (1 − MF)×100, MF = 0.98, and the expression for M.F; the solution stops there (the next page starts a new example) (⚠ C-F34).
  • Example (vibrometer on a motor) [VC-A4 p.32]: motor speed 1600 rpm; the seismic mass vibrates with amplitude 1.5 mm relative to the case; the vibrometer's natural frequency is 10 cycles/s; find the motor amplitude. ζ = 0: Z/X = (ω/ωn)²/(1 − (ω/ωn)²); ωn = 2πf = 20π, ω = 1600·2π/60 = 160π/3; Z/X = 1.5/X = (160/60)²/(1 − (160/60)²) = 64/(−55); X = −55×0.5/64 cm = 1.289 cm (as printed, ⚠ C-F34).

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

11.1 Introduction (book Ch. 5, headings numbered 4.x in the file)
  • Until now the study covered SDOF systems (the minimum number of generalized coordinates or independent variables sufficient to describe the motion). Systems described by more than one coordinate are multi-degree-of-freedom (M.D.O.F) systems. Two-degree-of-freedom (T.D.O.F) systems are a special case of M.D.O.F systems; because of their simplicity they are used to introduce the concepts and techniques for studying the dynamic characteristics and deriving the response of M.D.O.F systems [VA-BK p.144]. (PDF p.143 is the Ch. 5 title page "TWO DEGREE OF FREEDOM SYSTEMS"; the section numbers inside Ch. 5 restart at "4.1", ⚠ A-F49.)
  • When an undamped SDOF system is set in motion by initial excitation it vibrates at ωn, its natural state or mode. For M.D.O.F systems, natural vibration implies both a natural frequency and a displacement configuration of the masses during the motion, called a normal mode or modal shape. There are as many natural frequencies and associated modal shapes (natural modes of vibration) as degrees of freedom. So a 2-DOF system has: (1) two generalized coordinates, (2) two natural frequencies ("eigenvalues"), (3) two modal shapes or normal modes ("eigenvectors") [VA-BK p.144].
  • Examples of 2-DOF systems: two masses m1, m2 with springs k1, k, k2 between walls (x1, x2); a mass m on a spring with a pendulum of length l hanging from it (x, θ); two pendulums coupled by a spring k (θ1, θ2); a truck body (m, Io) on two springs k1, k2 (y, θ) [VA-BK p.145].
11.2 Equations of motion
  • Newton's method: translation m ẍ = ΣF; rotation J θ̈ = ΣT [VA-BK p.145].
  • Translation example: masses m1, m2 with springs/dampers k1,c1 (wall–m1), k2,c2 (m1–m2), k3,c3 (m2–wall) and forces F1(t), F2(t). From the FBDs: m1ẍ1 + (c1 + c2)ẋ1 − c2ẋ2 + (k1 + k2)x1 − k2x2 = f1(t) (1); m2ẍ2 − c2ẋ1 + (c2 + c3)ẋ2 − k2x1 + (k2 + k3)x2 = f2(t) (2) [VA-BK p.146].
  • Matrix form (needed for M.D.O.F problems): [m]{ẍ} + [c]{ẋ} + [k]{x} = {f} with [m] = [[m1, 0],[0, m2]], [c] = [[c1 + c2, −c2],[−c2, c2 + c3]], [k] = [[k1 + k2, −k2],[−k2, k2 + k3]]. [m] is the mass (inertia) matrix, [c] the damping matrix, [k] the stiffness matrix; {x}, {ẋ}, {ẍ} the displacement, velocity, acceleration vectors (the source lists them in the order "acceleration, velocity, displacement" as printed); {f} the force vector [VA-BK p.146].
  • Very important note: symmetry of the mass, damping and stiffness matrices is an inherent property of a vibrating system, i.e. the three matrices must be symmetric [VA-BK p.147].
  • Rotation example: torsional system with wall–(k2, c2)–J2–(k1, c1)–J1 and torque T on J1: J1θ̈1 + c1θ̇1 − c1θ̇2 + k1θ1 − k1θ2 = T (1); J2θ̈2 − c1θ̇1 + (c1 + c2)θ̇2 − k1θ1 + (k1 + k2)θ2 = 0 (2). Matrix form: [[J1, 0],[0, J2]]{θ̈} + [[c1, −c1],[−c1, c1 + c2]]{θ̇} + [[k1, −k1],[−k1, k1 + k2]]{θ} = {T, 0} [VA-BK p.147].
  • Characteristics of the matrices: (1) square; (2) symmetric ([m] = [m]ᵀ, [c] = [c]ᵀ, [k] = [k]ᵀ); (3) diagonal in the case of uncoupling: if [m] is diagonal the system is dynamically uncoupled; if [k] is diagonal it is statically uncoupled [VA-BK p.147–148].
  • Ex. (half car model): body (m, I) with CG at G, front spring/damper k1, c1 at distance a, rear k2, c2 at distance b; coordinates x (translation at G) and θ; xa = x − aθ, xb = x + bθ [VA-BK p.148].
    • Translation: m ẍ = −k1xa − c1ẋa − k2xb − c2ẋb → m ẍ + (c1 + c2)ẋ − (c1a − c2b)θ̇ + (k1 + k2)x − (k1a − k2b)θ = 0 (1) [VA-BK p.148].
    • Rotation about G: I θ̈ = k1xa·a + c1ẋa·a − k2xb·b − c2ẋb·b → I θ̈ − (c1a − c2b)ẋ + (c1a² + c2b²)θ̇ − (k1a − k2b)x + (k1a² + k2b²)θ = 0 (2). Matrix form: [[m, 0],[0, I]]{ẍ, θ̈} + [[c1 + c2, −(c1a − c2b)],[−(c1a − c2b), c1a² + c2b²]]{ẋ, θ̇} + [[k1 + k2, −(k1a − k2b)],[−(k1a − k2b), k1a² + k2b²]]{x, θ} = {0, 0} [VA-BK p.149].
  • Lagrange's method (§4.2.2): Newton's method formulates the equations in terms of physical coordinates and forces (vector quantities); it needs a free-body diagram for each mass and includes reaction and constraint forces as unknowns, so more equations than degrees of freedom are needed; for complex or high-DOF systems it loses its appeal. Lagrangian mechanics permits deriving all equations of motion from two scalar quantities, the kinetic energy T and the potential energy U; it needs no free-body diagrams, treats the system as a whole and is almost routine [VA-BK p.149].
  • Lagrange's equations: d/dt(∂T/∂q̇r) − ∂T/∂qr + ∂D/∂q̇r + ∂U/∂qr = Q_qr; T = kinetic energy of the whole system (½Jq̇r², ½mq̇r²), D = dissipative energy (½cq̇r²), U = potential energy (½kqr², mgh), qr = generalized coordinate (…, φ, θ, z, y, x), q̇r = dqr/dt, Q_qr = the external force associated with the generalized coordinate qr [VA-BK p.150].
  • Ex. (Lagrange): a disc of mass M and radius R rolling (spring k and damper c horizontally attached) with a pendulum m on a massless rod of length L hanging from the centre; generalized coordinates x(t), θ(t); Rφ = x. T = ½Mẋ² + ½Jφ̇² + ½mv² = ½Mẋ² + ½(½MR²)(ẋ/R)² + ½m(ẋ + Lθ̇)² = ½(3/2 M)ẋ² + ½m(ẋ + Lθ̇)² using v² = ẋ² + (Lθ̇)² + 2(Lθ̇)ẋ cos θ and cos θ ≈ 1 for small θ; U = ½kx² + mgL(1 − cos θ); D = ½cẋ² [VA-BK p.150–151].
    • Coordinate x: ∂T/∂ẋ = (3/2)Mẋ + m(ẋ + Lθ̇), d/dt = (3/2)Mẍ + m(ẍ + Lθ̈); ∂T/∂x = 0, ∂D/∂ẋ = cẋ, ∂U/∂x = kx, Qx = 0 → ((3/2)M + m)ẍ + mLθ̈ + cẋ + kx = 0 (1). Coordinate θ: ∂T/∂θ̇ = mL(ẋ + Lθ̇), d/dt = mLẍ + mL²θ̈; ∂D/∂θ̇ = 0, ∂T/∂θ = 0, ∂U/∂θ = mgLθ, Qθ = 0 → mLẍ + mL²θ̈ + mgLθ = 0 (2) [VA-BK p.151].
    • Matrix form as printed: [[(2/3)M + m, mL],[mL, mL²]]{ẍ, θ̈} + [[c, 0],[0, 0]]{ẋ, θ̇} + [[k, 0],[0, mgL]]{x, θ} = {0, 0} (⚠ A-F50) [VA-BK p.151].
11.3 Free undamped vibration: natural frequencies and normal modes (§4.3.1)
  • General form of the undamped 2-DOF equation of motion: M ẍ + K x = 0, two homogeneous second-order ODEs with four initial conditions x1(0), x2(0), ẋ1(0), ẋ2(0) [VA-BK p.151].
  • Synchronous motion: the whole system executes the same time motion with a fixed displacement pattern, so x2(t)/x1(t) stays constant: x1 = X1 F(t), x2 = X2 F(t), i.e. x(t) = X F(t), X = {X1, X2}ᵀ a constant vector (the displacement configuration) and F(t) the time function. Substituting: M X F̈ + K X F = 0 → KX/(MX) = −F̈/F; a function of position equal to a function of time must equal a constant, which can be shown to be real and positive, ω². So F̈ + ω²F = 0 (time-function equation) and [−ω²M + K] X = 0 (displacement-configuration equation) [VA-BK p.152–153].
  • F(t) = C sin(ωt + φ) is free (natural) motion, so ω → ωn; C, φ depend on the initial conditions and ωn on the system parameters. x(t) = X sin(ωn t + φ) [VA-BK p.153]. Substituting into the equation of motion gives [−ωn²M + K]X = 0; X = 0 is the trivial solution (rejected); the other requires |−ωn²M + K| = 0, the characteristic (frequency) equation, quadratic in ωn², with roots ωn1², ωn2² and natural frequencies ωn1, ωn2. The synchronous motion is harmonic and occurs in two ways: F1 = C1 sin(ωn1 t + φ1) and F2 = C2 sin(ωn2 t + φ2) [VA-BK p.153].
  • Substituting ωn1 and ωn2 in the configuration equation gives two configuration vectors X⁽¹⁾ (for ωn1) and X⁽²⁾ (for ωn2), the modal shapes, normal modes or eigenvectors. ωn1 with X⁽¹⁾ is the first natural mode, ωn2 with X⁽²⁾ the second; natural modes are characteristic properties, unique to the system [VA-BK p.154].
  • General motion (superposition, linear system): x(t) = A1X⁽¹⁾F1(t) + A2X⁽²⁾F2(t) = A1X⁽¹⁾ sin(ωn1 t + φ1) + A2X⁽²⁾ sin(ωn2 t + φ2). A1, A2 are the "percentage participation" of each mode; A1, A2, φ1, φ2 come from the initial conditions x(0), ẋ(0) [VA-BK p.154].
  • Ex. (two equal masses and three equal springs): m, m between walls with springs k, k, k; find the equations of motion, modal shapes, plot them, and the response for x(0) = {1, 1}ᵀ, ẋ(0) = {0, 0}ᵀ, and show the system vibrates in its first mode [VA-BK p.155].
    • m ẍ1 + 2kx1 − kx2 = 0, m ẍ2 − kx1 + 2kx2 = 0; M = diag(m, m), K = [[2k, −k],[−k, 2k]]. With x = X sin(ωn t + φ): [[−ωn²m + 2k, −k],[−k, −ωn²m + 2k]]{X1, X2} = 0 [VA-BK p.155–156].
    • Characteristic equation: (−ωn²m + 2k)² − k² = 0 → −ωn²m + 2k = ±k → ωn1 = √(k/m), ωn2 = √(3k/m) [VA-BK p.156].
    • Mode shapes: the two amplitude equations are dependent at ωn = ωn1, so only the ratio μ = X2/X1 = (−ωn²m + 2k)/k is found: μ1 = X21/X11 = 1, μ2 = X22/X12 = −1. X⁽¹⁾ = X11{1, 1}ᵀ, X⁽²⁾ = X12{1, −1}ᵀ; general solution x = A{1, μ1}ᵀ sin(ωn1 t + φ1) + B{1, μ2}ᵀ sin(ωn2 t + φ2), with normal modes X⁽¹⁾ = {1, 1}ᵀ and X⁽²⁾ = {1, −1}ᵀ [VA-BK p.156–157].
    • First mode {1, 1}: the two masses move in the same direction, the intermediate spring is not stretched and each mass obeys m ẍ + kx = 0, ωn1 = √(k/m). Second mode {1, −1}: opposite directions, a node (fixed point) at the middle of the intermediate spring, each mass obeys m ẍ + 3kx = 0, ωn2 = √(3k/m) (figures) [VA-BK p.157–158].
    • Initial conditions: 1 = A sin φ1 + B sin φ2 and 1 = A sin φ1 − B sin φ2 → sin φ1 = 1/A, B sin φ2 = 0; from the velocity conditions Aωn1 cos φ1 = 0 and Bωn2 cos φ2 = 0 → φ1 = π/2, A = 1, φ2 = 0, B = 0. So x1(t) = x2(t) = sin(ωn1 t + π/2), i.e. x = X⁽¹⁾ sin(ωn1 t + φ1): the system vibrates in its first mode [VA-BK p.158–159].
11.4 Coordinate transformation (§4.3.2)
  • For M ẍ + K x = 0 with M = [[m11, m12],[m21, m22]], K = [[k11, k12],[k21, k22]]: for certain coordinates q = {q1, q2}ᵀ, M is decoupled to M′ = diag(m′11, m′22) and K to K′ = diag(k′11, k′22), so M′q̈ + K′q = 0 gives independent equations m′11 q̈1 + k′11 q1 = 0 and m′22 q̈2 + k′22 q2 = 0. The idea is to choose new coordinates in which M and K are both diagonal, so each equation can be solved like an SDOF system [VA-BK p.159–160].
  • Static (elastic) coupling: the stiffness matrix is not diagonal, k12 = k21 ≠ 0 (the equations contain x1, x2 together). Dynamic (inertia) coupling: the mass matrix is not diagonal, m12 = m21 ≠ 0 (the equations contain ẍ1, ẍ2 together). Coupling is not an inherent property of the system but of the coordinates chosen to describe it [VA-BK p.160].
  • Natural (principal) coordinates (§4.3.2.1): a coordinate transformation that diagonalises the mass and stiffness matrices simultaneously removes static and dynamic coupling; the coordinates of the independent equations are called natural or principal coordinates, unique for a given system, and for free vibration they coincide with the time functions F1(t), F2(t). The independent equations are q̈i + ωni q_i = 0 (as printed, the square is missing, ⚠ A-F51) with qi(t) = Ci sin(ωni t + φi), i = 1 … n [VA-BK p.160–161].
  • Expansion theorem: the general motion of a free undamped linear system is the superposition of the normal modes multiplied by the natural coordinates: x(t) = X⁽¹⁾q1(t) + X⁽²⁾q2(t) + … + X⁽ⁿ⁾qn(t) = Σ X⁽ⁱ⁾qi(t). For 2 DOF: x = P q with P = [X⁽¹⁾ X⁽²⁾], the modal matrix (collection of modal shapes), which transforms motion coordinates x(t) to principal coordinates q(t) and the equations of motion to independent equations [VA-BK p.161–162].
  • Ex. (principal coordinates of the two-mass system): P = [[1, 1],[1, −1]]; x1 = q1 + q2, x2 = q1 − q2; substituting gives m q̈1 + kq1 = 0 (ωn1 = √(k/m), q1 = c1 sin(ωn1 t + φ1)) and m q̈2 + 3kq2 = 0 (ωn2 = √(3k/m), q2 = c2 sin(ωn2 t + φ2)); x = X⁽¹⁾q1 + X⁽²⁾q2 = c1X⁽¹⁾ sin(ωn1 t + φ1) + c2X⁽²⁾ sin(ωn2 t + φ2), proving that the principal coordinates are the synchronous time functions of the free undamped vibration [VA-BK p.162].
11.5 Orthogonality of normal modes (§4.3.2.2)
  • The modal vectors are orthogonal with respect to the mass and stiffness matrices: X⁽ⁱ⁾ᵀ M X⁽ʲ⁾ = m′ij δij (0 for i ≠ j, m′ii for i = j) and X⁽ⁱ⁾ᵀ K X⁽ʲ⁾ = k′ij δij (printed with q as the symbol). Consequently PᵀMP = diag(m′11, m′22) and PᵀKP = diag(k′11, k′22) [VA-BK p.163].
  • Transformation: M ẍ + K x = 0 with x = P q gives M P q̈ + K P q = 0; multiplying by Pᵀ: PᵀMP q̈ + PᵀKP q = 0, i.e. M′q̈ + K′q = 0 with M′ = diag(m′11, m′22), K′ = diag(k′11, k′22) [VA-BK p.163].
  • A coordinate transformation based on the modal vectors diagonalises the mass and stiffness matrices simultaneously and decouples the equations, so an M.D.O.F system is solved as easily as an SDOF one. A linear transformation x = Pq together with orthogonality turns the simultaneous equations M ẍ + K x = 0 into independent modal equations M′q̈ + K′q = 0; this process is known as modal analysis [VA-BK p.163–164].
11.6 Beat phenomenon (§4.3.3)
  • If two harmonic signals of equal amplitudes and nearly equal frequencies are added, the result is a harmonic function with frequency equal to the average of the two frequencies and a harmonically modulated amplitude [VA-BK p.164].
  • θ(t) = A cos ω1t + A cos ω2t with ω1 ≅ ω2. Using cos(α + β) + cos(α − β) = 2 cos α cos β with α = (ω2 − ω1)/2, β = (ω2 + ω1)/2 (so α + β = ω2, α − β = ω1): θ(t) = 2A cos((ω2 − ω1)/2 · t) cos((ω2 + ω1)/2 · t) = {2A cos((ω2 − ω1)t/2)} cos((ω2 + ω1)t/2) [VA-BK p.164–165] (⚠ A-F52).
  • Since (ω2 − ω1)/2 is very small, θ(t) behaves like 2A cos(ωav t), harmonic at the average frequency ωav = (ω2 + ω1)/2, with a slowly varying harmonic amplitude 2A cos((ω2 − ω1)t/2); ωB = (ω2 − ω1)/2 is called the modulating (beat) frequency. The modulated amplitude is the dashed envelope in the figure, and its period is T = 2π/ωB [VA-BK p.165].
  • When the two waves reinforce each other the amplitude doubles; when they cancel, the amplitude falls to zero. Many systems show beats, e.g. two identical SDOF systems joined by a weak spring (two masses with springs k, k1, k; two pendulums coupled by a spring): the resulting 2-DOF system has two natural frequencies very close in value [VA-BK p.166].
  • Famous application: the sound of a twin-engine propeller aircraft whose propellers turn at slightly different speeds; the noise grows and diminishes as the sound waves reinforce and cancel in turn [VA-BK p.166].
11.7 Example: two coupled pendulums (beats)
  • Statement: two identical pendulums (mass m, length L) joined by a spring k attached at distance a from the pivots; find θ1(t), θ2(t) for θ1(0) = θ0, θ2(0) = 0, and explain the beat phenomenon if k ≪ mgL/a² [VA-BK p.166].
  • Equations of motion from the FBDs (spring force ka(θ2 − θ1) on each): mL²θ̈1 + (mgL + ka²)θ1 − ka²θ2 = 0 and mL²θ̈2 − ka²θ1 + (mgL + ka²)θ2 = 0; matrix form M = diag(mL², mL²), K = [[mgL + ka², −ka²],[−ka², mgL + ka²]]. Assumed solution {θ1, θ2}cos(ωn t − φ); characteristic equation |mgL + ka² −ka²; −ka² mgL + ka²| (with the ωn²mL² terms) = 0 gives ωn1 = √(g/L), ωn2 = √(g/L + 2ka²/(mL²)); normal modes θ⁽¹⁾ = {1, 1}ᵀ, θ⁽²⁾ = {1, −1}ᵀ; θ(t) = c1{1, 1}ᵀ cos(ωn1 t − φ1) + c2{1, −1}ᵀ cos(ωn2 t − φ2). With θ1(0) = θ0, θ2(0) = 0: θ1(t) = ½θ0(cos ωn1 t + cos ωn2 t), θ2(t) = ½θ0(cos ωn1 t − cos ωn2 t) [VA-BK p.167].
  • With cos(α ∓ β) = cos α cos β ± sin α sin β and α = (ωn2 − ωn1)/2, β = (ωn2 + ωn1)/2: θ1(t) = θ0 cos((ωn2 − ωn1)t/2) cos((ωn2 + ωn1)t/2); θ2(t) = θ0 sin((ωn2 − ωn1)t/2) sin((ωn2 + ωn1)t/2) [VA-BK p.168] (⚠ A-F53).
  • Weak coupling: 2ka²/(mL²) ≪ g/L, i.e. k ≪ mgL/(2a²), gives nearly equal frequencies ωn1 ≅ ωn2 and beats, with the beat and average frequencies ωB = (ωn2 − ωn1)/2 and ωav = (ωn2 + ωn1)/2: θ1(t) = θ0 cos ωB t cos ωav t, θ2(t) = θ0 sin ωB t sin ωav t. The graphs (envelope period T) show a complete transfer of energy from one pendulum to the other every T/4 = π/(2ωB) [VA-BK p.168–169].
11.8 Forced harmonic vibration of a 2-DOF system (§4.4)
  • System: m1 (force F = F0 sin ωt) on spring k1 to the ground, with m2 attached to m1 by k2 (coordinates x1, x2). Equations: [[m1, 0],[0, m2]]{ẍ} + [[k1 + k2, −k2],[−k2, k2]]{x} = {F0, 0} sin ωt, i.e. M ẍ + K x = F0 sin ωt [VA-BK p.169].
  • The steady-state response to F(t) = F0 sin ωt is harmonic at the same frequency with different amplitude, x(t) = X sin ωt. Substituting: −Mω²X sin ωt + KX sin ωt = F0 sin ωt → (K − ω²M)X = F0, i.e. [[k1 + k2 − m1ω², −k2],[−k2, k2 − m2ω²]]{X1, X2} = {F0, 0} [VA-BK p.169–170].
  • Cramer's rule: X1 = F0(k2 − m2ω²)/Δ, X2 = F0k2/Δ, with the determinant Δ = (k1 + k2 − m1ω²)(k2 − m2ω²) − k2². Δ = 0 is the characteristic equation, whose solutions ω = ωn1, ωn2 [VA-BK p.170].
  • Dividing by k1k2 (ω11 = √(k1/m1), ω22 = √(k2/m2)): X1 = (F0/k1)(1 − (ω/ω22)²)/[(1 + k2/k1 − (ω/ω11)²)(1 − (ω/ω22)²) − k2/k1], X2 = (F0/k1)/[(1 + k2/k1 − (ω/ω11)²)(1 − (ω/ω22)²) − k2/k1]; equivalently X1k1/F0 and X2k1/F0 with the same bracket [VA-BK p.170–171].
  • Figures: X1k1/F0 and X2k1/F0 against ω/ω22 (two resonances; with μ = 0.20 and ω22/ω11 = 1.0 the resonances are at ω/ω22 = 0.8 and 1.25 and the X1 curve touches zero at ω/ω22 = 1) [VA-BK p.171].
  • Important note: the amplitudes of the two masses change with the exciting frequency so that the amplitude of m1 tends to zero at ω/ω22 = 1 (ω = ω22). Thus the vibration of m1 can be eliminated if the natural frequency ω22 of m2 (as if it vibrated alone) equals the exciting frequency ω; this has an important application called the vibration absorber (see §12) [VA-BK p.171].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

11.1 2-DOF systems (book)
  • Two-DOF systems require two independent coordinates to describe their motion (examples Fig. 1.25: two masses in series with springs k1, k2; double pendulum l1, l2 with θ1, θ2) [VB-AM p.43].
  • Damped 2-DOF (Fig. 1.26, walls–k1,c1–m1–k2,c2–m2–k3,c3–wall), coordinates x1, x2 from equilibrium, forces F1(t), F2(t). Newton: m1ẍ1 + (c1 + c2)ẋ1 − c2ẋ2 + (k1 + k2)x1 − k2x2 = F1(t); m2ẍ2 − c2ẋ1 + (c2 + c3)ẋ2 − k2x1 + (k2 + k3)x2 = F2(t); motion of m1 influences m2 and vice versa [VB-AM p.44].
  • Free vibration: x1 = X1 cos(ωt + φ), x2 = X2 cos(ωt + φ); characteristic determinant det[{−m1ω² + (k1 + k2)}, −k2; −k2, {m2ω² + (k2 + k3)}] = 0 → frequency (characteristic) equation (m1m2)ω⁴ − {(k1 + k2)m2 + (k2 + k3)m1}ω² + {(k1 + k2)(k2 + k3) − k2²} = 0 [VB-AM p.44] (⚠ B-F13).
  • ω1², ω2² = ½{[(k1 + k2)m2 + (k2 + k3)m1]/(m1m2)} ∓ ½[{[(k1 + k2)m2 + (k2 + k3)m1]/(m1m2)}² − 4{[(k1 + k2)(k2 + k3) − k2²]/(m1m2)}]^½; ω1, ω2 = natural frequencies [VB-AM p.44].
  • Amplitude ratios: r1 = X2(1)/X1(1) = [−m1ω1² + (k1 + k2)]/k2 = k2/[−m2ω1² + (k2 + k3)]; r2 = X2(2)/X1(2) = [−m1ω2² + (k1 + k2)]/k2 = k2/[−m2ω2² + (k2 + k3)] [VB-AM p.45].
  • Normal modes {X(1)} = {X1(1), r1X1(1)}, {X(2)} = {X1(2), r2X1(2)} = modal vectors [VB-AM p.45].
  • Torsional 2-DOF: two discs on a shaft in frictionless end bearings (Fig. 1.27: k1–I1–k2–I2–k3): I1θ̈1 + (k1 + k2)θ1 − k2θ2 = 0; I2θ̈2 + (k2 + k3)θ2 − k2θ1 = 0; ki = GiJi/li (Gi modulus of rigidity, Ji polar moment of inertia, li length); matrix form [I1 0; 0 I2]{θ̈} + [k1 + k2, −k2; −k2, k2 + k3]{θ} = {0} [VB-AM p.45–46].
  • Coupling = connection between the equations of motion. An n-DOF system needs n independent coordinates; any such set = generalized coordinates. Non-diagonal [M] → mass (dynamic) coupling; non-diagonal [K] → stiffness (static) coupling. Coordinates with neither coupling decouple the equations → principal (normal) coordinates [VB-AM p.46].
  • Undamped forced 2-DOF with F1 sin ωt, F2 sin ωt: X1 = (a22F1 − a12F2)/(a11a22 − a12a21), X2 = (a11F2 − a21F1)/(a11a22 − a12a21); the denominator defines ω1, ω2; because the motions are coupled, each mass shows resonance even if the force acts on one mass only [VB-AM p.46].
  • Damped forced 2-DOF: solved by mechanical impedance Zrs(iω) = −ω²mrs + iωcrs + krs (r, s = 1, 2) [VB-AM p.46].
  • Orthogonality: ω1²[M]X(1) = [K]X(1), ω2²[M]X(2) = [K]X(2) → for ω1 ≠ ω2, [X(2)]ᵀ[M]X(1) = 0; useful to check the accuracy of computed modes [VB-AM p.46–47].
11.2 Multi-DOF extension (book)
  • MDOF system: motion described by more than one generalized coordinate; n-DOF needs n coordinates, is governed by n coupled ODEs and has n natural frequencies (examples Fig. 1.28: 3-DOF torsional, 4-DOF spring–mass). Solution = homogeneous (free-vibration properties) + particular (forced response) [VB-AM p.47].
  • Newton on mass mi (Fig. 1.29): mi ẍi − ci+1 ẋi+1 + (ci + ci+1)ẋi − ci ẋi−1 − ki+1 xi+1 + (ki + ki+1)xi − ki xi−1 = 0 → [M]ẍ + [C]ẋ + [K]x = 0; here [M] is diagonal, but not necessarily for other coordinates [VB-AM p.47–48].
  • Stiffness influence coefficient kij: force required at xi to produce unit displacement uj = 1 at xj with zero displacement at all other points; Fi = Σj kij uj [VB-AM p.48].
  • Flexibility influence coefficient aij: displacement at xi due to a unit force Fj = 1 at xj; ui = Σj aij Fj; units m/N. For an SDOF with one spring, stiffness coefficient = spring constant, flexibility = its reciprocal [VB-AM p.48].
  • [A] = [aij] flexibility matrix, [K] = [kij] stiffness matrix, inverses of one another; stiffness coefficients are often easier to evaluate. Singular [K] → no flexibility matrix → rigid-body motion possible (supports do not fully restrain the system) [VB-AM p.48–49].
  • Inertia influence coefficients mij (elements of [M]): T = ½ẋᵀ[M]ẋ; obtained from impulse–momentum: m1j…mnj = impulses at points 1…n producing unit velocity at point j and zero elsewhere; F̃ = [M]Ẋ (impulse and velocity vectors n×1) [VB-AM p.49].
  • Free undamped n-DOF: [M]ẍ + [K]x = 0 ([M], [K] symmetric n×n); free vibration initiated by initial PE or KE; normal-mode solution x = X e^(iωt), X = mode shape; each natural frequency has at least one mode shape; general solution = superposition of modes [VB-AM p.49].
  • Eigenvalue equation −ω²[M]X + [K]X = 0; non-trivial only if det([M]⁻¹[K] − ω²I) = 0 (characteristic equation): ω² is an eigenvalue of [M]⁻¹[K]; the positive root is the natural frequency, the eigenvector the mode shape [VB-AM p.49] (⚠ B-F14).
  • Symmetric matrices → real roots; n real natural frequencies ω1 ≤ ω2 ≤ … ≤ ωn; [M]⁻¹[K]Xi = ωi²Xi; mode shape unique only to a multiplicative constant (normalization schemes); complexity grows exponentially with DOF, so numerical methods are used for large systems [VB-AM p.50].
  • Mode orthogonality: {X}rᵀ[M]{X}s = 0 and {X}rᵀ[K]{X}s = 0 (r ≠ s); expanded ΣΣ mij xi^r xj^s = 0; holds for any two modes; convenient normalization: kinetic-energy scalar product of a mode with itself = 1 [VB-AM p.50].
  • Response to initial conditions: x(t) = Σr [UrᵀM x(0) cos ωr t + (1/ωr) UrᵀM ẋ(0) sin ωr t] Ur; each mode can be excited independently [VB-AM p.51].
  • Damped free MDOF: characteristic polynomial has complex-conjugate roots and conjugate eigenvectors; modal analysis applies only to undamped systems or damping equivalent to mass/stiffness matrices; damping sometimes ignored in forced response [VB-AM p.51].
  • Proportional damping [C] = α[K] + β[M]: [M]Ẍ + (α[K] + β[M])Ẋ + [K]X = 0; X = Σ pi Ui; [U]ᵀ[M][U] = [I], [U]ᵀ[K][U] = [diag ω²] = [Ω]; decoupled p̈i + (αωi² + β)ṗi + ωi²pi = 0; modal damping ratio ξi = ½(αωi + β/ωi); for ξi < 1: pi(t) = Ai e^(−ξiωi t) sin(ωi√(1 − ξi²) t − φi) [VB-AM p.51–52].
  • General viscous damping: principal coordinates do not uncouple; reformulate as 2n first-order equations [M̃]ẏ + [K̃]y = 0, [M̃] = [O M; M C], [K̃] = [−M O; O K], y = {Ẋ; X}; solution y = φ e^(−γt), γ = complex-conjugate eigenvalues of [M̃]⁻¹[K̃] [VB-AM p.52].
  • Harmonic excitation (undamped, same phase): [M]ẍ + [K]x = F sin ωt; x = U sin ωt; printed result U = (−ω²[M] + iω[C] + [K])⁻¹F; the Laplace transform may be used instead [VB-AM p.52] (⚠ B-F15).
  • Modal analysis (undamped forced) MẌ + KX = F: Σ p̈i(XjMXi) + Σ pi(XjKXi) = XjF → p̈j + ωj²pj = gj(t), gj = XjF (normalized modes); zero initial conditions: pi(t) = (1/ωi)∫0^t gi(τ) sin[ωi(t − τ)]dτ. Proportional damping: p̈i + 2ξiωiṗi + ωi²pi = gi(t), pi(t) = (1/ωdi)∫0^t gi(τ)e^(−ξiωi(t−τ)) sin ωdi(t − τ)dτ, printed "1/ωdi = ωi√(1 − ξi²)" [VB-AM p.52–53] (⚠ B-F16).
11.3 Rao, Chapter 5 "Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems" (VB-2D, book pp.467–500)
  • Source note: the file is Ch. 5 of a Mechanical Vibrations textbook (S. S. Rao style: Learning Objectives, numbered Examples, "Approach/Solution" layout), pages 467–500 of the book (PDF p.1 = book p.467; PDF p.34 = book p.500); it stops in the first lines of §5.8 [VB-2D p.1, 34].
  • Chapter opener: Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782), Swiss, professor of mathematics at Saint Petersburg in 1725 after a doctorate in medicine (thesis on the action of lungs), later professor of anatomy and botany at Basel; developed hydrostatics/hydrodynamics (Bernoulli's theorem), derived the equation of motion for vibration of beams (Euler–Bernoulli theory), studied vibrating strings, and was the first to propose the principle of superposition of harmonics in free vibration [VB-2D p.1].
  • Chapter outline: 5.1 Introduction; 5.2 Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration; 5.3 Free-Vibration Analysis of an Undamped System; 5.4 Torsional System; 5.5 Coordinate Coupling and Principal Coordinates; 5.6 Forced-Vibration Analysis; 5.7 Semidefinite Systems; 5.8 Self-Excitation and Stability Analysis; 5.9 Transfer-Function Approach; 5.10 Solutions Using Laplace Transform; 5.11 Solutions Using Frequency Transfer Functions; 5.12 Examples Using MATLAB; Chapter Summary; References; Review Questions; Problems; Design Projects (only §5.1–5.7 and the start of §5.8 are in the file) [VB-2D p.1].
  • Chapter summary of contents: coupled equations of motion by Newton's second law, matrix form (mass, damping, stiffness matrices); harmonic motion of both masses gives eigenvalues (natural frequencies), modal vectors and the free-vibration solution of the undamped system with initial conditions; torsional systems analogously; coordinate coupling, generalized and principal coordinates; forced vibration in complex form with the impedance matrix; semidefinite (unrestrained, degenerate) systems; self-excitation and stability with the Routh–Hurwitz criterion for any n-DOF system; transfer-function approach, Laplace transform and frequency transfer functions; MATLAB solutions [VB-2D p.1–2].
  • Learning objectives: formulate the equations of motion of 2-DOF systems; identify the mass, damping and stiffness matrices; compute eigenvalues (natural frequencies) and modal vectors; determine the free-vibration solution from known initial conditions; understand coordinate coupling and principal coordinates; determine forced-vibration solutions under harmonic forces; understand self-excitation and stability; use the Laplace transform approach; solve free and forced 2-DOF problems using MATLAB [VB-2D p.2].
11.3.1 Introduction (§5.1)
  • Systems that require two independent coordinates to describe their motion are 2-DOF systems; the chapter is a simple introduction to systems with arbitrarily many DOF (Chapter 6 of the book) [VB-2D p.2].
  • Examples (all modelled as rigid bodies with two motion types): (i) lathe (Fig. 5.1): bed as elastic beam on short elastic columns with headstock and tailstock as lumped masses; simplified as a rigid body of mass m and moment of inertia J0 about the C.G. on springs k1 and k2 (distances l1, l2 from A and B); coordinates x(t) (vertical displacement of the C.G.) and θ(t) (rotation), or x1(t), x2(t) of points A and B; a particle would not need the rotation coordinate [VB-2D p.2–3]. (ii) automobile (Fig. 5.2): body idealised as a bar of mass m and J0 on rear and front suspensions k1 and k2; x(t) = vertical displacement of the C.G., θ(t) = pitching, or x1, x2 of A and B [VB-2D p.3–4]. (iii) multistorey building under an earthquake (Fig. 5.3): rigid bar of mass m and J0 with foundation/soil approximated by a linear spring k and a torsional spring kt; coordinates horizontal base motion x(t) and angular motion θ(t) about the point O [VB-2D p.3, 5]. (iv) packaged instrument (Fig. 5.4): mass m on springs in the x and y directions, one point mass with two DOF (translations along x and y) [VB-2D p.3–4].
  • Rule: number of degrees of freedom of the system = number of masses in the system × number of possible types of motion of each mass [VB-2D p.4].
  • A 2-DOF system has two equations of motion, one per DOF, generally coupled (each involves all coordinates). A harmonic solution for each coordinate gives a frequency equation with two natural frequencies. With suitable initial excitation the system vibrates at one natural frequency; the amplitudes of the two coordinates are then related in a specific manner, the configuration being a normal mode (principal mode, natural mode); there are two normal modes for the two natural frequencies [VB-2D p.4–5].
  • Arbitrary initial excitation gives free vibration that is a superposition of the two normal modes; under an external harmonic force the forced vibration takes place at the forcing frequency, and resonance (maximum amplitudes) occurs when the forcing frequency equals one of the natural frequencies [VB-2D p.5–6].
  • Any set of independent coordinates (lengths, angles, other physical parameters) specifying the configuration = generalized coordinates. Equations are generally coupled, but a particular set exists in which each equation contains only one coordinate (uncoupled, solvable independently): principal coordinates [VB-2D p.6].
11.3.2 Equations of motion for forced vibration (§5.2)
  • Viscously damped 2-DOF spring–mass system (Fig. 5.5(a): wall–k1,c1–m1–k2,c2–m2–k3,c3–wall, coordinates x1(t), x2(t) from the respective equilibrium positions, forces F1(t), F2(t); Fig. 5.5(b) free-body diagrams: k1x1, c1ẋ1; k2(x2 − x1) spring under tension for +(x2 − x1), c2(ẋ2 − ẋ1); k3x2, c3ẋ2). Newton's second law: m1ẍ1 + (c1 + c2)ẋ1 − c2ẋ2 + (k1 + k2)x1 − k2x2 = f1 (5.1); m2ẍ2 − c2ẋ1 + (c2 + c3)ẋ2 − k2x1 + (k2 + k3)x2 = f2 (5.2) [VB-2D p.6].
  • (5.1) contains x2 terms (−c2ẋ2, −k2x2) and (5.2) contains x1 terms, so they are two coupled second-order ODEs: the motion of m1 influences m2 and vice versa. Matrix form [m]ẍ + [c]ẋ + [k]x = f (5.3), with [m] = [m1 0; 0 m2], [c] = [c1 + c2, −c2; −c2, c2 + c3], [k] = [k1 + k2, −k2; −k2, k2 + k3], x = {x1; x2}, f = {f1; f2}; all matrices 2 × 2 and symmetric ([m]ᵀ = [m], [c]ᵀ = [c], [k]ᵀ = [k]) [VB-2D p.6–7].
  • The equations become uncoupled only when c2 = k2 = 0 (masses not physically connected; diagonal matrices). The solution involves four integration constants; usually x1(0), ẋ1(0), x2(0), ẋ2(0) are specified. Free vibration is considered first [VB-2D p.7].
11.3.3 Free vibration of an undamped system (§5.3)
  • With f1 = f2 = 0 and c1 = c2 = c3 = 0: m1ẍ1 + (k1 + k2)x1 − k2x2 = 0 (5.4); m2ẍ2 − k2x1 + (k2 + k3)x2 = 0 (5.5). Assume the same frequency ω and phase φ for both masses: xi = Xi cos(ωt + φ) (5.6); substituting: [−m1ω² + (k1 + k2)]X1 − k2X2 = 0; −k2X1 + [−m2ω² + (k2 + k3)]X2 = 0 (5.8). X1 = X2 = 0 is the trivial solution (no vibration); a non-trivial solution requires the determinant of the coefficients to be zero [VB-2D p.8].
  • Frequency (characteristic) equation: (m1m2)ω⁴ − {(k1 + k2)m2 + (k2 + k3)m1}ω² + {(k1 + k2)(k2 + k3) − k2²} = 0 (5.9) [VB-2D p.8].
  • Roots ω1², ω2² = ½{[(k1 + k2)m2 + (k2 + k3)m1]/(m1m2)} ∓ [¼{[(k1 + k2)m2 + (k2 + k3)m1]/(m1m2)}² − {[(k1 + k2)(k2 + k3) − k2²]/(m1m2)}]^½, equivalently ½{…} ∓ ½[{…}² − 4{…}]^½ as printed (5.10) [VB-2D p.9].
  • X1, X2 depend on ω; for ω1, ω2 denote X1(1), X2(1), X1(2), X2(2); only the ratios r1 = X2(1)/X1(1), r2 = X2(2)/X1(2) can be found (homogeneous equations): ri = [−m1ωi² + (k1 + k2)]/k2 = k2/[−m2ωi² + (k2 + k3)] (5.11), the two expressions being identical [VB-2D p.9].
  • Normal modes (modal vectors): X⃗(1) = {X1(1); r1X1(1)}, X⃗(2) = {X1(2); r2X1(2)} (5.12). Free-vibration solution in each mode: x⃗(1)(t) = {X1(1) cos(ω1t + φ1); r1X1(1) cos(ω1t + φ1)} = first mode; x⃗(2)(t) = {X1(2) cos(ω2t + φ2); r2X1(2) cos(ω2t + φ2)} = second mode (5.13) [VB-2D p.9–10].
  • Initial conditions: each equation is second order in time, so two initial conditions per mass. The system vibrates in its i-th normal mode if x1(0) = X1(i) (some constant), ẋ1(0) = 0, x2(0) = riX1(i), ẋ2(0) = 0. For general initial conditions both modes are excited and x⃗(t) = c1x⃗(1)(t) + c2x⃗(2)(t) (5.14); c1 = c2 = 1 with no loss of generality: x1(t) = X1(1) cos(ω1t + φ1) + X1(2) cos(ω2t + φ2), x2(t) = r1X1(1) cos(ω1t + φ1) + r2X1(2) cos(ω2t + φ2) (5.15); unknowns X1(1), X1(2), φ1, φ2 from x1(0), ẋ1(0), x2(0), ẋ2(0) (5.16) [VB-2D p.10].
  • Substitution gives x1(0) = X1(1) cos φ1 + X1(2) cos φ2; ẋ1(0) = −ω1X1(1) sin φ1 − ω2X1(2) sin φ2; x2(0) = r1X1(1) cos φ1 + r2X1(2) cos φ2; ẋ2(0) = −ω1r1X1(1) sin φ1 − ω2r2X1(2) sin φ2 (5.17): four algebraic equations in X1(1) cos φ1, X1(2) cos φ2, X1(1) sin φ1, X1(2) sin φ2 [VB-2D p.10–11].
  • Solution (5.18): X1(1) cos φ1 = (r2x1(0) − x2(0))/(r2 − r1); X1(2) cos φ2 = (−r1x1(0) + x2(0))/(r2 − r1); X1(1) sin φ1 = (−r2ẋ1(0) + ẋ2(0))/(ω1(r2 − r1)); X1(2) sin φ2 = (r1ẋ1(0) − ẋ2(0))/(ω2(r2 − r1)); X1(1) = [(X1(1)cos φ1)² + (X1(1) sin φ1)²]^½ = [1/(r2 − r1)]{[r2x1(0) − x2(0)]² + [(−r2ẋ1(0) + ẋ2(0))/ω1]²}^½; X1(2) = [1/(r2 − r1)]{[−r1x1(0) + x2(0)]² + [(r1ẋ1(0) − ẋ2(0))/ω2]²}^½; φ1 = tan⁻¹{[−r2ẋ1(0) + ẋ2(0)]/(ω1[r2x1(0) − x2(0)])}; φ2 = tan⁻¹{[r1ẋ1(0) − ẋ2(0)]/(ω2[−r1x1(0) + x2(0)])} [VB-2D p.11].
  • Example 5.1 (frequencies of a spring–mass system, Fig. 5.6, vertical motion only: m1 = m2 = m, k1 = k, k2 = nk, k3 = k, take n = 1, i.e. k1 = k2 = k3 = k): equations mẍ1 + 2kx1 − kx2 = 0; mẍ2 − kx1 + 2kx2 = 0 (E.1); xi = Xi cos(ωt + φ) (E.2); determinant → m²ω⁴ − 4kmω² + 3k² = 0 (E.3); ω1 = [(4km − (16k²m² − 12m²k²)^½)/(2m²)]^½ = √(k/m), ω2 = [(4km + (16k²m² − 12m²k²)^½)/(2m²)]^½ = √(3k/m) (E.4–E.5); amplitude ratios r1 = X2(1)/X1(1) = [−mω1² + 2k]/k = k/[−mω1² + 2k] = 1 (E.6), r2 = [−mω2² + 2k]/k = −1 (E.7) [VB-2D p.11–12].
    • Natural modes (E.8–E.9): first mode x⃗(1)(t) = {X1(1) cos(√(k/m)t + φ1); X1(1) cos(√(k/m)t + φ1)}, second mode x⃗(2)(t) = {X1(2) cos(√(3k/m)t + φ2); −X1(2) cos(√(3k/m)t + φ2)}. In the first mode the two masses have the same amplitude and move in phase (middle spring length constant, Fig. 5.7(a)); in the second mode the displacements are equal and opposite (180° out of phase), the mid-point of the middle spring stays stationary for all time: a node (Fig. 5.7(b)). General solution: x1(t) = X1(1) cos(√(k/m)t + φ1) + X1(2) cos(√(3k/m)t + φ2); x2(t) = X1(1) cos(√(k/m)t + φ1) − X1(2) cos(√(3k/m)t + φ2) (E.10) [VB-2D p.12–13].
    • Note: computing natural frequencies and mode shapes is lengthy and tedious; computer programs are convenient for multi-DOF systems (§5.12) [VB-2D p.14].
  • Example 5.2 (initial conditions that excite a specific mode of the system of Fig. 5.6): with r1 = 1, r2 = −1 the general solution reduces to Eq. (E.10). From (5.18): X1(1) = −½{[x1(0) + x2(0)]² + (m/k)[ẋ1(0) + ẋ2(0)]²}^½ (E.2); X1(2) = −½{[−x1(0) + x2(0)]² + (m/3k)[ẋ1(0) − ẋ2(0)]²}^½ (E.3); φ1 = tan⁻¹{−√m[ẋ1(0) + ẋ2(0)]/(√k[x1(0) + x2(0)])} (E.4); φ2 = tan⁻¹{√m[ẋ1(0) − ẋ2(0)]/(√(3k)[−x1(0) + x2(0)])} (E.5) [VB-2D p.14].
    • (a) First mode only if X1(2) = 0, which requires (E.3) x1(0) = x2(0) and ẋ1(0) = ẋ2(0) (E.7). (b) Second mode only if X1(1) = 0, requiring (E.2) x1(0) = −x2(0) and ẋ1(0) = −ẋ2(0) (E.9) [VB-2D p.14–15].
  • Example 5.3 (free-vibration response of the system of Fig. 5.5(a) with k1 = 30, k2 = 5, k3 = 0, m1 = 10, m2 = 1, c1 = c2 = c3 = 0; initial conditions x1(0) = 1, ẋ1(0) = x2(0) = ẋ2(0) = 0): the eigenproblem [−10ω² + 35, −5; −5, −ω² + 5]{X1; X2} = 0 (E.1); frequency equation 10ω⁴ − 85ω² + 150 = 0 (E.2); ω1² = 2.5, ω2² = 6.0, ω1 = 1.5811, ω2 = 2.4495 (E.3); X2(1) = 2X1(1), X2(2) = −5X1(2); modes X⃗(1) = {1; 2}X1(1), X⃗(2) = {1; −5}X1(2) (E.4–E.5); x1(t) = X1(1) cos(1.5811t + φ1) + X1(2) cos(2.4495t + φ2), x2(t) = 2X1(1) cos(1.5811t + φ1) − 5X1(2) cos(2.4495t + φ2) (E.6–E.7) [VB-2D p.15–16].
    • Initial conditions: 1 = X1(1) cos φ1 + X1(2) cos φ2 (E.8); 0 = 2X1(1) cos φ1 − 5X1(2) cos φ2 (E.9); 0 = −1.5811X1(1) sin φ1 − 2.4495X1(2) sin φ2 (E.10); ẋ2(0) = −3.1622X1(1) sin φ1 + 12.2475X1(2) sin φ2 (E.11, printed without "sin φ1" on the first term); solution X1(1) cos φ1 = 5/7, X1(2) cos φ2 = 2/7 (E.12); X1(1) sin φ1 = 0, X1(2) sin φ2 = 0 (E.13); X1(1) = 5/7, X1(2) = 2/7, φ1 = φ2 = 0 (E.14). Response: x1(t) = (5/7) cos 1.5811t + (2/7) cos 2.4495t; x2(t) = (10/7) cos 1.5811t − (10/7) cos 2.4495t (E.15–E.16); plotted in Example 5.17 (not in this file) [VB-2D p.16] (⚠ B-F67).
11.3.4 Torsional system (§5.4)
  • Two discs on a shaft (Fig. 5.8: torsional spring constants kt1, kt2, kt3 of the three shaft segments, inertias J1, J2, applied torques Mt1, Mt2, angles θ1, θ2): J1θ̈1 = −kt1θ1 + kt2(θ2 − θ1) + Mt1; J2θ̈2 = −kt2(θ2 − θ1) − kt3θ2 + Mt2 → J1θ̈1 + (kt1 + kt2)θ1 − kt2θ2 = Mt1; J2θ̈2 − kt2θ1 + (kt2 + kt3)θ2 = Mt2 (5.19); free vibration (5.20) with zero torques. Eq. (5.20) is obtained from (5.4)–(5.5) by substituting θ1, θ2, J1, J2, kt1, kt2, kt3 for x1, x2, m1, m2, k1, k2, k3, so the analysis of §5.3 applies with these substitutions [VB-2D p.17].
  • Example 5.4 (natural frequencies of the torsional system of Fig. 5.9: disc J1 = J0 below shaft kt1 from the ceiling, disc J2 = 2J0 below shaft kt2; kt1 = kt2 = kt, kt3 = 0): J0θ̈1 + 2ktθ1 − ktθ2 = 0; 2J0θ̈2 − ktθ1 + ktθ2 = 0 (E.1); θi = Θi cos(ωt + φ) (E.2); frequency equation 2ω⁴J0² − 5ω²J0kt + kt² = 0 (E.3); ω1 = √{(kt/4J0)(5 − √17)}, ω2 = √{(kt/4J0)(5 + √17)} (E.4); r1 = Θ2(1)/Θ1(1) = 2 − (5 − √17)/4, r2 = Θ2(2)/Θ1(2) = 2 − (5 + √17)/4 (E.5); the results also follow from Eqs (5.10)–(5.11) with k1 = kt1 = kt, k2 = kt2 = kt, m1 = J1 = J0, m2 = J2 = 2J0, k3 = 0 [VB-2D p.18].
    • Note: the two natural frequencies of a 2-DOF system are not equal to either natural frequency of the two SDOF systems built from the same components; here the SDOF systems kt1–J1 (ω̂1 = √(kt1/J1) = √(kt/J0)) and kt2–J2 (ω̂2 = √(kt2/J2) = (1/√2)√(kt/J0)) differ from ω1 and ω2 [VB-2D p.19].
  • Example 5.5 (natural frequencies of a marine engine propeller, Fig. 5.10(a): flywheel, engine, gear 1 (40 teeth) and gear 2 (20 teeth), propeller; shaft 1 steel, dia. 0.1 m, length 0.8 m; shaft 2 steel, dia. 0.15 m, length 1.0 m): mass moments of inertia (kg·m²) flywheel 9000, engine 1000, gear 1 250, gear 2 150, propeller 2000; find the torsional natural frequencies and mode shapes [VB-2D p.19–20].
    • Approach and assumptions: reduce all rotors to one shaft speed and use a 2-DOF model; (1) the flywheel is taken stationary (fixed) because its inertia is very large compared with the others; (2) the engine and gears are replaced by a single equivalent rotor. Gears with 40 and 20 teeth: shaft 2 rotates at twice the speed of shaft 1; (JG2)eq = (2)²(150) = 600 kg·m²; (JP)eq = (2)²(2000) = 8000 kg·m²; J1 = JE + JG1 + (JG2)eq = 1000 + 250 + 600 = 1850 kg·m² (engine and gears close together); J2 = 8000 kg·m² [VB-2D p.19–21].
    • Stiffnesses (G = 80 × 10⁹ N/m² for steel): kt1 = GJ01/l1 = G(πd⁴/32)/l1 = (80 × 10⁹)(π)(0.10)⁴/[(0.8)(32)] = 981,750.0 N·m/rad; kt2 = (80 × 10⁹)(π)(0.15)⁴/[(1.0)(32)] = 3,976,087.5 N·m/rad; the propeller is treated as a rotor at the end of shaft 2 (Fig. 5.10(b): kt1–J1–kt2–J2, θ1, θ2) [VB-2D p.19–20] (⚠ B-F68).
    • Frequencies from (5.10) with k3 = 0, k1 = kt1, k2 = kt2, m1 = J1, m2 = J2: ω1², ω2² = ½{[(kt1 + kt2)J2 + kt2J1]/(J1J2)} ∓ [¼{…}² − (kt1kt2)/(J1J2)]^½ = (kt1 + kt2)/(2J1) + kt2/(2J2) ∓ {[(kt1 + kt2)/(2J1) + kt2/(2J2)]² − kt1kt2/(J1J2)}^½, as (E.1) [VB-2D p.20–21]. Numbers: (kt1 + kt2)/(2J1) + kt2/(2J2) = (98.1750 + 397.6087) × 10⁴/(2 × 1850) + 397.6087 × 10⁴/(2 × 8000) = 1588.46; kt1kt2/(J1J2) = (98.1750 × 10⁴)(397.6087 × 10⁴)/[(1850)(8000)] = 26.3750 × 10⁴; ω², = 1588.46 ± [(1588.46)² − 26.3750 × 10⁴]^½ = 1588.46 ± 1503.1483 → ω1² = 85.3117, ω1 = 9.2364 rad/s; ω2² = 3091.6083, ω2 = 55.6022 rad/s [VB-2D p.21].
    • Mode shapes from (5.11): r1 = [−J1ω1² + (kt1 + kt2)]/kt2 = [−(1850)(85.3117) + 495.7837 × 10⁴]/(397.6087 × 10⁴) = 1.2072; r2 = [−(1850)(3091.6083) + 495.7837 × 10⁴]/(397.6087 × 10⁴) = −0.1916; modal vectors {Θ1; Θ2}(1) = {1; 1.2072}, {Θ1; Θ2}(2) = {1; −0.1916} [VB-2D p.21–22].
11.3.5 Coordinate coupling and principal coordinates (§5.5)
  • An n-DOF system needs n independent coordinates, usually geometrical quantities measured from the equilibrium position, but other sets are possible (origin away from equilibrium etc.); each such set of n coordinates = generalized coordinates [VB-2D p.22].
  • Lathe (Fig. 5.11: bed replaced by an elastic beam on short elastic columns with headstock and tailstock as lumped masses) can use: (1) deflections x1(t), x2(t) of the two ends of AB; (2) deflection x(t) of the C.G. and rotation θ(t); (3) deflection x1(t) of end A and rotation θ(t); (4) deflection y(t) of a point P located a distance e to the left of the C.G. and rotation θ(t) (Fig. 5.12) [VB-2D p.22–23].
  • Using x(t), θ(t) (Fig. 5.12(a): spring forces k1(x − l1θ), k2(x + l2θ)): mẍ = −k1(x − l1θ) − k2(x + l2θ) (5.21); J0θ̈ = k1(x − l1θ)l1 − k2(x + l2θ)l2 (5.22); matrix form [m 0; 0 J0]{ẍ; θ̈} + [(k1 + k2), −(k1l1 − k2l2); −(k1l1 − k2l2), (k1l1² + k2l2²)]{x; θ} = {0; 0} (5.23) [VB-2D p.23].
  • The equations are independent if the coupling term (k1l1 − k2l2) = 0, i.e. k1l1 = k2l2. Otherwise the motion of the lathe is both translational and rotational when a displacement or torque is applied through the C.G.: elastic or static coupling [VB-2D p.24].
  • Using y(t), θ(t) (Fig. 5.12(b)): mÿ = −k1(y − l1θ) − k2(y + l2θ) − meθ̈; Jpθ̈ = k1(y − l1θ)l1 − k2(y + l2θ)l2 − meÿ (5.24); matrix form [m, me; me, Jp]{ÿ; θ̈} + [(k1 + k2), (k2l2 − k1l1); (−k1l1 + k2l2), (k1l1² + k2l2²)]{y; θ} = {0; 0} (5.25). Both equations contain y and θ: coupled, with static (elastic) as well as dynamic (mass) coupling; if k1l1 = k2l2 the system has dynamic (inertia) coupling only: an up-and-down y motion makes the inertia force mÿ act through the C.G. and induces θ motion via the moment mÿe; similarly θ motion induces y motion by the force meθ̈ [VB-2D p.24].
  • General damped 2-DOF equation [m11 m12; m12 m22]{ẍ1; ẍ2} + [c11 c12; c12 c22]{ẋ1; ẋ2} + [k11 k12; k12 k22]{x1; x2} = {0; 0} (5.26). Stiffness matrix not diagonal → elastic (static) coupling; damping matrix not diagonal → damping (velocity) coupling; mass matrix not diagonal → mass (inertial) coupling; velocity and mass coupling together are dynamic coupling [VB-2D p.24].
  • The system vibrates in its own natural way regardless of the coordinates used (choice is a convenience); the nature of the coupling depends on the coordinates used and is not an inherent property of the system; coordinates q1(t), q2(t) exist that uncouple the equations both statically and dynamically: principal (natural) coordinates, whose uncoupled equations are solved independently [VB-2D p.24–25].
  • Example 5.6 (principal coordinates of the system of Fig. 5.6): define q1(t) = B1 cos(√(k/m)t + φ1), q2(t) = B2 cos(√(3k/m)t + φ2) (E.2) (B1 = X1(1), B2 = X1(2)); their equations q̈1 + (k/m)q1 = 0, q̈2 + (3k/m)q2 = 0 (E.3) (footnote: q = B cos(ωt + φ) satisfies q̈ + ω²q = 0) have natural frequencies √(k/m), √(3k/m) with neither static nor dynamic coupling; x1 = q1 + q2, x2 = q1 − q2 (E.4); hence q1(t) = ½[x1(t) + x2(t)], q2(t) = ½[x1(t) − x2(t)] (E.5) [VB-2D p.25–26].
  • Example 5.7 (pitch and bounce frequencies and oscillation centres (nodes) of an automobile, Fig. 5.13): m = 1000 kg, radius of gyration r = 0.9 m, front axle to C.G. l1 = 1.0 m, rear axle to C.G. l2 = 1.5 m, front spring kf = 18 kN/m, rear spring kr = 22 kN/m [VB-2D p.26].
    • With x, θ as coordinates Eq. (5.23) applies with k1 = kf, k2 = kr, J0 = mr²; free vibration x = X cos(ωt + φ), θ = Θ cos(ωt + φ) (E.1); [(−mω² + kf + kr), (−kfl1 + krl2); (−kfl1 + krl2), (−J0ω² + kfl1² + krl2²)]{X; Θ} = 0 (E.2), which becomes [−1000ω² + 40,000, 15,000; 15,000, −810ω² + 67,500] (E.3); frequency equation 8.1ω⁴ − 999ω² + 24,750 = 0 (E.4); ω1 = 5.8593 rad/s, ω2 = 9.4341 rad/s (E.5); amplitude ratios X(1)/Θ(1) = −2.6461, X(2)/Θ(2) = 0.3061 (E.6). Small angles (tan θ ≈ θ): the distance from the C.G. to the node is −2.6461 m for ω1 and 0.3061 m for ω2 (Fig. 5.14 mode shapes: nodes O at 2.6461 and 0.3061 from the C.G.) [VB-2D p.26–27].
11.3.6 Forced-vibration analysis (§5.6)
  • General 2-DOF equations under external forces: [m11 m12; m12 m22]{ẍ1; ẍ2} + [c11 c12; c12 c22]{ẋ1; ẋ2} + [k11 k12; k12 k22]{x1; x2} = {F1; F2} (5.27); (5.1)–(5.2) are special cases (m11 = m1, m22 = m2, m12 = 0). Harmonic forces Fj(t) = Fj0 e^(iωt) (5.28), steady state xj(t) = Xj e^(iωt) (5.29) with complex Xj depending on ω and the system parameters; substitution gives [(−ω²m11 + iωc11 + k11), (−ω²m12 + iωc12 + k12); (−ω²m12 + iωc12 + k12), (−ω²m22 + iωc22 + k22)]{X1; X2} = {F10; F20} (5.30) [VB-2D p.28].
  • Mechanical impedance Zrs(iω) = −ω²mrs + iωcrs + krs, r, s = 1, 2 (5.31); [Z(iω)]X⃗ = F⃗0 (5.32), [Z(iω)] = [Z11 Z12; Z12 Z22] = impedance matrix; X⃗ = [Z(iω)]⁻¹F⃗0 (5.33), [Z]⁻¹ = [1/(Z11Z22 − Z12²)][Z22, −Z12; −Z12, Z11] (5.34); X1(iω) = (Z22F10 − Z12F20)/(Z11Z22 − Z12²); X2(iω) = (−Z12F10 + Z11F20)/(Z11Z22 − Z12²) (5.35); substituting into (5.29) gives x1(t), x2(t) [VB-2D p.28–29].
  • The vibration-absorber analysis of a 2-DOF system is in the book's Section 9.11; Ref. [5.4] deals with the impact response and Ref. [5.5] with the steady-state response under harmonic excitation [VB-2D p.29].
  • Example 5.8 (steady-state response of Fig. 5.15: three springs k and two masses m in series between two walls, x1, x2; mass m1 excited by F1(t) = F10 cos ωt; also plot the frequency-response curve): [m 0; 0 m]{ẍ1; ẍ2} + [2k −k; −k 2k]{x1; x2} = {F10 cos ωt; 0} (E.1); xj = Xj cos ωt (E.2) (footnote: F10 cos ωt = Re(F10 e^(iωt)); Xj real for an undamped system); Z11 = Z22 = −mω² + 2k, Z12 = −k (E.3); X1(ω) = (−ω²m + 2k)F10/[(−ω²m + 2k)² − k²] = (−ω²m + 2k)F10/[(−mω² + 3k)(−mω² + k)] (E.4); X2(ω) = kF10/[(−mω² + 2k)² − k²] = kF10/[(−mω² + 3k)(−mω² + k)] (E.5); with ω1² = k/m, ω2² = 3k/m: X1(ω) = {2 − (ω/ω1)²}F10/{k[(ω2/ω1)² − (ω/ω1)²][1 − (ω/ω1)²]} (E.6); X2(ω) = F10/{k[(ω2/ω1)² − (ω/ω1)²][1 − (ω/ω1)²]} (E.7) [VB-2D p.29–30].
    • Fig. 5.16 shows X1k/F10 and X2k/F10 versus ω/ω1 (ordinates from −3 to 3, abscissa 0–4 with ω1, ω2 marked). The amplitudes become infinite at ω² = ω1² or ω² = ω2²: two resonance conditions (at ω1 and at ω2); at other values of ω the amplitudes are finite. There is a particular frequency at which the vibration of the first mass m1 (to which f1 is applied) is reduced to zero; this characteristic is the basis of the dynamic vibration absorber (Chapter 9 of the book) [VB-2D p.30–31].
11.3.7 Semidefinite systems (§5.7)
  • Semidefinite systems = unrestrained or degenerate systems. Examples (Fig. 5.17): (a) two railway cars of masses m1, m2 joined by a coupling spring k (coordinates x1, x2; free-body diagram (b): force k(x2 − x1)); (c) two rotors J1, J2 (turbine, air blower) connected by a shaft of torsional stiffness kt. A train rolling down the track is a system with rigid-body (unrestrained) translational motion while the cars also vibrate relative to one another; the unrestrained degree of freedom changes the analysis: the stiffness matrix of an unrestrained system is singular; one natural frequency of an unrestrained 2-DOF system is zero and the motion is composed of translation and vibration [VB-2D p.31–32].
  • Equations m1ẍ1 + k(x1 − x2) = 0; m2ẍ2 + k(x2 − x1) = 0 (5.36); xj = Xj cos(ωt + φj) (5.37); (−m1ω² + k)X1 − kX2 = 0; −kX1 + (−m2ω² + k)X2 = 0 (5.38); frequency equation ω²[m1m2ω² − k(m1 + m2)] = 0 (5.39); ω1 = 0 and ω2 = √[k(m1 + m2)/(m1m2)] (5.40). ω = 0 means no oscillation: the system moves as a whole without relative motion (rigid-body translation); such systems (one natural frequency equal to zero) are semidefinite. For ω2, X1(2) and X2(2) are opposite in phase: a node at the middle of the spring [VB-2D p.32].
  • Example 5.9 (free-vibration solution of the unrestrained system of Fig. 5.17(a): m1 = 1 kg, m2 = 2 kg, k = 200 N/m, x1(0) = 0.1 m, x2(0) = ẋ1(0) = ẋ2(0) = 0): ω1 = 0, ω2 = [200(1 + 2)/(1·2)]^½ = 17.3205 rad/s (E.1); [(−m1ω² + k), −k; −k, (−m2ω² + k)]{X1; X2} = 0 (E.2); for ω1 = 0: [200 −200; −200 200] → mode {X1; X2}(1) = a1{1; 1} (E.3–E.4); for ω2 = 17.3205: [−100 −200; −200 −400] → {X1; X2}(2) = a2{1; −0.5} (E.5–E.6) [VB-2D p.33].
    • Mode responses x⃗(1)(t) = {X1; X2}(1) cos(ω1t + φ1) = a1{1; 1} cos φ1; x⃗(2)(t) = a2{1; −0.5} cos(17.3205t + φ2) (E.7–E.8); general solution x⃗(t) = b1x⃗(1) + b2x⃗(2) = c1{1; 1} cos φ1 + c2{1; −0.5} cos(17.3205t + φ2) (E.9), c1 = a1b1, c2 = a2b2; velocities ẋ⃗ = −c2{1; −0.5}(17.3205) sin(17.3205t + φ2) (E.10). Initial conditions give x1(0) = c1 cos φ1 + c2 cos φ2 = 0.1 (E.11); x2(0) = c1 cos φ1 + 0.5c2 cos φ2 = 0 (E.12, printed); ẋ1(0) = −17.3205c2 sin φ2 = 0 (E.13); ẋ2(0) = −8.66025c2 sin φ2 = 0 (E.14, printed); c2 = ±0.06666, φ2 = 0 or π, c1 cos φ1 = 0.03333 (E.15); x1(t) = 0.03333 ± 0.06666 cos(17.3205t + φ2); x2(t) = 0.03333 ∓ 0.03333 cos(17.3205t + φ2) (upper sign for φ2 = 0, lower for π) (E.16–E.17). The response is composed of a constant (translation) and a harmonic term (vibration) [VB-2D p.33–34] (⚠ B-F69).
11.3.8 Self-excitation and stability (§5.8, start only)
  • §5.8 begins: the stability conditions of an SDOF system (Section 3.11 of the book) are expressed in terms of the physical constants; the procedure is extended to a 2-DOF system in this section; the file ends in the sentence "When the system is subjected to self-exciting …" [VB-2D p.34].

  • The 12-page file titled "مسائل المرجع وحلها" (reference problems and their solutions) contains, page for page, the textbook pages 477–488 (PDF p.1 = book p.477), i.e. the same content as VB-2D PDF pp.11–22: end of §5.3 (Eqs 5.17–5.18), Examples 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, §5.4 with Examples 5.4 and 5.5, and the start of §5.5 [VB-RP p.1–12]. No handwriting or added annotations appear on the pages. Its content is recorded in 11.3.3–11.3.5 above with the tags [VB-2D p.11–22]; the correspondence is VB-RP p.N = VB-2D p.N+10 (e.g. Fig. 5.6 on VB-RP p.2, Fig. 5.7 on p.3, Fig. 5.8 on p.7, Fig. 5.9 on p.8, Fig. 5.10 on p.10, Fig. 5.11 lathe photo and sketch on p.12) [VB-RP p.2–12].
