Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

13.1 Types of Simulink blocks (Section 9)
  • Integrator block (يستخدم في التكامل — used for integration): example ẍ → ∫ → ẋ → ∫ → x [VC-S9 p.7].
  • Scope block (يستخدم لرسم أي متغير — used to plot any variable): example x → Scope gives the response shape ("بيطلع شكل الـ Response") [VC-S9 p.7].
  • Gain block, a triangle (يستخدم في الضرب أو القسمة — used for multiplication or division): x → [K] → Kx; x → [1/K] → x/K [VC-S9 p.7].
  • Sum block (يستخدم في الجمع أو الطرح — used for addition or subtraction): inputs x (+), y (+) → x + y; x (+), y (−) → x − y; x (+), y (−), z (+) → x − y + z [VC-S9 p.8].
  • Derivative block d/dt (يستخدم في التفاضل — used for differentiation): x → d/dt → ẋ [VC-S9 p.8].
13.2 Example 1 — mass with two springs and two dampers (Section 9)
  • System: m hung between K2 ∥ C2 above (to the ceiling) and K1 ∥ C1 below (to the ground), with F(t) applied and x(t) measured downward [VC-S9 p.9].
  • Equation of motion (ΣFx = mẍ, downward positive): mẍ = F(t) − C1ẋ − C2ẋ − K1x − K2x [VC-S9 p.9].
  • Simulink diagram: ẍ → ∫ → ẋ → ∫ → x → Scope; gains −K2 and −K1 fed from x, −C2 and −C1 fed from ẋ, and a Source block F(t); all five signals enter a five-input sum block (all "+") whose output passes through a gain "1/m" and is fed back as ẍ [VC-S9 p.9].
13.3 Example 2 — pulley with a spring and a damper (Section 9)
  • System: pulley with J0 (angular displacement θ(t)), inner and outer radii r1, r2 in the sketch; a spring K attached to the wall at the pulley's horizontal cord and a damper C to ground on the vertical cord; x = rθ, ẋ = rθ̇ [VC-S9 p.10].
  • Equation of motion: ΣMO = J0θ̈: J0θ̈ = −Cẋ(2r) − Kx(r) → J0θ̈ = −2r²Cθ̇ − r²Kθ [VC-S9 p.10] (⚠ C-F24).
  • Simulink diagram: θ̈ → ∫ → θ̇ → ∫ → θ → Scope; gain −r²K from θ, gain −2r²C from θ̇, a two-input sum, then gain 1/J0 fed back as θ̈ [VC-S9 p.10].
13.4 Sherif Ehab's review notes on Simulink ([VC-RMS])
  • Base-excited SDOF model: mass M (x(t), ẋ(t), ẍ(t)) on K and C riding a wheel on a sinusoidal road y(t) = Y sin ωt; Newton's 2nd law: ΣF = Mẍ, Δ = x − y, Fs = KΔ, Fd = KΔ̇ (as printed, ⚠ C-F39): mẍ = −C(ẋ − ẏ) − K(x − y); Arabic note: isolate ẍ on one side → ẍ = −(C/m)(ẋ − ẏ) − (K/m)(x − y), "the equation of acceleration" [VC-RMS p.1].
  • Blocks (Arabic explanations): Signal Generator (input, gives y(t) and x(t) drawn together on the same plot); integrator ∫dt; derivative d/dt; gain (multiplies by a number); Sum (takes two or more inputs and gives one output; the same block can be used more than once); Scope (for plotting) [VC-RMS p.1].
  • Diagram [VC-RMS p.2]: ẍ → 1/s → ẋ → 1/s → x; x and y (from the sinusoidal input) enter a sum (+, −) giving x − y, then gain K/m; ẋ and ẏ (a d/dt block on y) enter a sum (+, −) giving ẋ − ẏ, then gain C/m; a two-input sum with both signs minus closes the loop as ẍ; scopes show x and, through a mixer, x(t) with y(t); Arabic side note: y is an input coming from a Simulink input block ("sinusoidal input"), which is chosen with the signal-generator block.
  • Quarter-car model [VC-RMS pp.3–4]: body mass mb (xb), suspension Ks and Cs, wheel mass mw (xw), tyre stiffness Kt (the tyre damping is neglected because rubber damping is small — Arabic side note, partly legible), road y(t) = Y sin(2πVt/λ) (as drawn). Body: ΣF = mbẍb: mbẍb = −Ks(xb − xw) − Cs(ẋb − ẋw) → ẍb = −(Cs/mb)(ẋb − ẋw) − (Ks/mb)(xb − xw) (a). Wheel: ΣF = mwẍw: mwẍw = Cs(ẋb − ẋw) + Ks(xb − xw) − Kt(xw − y) → ẍw = (Cs/mw)(ẋb − ẋw) + (Ks/mw)(xb − xw) − (Kt/mw)(xw − y) (b). Simulink: two chains of integrators for xb and xw, gains Cs/mb, Ks/mb, Cs/mw, Ks/mw, Kt/mw, sums with the signs of (a) and (b), a signal generator for y, and scopes for xb, xw and the relative motion; Arabic side note: xb − xw is the suspension working space and can be plotted.

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

14.1 Chapter 1 questions (book)
  • Define: physical system, analysis, synthesis, deduction, physical model, mathematical model [VA-CH p.12; VA-BK p.12].
  • Define vibration and its physical explanation. State the conditions for vibration to occur. Give four applications of desired vibration and four of undesired vibration [VA-CH p.12; VA-BK p.12].
  • Explain the methods used to study vibration systems, and the types of study required for them [VA-CH p.12; VA-BK p.12].
  • State the difference, with an example of each, between continuous and discrete systems; linear and non-linear systems; deterministically and non-deterministically excited systems [VA-CH p.12; VA-BK p.12].

  • Find the Fourier series of: a triangular wave between +A and −A with period τ; a rectangular pulse train of height 1.0 (period 2π, pulse width kπ); a rising sawtooth of height 1.0 and period 2π [VA-CH p.36; VA-BK p.36].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

14.1 Handwritten "Sheet (1) – Vibration Fundamentals" (VB-T1, 8 scanned pages)
  • Q1 Define: (a) degree of freedom: the minimum number of independent variables needed to describe the vibration motion [VB-T1 p.1]. (b) natural frequency: the frequency ("The of which", word missing) at which the system oscillates when not subjected to an external force; ωn = √(k/m) [VB-T1 p.1]. (c) magnification factor: ratio between the amplitude of vibration and the static deflection, M = A/(F0/k) [VB-T1 p.1]. (d) free vibration: oscillation caused by initial conditions without external forces [VB-T1 p.1]. (e) logarithmic decrement: the ratio between any two successive amplitudes, δ = (1/n) ln(xn/xn+1) [VB-T1 p.1] (⚠ B-F75). (f) resonance: the condition in which an object or system subjected to an oscillating force has a frequency equal to its natural frequency [VB-T1 p.1]. (g) physical system: a device or devices in the natural world acting together to perform a desired objective [VB-T1 p.1]. (h) analysis may be quantitative or qualitative: quantitative analysis determines the system response due to a certain excitation; qualitative analysis concerns general system properties such as natural frequency, damping ratio, settling time, and is very important because design techniques depend on it [VB-T1 p.1].
  • Q2 Discuss the effect of: (A) mass and stiffness on the natural frequency: ωn = √(k/m), ωn ∝ √k, ωn ∝ 1/√m; as mass increases the natural frequency decreases, as stiffness increases it increases [VB-T1 p.2]. (B) frequency ratio on the magnification factor: for r = 0…1 M increases with r; for r > 1 M decreases as r increases (sketch M vs r with curves ζ = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 … starting at M = 1 at r = 0, peak near r = 1, all decaying at large r) [VB-T1 p.2]. (C) damping force in case of resonance: used to avoid the destructive effects of resonance; damping reduces the magnification factor at resonance (sketch: no damping, low damping, large damping, over-damped curves) [VB-T1 p.2].
  • Q3 Condition for vibration motion to occur: the system must have mass and an elastic element such as a spring; ωn = √(k/m) [VB-T1 p.2].
  • Q4 Applications for desired vibration: music instruments, rock drilling, diggers, concrete compactor; for undesired vibration: ground vibration by earthquake, vibration of an aeroplane and its wings, in machines, robot [VB-T1 p.3].
  • Q5 Differences: (A) continuous system: infinite degrees of freedom, distributed mass, equations of motion are partial differential equations, e.g. beams, buildings, strings; discrete system: definite (finite) degrees of freedom, lumped masses, equations are ODEs, e.g. simple pendulum. (B) linear system: the highest power of any variable in the equation of motion is one, superposition principle can be applied, e.g. simple pendulum; non-linear system: highest power of a variable is more than one, superposition cannot be applied, e.g. simple beam. (C) deterministically excited system: the exciting force can be described as a function f(t), e.g. harmonic force; non-deterministically excited system: cannot be described as a function f(t), e.g. random force [VB-T1 p.3] (⚠ B-F76).
  • Q6 Deterministic vs random vibration: deterministic is harmonic or periodic (sketches: sine wave and a rectangular/square-pulse train), e.g. harmonic force, the magnitude of the exciting force is known; random vibration is non-deterministic (irregular sketches), e.g. earthquakes, the magnitude of the excitation is not known [VB-T1 p.4].
  • Q7 How to connect several springs to increase stiffness: connect the springs in parallel, keq = k1 + k2 + k3 + … (sketch of three parallel springs) [VB-T1 p.4]. Q8 Periodic vs harmonic motion: periodic motion repeats itself after equal intervals of time; harmonic motion is one form of periodic motion: all harmonic motions are periodic while the reverse is not always true [VB-T1 p.4].
  • Q9 Effect of a decrease in mass on the frequency: ωn = √(k/m), ωn ∝ 1/√m; as mass decreases the frequency increases (ω = 2πf) [VB-T1 p.4]. Q10 Effect of a decrease in stiffness on the natural period: T = 2π/ω, ω ∝ √k; written "as k↑, ωn↓ and T↑", T = 1/f [VB-T1 p.4] (⚠ B-F77). Q11 "Why does the amplitude of free vibration gradually diminish in a practical system?": no answer written [VB-T1 p.4].
  • Q12 Importance of finding the natural frequency: to design the system in a frequency range far from the natural frequency, because if the frequency of the excitation equals the natural frequency the system will fail ("resonance") [VB-T1 p.5]. Q13 Arbitrary constants of the general solution of a second-order ODE: two constants; roots D1,2 = (−c ± √(c² − 4mk))/(2m); determined from the initial conditions x(t0) = x0 and ẋ(t0) = ẋ0 [VB-T1 p.5]. Q14 Can the energy method find the equation of motion for all SDOF systems? No, it is used only for simple systems in which there is no dissipation of energy [VB-T1 p.5]. Q15 Assumptions for ωn of 1-DOF systems by the energy method: K.E. + P.E. = constant, d/dt(K.E. + P.E.) = 0 [VB-T1 p.5]. Q16 Is the frequency of a damped system smaller or greater than the natural frequency? ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²), so ωd < ωn [VB-T1 p.5].
  • Q17 Use of the logarithmic decrement: getting the ratio between any two successive amplitudes, δ = (1/n) ln(xn/xn+1) [VB-T1 p.6]. Q18 Critical damping and its importance: critical damping coefficient Cc = 2√(km); ζ = C/Cc, critical damping at ζ = 1; the system is critically damped when C = Cc [VB-T1 p.6]. Q19 ωn from the static deflection: δst = F0/k → k = F0/δst; ωn = √(k/m) = √(F0/(m δst)) [VB-T1 p.6]. Q20 Magnification factor: ratio between the amplitude of vibration and the amplitude of the zero-frequency deflection; M = A/δst = A/(F0/k) = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) [VB-T1 p.6]. Q21 Peak amplitude vs resonant amplitude: resonant amplitude Xres/X0 = 1/(2ζ) at r = 1 (ω = ωn); peak amplitude Xp/X0 = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) [VB-T1 p.6].
  • Q22 "What will be the frequency of the applied force with respect to ωn of the system if M < 1?": no answer written; margin scribbles: 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) < 1 → (1 − r²)² + (2ζr)² > 1 → 1 − 2r² + r⁴ + 4ζ²r² > 1 → r⁴ + (4ζ² − 2)r² > 0 [VB-T1 p.7]. Q23 Amplitude and phase in the neighbourhood of resonance: at ω = ωn, r = 1, M = Xp/X0 = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) → Xres/X0 = 1/(2ζ), φ = 90° [VB-T1 p.7]. Q24 "Is the φ corresponding to the peak amplitude of a viscously damped system over or larger than 90°?": no answer written [VB-T1 p.7]. Q25 "Why is damping considered only in the neighbourhood of resonance in most cases?": no answer written [VB-T1 p.7]. Q26 What happens to the response at resonance? "The response amplitude is a relative maximum" [VB-T1 p.7].
  • Q27 Why M is near one for small r and small for large r: M = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); r = 0 → M = 1; for large r M decreases; r → ∞ → M = 0 (sketch of M vs r with M = 1 line, ζ = 0, 0.2, … 3, r = 1 marked) [VB-T1 p.8]. Q28 Will the force transmitted to the base of a spring-mounted machine decrease with the addition of damping? "No, increasing damping will increase the transmitted force to base", Ft = kx + cẋ [VB-T1 p.8] (⚠ B-F78). Q29 A vehicle vibrates badly on a uniformly bumpy road; will a change in speed improve the condition? increasing velocity increases the frequency; the response amplitude will increase [VB-T1 p.8] (⚠ B-F78).
14.2 Handwritten oral-exam summary sheets (VB-T2, 15 scanned pages)
  • p.1 "Oral – Definitions" (boxed at the top: (X/δst)max = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²))): 1 degree of freedom: minimum number of independent coordinates needed to describe the vibration motion; 2 natural frequency: frequency at which the system oscillates when not subjected to external force, ωn = √(k/m); 3 free vibration: oscillation due to initial conditions, no external force, F(t) = 0; 4 logarithmic decrement: the natural logarithm of the ratio of any two successive amplitudes, δ = ln(xn/xn+1); 5 resonance: the frequency of the external force applied to the system equals the natural frequency, ωn = ω (boxed); 6 mode shape: the pattern of motion in which all parts of the system move sinusoidally with the same frequency and a fixed phase relation [VB-T2 p.1].
  • p.2: 7 magnification factor: ratio between the amplitude of vibration and the static deflection, M = X/(F0/k); 8 physical system: the device or devices in the natural world acting together to perform a desired objective; 9 vibration: any motion that repeats itself after an interval of time is called vibration or oscillation; 10 amplitude: the maximum displacement of the oscillating body from its original position; 11 periodic motion: motion which repeats itself after an interval of time (sketch of a non-sinusoidal periodic wave); 13 harmonic motion: a special case of periodic motion in which the wave takes the shape of a sine or cosine wave (numbering skips 12); 14 transient response: the behaviour of the system while it approaches the steady state, or the response of the system to a change of equilibrium; 15 periodic time: time in which the system produces one complete cycle (Arabic gloss: the time taken for the vibration to complete one full cycle); 16 frequency: number of complete cycles produced in one second; 17 beating vibration: the amplitude builds up and then diminishes in a regular pattern; 18 phase: a measure of how far some cycle's behaviour is displaced; phase angle is the difference between two waves [VB-T2 p.2] (⚠ B-F79).
  • p.3 Discuss the effects of: (i) mass and stiffness on ωn: ωn = √(k/m), ωn ∝ √k, ωn ∝ 1/√m; mass increase → ωn decreases; stiffness increase → ωn increases. (ii) damping force in case of resonance: used to avoid the destructive effects of resonance; damping reduces the magnification factor at resonance; at resonance the damping force becomes maximum (sketch M vs r: no damping (peak → ∞), low damping, large damping, over-damped, M = 1 marked, r = 1 marked). (iii) frequency ratio on magnification factor: 0 < r < 1: M increases as r increases; 1 < r: M decreases as r increases. (iv) frequency ratio on phase angle: for 0 < r < 1 with 0 < ζ: 0 < φ < 90°; for r = 1 with 0 < ζ: φ = 90°; for r ≫ 1 with ζ > 0: φ approaches 180° (sketches: M vs r for ζ = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 3…; φ vs r rising from 0 through 90° at r = 1 to 180°, ζ = 0 a step at r = 1) [VB-T2 p.3].
  • p.4 Effect of the frequency ratio on: (i) displacement transmissibility Td = X/Y: Td = 1 at r = 0; Td → ∞ at ζ = 0 and r = 1; Td = 1 at r = √2; Td < 1 for r > √2 (printed "Td ≮ 1"/"Td < 1 at r > √2"); Td ≫ 1 for r < √2 (near resonance); Td tends to be maximum for 0 < ζ < 1 at r = rm < 1 (sketch X/Y vs r for ζ = 0.05, 0.1, … with all curves through the point (√2, 1)). (ii) phase angle in X/Y (sketch φ vs r rising toward 180° for ζ = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1). (iii) force transmissibility Fr/(kY) versus r (sketch for ζ = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1 with all curves through the value 2 at r = √2); Note: increasing the damping force increases the forces transmitted to the base. (iv) vibration of Z/Y (or MX/(me)) versus r (sketch for ζ = 0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1 tending to 1 at large r) [VB-T2 p.4] (⚠ B-F80).
  • p.5 Differences: frequency response vs steady-state response vs time-domain response: frequency response X(ω) is the amplitude of the steady-state response for any frequency ω (sketch X(ω) vs frequency with marked points); time-domain response is the response of the system at any time t (sketch x(t) vs t decaying into a steady oscillation). Peak amplitude vs resonance amplitude: peak amplitude Xp/δst|max = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)), the amplitude which gives the maximum amplification factor; resonance amplitude Xres/δst = 1/(2ζ), the amplitude at r = 1 [VB-T2 p.5].
  • p.6 Steps of vibration analysis: 1 system modelling, 2 finding the equation of motion, 3 analysis (finding the solution of the equation of motion), 4 interpretation of the results. Damping = the mechanism by which vibration energy is converted into heat or sound; types: underdamped ζ < 1, critical damping ζ = 1, overdamped ζ > 1 [VB-T2 p.6].
    • Energy dissipated in one cycle by damping: dW/dt = force × velocity = Fv = −cv² = −c(dx/dt)²; ΔW = ∫0^(2π/ωd) c(dx/dt)² dt = ∫0^(2π) c X²ωd cos²(ωd t) d(ωd t) = πcωdX². Full force F = −kX sin ωd t − cωdX cos ωd t: ΔW = ∫F v dt = ∫kXωd sin(ωd t) cos(ωd t) d(ωd t) + ∫cωdX² cos²(ωd t) d(ωd t) = πcωdX² [VB-T2 p.6].
  • p.7 Free vibration – prove (free undamped): mẍ + kx = 0 (FBD with kx); ms² + k = 0 → s = ±i√(k/m) = ±iωn; x(t) = Ce^(st) = C1e^(iωn t) + C2e^(−iωn t); e^(±iωn t) = cos ωn t ± i sin ωn t; x(t) = A sin(ωn t) + B cos(ωn t); with X = √(A² + B²), φ = tan⁻¹(B/A): x(t) = X sin(ωn t + φ); or φ = tan⁻¹(A/B) (A = coefficient of sin, B = coefficient of cos): x(t) = X cos(ωn t − φ) [VB-T2 p.7].
  • p.8–10 Free damped vibration – prove: mẍ + cẋ + kx = 0 (FBD with kx, cẋ); s = d/dt → ms² + cs + k = 0; s1,2 = (−c ± √(c² − 4mk))/(2m); c/(2m) = [c/(2√(km))]√(k/m) = ζωn; 4mk/(4m²) = k/m = ωn²; s1,2 = −ζωn ± ωn√(ζ² − 1); general solution x(t) = C1e^([−ζωn + ωn√(ζ²−1)]t) + C2e^([−ζωn − ωn√(ζ²−1)]t); boxed "ωd = ωn√(ζ² − 1)"; cases ζ < 1 underdamped, ζ = 1 critically damped, ζ > 1 overdamped [VB-T2 p.8] (⚠ B-F81).
    • Case 1: ζ > 1 or (c² − 4mk)/(4m²) > 0: s1,2 = [−ζ ± √(ζ² − 1)]ωn < 0; x(t) = C1e^([−ζ+√(ζ²−1)]ωn t) + C2e^([−ζ−√(ζ²−1)]ωn t). Case 2: ζ = 1 or (c² − 4mk)/(4m²) = 0: s1,2 = −c/(2m) = −ωn (repeated roots); x(t) = (A + Bt)e^(−ωn t). Case 3: ζ < 1 or (c² − 4mk)/(4m²) < 0: s1,2 = −c/(2m) ± i√((4mk − c²)/(4m²)) = −ωnζ ± iωn√(1 − ζ²); x(t) = C1e^((−ζ+i√(1−ζ²))ωn t) + C2e^((−ζ−i√(1−ζ²))ωn t), using e^(±iθ) = cos θ ± i sin θ [VB-T2 p.9].
    • x(t) = e^(−ζωn t)[(C1 + C2) cos(ωd t) + (C1 − C2)i sin(ωd t)]; A = C1 + C2 (cos coefficient), B = i(C1 − C2) (sin coefficient); X = √(A² + B²); φ = tan⁻¹(A/B) if the sine form is used, φ0 = tan⁻¹(B/A) if the cosine form is used; x(t) = X e^(−ζωn t) sin(ωd t + φ) or x(t) = X e^(−ζωn t) cos(ωd t − φ0); sketch x(t) with period τd = 2π/ωd, curves for ζ < 1 (decaying oscillation between exponential envelopes), ζ = 1 and ζ > 1 (non-oscillatory) [VB-T2 p.10].
  • p.11–12 Prove logarithmic decrement: x1/x2 = X e^(−ζωn t1)cos(ωd t1 − φ)/[X e^(−ζωn t2)cos(ωd t2 − φ)]; t2 = t1 + τd, τd = 2π/ωd (period); cos(ωd t2 − φ) = cos(ωd t1 − φ + 2π) = cos(ωd t1 − φ); x1/x2 = e^(−ζωn t1)/e^(−ζωn(t1+τd)) = e^(ζωn τd); ln(x1/x2) = ζωn τd = ζωn(2π/ωd); δ = ln(x1/x2) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) (boxed). For m cycles: x1/xm+1 = (x1/x2)(x2/x3)(x3/x4)…(xm/xm+1) = (e^(ζωn τd))^m; ln(x1/xm+1) = mζωn τd; (1/m) ln(x1/xm+1) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = δ; δ = (1/m) ln(x1/xm+1) (boxed) [VB-T2 p.11–12].
  • p.13 Forced vibrations (summary in Arabic heading): forced damped: xp(t) = F0/√((k − mω²)² + (cω)²) · cos(ωt·(180/π) − tan⁻¹[cω/(k − mω²)]), i.e. amplitude Xp and phase φp (the 180/π converts radians to degrees); homogeneous part xh(t) = Xh e^(−ζωn t) cos(ωd t + φh) with constants from the initial conditions (Arabic note: the constants are found from the initial conditions, not from the equation); total x(t) = xp(t) + xh(t), the initial conditions being applied to the total; "C = 0 gives the forced undamped case" (Arabic note in the box) [VB-T2 p.13].
    • Beating happens at x0 = ẋ0 = 0 when the forcing frequency is close to but not exactly equal to ωn (ω ≈ ωn, ω ≠ ωn); ωbeating = ω − ωn = 2ε (written), ω + ωn = 2ω; x(t) = [(F0/m)/(2εω) sin εt] sin ωt; Tp = 2π/(2ε) = 2π/(ωn − ω); sketch of x(t): oscillation at period 2π/ω inside an envelope ±[(F0/m)/(2εω)] sin εt, the envelope repeating over 2π/ε [VB-T2 p.13] (⚠ B-F82).
  • p.14: δst = F0/k, r = ω/ωn; Xp = δst/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); M = X/δst = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); undamped case ζ = 0; quality factor Q = 1/(2ζ) = (X/δst) at ω = ωn, valid for ζ < 0.05 (boxed); power absorbed ΔW = πcωX² [VB-T2 p.14].
  • p.15 "Oral exam – Moving support" worked example: m = 250 kg, k = 4000 N/m, ζ = 0.2, v = 25 m/s, Y = 25 cm, wavelength L = 20 m; find Xp and the critical speed vcr [VB-T2 p.15]. ωn = √(k/m) = √(4000/250) = 4 rad/s; v = L/τ → τ = L/v = 20/25; ω = 2π/τ = 2π × 25/20 = 2.5π; X/Y = √(k² + (cω)²)/√((k − mω²)² + (cω)²) = √(1 + (2ζr)²)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²); r = 7.8/4 = 1.95 (boxed); Xp = 0.25 × √(1 + (2 × 0.2 × 1.95)²)/√((1 − 1.95²)² + (2 × 1.95 × 0.2)²) = 0.1089 m = 108.991 mm. Critical speed at resonance r = 1: Xres = 0.25 × √(1 + 4 × 0.04)/(2 × 0.2) = 0.673 m; ωcr = ωn = 4 → τcr = 2π/4 = 0.5π; vcr = 20/(0.5π) = 40/π = 12.7324 m/s (sketch: mass m on spring and damper riding on a sinusoidal road of wavelength L) [VB-T2 p.15] (⚠ B-F83).

14.4 Textbook review questions with answer keys (VB-RQ, book pp.210–213 and 334–335)
  • Source: pages of the textbook review-question sections of Chapter 2 "Free vibration of single-degree-of-freedom systems" (book pp.210–213, PDF p.1–4) and Chapter 3 "Harmonically excited vibration" (book pp.334–335, PDF p.5–6); the scans carry a typed grey solution key in the margin and a few handwritten marks (ticks, underlines, notes) [VB-RQ p.1–6].
Chapter 2, Q2.2 True/false (key: 1 T, 2 T, 3 T, 4 F, 5 F, 6 F, 7 T, 8 T, 9 T, 10 F, 11 T, 12 T, 13 F, 14 T, 15 T, 16 T, 17 T, 18 T, 19 T, 20 T, 21 T, 22 F) [VB-RQ p.1–2]
    1. The amplitude of an undamped system will not change with time (T). 2. A system vibrating in air can be considered a damped system (T). 3. The equation of motion of an SDOF system is the same whether the mass moves in a horizontal or an inclined plane (T). 4. When a mass vibrates in a vertical direction its weight can always be ignored in deriving the equation of motion (F). 5. The principle of conservation of energy can be used to derive the equation of motion of both damped and undamped systems (F). 6. The damped frequency can in some cases be larger than the undamped natural frequency (F). 7. The damped frequency can be zero in some cases (T; handwritten note: ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²), "in case of over & critical") [VB-RQ p.1].
    1. The natural frequency of a torsional system is √(k/m) with k the torsional spring constant and m the polar mass moment of inertia (T). 9. Rayleigh's method is based on conservation of energy (T). 10. The final position of the mass is always the equilibrium position in Coulomb damping (F). 11. The undamped natural frequency is √(g/δst), δst = static deflection (T; handwritten "mg = kδst"). 12. For an undamped system the velocity leads the displacement by π/2 (T). 13. For an undamped system the velocity leads the acceleration by π/2 (F). 14. Coulomb damping can be called constant damping (T). 15. The loss coefficient denotes the energy dissipated per radian per unit strain energy (T). 16. The motion diminishes to zero in both underdamped and overdamped cases (T). 17. The logarithmic decrement can be used to find the damping ratio (T). 18. The hysteresis loop of the stress–strain curve of a material causes damping (T). 19. The complex stiffness can be used to find the damping force in a system with hysteresis damping (T). 20. Motion in hysteresis damping can be considered harmonic (T). 21. In the s-plane the locus of constant natural frequency is a circle (T). 22. The characteristic equation of an SDOF system can have one real root and one complex root (F) [VB-RQ p.2].
Chapter 2, Q2.3 Fill in the blanks (key as printed) [VB-RQ p.2]
    1. Free vibration of an undamped system is an interchange of kinetic and potential energies. 2. A system in simple harmonic motion is a harmonic oscillator. 3. The mechanical clock represents a torsional pendulum. 4. The center of percussion can be used advantageously in a baseball bat. 5. With viscous and hysteresis damping the motion continues forever, theoretically. 6. The damping force in Coulomb damping is given by µN. 7. The loss coefficient can be used to compare the damping capacity of different engineering materials. 8. Torsional vibration occurs when a rigid body oscillates about an axis. 9. The property of critical damping is used in many practical applications such as large guns. 10. The logarithmic decrement denotes the rate at which the amplitude of a free damped vibration decreases. 11. Rayleigh's method can be used to find the natural frequency directly. 12. Any two successive displacements separated by a cycle can be used to find the logarithmic decrement. 13. The damped natural frequency ωd in terms of the undamped natural frequency ωn as _____ (no entry in the printed key; a handwritten tick appears; from VB-AM p.29 ωd = √(1 − ζ²)ωn). 14. The time constant denotes the time at which the initial response reduces by 63.2 percent. 15. The term e^(−2t) decays faster than e^(−t). 16. In the s-plane, lines parallel to the real axis denote systems having different damped frequencies [VB-RQ p.2].

For a critically damped system the motion will be (b) aperiodic (handwritten: non-periodic). 13. Energy dissipated per cycle in viscous damping for x = X sin ωd t: (a) πcωdX². 14. Specific damping capacity for total energy W and dissipated energy ΔW per cycle: (b) ΔW/W. 15. If the characteristic roots have positive real values the response is (b) unstable (handwritten: s = ξωn, +ve). 16. The frequency of oscillation is higher if the imaginary part of the roots is (c) larger. 17. If the characteristic roots have zero imaginary part the response is (b) nonoscillatory [VB-RQ p.3–4].

The shape of the root locus of an SDOF system as k is varied is: a vertical and horizontal lines, b circular arc, c radial lines; no key entries are printed for 18 and 19 [VB-RQ p.4] (⚠ B-F85).
Chapter 3, Q3.2 True/false (key: 1 T, 2 T, 3 T, 4 F, 5 T, 6 T, 7 T, 8 F, 9 F, 10 T, 11 T, 12 T, 13 T; no key for 14–16) [VB-RQ p.5]
    1. The magnification factor is the ratio of maximum amplitude and static deflection (T). 2. The response is harmonic if the excitation is harmonic (T). 3. The phase angle of the response depends on m, c, k and ω (T; handwritten φ = tan⁻¹[cω/(k − mω²)]). 4. The phase angle of the response depends on the amplitude of the forcing function (F). 5. During beating the amplitude builds up and then diminishes in a regular pattern (T). 6. The Q factor can be used to estimate the damping in a system (T). 7. The half-power points denote the frequency ratios where the amplification factor falls to Q/√2 (T). 8. The amplitude ratio attains its maximum value at resonance in viscous damping (F). 9. The response is always in phase with the harmonic forcing function in hysteresis damping (F). 10. Damping reduces the amplitude ratio for all values of the forcing frequency (T). 11. Unbalance in a rotating machine causes vibration (T). 12. The steady-state solution can be assumed harmonic for small dry-friction force (T). 13. In a system with rotational unbalance the effect of damping becomes negligibly small at higher speeds (T). 14. The transfer function is a property of the system and is not related to the input. 15. The transfer functions of several different systems can be the same. 16. If the transfer function of a system is known, its response can be found for all types of input (no key for 14–16) [VB-RQ p.5].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

14.1 Chapter 4 problem list (section 4.6) ([VC-A4])
  • P1 (bar, Fig. with damper and spring): the differential equation of the damped SDOF system shown is Io θ̈ + c(l/2)² θ̇ + kl²θ = F0 l sin ωt, Io the mass moment of inertia of the bar about O; uniform bar m = 5 kg, l = 1 m, Io = ml²; the undamped natural frequency ωn was found experimentally as 20 Hz; when the harmonic force at the end of the bar is applied at this frequency (ω = ωn) the steady-state amplification factor is 2.5; (a) determine the damping constant c from these data; (b) the amplitude of vibration if F0 = 10 N and ω = 35 Hz [VC-A4 p.56].
  • P2 (same system, part (a) show the equation of motion): Io θ̈ + c(L/2)² θ̇ + kL²θ = F0 L sin ωt; (b) IO = ⅓mL², m = 5 kg, L = 1 m, k = 2.5×10⁴ N/m; the steady-state amplification factor X/F0 = 2.5 when the force at the end of the bar is applied at this frequency; determine [b.1] the damping coefficient ζ or damping constant c, [b.2] the amplitude of vibration if F0 = 10 N and ω = 35 rad/s [VC-A4 pp.56–57].
  • P3: a uniform bar of mass m and length l pivoted at its centre; the spring of constant k at the left end is attached to a stationary surface, the right-end spring of constant k is attached to a support that undergoes harmonic motion yB = b sin ωt; determine the natural frequency of the system [VC-A4 p.57].
  • P4: the cam and follower of Fig. (meq, keq) impart a displacement x(t) as a periodic function to the lower end of the system (triangular wave of amplitude A, period τ): derive an expression for the response y(t) by Fourier analysis [VC-A4 p.57]. (Worked in §7.9.)
  • P5: a counter-rotating eccentric-mass exciter is used to determine the vibration characteristics of a structure of mass 181.4 kg; at 900 rpm a stroboscope shows the eccentric mass at the top at the instant the structure moves upward through its static equilibrium position (phase angle π/2, i.e. resonance) and the amplitude is 21.6 mm; the unbalance of each wheel is 0.0921 kg·m; find (a) the natural frequency, (b) the damping ratio, (c) the amplitude at 1200 rpm, (d) the angular position of the eccentrics at the instant the structure moves upward through its equilibrium position [VC-A4 p.58].
  • P6: an electric motor of mass 68 kg on an isolator block of mass 1200 kg; natural frequency of the total assembly 160 cpm, ζ = 0.10; unbalance produces F = 100 sin 31.4t; determine the amplitude of vibration of the block and the force transmitted to the floor [VC-A4 p.58].
  • P7: a car and suspension idealised as a damped spring–mass system, natural frequency 0.5 Hz, damping coefficient 0.2, drives at speed V over a road with sinusoidal roughness of wavelength 6 m and amplitude 10 cm (the figure shows 0.02 m); at what speed does the maximum amplitude occur and what is the corresponding vibration amplitude; the figure box gives |X/Y| = √[(1 + (2ξr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ξr)²)], r = ω/ωn, ω the base frequency [VC-A4 pp.58–59].
  • P8: the upper support of a dashpot moves in simple harmonic motion y(t) = Y sin ωn t with amplitude Y mm at the natural frequency of the system (m on K, C above); show that the amplitude of the damper force equals zero [VC-A4 p.59].
  • P9: a vibrometer fixed on the case of a motor rotating at 1600 rpm; the seismic mass vibrates with amplitude 1.5 mm relative to the case; natural frequency of the vibrometer 10 cycles/s; find the amplitude of the vibrating motor [VC-A4 p.59] (worked on p.32, §10.1).
  • P10: a seismometer with a seismic mass suspended by springs and a pointer of moment of inertia I about its pivot; a = 5 cm, b = 2.5 cm, m = 0.1 kg, I = 1.5×10⁻⁵ kg·m², k1 = k2 = 0.1 N/m; determine the natural frequency of the system [VC-A4 p.59].
  • P11: seismometer (pointer without the mass has moment of inertia I0 about its pivot); (a) draw the free-body diagram of the mass–pointer system, (b) determine the natural frequency, (c) with a = 5 cm, b = 2.5 cm, m = 0.1 kg, I0 = 2.5×10⁻⁴ kg·m², k1 = k2 = 0.8 N/m, an impulse gives the mass an initial velocity θ̇0 = 30 cm/s from θ0 = 0; determine the maximum angular deflection of the pointer [VC-A4 pp.59–60].
  • No answers are given for any of these problems [VC-A4 pp.56–60].
14.2 Review problems of the 2-DOF final-review set ([VC-R2D])
  • Statements without solutions to work through (all are solved in §11.8–11.19): vehicle pitch-and-bounce (Fig. 5.45) [VC-R2D p.1]; two-storey system on a moving base [VC-R2D p.4]; two-disc torsional system (J1 = J0, J2 = 2J0) [VC-R2D p.6]; two masses with three springs and dampers plus forces [VC-R2D p.13]; Examples 1–4 in matrix form [VC-R2D pp.19–24]; Examples 5–11 (Lagrange and Newton, natural frequencies and mode shapes) [VC-R2D pp.25–52].
  • The source marks the following exam-style tasks: "find the natural frequencies and mode shapes" (Ex. 5, 9), "find the normal modes, the natural frequencies and the free-vibration response" (Ex. 10), "find the equation of motion in matrix form" (Ex. 3, 11) [VC-R2D pp.21, 25, 42, 46, 51].

15.6 Appendix A: mathematical relations [VB-TB p.5–7]

Trigonometry:

  • sin(α ± β) = sin α cos β ± cos α sin β; cos(α ± β) = cos α cos β ∓ sin α sin β [VB-TB p.5].
  • sin(α + β) sin(α − β) = sin²α − sin²β = cos²β − cos²α; cos(α + β) cos(α − β) = cos²α − sin²β = cos²β − sin²α [VB-TB p.5].
  • sin α sin β = ½[cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)]; cos α cos β = ½[cos(α − β) + cos(α + β)]; sin α cos β = ½[sin(α + β) + sin(α − β)] [VB-TB p.5].
  • sin α + sin β = 2 sin((α + β)/2) cos((α − β)/2) [VB-TB p.5]; sin α − sin β = 2 cos((α + β)/2) sin((α − β)/2); cos α + cos β = 2 cos((α + β)/2) cos((α − β)/2); cos α − cos β = −2 sin((α + β)/2) sin((α − β)/2) [VB-TB p.6].
  • A sin α + B cos α = √(A² + B²) cos(α − φ1) = √(A² + B²) sin(α + φ2), where φ1 = tan⁻¹(A/B), φ2 = tan⁻¹(B/A) [VB-TB p.6].
  • sin²α + cos²α = 1; cos 2α = 1 − 2 sin²α = 2 cos²α − 1 = cos²α − sin²α; law of cosines for triangles: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C [VB-TB p.6].

Constants, logarithms, exponentials, hyperbolic functions and calculus:

  • π = 3.14159265 rad; 1 rad = 57.29577951°; 1° = 0.017453292 rad; e = 2.71828183 [VB-TB p.6].
  • log aᵇ = b log a; log10 x = 0.4343 loge x; loge x = 2.3026 log10 x [VB-TB p.6].
  • e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x; sin x = (e^(ix) − e^(−ix))/(2i); cos x = (e^(ix) + e^(−ix))/2 [VB-TB p.6].
  • sinh x = ½(eˣ − e⁻ˣ); cosh x = ½(eˣ + e⁻ˣ); cosh²x − sinh²x = 1 [VB-TB p.6].
  • d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx; d(u/v)/dx = (1/v) du/dx − (u/v²) dv/dx = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v² [VB-TB p.6].
  • ∫ e^(ax) dx = (1/a) e^(ax); ∫ u v dx = u ∫ v dx − ∫ (du/dx ∫ v dx) dx [VB-TB p.6].

Complex algebra [VB-TB p.7]:

  • z = x + iy ≡ A e^(iθ), with A = √(x² + y²) and θ = tan⁻¹(y/x).
  • For z1 = x1 + iy1, z2 = x2 + iy2: z1 ± z2 = (x1 ± x2) + i(y1 ± y2); z1 z2 = (x1x2 − y1y2) + i(x1y1 + x2y2) (as printed, ⚠ B-F88); z1/z2 = [(x1x2 + y1y2) + i(x2y1 − x1y2)]/√(x2² + y2²) (as printed, ⚠ B-F89).
  • For z1 = A1 e^(iθ1), z2 = A2 e^(iθ2): z1 + z2 = A e^(iθ) with A = [A1² + A2² − 2A1A2 cos(θ1 − θ2)]^(1/2) (as printed, ⚠ B-F90) and θ = tan⁻¹[(A1 sinθ1 + A2 sinθ2)/(A1 cosθ1 + A2 cosθ2)]; z1 z2 = A1A2 e^(i(θ1+θ2)); z1/z2 = (A1/A2) e^(i(θ1−θ2)).

Rod on three springs (m = 5 kg, L = 0.8 m, K = 200 kN/m) ⚠ C-F50 160 000, 56 000 rad²/s² θ/x = 2.5, −4 [VC-R2D pp.48–50]

Calculator candidates

In this section (3)
  1. Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book
  2. Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files
  3. Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

  • SHM peaks: inputs A, τ (or f); outputs ω = 2π/τ, ẋmax = Aω, ẍmax = Aω² [VA-CH p.16–17].
  • Equivalent stiffness: helical spring Gd⁴/(8nD³); cantilever 3EI/L³; simply supported 48EI/L³; axial EA/L; torsion GIp/L (Ip = πd⁴/32); springs in series and parallel [VA-CH p.29; VA-L1 p.10–15].
  • Natural frequency and period of a mass–spring system: inputs k, m → ωn = √(k/m), f = ωn/2π, τ = 2π/ωn [VA-CH p.40].
  • Spring stiffness from a timed test: inputs m, number of cycles N, time t → τ = t/N, k = m(2π/τ)² [VA-CH p.41].
  • g from a pendulum: inputs L, t for 20 cycles → g = (2π)²L/τ² [VA-CH p.42].
  • Disc inertia from a torsional pendulum: inputs d, L, G, cycles, time → k = GπD⁴/(32L), J = k/ωn² [VA-CH p.43–44].
  • Compound pendulum: inputs h, k (radius of gyration) → ωn = √(gh/(k² + h²)) [VA-CH p.45].
  • Damping: inputs m, k, c → cc = 2√(km), ζ = c/cc, ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²), δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²), amplitude ratio e^δ [VA-CH p.63–67].
  • Logarithmic decrement from a record: inputs X1, Xn+1, n → δ = (1/n) ln(X1/Xn+1), ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²) [VA-CH p.67].
  • Critically damped release with initial velocity: inputs v0, ωn → x(t) = v0 t e^(−ωn t), tmax = 1/ωn, xmax = v0/(eωn) [VA-CH p.72–76].
  • Fourier-series plotter for the square, triangular, sawtooth and half-sine waves (partial sums) [VA-CH p.19–27; VA-L1 p.5–8].
  • Equivalent mass and stiffness (energy method) of a rocker arm: inputs m1, m2, J0, k1, k2, kt, a, b → Meq = m2 + (a/b)²m1 + J0/b², Keq = k2 + kt/b² + (a/b)²k1 [VA-L2 p.21].
  • Tilted-spring combination: inputs ki, θi → Keq = Σ ki cos²θi [VA-L2 p.19, 22].
  • Composite (parallel) torsional shaft: inputs G, D, d, L for each tube → kt = Gπ(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32L), summed [VA-L2 p.20].
  • Spring-mass correction: inputs K, m, ms → ωn = √(3K/(ms + 3m)); cantilever with its own mass: Meq = M + 0.2357 mL, Keq = 3EI/L³ [VA-L2 p.29, 31].
  • Free-response from initial conditions: inputs ωn, x0, ẋ0 → X̄ = √(x0² + (ẋ0/ωn)²), α, x(t), ẋ(t), ẍ(t) plots [VA-L2 p.27–28, 32–35].
  • ωn from static deflection (vertical suspension): input δst → ωn = √(g/δst) [VA-L2 p.28].
  • Damped free response from initial conditions (all three cases): inputs m, k, c, x0, ẋ0 → ζ, ωn, ωd, x(t), plot [VA-LP p.1–3].
  • Design from a decay record: inputs amplitude ratio over n cycles (or a fraction of a cycle), τd, m → δ, ζ, ωn, c, k [VA-LP p.10–15].
  • Buffer/recoil maximum displacement: inputs m, k, c, v0 → tmax and xmax for under-, critically and over-damped cases [VA-LP p.4–6, 16–17; VA-CH p.72–76].
  • Forced response of an SDOF system: inputs m, k, c (or ζ), F0, ω → r, X0 = F0/k, X = X0/D, φ, resonance and peak values ωp, Xp [VA-BK p.87–89].
  • Damping ratio from a resonance test: inputs X0 (= F0/K), X_res → ζ = X0/(2X_res) [VA-BK p.89].
  • Rotating-unbalance response: inputs M, m, e, ω, ωn, ζ → X = (me/M) r²/D, φ [VA-BK p.92–93].
  • Transmissibility and isolator design: inputs ω/ωn (or k, m, ω), ζ → TR, force transmitted FT0 = TR·F0; base-motion amplitude X = TR·Y [VA-BK p.96–100].
  • Moving-support critical speed: inputs road wavelength L, ωn → Vcr = Lωn/2π, excitation ω = 2πV/L [VA-BK p.97–98].
  • Whirling shaft: inputs E, d, L, M, e, N, ζ → K = 48EI/L³ (I = πd⁴/64), ωn = √(K/M), critical speed Ncr = 60ωn/2π, r = e r²/D, bearing load Kr/2 (or (Kr/2)√(1 + (2ζr)²)), bending stress σb = (KrL/4)(d/2)/I [VA-BK p.102–108].
  • Vibration instrument error: inputs ζ, ω/ωn (vibrometer or accelerometer) → M.F and e%; solve for the frequency range for a given error [VA-BK p.110–113].
  • Fourier response to a periodic force or base motion: inputs a0, ai, bi, ω, ωn, ζ → sum of terms Xi = (ai/k)/√((1 − (iω/ωn)²)² + (2ζ iω/ωn)²) with phase [VA-BK p.115–126].
  • Impulse and step response: inputs m, ωn, ζ, F̂ or F0 → x = (F̂/mωd) e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t; step x = (F0/k)[1 − e^(−ζωn t)cos(ωd t − φ)/√(1 − ζ²)] (undamped (F0/K)(1 − cos ωn t), xmax = 2F0/K) [VA-BK p.129–134].
  • Convolution integral numerical evaluator: x(t) = ∫F(ξ)g(t − ξ)dξ for an arbitrary F(t) [VA-BK p.131].
  • Half-sine pulse peak: inputs ω/ωn → tm = 2π/(ω + ωn), x = (F0/K) sin(2π(ω/ωn)/(1 + ω/ωn))/(1 − ω/ωn) [VA-BK p.134–137].
  • 2-DOF free vibration: inputs M, K (2 × 2) → ωn1, ωn2, mode shapes, principal coordinates, response for initial conditions [VA-BK p.151–163].
  • Beats: inputs ω1, ω2 (or a coupled-pendulum k, m, L, a) → ωav, ωB, envelope period [VA-BK p.164–169].
  • 2-DOF forced response: inputs m1, m2, k1, k2, F0, ω → X1, X2 from Cramer's rule [VA-BK p.169–171].
  • Undamped absorber design: inputs ω, m1, k1, F0 (tuned) → k2 = ω²m2, X2 = F0/k2; range design: inputs ω1, ω2, M1 → ωn1, ωn2, μ, M2, k2 [VA-BK p.172–177].
  • Absorber parameter identification: inputs ωn1, ωn2, ω (and M2 or M1) → ω22 = ωn1ωn2/ω11, μ, M1 or M2 [VA-BK p.179–182].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

  • Equivalent mass of a distributed-mass member: inputs M, m (spring, cantilever 33/140, simply supported 0.5), select case → meq = M + m/3, M + 33m/140, M + 0.5m [VB-TB p.1].
  • Rack-and-gear equivalent: inputs m, J0, R → meq = m + J0/R², Jeq = J0 + mR² [VB-TB p.1]. Hinged bar: inputs m1..m3, l1..l3 → meq1 = m1 + (l2/l1)²m2 + (l3/l1)²m3 [VB-TB p.1].
  • Equivalent stiffness library: rod EA/l, tapered rod πEDd/4l, helical spring Gd⁴/(8nD³), fixed-fixed beam 192EI/l³, cantilever 3EI/l³, simply supported 48EI/l³, hollow shaft πG(D⁴−d⁴)/(32l); series and parallel combination [VB-TB p.1–2] [VB-AM p.23–24].
  • Equivalent viscous damping: parallel plates μA/h, dashpot μ(3πD³l/4d³)(1 + 2d/D), torsional damper πμD²(l−h)/2d + πμD³/32h, Coulomb ceq = 4fN/(πωX) [VB-TB p.2].
  • Section and solid properties: inputs shape and dimensions → area, centroid, I (Table 15.4) and mass moments of inertia (Table 15.5) [VB-TB p.3–4].
  • Phasor addition: inputs A1, θ1, A2, θ2 → A, θ (use the correct cosine sign, see ⚠ B-F90) [VB-TB p.7].
  • Harmonic analysis of a tabulated force: inputs N values F(ti), period T → a0, an, bn by the numerical formulas of 2.3 [VB-AM p.40–41].
  • Free-vibration quantities (ωn, ωd, ζ, logarithmic decrement δ = 2πζ/√(1−ζ²)), forced-response magnification factor and transmissibility, rotating unbalance, absorber design (m2, k2 from µ and r) and 2-DOF natural frequencies: see the formulas recorded in sections 5–12 [VB-AM p.29–30] [VB-T2 p.11–12] [VB-DA p.6–8] [VB-2D p.11–13].

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

  • Damped SDOF parameters: inputs m, K, C → ωn = √(K/m), Cc = 2√(Km), ζ = C/Cc, ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²), τd = 2π/ωd, δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²), s.d.c = 2δ, η = δ/π [VC-S34 pp.6–9].
  • ζ from measured decay: inputs X1, Xm+1 and m cycles (m may be ½) → ln(X1/Xm+1) = 2πmζ/√(1 − ζ²) solved for ζ [VC-S34 p.9; VC-S34 p.10].
  • Free response for any ζ: inputs m, K, C, x0, ẋ0, t → the underdamped, critical or overdamped x(t) formula [VC-S34 pp.7–8].
  • Foundation identification from a recorded free response: inputs W (or m), τd, X1/X2 → ωd, ζ, ωn, K, C [VC-S34 pp.52–53].
  • Forced damped SDOF steady state: inputs m, K, C, F0, ω → r, ζ, X̄p = (F0/K)/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), Mp, φp (quadrant-correct) [VC-S6 p.13].
  • Rotating unbalance: inputs M, m, e, N (rpm), K, C → ω = 2πN/60, F0 = meω², Xp, FTR [VC-S6 pp.3, 21–22].
  • Force transmissibility: inputs ζ, r → FTR = √{[1 + (2ζr)²]/[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]}, FT = F0·FTR, αp = tan⁻¹(2ζr) [VC-S6 p.19].
  • Road excitation: inputs m, K, ζ (or C), V, λ, Y0 → ω = 2πV/λ, F0 = √((CY0ω)² + (KY0)²), X̄p [VC-S6 pp.23–25].
  • Beating: inputs ωn, ω, F0, m → ε = (ωn − ω)/2, beat period π/ε, beat frequency ε/π, envelope (F0/m)/(2εω) [VC-S6 pp.9–10].
  • 2-DOF undamped eigenvalues: inputs m1, m2, K11, K12, K22 → frequency equation det([K] − ω²[m]) = 0 solved for ω1, ω2 and amplitude ratios X2/X1 = (K11 − m1ω²)/(−K12) [VC-S8 pp.16–18, 29; VC-R2D pp.26–29, 39–41, 44–45, 48–50].
  • Vehicle pitch-and-bounce road input: inputs V (km/h), λ, Y, L1, L2, Kf, Kr, M, rg → ω = 2πV/λ, J0 = M rg², phase lag φ = 2π(L1 + L2)/λ, matrix coefficients Kf + Kr, Kr L2 − Kf L1, Kf L1² + Kr L2², and force amplitudes Kf Y, Kr Y, Kr Y L2, Kf Y L1 [VC-R2D pp.2–3].
  • Two-DOF torsional chain: inputs J1, J2, Kt1, Kt2 → det [Kt1 + Kt2 − J1ω², −Kt2; −Kt2, Kt2 − J2ω²] = 0 solved for ω1, ω2 and θ2/θ1 = (Kt1 + Kt2 − J1ω²)/Kt2 [VC-R2D pp.7–11].

⚠ Flags

In this section (3)
  1. Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book
  2. Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files
  3. Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

  • A-F1 [VA-CH p.11] The simple pendulum is given as the example of a linear system, but the same book calls the pendulum equation non-linear because of sin θ and linearises it only for small θ [VA-CH p.42]. The "simple beam" given as a non-linear example is also doubtful.

  • A-F2 [VA-CH p.11] The third classification (deterministic vs non-deterministic excitation) repeats the heading "According to the mathematical modeling"; it is a classification by excitation.

  • A-F3 [VA-L1 p.3] sin nθ cos mθ is written as ½[sin(n+m)θ cos(n−m)θ]; the lecture's own later use [VA-L1 p.6] is sin A cos B = ½[sin(A+B) + sin(A−B)]. The e^(iθ) series has (iθ)³/5! where 3! is expected.

  • A-F4 [VA-CH p.18, 31] The coefficient formulas are swapped: an is printed with sin ωt and bn with cos ωt, and the n is missing (it should be an ↔ cos nωt, bn ↔ sin nωt). The worked examples on p.20 and p.22 repeat the swapped labels in their first line but then integrate the correct functions; p.26 uses the correct pairing. In the book form x = a0 + Σ…, a0 = (1/τ)∫x dt, whereas the lecture uses x = a0/2 + Σ… with a0 = (2/τ)∫x dt — both are consistent but differ by the factor ½ in a0.

  • A-F5 [VA-CH p.25–27] Falling sawtooth: the function is first written (A/τ)(τ − t) (= −(A/τ)t + A) and then "(2A/τ)(−t + τ)" (factor 2 inconsistent). bn = A/(nπ) is positive, but the final series is printed with a minus sign, "A/2 − (A/π)[sin nωt + ½ sin 2ωt + …]"; from the derived bn it should be A/2 + (A/π)[sin ωt + ½ sin 2ωt + ⅓ sin 3ωt + …] (the first term "sin nωt" should also read sin ωt). The line "x = a0 + Σ bn cos nωt" should read sin nωt.

  • A-F6 [VA-CH p.29] In the stiffness table the drawings and remarks for parallel and series springs are swapped: the row "Parallel spring, K = K1 + K2" shows springs end to end (series) with the remark "equivalent resistance in series", and the row "Series springs, 1/K = 1/K1 + 1/K2" shows springs side by side. The formulas themselves agree with the lecture [VA-L1 p.15]. The helical-spring figure labels 2R while the formula uses D. The printed "E = σ/E" should be E = σ/ε. The torsional (spiral) spring K = EI/L is kept as printed.

  • A-F7 [VA-L1 p.12] The symbol J is used both for the polar mass moment of inertia of the rotor and for the polar area moment of the shaft (kt = JG/L, J = πd⁴/32); the book writes k = GIp/L [VA-CH p.29, 43] to avoid the clash.

  • A-F8 [VA-CH p.40] "ẍ + ωn x = 0" is missing the square: it should be ẍ + ωn² x = 0 (as the book writes elsewhere, e.g. p.42 θ̈ + ωn²θ = 0).

  • A-F9 [VA-CH p.45] "K² = L³/3" for a rod is dimensionally inconsistent (k² must have units of length²); the value intended is not stated in the source.

  • A-F10 [VA-CH p.51] Preloaded springs on a disc: the torque −2krx with x = rθ is −2kr²θ, but it is printed "−2krθ²", and ωn = √(2Kr/J0) should then be √(2Kr²/J0) (dimension check: 2Kr/J0 is not s⁻²).

  • A-F11 [VA-CH p.58] The problem says "shell of hemisphere" but uses rc = 2R/π, and the final ωn = √(g/((π − 2)R)) is reached without showing how Ic was eliminated. The result is consistent with a thin semicircular ring (Ic = mR² − m rc²), not with a hemispherical shell; the source does not state the value of Ic it used.

  • A-F12 [VA-CH p.67] ζ = δ/√((2π)² − δ²) (minus sign) is inconsistent with δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²), which inverts to ζ = δ/√((2π)² + δ²). The worked example on p.71 uses the same formula; with δ = 0.020 both give 0.003215.

  • A-F13 [VA-CH p.68] The critical-damping example first writes K = 0.7 N/cm and then K = 7.0 N/cm = 700 N/m, and leaves the answer blank; 2√(700 × 0.907) = 50.4 N·s/m (see checks). The dashpot example (p.69) asks for ζ but computes only c.

  • A-F14 [VA-CH p.70–71] "ωn = 27.784 K" (a stray K; unit rad/s); δ = ln(1/0.92) is printed where the data give 1/0.98 (the value 0.020 matches 0.98); c = 2ζmωn = 0.545 is wrong — 2 × 0.003215 × 2.267 × 27.78 = 0.405 N·s/m.

  • A-F15 [VA-CH p.71–72] The data C = 70.0 N·s/cm are rewritten as C = 0.7 N/(cm/s) (a factor-of-100 change), K = 70 N/cm is substituted as 7 × 100 N/m (it should be 7000 N/m), and m = 17.5 kg becomes 17.9 in ωn. The answers (b)–(d) are blank. With the stated data (C = 7000 N·s/m, K = 7000 N/m) ζ = 10 (overdamped, no ωd); the source's own substitution gives 0.316. The intended data are unclear.

  • A-F16 [VA-CH p.74] From ma²θ̈ + Ca²θ̇ + KL²θ = 0 (the damper at a, the spring at L) the mass term should be mL²θ̈ if m is at L as drawn. The source divides by ma² and writes C/m, which is consistent with its own first line but not with the figure.

  • A-F17 [VA-CH p.76] Gun barrel: B = e × 20 × 1.25 = 67.96 m/s, but it is printed "62 m/s", and part (c) then uses 68. Part (c) writes "1 = 68 e^(−20t)" without the factor t (x = Bt e^(−ωn t)) and is left unsolved. Correct: 1 = 67.96 t e^(−20t) → t = 0.0236 s on the outward recoil (and 0.0912 s on the return).

  • A-F18 [VA-L2 p.20] Composite shaft: (kt)st and (kt)Al are both written "× 10⁵", but their sum is given as 5.54811 × 10⁶. The correct values are (kt)st = 5.3407 × 10⁶ and (kt)Al = 0.2074 × 10⁶ N·m/rad; the final Keq = 5.548 × 10⁶ N·m/rad is correct.

  • A-F19 [VA-L2 p.27] Case (2) of the root solutions is written x = e^(at)(C1 cos D1t + C2 sin D2t); for roots a ± ib it should read e^(at)(C1 cos bt + C2 sin bt) (the lecturer marked "b" above D1 and D2).

  • A-F20 [VA-L2 p.31] ẏ² is written with the denominator 4L⁵; it should be 4L⁶ (the next line uses 8L⁶ correctly, and the result 0.2357 mL is correct).

  • A-F21 [VA-LP p.2–3] Ex. 1: with the given data C2 = (ẋ0 + ζωn x0)/ωd = 0.0000 exactly (the data were chosen so that it vanishes), not "0.009". For ζ = 1 the coefficient of t is ẋ0 + ωn x0 = 0.2192 m/s (printed "2.4744"). For ζ = 1.7 the sinh coefficient is (ẋ0 + ζωn x0)/ω′d = 0.00916 (printed "0.098"). τd is computed with ωn (2π/31.32 = 0.2006 s) instead of ωd (2π/31.074 = 0.2022 s) — negligible here.

  • A-F22 [VA-LP p.6] Ex. 2: "e^(−√5 t) = 0 → t = 318.31 s" is meaningless (the exponential is never zero; the root is t → ∞). The rest is correct (t = 0.2704 s, xmax = 1.2215 m).

  • A-F23 [VA-LP p.8–9] Ex. 3: X̄d = √(C1² + C2²) = √(0.05² + 0.01277²) = 0.0516 m, not 0.05; ζωn = 6.13 is correct. Only the case with x0 = 0.05, ẋ0 = 0 is solved by hand (the critical and over-damped cases and the ẋ0 effect appear only in the typed figure). The source does not state how x0 and ẋ0 follow from the step and the 5 m/s speed.

  • A-F24 [VA-LP p.15] Ex. 5: from tan ωd t = 2.26676 the time is t = 1.15532/ωd = 1.15532/π = 0.3677 s, but the source divides by ωn (3.433) → 0.3365 s; in the next line it uses ωn instead of ωd in the amplitude and the sine, and drops t from the exponent (e^(−1.385)). The answer 3.747 m/s is crossed out. Recomputed: ẋ0 = 0.25ωd/(e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t) = 1.429 m/s.

  • A-F25 [VA-BK p.87] The line that substitutes x_p.I into the equation of motion is printed as scrambled text ("t ω sin ₀) = Fϕ -t ω sin ( X) + …"); the intended step is −mω²X sin(ωt − φ) + CωX cos(ωt − φ) + KX sin(ωt − φ) = F0 sin ωt, which the force polygon then solves.

  • A-F26 [VA-BK p.88] For ζ = 0 and ω/ωn > 1 the phase is printed "φ = 1"; it should be φ = 180° (π), as the same page gives φ = 0°, 180° and the phase figure shows a jump to π.

  • A-F27 [VA-BK p.90] Resonant-amplitude example: the statement gives X_res = 1.5 cm but the solution uses 1.25 cm (with 1.25 cm ζ = 0.49698 as printed; with 1.5 cm ζ = 0.414 and C = 52.0). ζ is printed as "0.25sec" in the data line. C = 2mωnζ = 2 × 2 × 31.416 × 0.497 = 62.45 N·s/m (the source writes N·s/cm).

  • A-F28 [VA-BK p.90–91] Example with k = 0.54 kN/m: the statement gives period 1.8 s and force F(t) = 2 cos 3t, but the solution first writes τd = 1.2 s (then uses 1.8 s), the ratio as 4.2/10 (statement 4.2 to 1.0), and solves with F = 9 sin 3t (F0 = 9), x(t) = X cos(ωt − φ). Printed typos: "ωn = 3.58 sec", "K = 540 N/m²" and "3/358", "3/3.52" in the X and φ lines. With the solution's own values (ζ = 0.2227, ωn = 3.58, F0 = 9) X = 0.0349 m and φ = 51.4° (source 51.54°); with F0 = 2 as stated X = 7.76 mm. The mass is never given, so K = mωn² = 540 is really the given stiffness (it would imply m = 42.1 kg).

  • A-F29 [VA-BK p.94–95] Grinding machine: the data line is garbled ("ζ = 0.33m = 0.2 Kg", read as τ = 0.33 s, m = 0.2 kg). ωd = 2π/0.33 = 19.04 rad/s, so ωn = ωd/0.99 = 19.23 rad/s, but the source calls 19.05 the ωn (it is ωd) and gets K = 23.589 kN/m; with ωn = 19.23, K = 24.04 kN/m (8.01 kN/m per spring). The amplitude is 0.0508 cm (0.5 mm) for e = 0.05 m; the source prints X = 0.5 cm (factor 10, or unit slip).

  • A-F30 [VA-BK p.95] Motor on a table: the statement gives e = 15 mm and δst = 3 mm, the solution lists e = 15 cm and δst = 3 cm but still uses 0.003 m in ωn. With e = 15 mm, X = 6.10 mm (0.61 cm); "6.09 cm" is 10 times too large unless e is 15 cm. The statement does not give the speed 875 rev/min used in the solution; ln(X1/Xn+1) = ζωn(nτd) is used with nτd = 1 s.

  • A-F31 [VA-BK p.103] r/e is printed with (ω/ω)² in the numerator (the n subscript is lost). Also, "F_s in the direction SO" while r is defined as OS; only the magnitude matters.

  • A-F32 [VA-BK p.104] For ω/ωn > 1 the source says S lies "between O, S"; a point cannot lie between itself and another. As r/e becomes negative, G (not S) should be the point that lies between O and S — the source does not say. Also the ζ = 0, φ = 0 statement on p.103 is only valid below resonance (φ = 180° above it).

  • A-F33 [VA-BK p.105] Turbine wheel: the printed final line uses "πd²/64" (should be πd⁴/64). Recomputed: r = 0.174 mm, Kr = 2588 N, Mb = KrL/4 = 194 N·m, σb = 194 × 0.015/3.976 × 10⁻⁸ = 73.2 N/mm²; the source gets 142 N/mm² (almost twice). The other steps (K, ωn, ω, r/e) check.

  • A-F34 [VA-BK p.106] Turbocharger: ωn = √(K/M) with K = 3.02 × 10⁶ N/m, M = 10 kg is 549.5 rad/s, not "459.5" (Ncr = 5247.8 rev/min and r/e = 0.8 are consistent with 549.5). F/bearing = Kr/2 = 3.02 × 10⁶ × 0.012 × 10⁻³/2 = 18.1 N, printed "18.14 KN" (unit). Part (c) at 500 rev/min is not worked (r/e = 0.00916, r = 0.137 µm, F = 0.21 N).

K = 3.673 × 10⁶ is printed; recomputed 3.693 × 10⁶ (ωn = 549.5). r = 0.8 × 0.025 mm = 0.02 mm, but "0.02 cm" and "0.002 cm" are printed (0.002 cm = 0.02 mm is the second value, so the first is a slip). With r_res/e = ωn t/2 (this relation is not derived in the source) and r_res/e = 0.8, t = 1.6/549.4 = 2.91 × 10⁻³ s, not 2.91 × 10⁻⁴ s. The maximum bearing force asked in (b) is not computed.

M = "1.0/9.21" kg is 100/9.81 = 10.19 kg (the printed ωn = 261.6 and ζ = 0.206 use 10.19). r = 0.147 × 0.0025 = 3.67 × 10⁻⁴ m, printed "0.037 m"; F(bearing) = Ks r/2 = 84.1 N, printed 8.48 N; F(III) is not evaluated (≈ 96 N). The unsafe-range answer ω1 = 300.9, ω2 = 227 (rad/s) cannot be reproduced: r = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m needs r/e = 0.2, and for ζ = 0.206 this happens only at ω/ωn = 0.412 (ω = 107.8 rad/s = 1029 rev/min); above it r/e stays greater than 0.2 for all speeds (900 rev/min is below it, safe).

With 40 kN/m the answers X = 0.4 m and Vcr = 40 m/s check (0.407 m, 40.26 m/s); with 4000 N/m, ωn = 4 rad/s, Vcr = 12.7 m/s and X = 0.107 m. The stated ζ = 0.20 is ignored ("in the case of no damping"); with ζ = 0.2 and K = 40 kN/m, X = 0.389 m. The road wave is drawn as y = Y sin(2πx/L).

  • A-F38 [VA-BK p.109] The book writes y for the seismic-mass displacement and x for the container, while the figure labels the base motion y = A sin ωt; the derived relative-motion equation and Z/X are consistent with z = y − x only if y is the mass and x the base, as the text states.

  • A-F39 [VA-BK p.112–113] Vibrometer example: the result ω/ωn = 0.728 (from r² = 0.53; the quartic gives r² = 0.5364 as its positive root, r = 0.7324) is the point where M.F first rises to 0.95, on the rising branch before resonance; for ζ = 0.22 M.F then passes through a peak of 2.33 and comes back within 5% of 1 (M.F ≤ 1.05) only for ω/ωn ≥ 4.34. The formula e% = 100(1 − M.F) also ignores M.F > 1 (negative error). The mass and stiffness given (2.5 kg, 60 N/m; ωn = 4.9 rad/s) are not used. The printed square root is √(16.71² + 4 × 9.25) = 17.78 (printed 17.71 in the numerator line).

  • A-F40 [VA-BK p.113] Second vibrometer example: "e% = (1 + MF) × 100" is written where (1 − MF) × 100 is meant (the next line uses 1 − MF) and the solution stops after M.F = 0.98. Recomputed (ζ = 0.6): M.F = 0.98 at ω/ωn = 1.264 (6.32 Hz); M.F stays within ±2% only for ω/ωn ≥ 3.51 (17.6 Hz), because M.F exceeds 1.02 between 1.445 and 3.51.

  • A-F41 [VA-BK p.114] Motor-mounted vibrometer: the statement gives 1.5 mm, the solution writes 1.5 and then "X = −55 × 0.5/64 cm = 1.289 cm" (0.5 for 1.5 and cm for mm). Correct: X = 1.5 × 55/64 = 1.289 mm (the negative sign means the motion is opposite in phase to the mass motion).

  • A-F43 [VA-BK p.117–119] Relay example: tan φ1 is printed with a square root, tan φ1 = 2ζ(ω/ωn)/√(1 − (ω/ωn)²)²; it should be 2ζ(ω/ωn)/(1 − (ω/ωn)²). The Y3 formula keeps 2ζ(ω/ωn) instead of 2ζ(3ω/ωn) in its second term, and its phase is written φ1 with 3ω/ωn in the denominator (a separate φ3 with 3ω is meant). The step "−4a/(iω · 2π/ω) = −2a/(πi)" is printed with "π^i" for πi.

  • A-F44 [VA-BK p.123–126] Second cam function: the input is written −(A/τ)t + A and then "(2A/τ)(−t + τ)" (same factor-2 slip as ⚠ A-F5). Here the derived bn = A/(nπ) is carried through with a plus sign, x(t) = A/2 + (A/π)[sin ωt + ½ sin 2ωt + …], which confirms the sign correction proposed in ⚠ A-F5. In the first function the intermediate line (4A/τ²n²ω²)(2 cos nω(τ/2) − 1 − cos nωτ) is correct; the response uses undamped k_eq y = k_eq x, so φn = 0 is valid only for n ω < ωn (φ = π above).

  • A-F45 [VA-BK p.128] ∫ F(t) δ(t − ζ) dt is printed "= F/ζ"; the sifting property gives F(ζ), the value of F at t = ζ.

  • A-F46 [VA-BK p.129] The ζ < 1 impulse response is first written x = X e^(ζωn t) sin(ωd t + φ) with a positive exponent; the next line and the following pages use e^(−ζωn t).

  • A-F47 [VA-BK p.135] The half-sine response is printed x(t) = (F0/k)[sin ωt + (ω/ωn) sin ωn t]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²). The preceding line (−2ωn sin ωt + 2ω sin ωn t) gives a minus sign: x(t) = (F0/k)[sin ωt − (ω/ωn) sin ωn t]/(1 − (ω/ωn)²), which also matches the printed derivative (cos ωt − cos ωn t) on p.135.

  • A-F48 [VA-BK p.137] The bound i < ½(1 + ωn/ω) with ω/ωn = ½ (ωn/ω = 2) equals 3/2, not "½(1 + ½) < 3/4"; only i = 1 satisfies it, so tm = 2π/(ω + ωn) = 4π/(3ωn) (0.667 of the natural period), and the peak is x = (F0/K) sin(2π/3)/(1 − ½) = 1.732 F0/K (computed here; the source stops at tm). The source also equates the pulse length T with the natural period (ω = π/T, ωn = 2π/T) without saying so in the problem statement, and uses T for both the pulse length and the period (T = 1/f).

  • A-F49 [VA-BK p.144–166] The section headings of Ch. 5 are numbered 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 … (the numbering of Ch. 4 is repeated), and the contents pages list Ch. 5 as the 2-DOF chapter; the source's "4.1 Introduction" of Ch. 4 (PDF p.84) is also an empty heading.

  • A-F50 [VA-BK p.151] Matrix form of the disc–pendulum example: the mass matrix is printed with (2/3)M + m, whereas the equation (1) and the kinetic energy T = ½(3/2 M)ẋ² + … give (3/2)M + m.

  • A-F51 [VA-BK p.161] The independent equations are printed q̈i + ωni qi = 0 (missing the square); they should be q̈i + ωni² qi = 0. Also p.156: μ = (−ωn m + 2k)/k lacks the square on ωn.

  • A-F52 [VA-BK p.164–165] The beat sum is printed "cos ω2 + cos ω1 = 2 cos((ω2 − ω1)/2) cos((ω2 + ω1)/2)" without t; and ωB = (ω2 − ω1)/2 is called "the beat frequency" with period T = 2π/ωB, but the envelope |cos ωB t| repeats (successive amplitude maxima) every π/ωB; 2π/ωB is the period of the modulating cosine itself. The source keeps the two sign conventions (ω1 ≅ ω2) without giving numbers.

  • A-F53 [VA-BK p.168] The first line of θ2(t) is printed "½θ0 cos ωn1 t + ½θ0 cos ωn2 t"; from the previous page (½θ0[cos ωn1 t − cos ωn2 t]) and the sin·sin result it should be a minus sign.

  • A-F55 [VA-BK p.177–178] Beam and motor example: the statement gives a 1 cm deflection under 1200 N (k = 120 000 N/m, which is the value used); the solution writes "δ = 1 mm = .001 m" and "k = 1200/.001 = 120000", which would be 1.2 × 10⁶ N/m. With k = 120 000 the source's numbers check (ωn = 49 rad/s, F0 = 369 N, k2 = 2305 N/m, X2 = 0.16 m).

Recomputed: ω22 = ωn1ωn2/ω11 = 198 × 272/232 = 232.1 rev/min; μ = (198² + 272²)/ω22² − (232/232.1)² − 1 = 0.1016; M1 = 1/μ = 9.84 kg; k1 = M1ω11² = 5808 N/m. Design: ωn2 = 232²/160 = 336.4 rev/min (printed 336); μ = (160/232)² + (336.4/232)² − 2 = 0.578 (printed 0.577; 0.573 with 336); M2 = μM1 = 5.69 kg; k2 = M2ω22² = 3358 N/m. These are computed here, not from the source.

  • A-F57 [VA-BK p.181–182] Pump example: "M2 = 204.8 kg" is printed after μ = 0.0977 = M2/M1 with M2 = 20 kg given; 204.8 kg is M1 (= 20/0.0977), the equivalent mass asked for. Recomputed μ = 0.0974 (M1 = 205.3 kg) using ω22 = 50 × 68/59.33 = 57.30. The frequencies are called "HZ" while ω = 2 × 1780/60 = 59.33 is a frequency in Hz (the pulsation frequency of a double-acting pump, twice the speed); k2 = ω22²M2 is not evaluated (with ω22 in rad/s, 2.59 × 10⁶ N/m).

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

  • ⚠ B-F1 [VB-AM p.18–19]: "Self-excited vibrations … the exciting force is independent of the vibrations and can still persist even when the system is prevented from vibrating" is stated "in contrast to forced vibrations"; the contrast is reversed (for self-excited vibration the exciting force depends on the motion and vanishes when the motion stops; for forced vibration it is independent). Kept as printed.
  • ⚠ B-F2 [VB-AM p.21]: the text announces "four steps" but the numbered list shows only three (1–3, with step 1 repeated as a heading); step 4 "Physical interpretation" appears only in the following text (p.22).
  • ⚠ B-F3 [VB-AM p.21]: "assuming that the earth is an internal frame" — should read "inertial frame".
  • ⚠ B-F4 [VB-AM p.24]: series-spring formula printed as 1/keq = 1/Σ(1/ki); the correct relation is 1/keq = Σ(1/ki) (i.e. keq = 1/Σ(1/ki)); the sentence also omits "the sum of" the reciprocals.
  • ⚠ B-F5 [VB-AM p.27]: J is called "the polar mass moment of inertia of the shaft"; J = πd⁴/32 is the polar (area) second moment of the cross-section. Also Mt = GJ/l is the torque per unit twist (Mt = GJθ/l).
  • ⚠ B-F6 [VB-AM p.29]: for ζ < 1 the roots are complex conjugates (−ζωn ± iωd), not "both imaginary"; ωd is compared with "ω" meaning ωn.
  • ⚠ B-F7 [VB-AM p.31]: the Coulomb-damping cases are keyed on ẍ > 0 / ẍ < 0; the friction force direction depends on the velocity (ẋ > 0 / ẋ < 0), as the next line (ẋ < 0) itself uses.
  • ⚠ B-F8 [VB-AM p.32]: ce = βk/ω is then set equal to β√(mk); this equality holds only at ω = ωn (it is not stated).
  • ⚠ B-F9 [VB-AM p.33]: ζ printed as c/(2mω); the damping ratio is c/(2mωn).

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

  • C-F1 [VC-S1 p.3] Fourier coefficients are written with limits 0→t and factor 2/t, using t both as the period and as the variable of integration; the period τ is presumably meant.
  • C-F2 [VC-SOL1 p.3] In the TA's Q4 Fig. 1 meq the link-1 and cylinder terms are written with "m" (m l1²/(3rp²), 3m l1²/(2rp²)) although the sheet names them m1 and mc; the block mass is also m. With J1 = m1 l1²/3 and the cylinder about the contact point, the terms should read m1 l1²/(3rp²) and 3mc l1²/(2rp²), which agrees with [VC-S2 p.15].
  • C-F3 [VC-SH1S pp.1–2] Student DOF answers for Sheet 1 Q2 Fig. 3 (mass m hung from the bar by spring k2) and Fig. 6 (bar m on two springs) are "one degree of freedom" even though the student first lists "2 or 1"; in Fig. 3 the mass can move relative to the bar end through k2, so a second coordinate appears to be needed. No TA answer is available to confirm.
  • C-F4 [VC-SH1S p.7] The sphere term is written Is(L2/(r2 L1))²; the sphere radius is rs (the student also writes Is = (2/5)ms r²), so "r2" is presumably rs.
  • C-F5 [VC-SOL1 p.5] The TA's own line gives ((2/5)m rs² + m rs²)(l2/(l1 rs))² = (7/5)m(l2/l1)², but the boxed result says (7/5)m(l1/l2)² (ratio inverted). The sphere mass is also written m (the sheet calls it ms). [VC-S2 p.19] gives ms l2²/l1² + Js l2²/(l1² rs²), consistent with (l2/l1)².
  • C-F6 [VC-S3 p.9] Sheet 2 P1 Fig. 1 takes J = mL² for the bar about A. For a uniform bar of length L pivoted L/3 from its end, J about A would be mL²/12 + m(L/6)² = mL²/9; J = mL² would only hold for a point mass at distance L. The sheet figure [VC-SH2 p.1] labels the bar itself "m" (arrow to the bar, springs k at both ends, kt at A, A at l/3 from the top), so the bar is the mass and J = mL² does not fit a uniform bar. Sherif's solution [VC-SH2S p.1] uses IA = (1/12)mL² + m(L/6)² = (1/9)mL² for the same bar (ωn² = ((10/9)KL² + Kt + mgL/6)/IA), consistent with this flag.
  • C-F7 [VC-S3 p.20] Sheet 2 P2(c): from ωnt = π/2 the time is t = (π/2)/ωn = 1.5708/17.234 = 0.0911 s, not 1.572 s (π/2 was taken as the time). The maximum displacement is ẋ0/ωn = 4.95/17.234 = 0.2872 m; the value 0.26584 m comes from evaluating the sine at the wrong time. The separate solution [VC-SOLU p.4] gives t = π/(2ωn) = 0.09115 s and xmax = 0.287 m, in agreement with these corrected values.
  • C-F8 [VC-S3 p.21] Sheet 2 P3: K2 is first written 48E2I2/L2³ but the boxed Keq and ωn use 48E2I2/L2² (exponent 2 instead of 3).
  • C-F9 [VC-SH2 pp.3–4] Sheet 2 numbering: two different problems are both numbered "Problem (8)" (Figs. 12 and 13), and Problem 9 says "the system shown in figure 13" although its data (m, Jo, r1, r2) belong to Figure 14.
  • C-F10 [VC-S34 p.38] Sheet 2 P7(d): 0.1 = 4.863 t e^(−4.4721t) has two roots, t = 0.0228 s (still moving outward, before the maximum at 0.224 s) and t = 0.826 s (on the way back). The question asks for the time "to return to a position 0.1 m from its initial position", which is the second root; the source gives only the first (0.02276 s). [VC-SH2S p.19] also gives only 0.023 s.
  • C-F11 [VC-S34 pp.39–40] Sheet 2 P8 (Fig. 13): (i) the tip spring k, which carries the hanging mass m, is treated as if grounded (−Kx l) and the inertia is written Jo although the bar is massless and the moving mass is m on its own spring — the figure really needs the mass coordinate x(t); (ii) the ωn box first writes K(l1² + l1²) and later K(l1² + l2²), while the sheet names the tip distance l; (iii) the ωd line equals ωn√(1 − ζ) (ζ not squared) instead of ωn√(1 − ζ²); (iv) δ is written 2πmζ/√(1 − ζ²) with the cycle count m left in.
  • C-F12 [VC-SH2 p.5 vs VC-S34 p.19] Sheet 2 P11 has two versions: the sheet file gives c = 8.9443 N·s/mm (ζ = 0.5, underdamped) and the copy in Section 3&4 gives c = 20 N·s/mm (ζ = 1.118, overdamped). The solved answer (tmax = 0.2159 s, xmax = 0.7628 m) belongs to c = 20 N·s/mm only; for c = 8.9443 N·s/mm the underdamped formulas give tmax ≈ 0.270 s and xmax ≈ 1.22 m (computed here, not in any source). [VC-SH2S pp.30–31] solves the c = 8.9443 N·s/mm version and prints tmax = 36.7385 s and xmax = 3.325×10⁻³⁶ m (it does not solve ẋ = 0 as tan ωdt = ωd/(ζωn), which gives ωdt = π/3); these values are wrong (computed: tmax = π/(3√15) = 0.2704 s, xmax = 1.2215 m).
  • C-F13 [VC-S6 pp.14–15, 27] The constant B of the forced damped transient is written B = [ẋ0 + ζωn(x0 − X̄p cos φp)]/ωd. Applying ẋ(0) = ẋ0 to the total response also brings in the derivative of X̄p cos(ωt − φp), i.e. B = [ẋ0 + ζωnA − ωX̄p sin φp]/ωd. In the worked example (φp = 3.814°) this changes B from −1.176×10⁻³ to about −2.27×10⁻³ (computed here).
  • C-F14 [VC-S6 p.18] For ζ > 0 and r > 1 the note says the response "leads" the excitation by φp (90° < φp < 180°). With xp = X̄p cos(ωt − φp) the response lags the excitation by φp for every r; only the size of the lag changes. Also "in plane / out of plane" [VC-S6 p.17] means in phase / out of phase.
  • C-F15 [VC-S6 p.20] Energy dissipated per cycle in forced vibration is written Wd = πCωX̄p; the amplitude should be squared (πCωX̄p²), as in the free-vibration formula Ed = CπX̄²ωd [VC-S34 p.9].
  • C-F16 [VC-S6 pp.32, 35, 44] In three examples φp = tan⁻¹[Cω/(K − mω²)] is taken straight from the calculator as a negative angle (−13.13°, −26.96°, −8.25°) because K − mω² < 0 (r > 1), and the response is then written cos(ωt + |φp|). For r > 1 the phase lies between 90° and 180° (166.87°, 153.04°, 171.75°), so the responses should read cos(ωt − 166.87°) etc. In the pulley example the amplitude 0.01136 is an angle θ̄p in rad (the equation is in θ), not metres.
  • C-F17 [VC-S6 p.39] The conclusion "if C negligible θ̄p)1 < θ̄p)2, so case 1 desirable" does not follow: with C ≈ 0, θ̄p)1 = (L/2)F0/|(9/16)L²K − mL²ω²/3| and θ̄p)2 = (L/2)F0/|KL² − mL²ω²/3|; below resonance Case 2 has the larger stiffness term and therefore the smaller amplitude. Which case is better depends on ω; the source gives no numbers.

Not covered by the sources

In this section (3)
  1. Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book
  2. Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files
  3. Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

Group A: Dr. Abdallah Kabil's lectures and the course book

  • Coulomb (dry-friction) damped free response (amplitude decrease per cycle): only FF = μR is given [VA-CH p.30].
  • Chapter 1.1 and 2.1 "Introduction" pages are blank headings in the book [VA-CH p.6, 14].
  • Ch. 6 (multi-DOF) is listed in the contents only [VA-BK p.4].
  • Reciprocating unbalance (inertia forces of a piston, primary and secondary): not in these files [VA-BK p.92–108].
  • Hysteretic (structural) damping and equivalent viscous damping of dry friction under harmonic force: only the definition Fd = Ceq ẋ is given [VA-CH p.31].
  • Dynamic amplification of transient (shock) inputs beyond the step and half-sine pulses; shock spectra: not covered [VA-BK p.126–137].
  • Damped 2-DOF forced response, damped absorbers (optimum tuning, mass-ratio graphs): only the undamped absorber is given [VA-BK p.169–182].
  • Chapter 6 (multi-DOF, more than two coordinates) is only listed in the contents [VA-BK p.4].
  • Rayleigh or Dunkerley estimates, Holzer/matrix iteration, continuous systems (strings, beams): not in these files.
  • Answers to the Ch. 4 and Ch. 5 problem sets (§14.5, §14.6): not given in the sources.
  • Any vibration-standard limits, balancing grades or isolator materials data: not given [VA-BK p.98].

Group B: Dr. Ayman Mansour's lectures and the theory / definition files

  • Vibration-measuring instruments (seismometer/accelerometer theory, frequency-range design): only definitions are given (see section 10); no derivations or design rules.
  • Hysteretic (structural) damping analysis, Coulomb-damping response formulas beyond the short statements recorded in section 6, and self-excited vibration theory: only defined in the glossary (1.1, 1.3), no equations of motion.
  • Random vibration, shock response and shock spectra: only glossary definitions (1.3).
  • Answers for the unkeyed review-question items listed in ⚠ B-F85 (Ch. 2 Q2.3-13, Q2.4-18/19; Ch. 3 Q3.2-14 to 16, Q3.3-8, 9, 13, 14, 16 to 21).
  • Diagram-free descriptions in Tables (15.1–15.5): the dimensions on the figures that carry no formula (e.g. axes labelled only in the drawing) are not transcribed; derivations of the equivalent-mass and equivalent-spring formulas are not given.
  • Values of material properties other than the four materials of Table 15.7; damping coefficients or experimental damping data.

Group C: Sections, sheets, student notes and final reviews

  • The forced (steady-state) response of a general 2-DOF system to a harmonic force is not derived; only the dynamic-absorber amplitudes X1 and X2 are given [VC-S10 pp.3, 5; VC-RDA pp.2–7].
  • Numerical response of the pitch-and-bounce vehicle model (amplitudes and phases of x and θ under the 8.73 rad/s road input) is not computed [VC-R2D p.3].
  • Free responses with initial conditions: the two-mode sum is written but the constants are never evaluated (no initial conditions are given) [VC-R2D pp.29, 41, 50].
  • Node locations asked for in the double-pendulum problem and the eigenvectors of the damped coupled pendulums are not calculated [VC-S8 pp.20, 26, 30–31]; the double pendulum and coupled pendulum of [VC-R2D pp.30–36] stop before solving.
  • Orthogonality of mode shapes, modal (normal-coordinate) decoupling and the beating of the two modes are not mentioned in any 2-DOF page.
  • Coulomb (dry-friction) free vibration: only the element Fd = μN is stated [VC-S1 p.4]; no equation of motion or decay law appears. Hysteretic damping is only described qualitatively [VC-S1 p.5].
  • The tuning condition for the damped absorber and optimum damping are not given [VC-S10 pp.4–5; VC-RDA pp.6–8].
  • No oral-exam questions as such appear; only problem lists (§14).
  • Section 15 tables: no standard formula tables (beam stiffness, moments of inertia) are provided beyond the equivalent-stiffness summary of [VC-S2 p.3].
